AI Expansion Boom Spurs Land and Factory Purchases by Taiwan’s “Thousand-Dollar Stock” Companies (Those with Share Prices of NT$1,000 or More)—12 Firms Spend NT$37.3 Billion on 20 Industrial Properties

Unimicron’s NT$10.09 billion acquisition of Bridgestone’s plant in Hsinchu Industrial Park marks the largest factory purchase by a company in this group so far this year.

October 18, 2026

The AI boom has lifted Taiwan’s stock market, bringing the number of companies whose shares currently trade—or have previously traded—at NT$1,000 or more to nearly 60. These companies, whose earnings and growth prospects have drawn considerable market attention, have been actively purchasing land and factories to accommodate their expanding businesses. According to compiled figures, 12 companies in this group have acquired a combined 20 industrial properties so far this year, spending approximately NT$37.3 billion. Taiwan’s “thousand-dollar stock” club has become a major buyer of factories and industrial land.

Real estate experts say that as AI business opportunities spread across the materials, components and equipment supply chains, companies must not only expand production lines to meet current needs but also plan ahead by securing manufacturing space for their next stage of growth.

The most prominent transaction was Unimicron’s NT$10.09 billion purchase of Bridgestone’s plant in Hsinchu Industrial Park, the largest factory acquisition by a company in this group this year. Kinsus acquired the former Chu Shui Che factory site in Pingzhen, Taoyuan, for NT$6 billion, while Largan Precision spent NT$8.08 billion on factory properties in Taichung through seven successive transactions. These deals have also become major talking points in the real estate industry.

Other buyers include copper-clad laminate manufacturer Elite Material, which has spent approximately NT$3.32 billion on factories and land this year, and liquid-cooling specialist Kaori, which acquired a factory property in Zhongli, Taoyuan, for NT$2.38 billion. Phison and MPI invested NT$2.05 billion and NT$2 billion, respectively, in factory acquisitions. Innostar Service, Hon Precision, All Ring Tech, Holy Stone Enterprise and Lianyou Metals have also stepped up investment, spreading expansion-driven property purchases across a range of industries.

Erin Ting, an associate director at Savills Taiwan, said companies in the group prefer to expand near their existing production bases. As the stock market gained momentum in the second half of the year, the scale of their property purchases also increased. Major transactions involving companies such as Unimicron, Kinsus and Largan Precision were concentrated in the second half, indicating that corporate expansion is accelerating.

Factories account for 81% of the group’s industrial property acquisitions, far exceeding industrial land’s 19% share. Industry sources say acquiring an existing factory can shorten the time needed to establish production facilities compared with buying land, designing a facility and constructing it from scratch. A location close to an existing production base also makes staff deployment and production management easier. This preference reflects companies’ urgent need to bring additional capacity online when required.

Research by Cushman & Wakefield shows that AI-related industries have invested a cumulative NT$260 billion in real estate since 2023, accounting for 37% of total commercial real estate transactions over the same period. AI server, PCB and semiconductor supply chains continue to drive large factory transactions. With major manufacturers rushing to fulfill urgent orders, some factories previously offered for sale are now changing hands at their asking prices.

text:
“A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another.” — John 13:34

Over Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, USA.

On the last night before the cross, Jesus shared a meal with His friends in an upper room in Jerusalem. The roads were dusty in those days, and washing guests’ feet was a job for the lowest servant. No one at the table offered to do it. Then Jesus stood up, set aside His outer robe, wrapped a towel around His waist, poured water into a basin, and knelt in front of each of them, one by one. Peter protested, embarrassed to see his Teacher on His knees. Jesus answered gently that this was exactly what love looks like.

When He had finished, Jesus sat back down and handed them a command to carry into every day that followed: love one another the way I have loved you. That simple, humble act became a picture His friends never forgot. In the years to come, those same disciples served the hungry, welcomed strangers, and cared for one another so faithfully that people noticed, and the good news spread across the world on the strength of that kind of love.

Love rarely arrives with a spotlight. Most days it looks like a towel and a basin. It is picking up the extra shift so a coworker can see her son’s game, listening all the way to the end when your spouse has had a rough week, or bringing soup to a neighbor who is too worn out to cook. It is choosing patience with the teenager who slammed the door, and understanding with the friend who forgot to call back. None of it feels grand, yet every small act of care carries the same heart Jesus showed in that upper room.

So as this Sunday unfolds, look for one quiet place to kneel. Send the encouraging text. Make the phone call you have been putting off. Offer a kind word to someone running on empty. You were loved first, fully and freely, and that love was always meant to flow through you. Like the countless layers of stone glowing in the morning sun, small faithful kindnesses add up over time into something breathtaking.

text:
Then she whispered:

“You’re not one of the twins, Daddy.”

She pointed at the mirror.

“You’re the person who decided which twin would survive.”

I looked at my reflection again.

It was smiling now.

And for the first time in my life, I recognized the expression.

It was the same smile I’d seen in every photograph of Dr. Dev Malhotra.

The clock struck 2:13 AM.

The mirror cracked from top to bottom.

And my reflection spoke.

“Good. Now that you remember who you are, we can finally begin the first death.”

My reflection stepped out of the mirror.

Not through a crack.

Not through the broken glass.

It simply placed one foot beyond the frame, as though the mirror had always been a doorway and I had been too stupid to notice.

It wore my face.

But it was not the face I saw every morning.

This version looked older. Its hair was almost entirely white, its skin was covered in tiny surgical scars, and its eyes were so tired that looking into them felt like looking at the end of a very long life.

It was wearing a doctor’s coat.

The name badge read:

DR. DEV MALHOTRA.

I stumbled backward.

The little girl in the corner began to cry.

“Don’t let him touch you,” she whispered.

The man in the doctor’s coat ignored her.

He studied me with the detached curiosity of a scientist examining an experiment that had finally produced an unexpected result.

“Twenty-eight years,” he murmured. “Twenty-eight years of resetting the same mistake.”

“Who are you?”

He sighed.

“You really do make me repeat everything.”

He took a pen from his pocket and wrote something on the wall.

18 OCTOBER 1998.

Then he wrote another date beneath it.

18 OCTOBER 2026.

Then another.

18 OCTOBER 2054.

There were dozens of dates, stretching across the wall in neat columns.

Every date was exactly twenty-eight years apart.

“What are these?” I asked.

“Your birthdays.”

I stared at him.

“I was born in 1997.”

“No,” he replied. “You were given a birth certificate in 1997.”

He tapped the first date.

“This is when your life began.”

Then he tapped the second.

“This is when it ends.”

Finally, he tapped the third.

“And this is when it begins again.”

I looked at the dates.

October 18, 2026.

Today.

My twenty-ninth birthday was in 2026 according to the identity I’d been given.

But the date on the wall said I was supposed to be born today.

I couldn’t make the numbers fit.

The doctor noticed my confusion.

“Time isn’t passing in this house the way you think it is. Every twenty-eight years, the family is offered a choice. One person is allowed to leave. Everyone else must remain.”

“Who gets to leave?”

“The person who remembers.”

He pointed at the little girl.

“She remembers everything.”

Then he pointed at me.

“And you remember nothing.”

I looked at the girl.

“What’s your name?”

She wiped her eyes.

“Ananya.”

The name struck me with the force of a physical blow.

Ananya Sharma.

My grandmother.

The woman who had died giving birth to the twins.

Except this girl was six years old.

And she had my eyes.

The doctor crouched beside her.

“Tell him what happened the first time.”

She shook her head.

“Tell him.”

“No.”

He gripped her chin.

“Tell him!”

She screamed.

The walls began to tremble.

Every photograph in the room turned toward us.

Every painted eye.

Every drawn face.

Every image of the little girl outside the house.

Then Ananya spoke.

“On October 18, 1998, I was six years old. My mother told me that if I went to sleep before midnight, I would wake up with a baby brother.”

She looked at me.

“I didn’t know she meant forever.”

The doctor released her.

She continued.

“When the clock struck 2:13 AM, my mother died. My father disappeared. The doctor told everyone that two babies had been born.”

She paused.

“But there were three.”

My stomach tightened.

“Three?”

She nodded.

“My brother. My sister. And me.”

I looked at the doctor.

He didn’t deny it.

text:
I would be quite remiss to not credit @Streetlight0502 for having inspired the recent happenings in my side of the #Malfoid #fanfic series pond. Please give them all your love!

The Second Task - Part 2 - 

Harry's heart was still racing from the sprint as he entered the tent to prepare, apparently having arrived about a half hour before the starting gun. Already were the other Champions at the platforms to the center of the lake, surrounded by their closest supporters as well as some members of the press and important figures of the Ministry of Magic fit to oversee the whole thing. 

It wasn't any of them, however, that greeted him as he came out of the tent with that oddly Muggle-like wetsuit on. Instead it was Dumbledore, Professor McGonagall, Percy and Ludovic Bagman who did so, the latter of which pressing a fat little hand to his shoulder and giving him a sweet but ultimately showy smile from his portly cheeks. 

"How are you feeling, my dear boy? Catch your breath, please! You've arrived with plenty of time to spare to do so, thanks to that friend of yours. She practically rushed through the entire grounds just to get you, she did!"

Percy sneered, a bit off and to the side, and Harry could've sworn he heard the most odious Weasley complain to McGonagall and Dumbledore both about the 'preferential treatment' that he was receiving. He paid it no further mind mind however, giving Ludovic a smile and a nod of his head. 

"I'm fine, sir. Thank you."

The showman leant in real close and whispered as they shuffled their way onto the boat. "Say, my boy... You do have a plan, don't you? We're not allowed to assist you further than telling you to go to the center of that lake, but I'd be remiss to send a boy as sweet and inspiring as you to an early grave." Ludovic's eyes glinted as he spoke of the word 'inspiring', and Harry could tell that he was seen more as the centerpiece of a story cooked up by the Ministry than anything resembling a person in his eyes. 

"I do, sir. A good one." Harry smiled, and his smile was far more of a confident one than the true feelings he hid behind it. 

The preparations met, he was ushered off on the boat towards the platforms, and as he looked to the side he saw another small skiff with Ronnie on it, waving at him in that animated way that always brought him some measure of ease. She was there alongside Neville and Seamus, and the two of them helped hoist her up to cheer for him, with Longbottom barely holding it together as the boat rocked violently from the other two's valiant efforts. 

He waved right back, unable to resist laughing at the sight, his heart just a bit lighter for it. It was good to be reminded that one held such dear friends, nearly good enough to make him forget the odd feeling of dread deep within his stomach. 

Ronnie was there, but where was Hermione? He didn't see her in the boat with them, and he seriously doubted that, in spite of all that Ronnie had complained about regarding her 'turncoating', that she'd actually go as far as to join Viktor Krum's float before coming to wake him with Ronnie or even so much as saying hello to him. 

No, Hermione would never do that to him, or them for that matter. So where was she? 

For that matter, where was Dracaena?

His eyes sought the center platform as they arrived to it, and then the other ones beside. Those that were decorated in the yellows of Hufflepuff. There, he saw what looked to be the top of the heads of Crabbe and Goyle, those odious orbiters of Dracy's who had as much wit between them as they did charm. But he couldn't quite see either of them fully, huddled in the midst of a crowd which cheered in racuous manner towards Cedric.

No sign of the Queen Serpent there, nor on the float covered in blue silks and tapestries for the Beauxbatons, nor in the red and blacks of the Durmstrang Institute. The bushy head of Hermione was nowhere to be seen on the latter, either, and Harry's heart sank even further.

He stepped onto the center platform, and saw that the other three seemed just as anxious as he, their eyes seeking towards the platforms, Viktor's even going so far as to awkwardly peer towards the bridge which overlooked the lake as if his eyesight had suddenly turned as good as a hippogriff's. 

Still, there was no time to ruminate on it. Already was Albus announcing their task. His voice boomed through the Sonorus charm, echoing across the entirety of the Lake's surface. 

The four Champions were pushed forward towards the Lake's surface at the edge of the platform, and as they were Harry steeled his resolve.

He pulled the gillyweed from his pocket, closing his eyes and taking a deep inhale. Then, he shoved it in his mouth, and immediately began to retch. Dracaena had warned him of the taste, of course, but the reaction had been immediate. It went down most unpleasantly, owing to its slimy and rat-tailed texture and the sheer amount of fibers which wove into each other, making it difficult to chew and harder still to swallow. But the taste? The taste was awful. Like stagnant water or murk at the bottom of the deepest, dankest of marshes. 

Immediately, Harry felt his chest throb, a sudden and jarring pain taking over the inside of his ribcage and the sides of his collar. He twisted on the spot, grabbing at his head with a choked gasp and falling to one knee. Behind him, a cannon's fire echoed and a gruff and calloused hand pushed onto his back and with a harsh shove that he'd later learn had come from Proffesor Moody, threw him into the water.

His ears and nose felt it first, the thoroughly unpleasant sensation of the blood-vessels within them coming into contact with the water only exacerbating the sharp aches that were now traveling up and down his arms and his legs and into his chest. 

There in the water he began to write like an eel, twisting to and from as he felt his breath fail him.

But just as quick as the transformation pain's came, they ceased, and all of a sudden Harry felt a rush of oxygen flow into his system. He looked down at his hands, and saw that he'd grown claws and webs between his fingers, and down beneath his calves and his shins had elongated into his ankles, and his feet had further lengthened into disquieting flippers. 

He kicked his feet for a moment, and realized that the eyesight that a moment before had stung and felt utterly overwhelmed by the murk now managed to see perfectly down towards the yawning abyss. His ears and nose no longer throbbed, and more than that he could hear and scent the world around him in novel and singularly curious ways. 

Down below he saw the other three, all of whom used that 'Bubblehead' Charm that he and Dracy had been too pressed to properly teach him, dive down beneath the waters and disappear behind long stalks of kelp and algae below. He grimaced then, and quickly made his way down and into the murky abyss.

What he found was utterly singular. He'd expected some form of dark and dank cavern, or perhaps a collection of ancient spires which held within them horrors unknown. Instead, through the weeds and the kelp and lighting up beacons of tenuous light in the dark... was a town.

Calling it a town would be a disservice to what it actually seemed like, for what was there was so unlike the likes of marvelous Hogsmeade. It was a fishing hamlet, morbid and tenebrous, each building within it seemingly wrought from the rock itself. All around it, creatures in the dark swum about with makeshift spears made out of bone and flint, their long red hairs the only part of them that Harry recognized from the fairytales of Muggles he'd come to know.

They were long and sinister, their arms a pair of elongated limbs contorted around their weaponry if they had any, or lazily drifting behind them in such a manner that their claws gleamed against the tenuous light of the curious lamplights above each and every little hovel of the 'village'. Their songs echoed, a dozen different melodies both disparate and in complete synchronization, as beautiful to Harry's mind as they were horrifying, and as he approached did he espy some of their faces within the darkness of windows and trapdoors which lead to each of their "homes".

Their faces were elongated, with gigantic eyes that looked glassy, dead, and maws which stretched from ear to sunken ear in a Cheshire's smirk most reminiscent of an angler fish's. Their fangs grew over each other in sharpened rows that protruded from thin lips, and their hair was snakes and tentacles and crests of bone and woven flesh which followed their every move at the root before turning unruly and of a deep, striking blood red. 

Every single one of them looked to him, their song washing over his soul to find purchase and provide little comfort after.

Some of it he could understand, verses and syllables distinguished through the cacophony. 

An hour-long you'll have to look, 
To recover what we took.

He pushed forward, kicking his feet against the water in ways that felt concerningly natural, and brushing deep into the "alleys" (perhaps canyons would be a better descriptor, considering the way that some of the hovels resembled the craggy outcrops of rock ravaged by time's wiles) with trepidation in his heart and an itching to grasp onto the wand strapped to his leg. 

Their songs grew in might as he passed them, some of them tempting him to stay, to sleep, to rest. 

But he ignored them all, singular in his purpose and driven forward by bravery tempered in fear. Fear of the unknown, fear of what surrounded him. Fear of what he'd find, what they might've taken from him.

At the center of the square, the treasures hung by the feet and floated a dozen arm lengths from the abyss. Four figures, four treasures. 

Harry exclaimed, but his voice was drowned and turned into a garbled mess, utterly unrecognizable. Tears welled in his eyes that dissipated as a salty offer into the water, and his teeth grit and his chest swelled with rage.

With worry.

With newfound purpose.

She looked so different from the time he'd seen her beneath the hot waters of the Prefect's Bathroom. Her hair did not flow naturally, spreading out into a beautiful sun to frame her face as it had back then, but instead it was pulled downwards by some unseen source, stiff like her body. A body which was covered in their student robes, which clung to her body with as much casual demesne as they did during any random day, and which seemed soaked to the very threads.

Her eyes were closed, but her face was not peaceful. Indeed, Dracaena looked not asleep, but dead. And it was as he stared at her face that Harry felt a deep, deep fear strike his heart.

He got to her quickly, kicking his legs harsh and grabbing onto her shoulders with his webbed fingers. He kicked at the rope which bound her at the ankles, and groaned out a bubble-filled echo of frustration as he found it unmoved. 

He panicked, squeezing onto her neck and her face. She was cold like stone, yet her heart still beat, and the paradox only served to panic him further. His eyes sought out the rest of the 'treasures' then, and what had begun as anger for his (his?!) Dracy soon shifted into indignant fury for them, too. 

The first of the figures was small in the way only children could be, with an adorable face and long streaks of cherry blonde hair which framed it just so. Hers was a uniform unrecognizable as anything but the Beauxbatons', and from it Harry took little to no wondering at all to realize it must've been Fleur's 'treasure'. She floated haphazardly, the natural difference of buoyancy given her build and her age clearly causing her to jerk from time to time due to the currents. 

To her right, another figure. Shrouded by the murk, her closed eyes did no favors to the kindness in her expressions that Harry knew her most by, and her normally beautifully straight and shiny raven hair was now dulled and split at the ends, sort of idly floating behind her in ways that felt almost sacrilegious. 

Cho. Cedric's treasure, no doubt. 

The final figure floated a bit further back, and it only took harry a second of staring before he realized exactly who it was, bushy head of hair and all.

Hermione.

Suddenly, everything made horrific, heavy sense. 

Harry rushed forward, towards his bookish and dear best friend, but a hiss and a sudden screeching halt to the song put hesitance in his heart. Some of the mermaids had emerged from their hovels, eyes staring out as the boy made his choice. The lot of them stared at each other and sang, but the one he'd angered had done no such thing. It had hissed at him instead, pointing a spear towards his chest and whispering in the waters:

"One! You take one! Take any more, and spear shall strike!" 

What was he doing?

Dracy!

He grabbed her, pulling her deep into his arms. Squeezed there, and pressed their foreheads together, tight.

Wake up. He begged, though he wasn't sure how or why.

Please, wake up.

He kissed her. He held her. He bit back the tears in his eyes when the fairytale methods didn't work. 

And he steeled his resolve again, looking up to the greys of the late winter's chill above, before turning towards the others.

He had to help them. He had to.

To the side, the girl of platinum blonde hair and silver eyes... stirred.

text:
Antora and Pratt Energy plan to build a 5.8 GWh thermal energy storage system for a bio-refinery in Kansas, USA.
Industrial decarbonization cannot focus solely on electricity; it must also address the low-carbon supply of industrial heat.
In-depth analysis
Industrial decarbonization faces a structural issue that is often overlooked: decarbonizing electricity does not equate to comprehensive decarbonization of industrial energy consumption.
Industries such as steel, chemicals, cement, and food processing not only consume electricity but also require a significant amount of industrial heat at various temperature levels.
If zero-carbon solutions are designed solely around photovoltaic, wind power, and electrochemical energy storage, the important market of industrial thermal load may be overlooked.
The value of thermal energy storage lies in decoupling energy supply from thermal demand over time. It offers the opportunity for businesses to utilize low-cost electricity or other low-carbon energy sources to provide industrial heat when needed.
However, the specific economic feasibility still depends on the heat load curve, required temperature, equipment efficiency, alternative fuel costs, and operational methods.
My view: The competition for industrial decarbonization in the future will not only be about the power system but also about the industrial thermal energy system.

text:
Cover3 #NFL Week 6 Preview - Chargers at Chiefs

The Chargers are 0-5. Kansas City is 4-0 and coming off a bye. Desperation is understandable. Turning it into a game plan would be a mistake.

The temptation for Los Angeles will be to treat every fourth down like the season depends on it. But aggression only helps when the execution justifies the decision. Last week, a failed Justin Herbert sneak offered a painful reminder.

My angle Sunday is whether the Chargers can distinguish urgency from impatience.

Give Herbert manageable third downs. Finish a drive without needing him to rescue it. Make Kansas City earn possession instead of handing it a short field because the scoreboard feels like a referendum on the entire season.

The Chiefs can afford to let this game develop. Los Angeles has to resist the urge to settle everything in one quarter.

An upset starts with playing better football, not proving how desperately you want one.

Against a rested Kansas City team, desperation is something the opponent can use.

Sir, an excellent piece. Three observations.

First, it is clear that administrative lapses have occurred during the SIR exercise, and these must be investigated and rectified. However, my experience has been that when electoral malpractice is perceived to have occurred on a scale capable of overturning election results, as in Ukraine and Georgia, public anger often spills onto the streets. We have witnessed nothing comparable in India. This suggests to me that while errors have occurred, they are not on the scale claimed by the opposition.

Second, I particularly liked your concluding paragraph about the need for a credible and acceptable alternative. The opposition seems to offer little beyond criticism and cynicism. Where is the compelling alternative vision for India?

Finally, Indian democracy operates in an almost 24/7 election mode. Political battles should be fought at the ballot box and not through anarchic means.

text:
🚨Casemiro on his conversation with Lionel Messi after Inter Miami vs Atlanta United:

🗣️Reporter: Casemiro, there was a moment when you appeared to exchange a few words with Lionel Messi. What did you tell him?

🎙️Casemiro: 

 Honestly, I told him something I've been thinking about for a long time.

I spent years at Real Madrid playing alongside Cristiano Ronaldo. I saw his mentality, his hunger, his goals and the incredible standards he set for himself every single day. Back then, I thought I had seen everything football could offer from an individual player.

I thought, “This is the highest level. This is what greatness looks like.”

But then you face Messi, and you realise that football can surprise you all over again.

I told Leo, “During my Madrid days, I thought I had seen everything from Cristiano. I thought I knew what the highest level looked like. But you have shown me that there is another level to this game.”

And I meant every word. It's not about disrespecting Cristiano. I shared some of the greatest moments of my career with him, and I know exactly how special he is.

But Messi has this ability to make you question what you thought was possible. You can prepare for him, study him and talk about tactics all week, and then he does something that makes you look at your teammates as if to say, “How are we supposed to stop this man?” 

🗣️Reporter: And what did Messi say when you told him that?

🎙️Casemiro:

 That was the funny part!  He smiled at me and said, “You haven't seen anything yet.”

Imagine that! This is a man who has won everything, broken countless records and spent years making defenders suffer, and he still talks as if he has more to show the world.

That answer told me a lot about his mentality. He doesn't seem to believe he's finished surprising people. Even at this stage of his career, he's still looking for ways to improve and enjoy the game.

I've played against some extraordinary footballers, but there are moments when you have to put the rivalry aside and appreciate what you're witnessing.

I thought Cristiano had shown me the limits of football. Then Messi came along and made me wonder whether football has limits at all.

Wild Boars in Archaeology and the Gothic Period
https://t.co/mSxY1P5xoK

Wild boars (Sus scrofa) have a long and complex archaeological record, with evidence from the Iron Age through the medieval period, including the Gothic era in Europe. They appear in both material remains and symbolic contexts, and their presence is often tied to hunting, diet, and cultural symbolism.
Archaeological evidence
https://t.co/k4AS7rml8w
Zooarchaeological studies show that wild boars were present in Britain and continental Europe well into the early medieval period, sometimes persisting alongside domestic pigs
https://t.co/tOcow7P0WL
Excavations have recovered boar bones, tusks, and teeth from archaeological sites, often in hunting contexts or as part of faunal assemblages. The “BOAR” project at the University of Exeter is using geometric morphometrics and stable isotope analysis on archaeological suid remains to distinguish wild boar from domestic pigs, reconstructing their size, diet, and ecological changes over time
This work integrates zooarchaeology with historical texts and iconography to build a chrono-cultural timeline of the species.
Gothic period context
https://t.co/jfixCRbXWm
In the Gothic period (roughly 11th–14th centuries in Europe), boars were still part of the archaeological record in some regions, though their numbers may have declined due to hunting pressure and habitat change
They appear in medieval bestiaries and hunting manuals, such as Modus et Ratio and Gaston de Foix’s La Chasse, which describe the boar as dangerous, proud, and a challenging hunt
These texts reflect both the practical dangers of boar hunting and the animal’s symbolic role.
Symbolism in medieval culture
https://t.co/OZw87Xf7gq
Medieval bestiaries and Christian allegories often depicted the boar as a symbol of wrath, unbridled violence, or pagan/heretical forces
In some contexts, it also represented courage and resilience. Biblical references (e.g., Psalm 80:13) and moral tales linked the boar to destruction and wildness
https://t.co/HKHE3KfObp
Iconographically, boars appear on medieval art, heraldry, and even on Iron Age gold coins, showing their enduring cultural significance
https://t.co/GpjWAI2alO
Archaeological and cultural significance
https://t.co/XIdhr67bSv
The combination of physical remains and symbolic depictions means that boars in the Gothic period are studied not only as a faunal species but also as part of the cultural imagination. Their tusks, for example, are often preserved as artifacts, and their hunting is recorded in both material and literary sources. This dual evidence—archaeological finds and textual/iconographic records—helps reconstruct the role of boars in medieval society.

In summary:

Wild boars are well-documented in archaeological sites from the Iron Age into the medieval period, including the Gothic era. They are found in hunting assemblages, symbolic art, and literary works, and modern research is using advanced analytical methods to refine their identification and ecological history

This makes them a rich subject for both archaeological and cultural-historical study.

Winged Orb Magazine X Fairy Mythology
Fairy Mythology: Boars, Winged Orbs, and Gothic Folklore

In older European folklore, fairies were often linked to boars as companions, shapeshifters, or guardians, and “winged orb” imagery appears in later Romantic and Gothic literature as a symbolic or supernatural motif.

Boars in Fairy Folklore

Across British and Celtic traditions, the wild boar is a recurring faery animal. It is not just a domesticated beast but a supernatural companion or form for certain fae beings

Examples include:

Cailleach bheur (Highland hag) keeps herds of pigs alongside deer and cattle.

Mala Liath (Ross and Cromarty) protects swine herds and is linked to the wild boar of Glen Glass.

Gyre Carlin (Fife) rides a sow and can take pig form

Fairy Mythology: Boars, Winged Orbs, and Gothic Folklore

In older European folklore, fairies were often linked to boars as companions, shapeshifters, or guardians, and “winged orb” imagery appears in later Romantic and Gothic literature as a symbolic or supernatural motif.

Boars in Fairy Folklore

Across British and Celtic traditions, the wild boar is a recurring faery animal. It is not just a domesticated beast but a supernatural companion or form for certain fae beings

Examples include:

Cailleach bheur (Highland hag) keeps herds of pigs alongside deer and cattle.

Mala Liath (Ross and Cromarty) protects swine herds and is linked to the wild boar of Glen Glass.

Gyre Carlin (Fife) rides a sow and can take pig form

In the English ballad The Jovial Hunter, a knight kills a boar only to learn the “lady” in trouble was a wild woman whose “spotted pig” was her familiar

Shapeshifting faeries also appear as pigs: the Manx glastin/glashtyn (horse and pig), Highland fuathan (pig and dog), barguests (dogs, donkeys, calves, pigs), and Manx bugganes (pig, cow, dog, cat)

These boar associations often carry ominous or protective overtones, and in some tales the boar is a dangerous predator in the faery realm.

Winged Orbs in Folklore and Gothic Imagery

There is no widespread medieval or early modern oral tradition of “winged orbs” as faery creatures, but the orb motif appears in later Romantic and Gothic literature as a magical sphere, sometimes with wings, symbolizing the otherworld, fate, or a faery’s essence

In Victorian and Edwardian fairy art, “winged” imagery was often added to older human-sized, dangerous fairies, creating the small, glowing, winged sprite form

Gothic writers (e.g., Shelley, Poe, and later fantasy authors) sometimes used orb-like magical objects or winged spheres as emblems of faery power, blending the ancient “orb” (a universal symbol of cosmic order or magic) with the “wing” (a Romantic symbol of transcendence).

In some European folktales, “wings” are a later Victorian addition; older Irish fairies (aos sí) were human-sized and not winged

Gothic Period Context

The Gothic period (late 18th–19th centuries) reimagined fairy lore through Romantic and Gothic lenses:

Writers often retrofit older, dangerous, human-sized fairies with winged, ethereal traits for aesthetic effect

The “winged orb” can be seen as a literary hybrid of the faery’s magical essence and the Romantic fascination with celestial or cosmic symbols.

Gothic tales sometimes merge faery beings with animal forms (like boars) and astral imagery (orbs) to create hybrid, unsettling figures—fitting the Gothic’s love of the uncanny and the supernatural.

In short: Boars in fairy myth are well-documented in British/Celtic lore as companions, shapeshifters, and guardians, while “winged orbs” are more a later literary and Gothic motif, blending older faery symbolism with Romantic imagery. Together, they reflect the evolution from ancient oral tradition to the Gothic reimagining of the fae.

text:
St. Patrick’s connection to opposing Samhain is primarily legendary rather than a matter of detailed contemporary history, and the broader Christianization of the festival happened gradually over centuries.
The Legendary Account: Destruction of Crom Cruach
Medieval Irish Christian sources (especially the 9th-century Tripartite Life of Saint Patrick, place-lore texts like the Dindsenchas, and the Annals of the Four Masters) credit Patrick with destroying the idol of Crom Cruach (also called Cenn Cruach or similar variants) at Magh Slécht (“Plain of Prostrations”) in County Cavan.
In these accounts:
•Crom Cruach was portrayed as the “chief idol of Ireland,” a gold-covered figure surrounded by twelve stone or bronze companions.
•Worship involved prostrations and, according to the Christian writers, human sacrifices (especially of firstborn children) offered in exchange for fertility, milk, and grain.
•High King Tigernmas and a large portion of his host (three-quarters of the men of Ireland in some versions) died while worshipping the idol on the eve of Samhain.
•Patrick confronted the site, struck or threatened the idol with the Staff of Jesus (Bachall Ísu) or a sledgehammer, caused the central figure to fall (leaving a mark from the staff), and saw the surrounding figures sink into the earth. He then cursed and banished the demon said to inhabit it, baptized survivors, and founded a church nearby.
These stories cast Patrick as the decisive overthrower of a major pagan cult center explicitly linked in the texts to Samhain-period worship. They were written centuries after his lifetime (traditionally placed in the 5th century) and serve hagiographical purposes—emphasizing the triumph of Christianity over paganism.
What Patrick’s Own Writings Show
Patrick’s authentic writings (his Confessio and Letter to Coroticus) do not mention Samhain, Crom Cruach, or any specific seasonal festival. He does refer generally to the Irish having previously worshipped “idols and unclean things” before conversion, and he describes his mission as bringing people from the ends of the earth to faith, with clerics being ordained for the newly converted.
Later hagiographies (such as Muirchú’s Life of Patrick) portray him confronting druids and pagan kings at Tara, lighting the Easter fire in defiance of a royal ban on fires (sometimes associated with a major pagan feast, often linked in later retellings to Beltane rather than Samhain), and systematically challenging idolatry. These are literary expansions, not contemporary reports.
The Wider Christianization of the Season
Patrick’s mission helped establish Christianity in Ireland, which over time redirected or overlaid existing seasonal practices. However, the specific placement of All Saints’ Day on 1 November (with All Souls’ Day on 2 November) was a later development:
•An earlier feast of all martyrs was observed on 13 May (linked to the dedication of the Pantheon in Rome by Pope Boniface IV around 609–610).
•The November 1 date gained ground in parts of northern Europe (England, Germany, and the Frankish realms) in the 8th century under figures such as Pope Gregory III and was more widely mandated under Gregory IV in the 9th century.
Historians such as Ronald Hutton argue that the November date for All Saints developed independently of Irish Samhain (early Irish sources show the Irish church still observing All Saints in April). There is no clear contemporary evidence that the Church deliberately chose 1 November specifically to suppress Samhain. In Ireland and Scotland, the Christian feasts of the dead and the older seasonal festival eventually blended in folklore, contributing to the later association of the period with ancestors, spirits, and the “thinning of the veil.” Many of the customs now linked to Halloween (costumes, turnip lanterns, offerings, guising) developed or were reshaped in the medieval and early modern periods through this interaction, then spread further via

Regarding the third point in the original post—concerning the validity of "whether a proxy retains powers after succession"—I have received pointing out of flaws. I believe that my previous description was severely lacking in explanation and that my phrasing was inappropriate.

​As for the flow of events, a method where the original proxy retains their powers while simultaneously allowing another to use them in the same state did not exist in the established lore. Therefore, I interpreted "succession" simply as "handing over"—equivalent to the separation of powers that Chongyue performed.

​While there was an instance where an item infused with the power was sent to Wan, my understanding was that this did not mean the power itself could be used ​(Even if the power of cause and effect can be partially used through Shu's rice sheaf, it does not mean that the authority itself is retained, nor does it allow one to see through cause and effect like Shu can.)

​Furthermore, my understanding was that the powers themselves did not disappear, but merely changed owners, meaning the creations generated by the siblings would not vanish either.

However, as pointed out, I cannot deny that an interpretation is involved here, and this premise could drastically change depending on unrevealed information (such as the discovery of a method to replicate powers) or future developments. Furthermore, other interpretations of the depictions are entirely possible.

​Focusing only on one side of uncertain possibilities while ignoring the opposite possibility was an unfair way to act. I offer my sincere apologies.
​───────​───────
 
・一部の言語の自動翻訳では、「権能の継承によって兄妹姉妹たちは特技を失った」といった意図しないニュアンスになってしまっているようです。

実際には権能と生業、シュウで言えば前者は「因果」、後者は「農」ですが、これは繋がりはあれど別個のものであり、故に区別して表記していました。仮に前者が無くとも後者が失われる訳ではないのですが、この二つが同一のものとして訳され混乱を招いてしまったパターンがあったようです。
(ウァンから碁を奪うのか！など)

大変申し訳ありませんが全ての言語で翻訳を確認して事前に文面を修正することは不可能なため、ご理解いただけますと幸いです。

It heard that due to machine translations in some languages, an unintended nuance has been conveyed, suggesting that "the siblings lost their specialized skills as a result of the succession of powers."

​In reality, powers and livelihoods—taking Shu as an example, the former is "cause and effect" and the latter is "agriculture"—are distinct things, even if they are connected, which is why I distinguished between them in my original writing. Even if the former were absent, the latter would not be lost. However, it seems that these two were translated as if they were the same thing, leading to confusion.
​(Such as: "Are they taking the Go board away from Wang?!", etc.)

​I am terribly sorry, but it is impossible for me to check the translations in every language and revise the wording in advance, and I would appreciate your understanding.

text:
🚨PART 1: Life under communism/socialism rule. 
Growing up during the communist era in Poland. 
I saw the Polish People's Republic being shaped and changed daily to a different more limited life. It affected social behavior, and the psychology of millions of Polish people.
Poland and across the Eastern Bloc was a daily grind of scarcity, surveillance, and lost agency that turned ordinary existence into a series of humiliating calculations. Central planning eliminated price signals, so factories and farms could only produced what communistic bureaucrats ordered rather than what people needed. The result was a permanent shortage of food, other daily essentials, labor and extremely bad economy.
Stores were routinely stripped bare. Iconic memories from the 1970s–80s include entire shops stocked with nothing but vinegar and tea. I know that many of you today can even imagine how it felt being in that situation. 
Basic goods—meat, butter, flour, sugar, toilet paper, soap, shoes, even matches—were either absent or available only sporadically via “rzuty” (sudden deliveries that triggered stampedes). By the early 1980s, ration cards (kartki) covered meat, butter, flour, rice, chocolate, alcohol, cigarettes, and petrol. An average adult might be allotted roughly 2.5–4 kg of meat and meat products per month (miners got more, office workers less), but even that was theoretical: high-quality cuts were severely limited (often only ~400 g), lower-grade meat, offal, and processed items made up the rest, and shops frequently ran out anyway. People spent hours or days in queues; some estimates put average daily queue time at around three hours. Informal “queue committees” kept lists, and retirees or children could be hired as stand-ins. 
Money itself became nearly useless when there was nothing to buy.
Housing was another long wait—often years or a decade-plus for a small apartment in a prefabricated block, frequently shared with many family members or completely overcrowded. 
Getting a private landline 📞 phone could take up to ~ 
20 years. 
Cars, appliances, and decent clothing required connections (“dojścia”), bribes, or the black market. 
Special hard-currency stores like Pewex existed for the elite and those who may have dollars; everyone else made with poor-quality substitutes. 
Freedom was tightly constrained and limited to almost none. Travel aboard required rare passports and exit permissions. 
Travel from city to city required special permission from authorities. 
Media, books, and education were censored. The secret police (SB) and a network of informers created a climate of caution—neighbors reported neighbors. 
By the end of 1978 my father was killed by them. He was only 38 years old. He didn’t wanted to become a communist so he was killed on the sidewalk walking home. I was 9. Three years later in the middle of the night my mother left me and my younger brother behind in this big city. She escaped to America. 
Every day I continue to live by myself and making sure that my brother and I are safe. We went to school every day and pretend that our mom is at home. I learn how to cook from whatever I could get at the vegetable market, because stores were always empty by the time I got home from school. 
One day in the morning I woke up to the news that Poland was under martial law (December 1981–1983), and everything intensified: curfews (often 10 p.m.–6 a.m.) no one was allowed outside their apartments or house, sealed borders and no travel outside the country. Internment of thousands of Freedom Solidarity activists, militarized workplaces, restricted intercity travel, and suspended civil liberties. 
Official propaganda still claimed record harvests and full employment while shelves stayed empty and people pretended to work at idle factories. State television and newspapers offered heavily filtered propaganda. Phones were frequently tapped, public gatherings were restricted, and….

A Psalm of David when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.
 
“Have mercy on me, O God..
   According to Your unfailing love..
According to Your abundant mercy..
   Blot out my transgressions..
Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity..
   And cleanse me.. from my sin..
 
“For I acknowledge my transgressions..
   And my sin is always before me..
Against You, You only, have I sinned..
   And done this evil in Your sight..
So that You may be proved right in Your charge..
   And just in passing sentence..
 
“Surely I was sinful at birth..
   Sinful from the time my mother conceived me..
Yet you desire truth in my inward parts..
   You teach me wisdom in the inmost place..
 
“Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean..
   Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow..
Let me hear the sounds of joy and gladness..
   That the bones You have broken may rejoice..
Hide Your face from my sins..
   And blot out all my iniquities..
 
“Create in me a clean heart, O God..
   And renew a steadfast spirit within me..
Do not cast me away from Your presence..
   And do not take Your Holy Spirit from me..
 
“Restore to me the joy of Your salvation..
   And uphold me with a willing spirit..
Then I will teach transgressors Your ways..
   And sinners will return to You..
 
“Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God..
   O God of my salvation..
   And my tongue shall sing aloud of Your righteousness..
O LORD, open my lips..
   And my mouth shall declare Your praise..
You do not desire sacrifice.. or else I would give it..
   You do not delight in burnt offerings..
The sacrifice You desire is a broken spirit..
   A broken and a contrite heart..
   These, O God.. You will not despise..
 
“Do good in Your good pleasure to Zion..
   Build the walls of Jerusalem..
Then You will be pleased with the right sacrifices..
   With burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings..
   Then bulls will be offered on Your altar..” (Psalm 51)

text:
In the vast landscape of crypto innovation, most projects are still racing over who builds the fastest car. But Telcoin? Telcoin is rewiring the highways that already pulse through nearly every human on Earth—and putting the architects of these roads firmly in the driver’s seat.

Think of the global telecommunications network as a sprawling web of highways painstakingly laid over decades by mobile network operators. These are the true infrastructure giants who transformed phones into the world’s default connection and payment devices. Banks may have ridden these rails for years, but their reliance—while significant—has always been on infrastructure they did not own. The pipes existed; banks simply utilized them. Telcoin’s vision flips the script: it’s not about the car alone, but who controls the roads, who manages the traffic, and who earns from every vehicle passing through.

Telcoin Network is architected for mobile operators—not as passive conduits, but as validators who stake the TEL token, produce blocks, and earn directly from transactional flows. These operators, intimately familiar with every SIM card and mobile money account, evolve from silent pipes into active guardians of value settlement. This shift is protocol design at its finest, not a mere marketing alignment.

On the financial frontier, Telcoin Digital Asset Bank stands as a trailblazer with its Nebraska Digital Asset Depository Institution charter—the first in the United States of its kind. It issues eUSD, a fully regulated, bank-issued stablecoin backed one-to-one by US dollars and short-term Treasuries. Complementing this, it offers on-chain bank accounts inside the Telcoin Wallet, marrying regulatory compliance with digital-native convenience. Here, issuer, depository, and regulator coexist under one roof, forging a fortress of trust in the crypto wild west.

Combined, these elements reshape the narrative. The mobile operator reaching the last mile now validates the blockchain that settles digital cash. Remittances—once a labyrinth of banks and agents—can now move seamlessly as eUSD across rails secured by those very operators. It’s not just innovation; it’s evolution of the entire value chain.

Contrast this with XRP and Ripple, which meticulously built institutional corridors for payments. Telcoin’s differentiator lies not in one side wielding dominance, but in fusing two formidable moats: a public chain powered by GSMA mobile network operators as consensus validators, coupled with a state-chartered digital asset bank. This architectural duality is rare, potent, and still unproven—but undeniably bold.

The gauntlet is no longer theoretical. Live since 2026, eUSD and on-chain bank accounts serve U.S. residents today. TEL token’s upgrade is complete. Telecom data centers are increasingly hosting validators. Security audits near their finisher’s line. Mainnet is slated to launch later this year. While adoption remains the ultimate test, Telcoin has transcended vision—it now operates a live bank, a live stablecoin, and a blockchain secured by the very networks connecting billions.

Where others race to build the fastest cars, Telcoin is staking claim to the roads that already exist, issuing regulated fuel to power every transaction, and empowering those who built these pathways to have skin in the game. This is a more difficult path—a path less taken—but it’s the one ready to redefine financial inclusion for the next billion smartphone holders still waiting for a true digital banking gateway.

text: If you haven’t read The Billion Dollar Spy by David E. Hoffman yet... you’re missing the best spy story of the Cold War. In 1977, a Soviet engineer named Adolf Tolkachev walked up to Americans on the streets of Moscow and offered to give them military secrets. The CIA ignored him, again and again. They thought it was a trap. He kept coming back. When they finally trusted him, he spent six years photographing top-secret Soviet radar and weapons plans and passing them to the Americans. The US Air Force valued what he gave them in the billions of dollars. It is the best book ever written on how spying really works.

I find it frankly astonishing that Vatican News @VaticanNews  has chosen to publish this glowing tribute to Cardinal Joseph Bernardin under the headline “An example for the Church and the world.”

@CardinalBCupich  offers what amounts to an unqualified celebration of a man whose ecclesiastical legacy remains profoundly controversial. More troubling still is his apparent blindness to some of the gravest failures of Bernardin's episcopal governance. I am not just talking about his much-debated “seamless garment” approach to Catholic moral teaching, or the culture of doctrinal accommodation and institutional consensus that George Weigel famously identified with the “Bernardin Machine”, although these are serious questions in themselves, particularly when considering the damage done to Catholic identity in the postconciliar Church. I'm talking about the protection of children.

The Illinois Attorney General's devastating 2023 investigation documented that Bernardin was informed in 1989 that Fr Vincent McCaffrey was a paedophile, yet McCaffrey remained in ministry. It also recorded how Bernardin allowed Fr Robert Mayer to continue in parish ministry despite serious allegations and restrictions on his contact with minors. Mayer was subsequently imprisoned for child sexual abuse. Bernardin eventually introduced important safeguarding reforms which I duly acknowledge, but those reforms do not erase the earlier failures & they certainly don't justify pretending that his record represents exemplary episcopal leadership.

Despite this Cupich celebrates Bernardin's “gentle and wise spirit”, presents his approach as a model for today's Church & says virtually nothing about these profoundly troubling aspects of his legacy. That Vatican News should reproduce this panegyric without any accompanying historical context or critical qualification is an extraordinarily poor editorial judgement.

The Church has spent decades confronting the consequences of bishops who prioritised institutional harmony, reputation and accommodation over the uncomfortable demands of truth and accountability. Have we really learned so little that we are now being invited to celebrate precisely this model of episcopal leadership? Charity towards the dead does not require historical amnesia & respect for the episcopal office surely demands that we judge its exercise by something more substantial than a bishop's ability to build consensus. https://t.co/v35gEdRomU

HAN DONG-CHEOL

THE WHITE HORSE — 백마
SUPREME CHAIRMAN OF HEUKCHEONHOE
BLACK HEAVEN SOCIETY — SOUTH KOREA

GENERAL PROFILE
Name: Han Dong-cheol (한동철)
Alias: White Horse (백마)
Age: 76
Nationality: Korean
Height: 168 cm
Weight: 58 kg
Position: Supreme Chairman
Organization: Heukcheonhoe (Black Heaven Society)
Military Background: Republic of Korea Army, 9th Infantry Division — White Horse Division
Combat Experience: Vietnam War Veteran

THE MAN BEHIND THE MASK

Han Dong-cheol is the supreme chairman of Heukcheonhoe, one of South Korea's largest and most powerful criminal organizations.
The right half of his face is concealed behind a battered metal mask, a permanent reminder of the war that shaped his life.
Though thin and elderly, he stands with an unnaturally straight back, carrying himself with the discipline of a soldier who never truly left the battlefield.
He has no interest in wealth, luxury, or personal indulgence.
Above everything else, he values loyalty, obligation, and honor.
He speaks little, but every word carries absolute authority.
Within Heukcheonhoe, his commands are unquestioned. His followers regard him not merely as their chairman, but as an irreplaceable figure whose authority has been earned through decades of sacrifice and survival.
VIETNAM — 1972
In 1972, while serving with the South Korean White Horse Division in central Vietnam, Dong-cheol's unit was devastated in battle.
Despite suffering catastrophic facial injuries, he gathered the surviving soldiers, assumed command, and maintained their defensive position until reinforcements finally arrived.

When a rescue soldier approached and demanded to know who was in command, Dong-cheol gave a simple answer:

"...I am."

He almost never speaks about Vietnam.

When questioned about the war, he offers only one observation:

"Over there, the strong died first."

For Dong-cheol, survival was never proof of superiority.

It was a burden he would carry for the rest of his life.

THE LAST COMRADE — M1911A1

Weapon: M1911A1
Caliber: .45 ACP
Service History: More than 50 years

Dong-cheol has carried the same M1911A1 pistol since the Vietnam War.

Its metal surface is covered with scratches and scars accumulated over decades of use.

There are no decorations, no precious metals, and no modifications intended to impress.

Even as the supreme chairman of Heukcheonhoe, he refuses to replace it.

He personally cleans, maintains, and inspects the weapon.

When a subordinate once suggested that he acquire a newer pistol, Dong-cheol replied:

"This one won't die before I do."

To him, the M1911A1 is more than a firearm.

It is the last surviving comrade who returned from Vietnam by his side.

THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE WHITE HORSE

Han Dong-cheol does not believe that strength guarantees survival.
He has witnessed the strongest men die and the weakest survive.
He understands the difference between fear and cowardice, obedience and loyalty, power and honor.

He does not demand loyalty through wealth alone.

He expects it to be earned, honored, and repaid.

And betrayal is the one offense he will never forgive.

At seventy-six, he remains the undisputed supreme chairman of Heukcheonhoe.

The war ended more than fifty years ago.

But Han Dong-cheol never truly came home.

text:
Lessons 4-6 from the Divine Office for the Third Sunday of October:
From the Treatise on Duties by St. Ambrose the Bishop.
.
Because courage is proved not only by success, but also by misfortune, let us consider the death of Judas Maccabeus.  For after he had conquered Nicanor, the general of King Demetrius, he was valiant enough to offer battle with his eight hundred men against a royal army of twenty thousand.  And when his own troops wished to surrender, lest they should be overwhelmed by superior numbers, he persuaded them to choose a glorious death rather than a shameful flight, saying: Let us die manfully for our brethren, and let us not stain our honour.  Therefore he joined battle, and after the strife had raged from dawn till evening, he attacked on the right wing, where he perceived the strongest forces of the enemy to be, and easily discomfited them.  But when he followed up the retreating force, he exposed himself to an attack from the rear, whereby he was wounded unto death, which same was more glorious than a victory.
Why should I add anything concerning his brother Jonathan?  This same was he, who in fighting with a small force against the royal armies, was deserted by his own troops, and left with two men only; and yet he renewed the battle, and discomfited the enemy, and recalled his own deserters to share this his triumph.  Ye thus examples of warlike courage, wherein is no ordinary nobility and dignity, in that death was preferred to slavery and shame.  But what shall I say of the sufferings of the Martyrs?  And lest we should digress further, let us remember how the sons of the Maccabees gained no less a triumph over the proud King Antiochus, than did their fathers; as the latter overcame by arms so did the former without arms.
The unconquered band of seven boys stood encompassed by the royal legions; tortures failed, executioners became weary; but the martyrs failed not in their witness.  One of them suffered the stripping of the skin from his head, whereby his outward appearance was changed, but his courage was increased.  Another, when ordered to put forth his tongue that it might be cut off, thereby put forth his testimony, as it were, on this wise: The Lord, who heard Moses when he was silent, can hear them that speak not; yea, he heareth the silent thoughts of his own people more than the much speaking of other folk; and ye that fear the scourge of the tongue, fear ye not the scourge of blood? for blood, too, hath its own voice, which crieth unto God as crieth the blood of Abel.

text:
Thinking Zone. It is Sunday morning in my little Black Sea village, my coffee is ready, and I am absorbed in one of the strangest stories about the love of art that Stefan Zweig recounts in “The World of Yesterday”: the Belgian painter James Ensor loved his paintings so much that he fell into genuine despair whenever someone wished to buy them, although he was equally sincere in his affection for the money he might receive in exchange.
His friends claimed that Ensor's ideal transaction would have been to sell a painting for the highest possible price, while the buyer displayed sufficient delicacy to leave it with him. I confess that this strikes me as a magnificent economic theory, particularly for those who wish to enjoy simultaneously all the advantages of ownership and all the proceeds from its disposal.
The encounter takes place in the summer of 1914 in Ostend, where Zweig visits Ensor with Belgian friends, among them the writer Fernand Crommelynck. The painter, famous for his grotesque masks and fantastic figures, takes considerably greater pride in the little waltzes and polkas he composes for military bands than in his paintings, which is a particularly exquisite way for a genius to place his admirers in the awkward position of appreciating something other than what he himself considers most important.
And outside, Europe still looks beautiful.
On the beaches near Ostend, Germans, Belgians, and French people share the sea with that easy familiarity which makes national borders almost invisible during a holiday; children fly kites, the cafés are crowded, and the alarming newspaper headlines manage to darken the mood only until the sunshine once again makes swimming more attractive than international politics.
And yet something has already changed. Belgian soldiers pass along the seafront with machine guns pulled by dogs, and when one of Zweig's friends strokes an animal, the officer takes offence at such an affront to the dignity of military equipment.
Ensor might have painted this scene among his most extraordinary carnival masks, although reality has evidently decided, on this occasion, to take care of the grotesque itself.
In the conversation that follows, one of the Belgians mentions the possibility that the German army might violate the country's neutrality. Zweig finds the suggestion so absurd that he offers to be hanged from a nearby lamppost if the Germans actually invade.
How extraordinary this confidence seems when we know what follows! But it is easy to be far-sighted once history has already run its course. Zweig was not naive through lack of education, nor blind to political contradictions; he simply knew so many people personally across national borders that he could not imagine how states would turn friendships between their citizens into a historically insignificant detail.
A few days later, he leaves Belgium on the last train bound for Germany, and at the border he sees military trains already travelling in the opposite direction.
It is precisely this image that holds me over the book: two trains, two opposite directions, and one man still attempting to reconcile what he knows about human relationships with what he sees before his eyes.
Meanwhile, my coffee is growing cold, and I return to Ensor, who was so reluctant to part with his paintings. How strange that, of all the participants in that summer afternoon, the painter, with his amusing attachment to his own canvases, understood best one very simple truth: once something precious leaves your hands, nobody is obliged to return it.
Zweig was yet to learn the same thing about Europe.
And that was no longer a painting one could buy back.

🇺🇸 WHY BUILD EVERYTHING FROM SCRATCH WHEN AMERICA COULD TURN ITS INDUSTRIAL PAST INTO THE FUTURE OF AI?

The global data center industry is expanding rapidly. ABI Research forecasts that the number of operational data centers worldwide will rise from approximately 8,821 in 2026 to more than 10,000 by 2030 and over 12,000 by 2035. Meanwhile, BloombergNEF projects that US data center capacity could reach 118 GW by 2030.

This expansion raises critical questions: Where will we build these facilities? Where will the electricity come from? And how can we reduce their environmental impact?

💡 ONE OPPORTUNITY DESERVES MUCH MORE ATTENTION: REPURPOSING ABANDONED SHIPYARDS AND INDUSTRIAL WATERFRONTS.

Former American shipyards could offer large industrial sites, existing infrastructure and direct access to coastal waters. Instead of consuming more undeveloped land, suitable locations could be transformed into modern AI data centers.

🌊 SEAWATER COOLING COULD BE A GAME CHANGER.

Using heat exchangers and closed-loop cooling systems, seawater can carry heat away from servers without coming into direct contact with sensitive computer equipment. This could substantially reduce reliance on freshwater and groundwater for cooling, particularly in water-stressed regions.

This is not science fiction. Google already uses seawater to cool its data center in Hamina, Finland, where an existing paper mill was repurposed into a digital infrastructure hub.

⚡ A NEW INDUSTRIAL MODEL

Imagine combining:
• Former shipyards and industrial brownfield sites.
• Seawater-based cooling and advanced liquid cooling for AI servers.
• Upgraded electricity infrastructure and renewable energy.
• Modular data centers that can expand as demand grows.
• Heat recovery for nearby homes, businesses and industrial facilities.

The benefits could include revitalized industrial regions, new jobs, additional tax revenue, reduced pressure on freshwater resources and less development of untouched land.

Of course, not every shipyard will be suitable. Grid capacity, fiber connectivity, contamination, construction costs, coastal risks and marine ecosystem protection must be assessed individually. Seawater cooling also does not solve the enormous electricity demands of AI.

But the principle is worth serious investigation: reuse existing industrial infrastructure wherever technically and economically feasible before automatically building on new land.

As America invests billions in AI infrastructure, governments, technology companies and investors should systematically evaluate former shipyards, retired power stations and other industrial brownfields as potential data center locations.

THE QUESTION IS SIMPLE: WHY NOT TURN ABANDONED INDUSTRIAL SITES INTO THE FOUNDATION OF A MORE RESOURCE-EFFICIENT AI FUTURE?

The request was for something Cristiano Ronaldo could sign: a shirt and a pair of boots that might help a family raise money for their baby’s brain surgery. His response went much further.

In March 2014, reports in Spain and Portugal described the situation facing Erik Ortiz Cruz, a 10-month-old boy with cortical dysplasia. The condition was reported to be causing as many as 30 epileptic seizures a day. His family was trying to raise €60,000 for an operation, roughly $83,000 at the exchange rate then.

Ronaldo, who was playing for Real Madrid, was approached about contributing items to an auction. According to the contemporary reports, he donated the football gear and offered to pay for the operation himself. The family’s request for help with fundraising had reached someone willing to take on the full surgical cost.

In Erik’s hometown of Villaluenga de la Sagra, near Toledo, people had already been organizing collections and charity stalls. Even donated bottle caps were part of the fundraising effort. A friend brought the appeal to Ronaldo’s attention, connecting that local effort with the player.

The boots and shirt could still help the appeal. But the larger promise changed what the auction needed to achieve: the €60,000 operation no longer depended on how much those items might fetch.

Sources: Diário de Notícias; Record; El Universal.
