The following is Part 3 of a feature on American history first published in EIR on February 9, 1996. Part 1 is available here, Part 2 here.
America 250

The year 2026 marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence by what would soon become the United States of America. That instrumental document laid down the principles of an anti-oligarchic republican form of government, and would go on to be the inspiration for countless other peoples around the world, forever changing the shape of history. Today, this history is either misunderstood or intentionally misconstrued, and the U.S. has nearly abandoned the outlook of its Founding Fathers. Over the course of this year, EIR will be publishing key articles on the true anti-oligarchic history of the United States in the hopes of contributing to the widest possible discussion of these principles, the rediscovery of which has enormous implications for whether the world can get out of its current state of turmoil today.
7. The ‘Philadelphia Interests’: The World after Lincoln

Following the American Civil War, U.S. statesmen, industry builders, military officers, scientists, and inventors in the nationalist faction fought against terrible odds to advance global technology and civilization. Assassins struck down their President in 1865, another President in 1881, and another in 1901. The nationalists were bankrupted in 1873, and U.S. government finances came under foreign control; piratical foreign representatives seized the great industries. By 1902, adherents of British policy governed the United States top-down and blocked any further revolutionary technological advance.

Despite these obstacles, in the post–Civil War period the tightly knit nationalist faction created new infrastructure and industries which vastly expanded the power of man over nature in the United States and abroad. Their crowning victory was the electrification of the United States and other nations by their protégé and fellow fighter, the inventor Thomas A. Edison.

“But wait!” the reader may be thinking. “Your history may suit a communist country, but not the United States. In capitalist countries, no one planned new technology. Sure, some inventors might have been idealistic at times; but money and the market drive our economy!” The idea that forethought and strategic purpose have guided man’s progress is perhaps even more unsettling to some people than the thought that evil men conspire against that progress. This may be because, in 1996, such real progress is unthinkable, is banned by “budget cuts” and “ecology.”

Yet, in 1870, there still existed a powerful American alternative to Wall Street, to British ideology. There was a general expectation of dramatic material progress; there were men and institutions determined to bring it about, and they had allies abroad. We report here on how some of the main industries were built with their new technologies. In order to unmistakably identify the strategists behind these enterprises we will review some of their other objectives, political and military, and explain how the nationalists were ultimately brought down.

At the heart of America’s post–Civil War development were the political and intellectual associates of Henry C. Carey and Alexander Dallas Bache, and the complex of government and private institutions they and their predecessors had built since Benjamin Franklin.

The nationalists’ power revolved around the Pennsylvania Railroad (PRR) and the banking house of Jay Cooke. The PRR had been built in the late 1840s; the city of Philadelphia bought a quarter of the corporate stock to subsidize construction. In 1857, PRR President J. Edgar Thomson hired the young engineer William J. Palmer—to become the sponsor of Thomas Edison—as his personal secretary; Palmer converted the railroad from wood- to coal-burning locomotives. The Pennsylvania Railroad grew to become the largest American corporation, with 6,000 miles of lines.
Philadelphia nationalist Jay Cooke raised $1 billion for the war effort by selling U.S. bonds to ordinary citizens, and beat Wall Street’s attempt to blackmail President Lincoln by denying credit to the government. With huge government land grants under Lincoln’s law, he began construction of the 2,000-mile Northern Pacific Railway.

During the Civil War, PRR executives Thomas Scott and Andrew Carnegie organized the U.S. military telegraph office. William J. Palmer became a cavalry general and was awarded the Congressional Medal of Honor. Philadelphia nationalist Jay Cooke raised $1 billion for the war effort: He sold U.S. bonds to ordinary citizens, and beat Wall Street’s attempt to blackmail the President by denying credit to the government. Cooke continued marketing most of the federal government’s bond sales after the war.

Thus a combination arose, involving banking, government, and Bache’s naval and military connections, with immense potential power for technological transformation. At the center was economist Henry C. Carey, the grand old man of nationalist strategy. His books and articles defined the purposes of the nationalists’ efforts. Carey’s ideas informed the federal policy that protected the mills and kept federal finances out of the hands of the London-Wall Street banking axis. And Carey’s behind-the-scenes relationships with the military, the scientists, and the pro-modern parties in each foreign country, were the web which held everything together.

By 1871-72, a unified set of large industrial companies was owned by a partnership, known informally as the “Philadelphia Interests,” including J. Edgar Thomson, Thomas A. Scott, Andrew Carnegie, William J. Palmer, Matthew Baird, Samuel Felton, and others. They ran the Pennsylvania Railroad, the Baldwin Locomotive Works, the Denver & Rio Grande Railroad, the Pennsylvania Steel Company, the Kansas Pacific Railway, the Mexican National Railways, the Automatic Telegraph Company, and numerous other railroads, iron forges, machine builders, and coal mines.

Partner Andrew Carnegie was building the J. Edgar Thomson Steel Works in Pittsburgh, the world’s largest and first truly modern steel mill. The Philadelphia Interests had just taken control of the Union Pacific Railroad, and had started George Westinghouse’s career by installing his air brake on PRR trains.

Meanwhile the group’s banker, Jay Cooke, with huge government land grants under Lincoln’s law, began construction of the 2,000-mile Northern Pacific Railway.

The management of these enterprises overlapped with the Franklin Institute, the University of Pennsylvania, and the American Philosophical Society. The cadres developed under Alexander D. Bache’s leadership, and otherwise nested within this extended Philadelphia research/industrial complex, supplied the genius and drive for the most important U.S. engineering and scientific endeavors. For example: Samuel Felton, president of several of the partners’ railroads and steel companies, was the brother of Bache-Lazzaronian Cornelius C. Felton, who presided over vital scientific capabilities as president of Harvard College. Another example: Bacheite Benjamin Silliman, Jr. had published in 1855 a “Report on the Oil Rock, or Petroleum, from Venango County, Pennsylvania,” on the chemical composition of underground oil and how to refine it; this was the beginning of America’s oil industry, which was first promoted by the Philadelphia Interests.

Henry Carey’s disciple Joseph Wharton, founder of the Bethlehem Steel Company, led the Washington, D.C. lobbying on behalf of Carey and the PRR group. They secured protective tariffs so high as to block any British interference with U.S. development. Joseph Wharton founded the Wharton School of Business (later a school for swindlers and parasites) as a Careyite nationalist center.
British Financiers Open Fire

In 1871, at the height of the nationalists’ power, the British forged a new Philadelphia–New York–London axis that would be used to break the entire American political leadership. London banker Junius S. Morgan merged his New York son, J.P. Morgan, into the Austrian-origin Drexel banking house of Philadelphia. The new firm was Drexel, Morgan & Co.—later, J.P. Morgan & Co.

Anthony Drexel owned the Philadelphia Ledger, which had a joint editorial operation with the London Times. The Ledger began relentlessly slandering Jay Cooke, the main banker for the U.S. government and the Philadelphia Interests; they said Cooke was going bankrupt, that his depositors and lenders would lose everything. These articles were circulated throughout the world while Drexel, Morgan & Co. coordinated an all-out war against Cooke’s credit standing within the financial community. Furious “anti-corruption” propaganda by the Anglophiles against all railroad building had already caused the Congress to shrink from further support for Cooke and his colleagues, and Cooke was weakened. Drexel’s campaign struck its target with explosive effect.

Jay Cooke & Co. folded and closed its doors on Sept. 18, 1873. Within two days the Northern Pacific and most other American railroad construction halted. The new steel mills shut down, banks collapsed, stocks crashed. In this Panic of 1873, the Philadelphia industrialists were totally removed from the transcontinental railroad business. The overall pace of development in the American economy was never again to be recaptured. The goal of densely settling populations along the western routes of transcontinental railroads was abandoned by the men who took over the lines.

In 1879, the year that Henry Carey died, the Specie Resumption Act was officially implemented, ceding sovereignty over U.S. monetary policy to the international holders of gold.

Britain’s Newcomen Society gloated over the change: “Drexel, Morgan & Co. achieved a major position in the distribution of U.S. Government bonds, a field that previously had practically been dominated by the Philadelphia banking firm of Jay Cooke…. After Cooke was forced into bankruptcy by the Panic of 1873, the Drexel-Morgan firm held an unrivaled position in this field of finance…. To the United States Treasury, [Morgan] could now offer distribution facilities … [involving] Drexel-Morgan … J.S. Morgan & Co. in London … [and] international distribution through Levi Morton and the Rothschild firm.” In fact, those very British firms constituted a syndicate which had gained iron control over U.S. government finances.

But in the darkening 1870s, Henry Carey and his associates did not submit. We will here offer thumbnail sketches of four “projects”—three foreign nations, and one famous man’s career—projects which were carried out under conditions akin to enemy military occupation, and which the nationalists would continue for a few crucial years after Carey’s death.
Japan Gets on the Track

The U.S. nationalists had opened up Japan in the 1850s, when Commodore Matthew Perry brought a fleet loaded with a railroad train and a telegraph system; with U.S. backing, Japan went on to create a new pro-modernization government. In 1872, Japanese Prince Iwakura and much of his regime came to visit, staying in the home of Jay Cooke. His delegation was preparing a trade treaty and a loan of $15 million for Japanese development, and Cooke was negotiating for Asian connections with the Northern Pacific system. The allied nationalists envisioned a global belt of railways, canals, and shipping operations to vastly increase the effectiveness of their economies.

At that time, Henry Carey’s associates, led by geologist/industrial planner Benjamin Smith Lyman and economist E. Peshine Smith, were in Japan coordinating the American-allied government’s identification of mineral resources, planning railroads, and outlining tariff strategies. This was the birth of Japan’s industrial might.

The fiercely anti-British John Bingham became ambassador to Japan in 1873. Bingham hung on to his post through several U.S. administrations until 1885, battling British diplomat Harry Parkes for influence over Japan’s destiny: Should it be a powerful technological republic or a British-model chauvinist empire, a plaything of British geopolitics?

The eventual collapse of America’s nationalist faction was a tragedy for Japan as well as for the United States. The Japanese entered modern times on an American train, but the British sidetracked it.
Russia’s Western Start

As America’s most influential newspaper writer, Henry Carey had swung public opinion behind Russia in its 1854-56 Crimean War with Britain. Carey himself went to Russia in 1859, apparently to secure a U.S.-Russian alliance in the deepening U.S. sectional crisis. During the Civil War, Czar Alexander II did send his fleet to New York and San Francisco to prevent British direct intervention on behalf of the Confederacy, and the United States began supplying ironclad warships to Russia.

Former Pennsylvania Gov. Andrew Curtin went to Russia as U.S. ambassador in 1869. Henry Carey hosted a send-off dinner for Curtin, where a U.S. general proposed that the czar should build a trans-Siberian railway to link up with the United States and to break British hegemony.

Carey’s Philadelphia friend, George H. Boker, was ambassador to Russia from 1875 to 1878, and a new venture was undertaken.

The Russians appointed the publisher of Carey’s polemical anti-British magazine articles, banker Wharton Barker, as Russia’s American financial agent. In 1878 Barker built four battle cruisers for the Russian Navy in Philadelphia. Wharton Barker went to Russia to plan iron and coal mines, forges and factories, for the transformation of southern Russia. He formally proposed that the two nations prepare as allies for a war against Great Britain, aiming at “the accomplishment of the common work of Russia and America, namely the dismemberment of the British Empire.”

Wharton Barker and his closest associates brought about the nomination of their candidate, James A. Garfield, who was elected U.S. President in November 1880. The czar signed the industrial development contracts with the Philadelphia organization on March 10, 1881; on March 13, Czar Alexander II was assassinated. One week later, Garfield was inaugurated; President Garfield was shot in July, and died in September. The new czar, Alexander III, continued some of the proposed southern Russian development, but now without participation by the clearly dangerous Philadelphians.

Count Sergei Witte, an advocate of Friedrich List’s nationalism, would build Russia’s Lincoln-style trans-Siberian railway and begin the country’s industrial modernization in the 1890s. But the Russian Revolution overthrew Witte and cut the American tie.
Ireland and the Carey Submarine

One hundred years after Mathew Carey had become an Irish revolutionary, his son, Henry Carey, plunged in and took responsibility for reviving the Irish struggle for independence from Britain. Carey’s disciple, Philadelphia Irish immigrant physician William Carroll, was designated head of the Irish revolutionary underground—the Fenians, or Clan na Gael—in 1875. Dr. Carroll was chairman of the Clan na Gael executive committee from 1875 to 1880; he was backed in the movement’s leadership by other Carey allies, notably Knights of Labor chief Terence V. Powderly and University of Pennsylvania economics Prof. Robert Ellis Thompson.
Irish immigrant John Holland was paid approximately $60,000 from the Clan na Gael “skirmishing fund” to build prototype underwater warships. The first submarine was tested in New York harbor in May 1881, and the U.S. Navy in the 1890s paid him to build the Navy’s first battle submarines. Shown here, Holland stands in the hatch of a submarine.

The first submarine was tested in New York harbor in May 1881, and the U.S. Navy in the 1890s paid him to build the Navy’s first battle submarines. Shown here, Holland stands in the hatch of a submarine. Credit: Unknown photographer

Carroll and his colleagues sent cash and guns to Ireland, and in 1878 Carroll toured the British Isles, reuniting the bickering Irish underground into a cohesive force of 20,000 members. (Twenty years later this Careyite initiative would result in the formation of the Sinn Féin, which went on to free most of Ireland from British rule.) Dr. Carroll’s main partner in this work was Irish revolutionary John Devoy, who had become foreign editor for James Gordon Bennett, Jr.’s New York Herald. Several others of the Carey-allied Irish nationalist movement joined Devoy in guiding the Herald—a newspaper that would be useful to Thomas Edison.

Perhaps Dr. Carroll’s most spectacular enterprise was the invention of the submarine. The Clan na Gael “skirmishing fund” paid Irish immigrant John Holland approximately $60,000 to build prototype underwater warships; Carroll justified the expenditure by reference to Robert Fulton’s similar craft in the 1790s. The three-man submarine, Fenian Ram, was tested in New York harbor in May 1881; the British embassy protested, but Garfield refused to interfere with the Irish operation. (Garfield died soon afterwards.) The U.S. Navy in the 1890s decided to revive the Clan na Gael’s project, and paid John Holland to build the Navy’s first battle submarines.
8. The Real Thomas Edison

Thomas Edison was called by admirers “the Franklin of the Nineteenth Century,” and it is not surprising that he should be slandered by his detractors precisely as was Franklin: “a mere tinkerer,” “uneducated,” “unscientific,” “an empiricist.” The Dec. 31, 1995, Washington Post labeled Edison “a grease monkey. A putterer. A mechanic.” As the lie was put about that Franklin was a “British agent,” so had Edison been called a Wall Street stooge. It is said that J.P. Morgan sponsored Edison’s work, or that speculator Jay Gould gave Edison his start.

These and other calumnies constitute an outpouring of Anglo-establishment rage which is puzzling until one knows who Edison really was.

At the height of their power, the Philadelphia industrial-scientific-political grouping (see previous sections) discovered Thomas Edison as a young, clever inventor of telegraphic devices. They set him up as an independent full-time inventor. They encouraged him into astonishing inventions. When they were grievously weakened, financially and politically, they schemed to make Edison famous. Recognizing the force of his genius, they asked him to invent the electric light and tutored him in the history of the field. They protected Edison as far as possible from the brutal sabotage of J.P. Morgan, their enemy, and they stayed with Edison, through to the victorious electrification of the world.

The following report is, as far as is known, the first published attempt to systematically account for Edison in his real relations to the “principalities and powers,” and to see Edison’s own thinking in the context of America’s technological optimism—something considered quite “incorrect” today.

It was William Jackson Palmer who directed the initial rescue of Edison out of Wall Street’s employ. By the end of the Civil War, Palmer had become a full partner in the Philadelphia Interests. He had converted the Pennsylvania Railroad to coal. As a Union officer, his cavalry had routed and captured an entire Rebel regiment in Alabama. The partners in 1866 sent Palmer and his assistant, telegraph expert Edward H. Johnson, out west to build the Kansas Pacific Railroad.

Backed by their industrial power, and the land grants and greenback-issuance policies put in place by President Lincoln, Palmer and Johnson surveyed the Kansas Pacific route through untracked wilderness in New Mexico and Arizona to the West Coast, and built the line from Kansas City, Missouri, to Denver, Colorado. Johnson served as telegraphic constructor, surveyor, and Palmer’s secretary. With Johnson’s assistance, Palmer began building a line from Denver to Mexico City, with plans to develop modern manufacturing in both of the United States’ North American sister republics.

Entries in Edison’s notebooks, 1886. Edison hypothesized on the force geometries shaping the solar system, and theorized that overlapping force lines from the Sun and the Earth produced the Earth’s rotation. Left, an “apparatus to prove the theory.” Like Franklin, Edison had no use for Isaac Newton’s dead, purposeless universe.

But Wall Street was pressing everywhere to take over and milk or destroy productive enterprises. Jay Gould would get into the Kansas Pacific; the Boston Brahmins would move to shoot down Palmer’s operations.
Backed by the Philadelphians

In 1870, Palmer, one of his Kansas Pacific executives named Josiah Reiff, and Philadelphian George Harrington, formerly Lincoln’s Assistant Secretary of the Treasury, set up the Automatic Telegraph Company in New York City. The firm was supposed to compete with the Western Union Company, which only bought inventions in order to silence a potential challenge to its communications monopoly, and would suppress or make use of them as necessary.

Palmer sent Johnson back East to supervise Automatic’s work, and Johnson hired the 24-year-old Edison to invent their technology. Edison had made a name for himself as an employee or contractor developing telegraphic devices, but Wall Street had hemmed him in. The Automatic Telegraph Company now gave Edison $40,000 to set up a new shop; Reiff later arranged that Edison would be on salary while doing his telegraphic inventing. Edison accepted on condition that Johnson be assigned as his chief assistant. Johnson became Edison’s closest friend, and was Edison’s business manager for the next two decades.

Socialist author Matthew Josephson helped lay the basis for populist error by misidentifying Edison’s backers, in his Edison: A Biography:

    One of the directors of Automatic Telegraph was George Harrington, formerly assistant secretary of the United States Treasury, but reputed to be the financial agent of the sinister Jay Gould. Another director was Josiah C. Reiff … Washington lobbyist for the Gould-controlled Kansas & Pacific Railroad. These people were all for technical progress … but … they were in hopes [of] a good stock-jobbing venture.

This is anachronistic fallacy of composition. Harrington eventually sold out to Gould; and Gould was contending for and eventually took over the Kansas Pacific. But Reiff and Automatic’s international representative, Colonel Gouraud, were both agents of the anti-Wall Street Gen. William J. Palmer. Gouraud would become Edison’s personal representative in England, dealing with British invention-stealers. On Jan. 17, 1870, Palmer wrote to his fiancée that he daydreamed of an “ideal railroad” under his own total control, staffed by only his closest and most trusted comrades: “Mr. Reiff [should be] general agent, Colonel Gouraud New York representative … and a host of good fellows from my regiment should occupy … various positions.”

Edison himself explained the speculator’s thinking:

    Gould took no pride in building up an enterprise. He was after money, and money only. Whether the company was a success or failure mattered little to him. His conscience seemed to be atrophied, but that may have been due to the fact that he was contending with men [of Western Union] who never had any to be atrophied.

To understand Edison’s mental map, it helps to consider the background of his Canadian immigrant father, Samuel Edison, who assisted Thomas in his Automatic Telegraph work and would help construct his famous Menlo Park, New Jersey, laboratory. Like Henry Carey’s father, Mathew Carey, Thomas Edison’s father was indicted for treason against the British Crown. Samuel Edison organized his townsmen against British rule, and, in 1837, he was forced to flee through the woods from British troops pursuing him. He escaped across the river-border from Ontario to Michigan, and later moved to Ohio, where Thomas was born in 1847.
Attacking a Problem

Johnson described Edison’s probe of everything ever done before on the telegraph problem under study—how to send several messages simultaneously on the same wire, at high speed:

    There were numerous theoretical solutions in French books, but none of them enabled him to exceed the rate of 200 words a minute…. I came in one night and there sat Edison with a pile of chemical books that were five feet high when laid one upon another. He had ordered them from New York, London and Paris. He studied them day and night. He ate at his desk and slept in a chair. In six weeks he had gone through the books, written a volume of abstracts, made 2,000 experiments … and produced a solution, the only one that could do the thing he wanted.”

LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM

MOHAMMED BIN SALMAN’S TRILLION-DOLLAR GAMBLE: HOW TRUMP LEFT SAUDI ARABIA TO FACE THE HOUTHIS ALONE

By Kio Amachree | 18 October 2026

There is a very expensive lesson being taught in the Middle East today, and the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia, Mohammed bin Salman, is discovering that friendship with Donald Trump does not necessarily come with American military protection.

For years, MBS believed that Saudi Arabia’s enormous wealth could purchase something more valuable than weapons, technology or influence. He believed it could purchase the loyalty of the United States of America.

He cultivated Donald Trump, embraced his family, welcomed American investors, promised hundreds of billions of dollars in investments and eventually allowed the figure of almost one trillion dollars to become the centrepiece of his relationship with Washington.

What he failed to understand was that Donald Trump is a businessman first, a transactional politician second, and a strategic ally only when American interests coincide with those of his partners.

Today, Saudi Arabia is being attacked by Iranian-backed Houthi forces. Its airports and oil infrastructure have come under fire. Its ambitious economic transformation is under enormous pressure. And when MBS turned to his powerful American friend for military assistance, Trump refused to give him the direct intervention he wanted.

The Saudis are now discovering that a trillion-dollar promise does not automatically buy a single American airstrike.

THE TRILLION-DOLLAR ILLUSION

In November 2025, Mohammed bin Salman visited Washington and discussed expanding Saudi investment commitments in America from $600 billion to almost $1 trillion.

Trump celebrated the announcement as an extraordinary economic victory.

But there was a fundamental problem. The trillion dollars was not a completed transfer of money. It was an ambitious collection of investment commitments, agreements and opportunities without a clearly defined timetable.

Nevertheless, the political message was unmistakable. Saudi Arabia was presenting itself as one of America’s most important financial partners.

In return, MBS secured promises of strategic defence cooperation, advanced American military equipment, access to sophisticated technology and recognition of Saudi Arabia as a major non-NATO ally.

He believed he was building an insurance policy for the survival of his kingdom.

But insurance is only useful when the insurer honours the policy.

TRUMP LISTENED TO THE HOUTHIS

This is perhaps the most humiliating development for the Saudi Crown Prince.

As Houthi forces threatened vital Saudi interests around the Red Sea, MBS reportedly telephoned Trump twice in September, requesting American military strikes against the movement.

Trump declined.

Then came the extraordinary development. American officials met Houthi representatives in Oman, where the Houthis assured Washington that they intended to respect their ceasefire with the United States and would not attack American shipping.

In effect, the Houthis were telling Trump that their quarrel was not with America.

Their confrontation was with Saudi Arabia.

And Trump decided that America did not need another military campaign against the Houthis simply because the Saudis wanted one.

Think about that.

A movement operating from impoverished Yemen had managed to separate American security interests from Saudi security interests, despite the enormous sums Riyadh had promised Washington.

MBS had invested years in cultivating Trump, only to discover that the Houthis could offer Washington something more immediately attractive: an assurance that American interests would not be attacked.

This is the danger of building a country’s national security around the personal relationship between two leaders.

SAUDI ARABIA’S INFRASTRUCTURE IS NOW A TARGET

The consequences are no longer theoretical.

Houthi missile attacks have struck Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, killing civilians, injuring hundreds and disrupting flights.

Saudi Aramco facilities have also been attacked, with fires and damage threatening the infrastructure on which the kingdom’s economy depends.

The attacks have disrupted major international business events and raised serious questions about Saudi Arabia’s ability to protect the investors it has spent years trying to attract.

The Houthis understand something that MBS appears to have underestimated.

Saudi Arabia has vastly more valuable infrastructure to defend than Yemen.

An inexpensive drone or missile can threaten an airport, refinery, pipeline, hotel district or investment conference worth billions.

And Saudi Arabia cannot build a modern international economy if investors, tourists and airlines are constantly wondering where the next missile will land.

The kingdom’s wealth has become both its greatest strength and its greatest vulnerability.

THE COLLAPSE OF THE MEGACITY DREAM

Then there is NEOM.

Remember the spectacular promises?

A futuristic desert metropolis. The Line, a proposed 170-kilometre linear city. Luxury resorts, artificial intelligence, autonomous transport and an entirely new model of urban civilisation.

MBS presented these developments as the foundation of a Saudi economy that would no longer depend overwhelmingly on oil.

Yet long before the latest Houthi attacks, the financial reality was already catching up with the publicity.

In 2026, reports revealed that further work on The Line had been postponed until at least after 2030. Other tourism developments were delayed, and Saudi authorities faced the prospect of approximately $16 billion in contract termination costs.

Imagine spending billions planning projects, only to face another enormous bill for cancelling parts of them.

These projects have not all disappeared, but the original vision has been substantially reduced.

Now add missile attacks, disrupted oil infrastructure, regional instability and declining investor confidence.

Who will commit billions to futuristic cities when the country cannot guarantee the security of its existing airports?

MBS wanted to build the cities of tomorrow before resolving the security problems of today.

He may now be forced to choose between financing his dreams and defending his kingdom.

THE TWO BILLION DOLLARS GIVEN TO TRUMP’S SON-IN-LAW

And we must not forget Jared Kushner.

After Trump left office in 2021, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund committed $2 billion to Kushner’s newly established investment firm, Affinity Partners.

What makes this extraordinary is that the fund’s own investment advisers reportedly raised serious objections.

They questioned Kushner’s experience, the proposed fees and the risks involved.

Yet MBS, who chaired the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, approved the investment.

The kingdom also invested approximately $1 billion in a fund associated with Trump’s former Treasury Secretary, Steven Mnuchin.

These were investments, not proven personal payments to Trump, but they raise an unavoidable political question.

What did Saudi Arabia expect to gain from placing such enormous sums with people so closely connected to the American president?

Access? Influence? A sympathetic ear in Washington? Greater security?

Whatever the calculations, the outcome has exposed the limitations of financial diplomacy.

Saudi Arabia helped finance the business interests of people close to Trump, but when the kingdom faced a direct security crisis, those relationships did not produce the American military intervention MBS requested.

That should concern every government that believes political protection can be purchased through private financial relationships.

THE UAE, THE MUSLIM WORLD AND THE PRICE OF ISOLATION

Saudi Arabia’s difficulties are compounded by its deteriorating relationship with the United Arab Emirates.

For years, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi appeared to be natural partners, sharing economic ambitions, regional security interests and opposition to Iranian expansion.

But competition for investment, regional influence and conflicting policies in Yemen have strained that relationship.

There are claims that MBS sought an emergency $8 billion loan from the UAE and was refused. I have not seen sufficient independent confirmation of that specific transaction to present it as established fact.

Nevertheless, the larger financial problem is undeniable.

Saudi Arabia faces extraordinary spending commitments at the same time as its security requirements are increasing.

Its sovereign wealth fund cannot finance everything indefinitely. Its ambitious development programme, defence expenditure and foreign investment commitments all compete for resources.

And where is the great Islamic military coalition that Saudi Arabia might once have expected to defend the kingdom?

There has been no broad mobilisation of Muslim countries willing to enter a major war against the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf.

Pakistan, Egypt, Turkey and the Gulf monarchies have their own national interests, economic pressures and security calculations.

The absence of a united military response illustrates a basic principle of international relations: religious solidarity does not automatically translate into military solidarity.

Saudi Arabia may be the custodian of Islam’s two holiest mosques, but that does not mean other Muslim governments are prepared to sacrifice their soldiers for Mohammed bin Salman’s political decisions.

THE WAHHABI ESTABLISHMENT AND THE DANGER WITHIN

There is another dimension to this crisis that deserves serious attention.

The Saudi royal family’s authority has historically rested on an alliance between the House of Saud and the kingdom’s conservative religious establishment.

MBS has radically altered that relationship.

He has restricted the religious police, weakened the political influence of conservative clerics, expanded entertainment, promoted tourism and introduced social reforms that would once have been unimaginable in Saudi Arabia.

Some of these reforms have been welcomed, particularly by younger Saudis.

But they have also challenged the traditional religious foundations of the monarchy.

The question is what happens when a ruler weakens the old sources of legitimacy while failing to deliver the economic transformation promised as their replacement.

There are concerns about conservative religious opposition, although claims of an organised Wahhabi insurrection against MBS have not been independently established.

Nevertheless, the potential political danger should not be dismissed.

A prolonged war, economic austerity, unemployment, frustrated expectations and religious opposition could become a dangerous combination for any authoritarian government.

The House of Saud has survived crises before. It would be premature to declare its imminent collapse.

But MBS has concentrated extraordinary political authority in his own hands, meaning that failures of national policy increasingly become failures of his personal leadership.

THE IRANIAN STRATEGY IS WORKING

Iran does not need to invade Saudi Arabia to weaken it.

It can exploit the kingdom’s economic vulnerabilities through regional allies, missile threats, disruption of shipping routes and sustained pressure on strategic infrastructure.

The Houthis understand that Saudi Arabia cannot easily absorb years of attacks on airports, refineries and international investment projects.

Iran also understands that Trump has domestic political calculations.

An American president facing economic pressure, expensive military commitments and congressional elections may be reluctant to begin another prolonged conflict in Yemen.

This creates a strategic imbalance.

Saudi Arabia wants American military protection.

America wants to avoid another costly war.

The Houthis want concessions and recognition.

Iran wants to increase the pressure on Washington through its regional partners.

And MBS finds himself caught between them.

He cannot afford an endless war, but neither can he easily accept Houthi demands without appearing to surrender to a movement he has spent years trying to contain.

THE FUTURE OF THE HOUSE OF SAUD

The real danger for Mohammed bin Salman is not simply that Trump has disappointed him.

It is that his entire political strategy is being tested simultaneously.

His foreign policy depended heavily on American protection.

His economic strategy depended on international investment and stability.

His domestic political authority increasingly depends on delivering prosperity and demonstrating that his modernisation programme can succeed.

All three are now under pressure.

The Saudi monarchy has enormous financial reserves, formidable security institutions and decades of political experience. Nobody should underestimate its capacity to survive.

But neither should anyone assume that royal families are permanent fixtures of history.

The Shah of Iran believed his armed forces, oil wealth and American connections would protect his throne.

They did not.

That does not mean Saudi Arabia is about to experience another Iranian Revolution. It means that history offers warnings to rulers who confuse foreign patronage with domestic legitimacy.

THE LESSON FOR THE REST OF THE WORLD

What has happened to Saudi Arabia should be studied carefully by governments across Africa, the Middle East and the developing world.

Mohammed bin Salman gambled that personal friendship with Donald Trump, enormous investment promises and close relationships with the American president’s associates would strengthen the kingdom’s security.

Instead, he has discovered that the United States will ultimately calculate its own interests before those of Saudi Arabia.

Trump accepted the promise of Saudi investment, celebrated the strategic partnership and maintained his personal relationship with MBS.

But when the Houthis threatened Saudi Arabia, Washington drew a line between defending American interests and fighting another country’s war.

That is the difference between being an American partner and being an American priority.

I believe Mohammed bin Salman has made a fundamental strategic miscalculation.

He attempted to purchase influence abroad while undertaking an extraordinarily expensive economic transformation at home, without first establishing a sustainable regional security settlement.

Today, the airports are being attacked, the oil infrastructure is vulnerable, the megacity projects are being scaled back and the American military protection he expected has proved conditional.

And the most extraordinary aspect of this entire affair is that the Houthis, a movement operating from one of the poorest countries in the Arab world, have demonstrated the ability to impose enormous economic and political costs on one of the richest.

Saudi Arabia is not bankrupt. Its monarchy has not fallen. Nor is its future predetermined.

But MBS has learned a lesson that every political leader should understand.

You can buy American weapons. You can invest in American companies. You can cultivate American presidents and their families. But you cannot buy an unconditional guarantee that America will fight your wars.

And if the Saudi Crown Prince cannot restore security, economic confidence and political stability, the consequences may eventually threaten far more than his futuristic cities.

They could threaten the political foundations of the House of Saud itself.

The trillion-dollar gamble has become a trillion-dollar warning.

Kio Amachree
Letters from Stockholm
Worldview International

"On recognition, there is a growing willingness in Washington to assess Somaliland based on today’s geopolitical realities and security and commercial interests rather than outdated diplomatic conventions," Bashir Goth, Somaliland’s representative to Washington and #Canada, told The Sun.

Bashir Goth highlighted Somaliland’s three-decade record of democratic self-governance, independent currency, security forces, and regular one-person, one-vote elections, contrasting Hargeisa's stability with Mogadishu's ongoing security challenges.
"Somaliland has governed itself, held free and fair elections and maintained security along its coastline," Goth told the Sun, adding: "Somaliland is not creating new borders; it reclaims its borders of the former British Somaliland protectorate, which became independent in 1960 before entering a voluntary union with Somalia."

The growing Houthi threat has raised the value of bases near the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and “this makes Somaliland more tempting as a partner to the U.S.,” a professor of international relations at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences, Stig Jarle Hansen, tells the Sun.

Somaliland’s firm alignment with #Taiwan has also drawn sharp reactions from Beijing, particularly after President Abdirahman defended ties with Taipei during his @HudsonInstitute appearance.
"Somaliland has demonstrated that it is prepared to stand by its like-minded partners even when doing so carries a cost," Bashir Goth says, emphasizing that "Berbera’s capabilities and location make it a valuable platform for supporting maritime security in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden."

text:
🍇 THE DUKE’S VINEYARD — PART 17

THE SECRET BENEATH THE ROYAL ALTAR

The coronation bells rang for the third time.

William did not wait for an explanation.

He rushed toward the royal carriage, with Robert, Edward and Eleanor following close behind. Margaret climbed in last, her expression unreadable.

Adrian remained under guard.

As the carriage raced toward the capital, William turned to his mother.

“You said you hid me to protect me. You said Father was murdered. Now Adrian claims you were in the chapel that night.”

Margaret stared through the window.

“I was there.”

“Then tell me what happened!”

She closed her eyes.

“Your father discovered that several noble families had been secretly selling royal land to foreign merchants. He planned to expose them at dawn. That night, I went to the chapel to warn him that the conspirators knew about his plans.”

“Did you see the killer?”

“Yes.”

William leaned closer.

“Who was it?”

Margaret looked directly at him.

“Your grandfather’s most trusted knight. A man who was supposed to protect the royal family.”

Before William could ask another question, the carriage stopped abruptly.

Outside, the streets were filled with armed soldiers. The royal guards who had escorted them were now pointing their weapons toward the carriage.

Their commander approached the door.

“Your Majesty, I am sorry. The palace has fallen under the control of the royal council. No one enters without their permission.”

Margaret reached beneath her cloak and produced a small silver medallion.

The commander saw it and immediately lowered his sword.

“My Queen,” he whispered. “We thought the medallion had been destroyed.”

“What does it mean?” William asked.

“It proves that the royal guard has a second oath,” Margaret replied. “One sworn not to the crown, but to the rightful heir.”

The commander opened the carriage door.

“Your Highness, we can take you through the old aqueduct. It leads directly beneath the royal chapel.”

They descended into a dark passage beneath the city.

At its end, William heard voices above them.

Someone was speaking inside the chapel.

He recognized the voice immediately.

It belonged to the King’s adviser, Lord Vane.

But Vane was supposed to be a prisoner.

William crept toward a narrow opening and looked through.

Vane stood beside the royal altar, speaking to a hooded figure.

“The prince is on his way,” Vane said. “Once the crown is placed on his head, the old succession laws will be meaningless.”

The hooded figure removed the covering.

William stopped breathing.

It was the Duke.

The same man who had offered William a chance to learn the estate, defended him against accusations, and helped uncover the royal conspiracy.

The Duke handed Vane a document.

“Once William enters this chapel,” he said, “the final piece of the plan will be complete.”

William backed away in horror.

Had the Duke been protecting him all along—or guiding him into a trap?

Then the Duke spoke words that made William’s blood run cold.

“The boy must never discover that I ordered his father’s execution.”

Behind William, Margaret whispered:

“Now you understand why I kept you away from the palace.”

A hand suddenly clamped over William’s mouth.

Someone had found them in the passage.

And a familiar voice whispered into his ear:

“Don’t make a sound, Your Highness. If you want to survive, you must come with me.”

William turned his eyes toward the stranger.

It was Adrian.

text:
🍇 THE DUKE’S VINEYARD — PART 16

THE QUEEN WHO GAVE BIRTH TO A LIE

Nobody dared to speak.

Margaret stood before them wearing the crown jewels, while the royal guards bowed as though she had ruled the kingdom for years.

William stared at Robert.

“Tell me she is lying.”

Robert’s eyes filled with tears.

“I raised you as my son because I promised your mother I would protect you. But the truth is… I am your uncle.”

William stepped backward.

“Then who is my father?”

Margaret approached him, but he refused to let her touch him.

“Your father was King Edmund, the elder brother of the man who now lies dead,” she said. “Before his death, he discovered a conspiracy within his own court. He entrusted me with his infant son and ordered me to hide him until the kingdom was safe.”

William shook his head.

“You expect me to believe I am the son of a king?”

“I expect you to understand why I sacrificed everything to keep you alive.”

Adrian suddenly rose from his knees.

“Then why did you let me believe I was the rightful heir?”

Margaret turned toward him.

“Because you were.”

The answer stunned everyone.

She explained that Adrian had been the late king’s chosen successor after Edmund’s death. But the succession agreement had one condition: if Edmund’s legitimate son ever returned, the crown would pass to him.

William.

Adrian’s face twisted with anger.

“You hid the boy for twenty years and allowed me to carry the burden of a throne that was never truly mine!”

“No,” Margaret replied. “I hid him because your father’s murderers were still inside the palace.”

“And now the King is dead,” Eleanor said. “Who killed him?”

Margaret’s expression changed.

“I did not order his death.”

Vane laughed from where the soldiers held him.

“Then explain the message bearing your signature.”

Margaret looked at him coldly.

“Because you forged it.”

For the first time, Vane stopped smiling.

Margaret revealed that she had spent years gathering evidence against the royal adviser and his allies. The King had finally agreed to expose them, but someone reached him first.

Someone who knew exactly when he would be alone.

William remembered the fresh ink on Adrian’s succession parchment.

He looked at the prince.

“Where were you when the King died?”

Adrian said nothing.

Then Edward noticed blood on the cuff of Adrian’s sleeve.

The commander drew his sword.

“Prince Adrian, you will come with us.”

Adrian slowly raised both hands.

“You have no idea what you are doing.”

He looked directly at William.

“Ask your mother why she was in the royal chapel the night your father died.”

Margaret’s face went pale.

And William understood something terrible.

His mother had told them the truth about his birth—but not the truth about his father’s death.

Before anyone could question her, a bell rang from the direction of the capital.

The coronation bell.

Someone had entered the royal chapel.

And whoever reached the altar first would decide who ruled the kingdom.

text:
🍇 THE DUKE’S VINEYARD — PART 15

THE MOTHER WHO KNEW THE KING’S KILLER

Margaret had vanished.

One moment, she stood beside William in the courtyard. The next, she was gone, leaving only a torn piece of parchment beneath the ancient tree.

William unfolded it with trembling hands.

My son, if you are reading this, the truth has finally caught up with us. Do not trust the man who wears the black ring. And whatever happens, do not allow Adrian to enter the royal chapel before sunrise.

William looked toward the prisoner.

Adrian was watching him.

“You found her message,” the prince said quietly.

William grabbed him by the collar.

“What have you done to my mother?”

Adrian did not resist.

“Nothing. Margaret is the only person alive who knows what truly happened the night your grandfather died.”

Robert stepped forward.

“You said your grandfather died of illness.”

“That is what the official record says,” Adrian replied. “But the old king was poisoned. And the person who served him his final cup was Margaret.”

William released him in disbelief.

“My mother was a servant in the royal household. She was barely seventeen.”

“She was more than a servant,” Adrian said. “She was the king’s personal messenger. She carried a letter that could have changed the succession forever.”

Suddenly, Edward rushed into the courtyard holding a small brass key.

“I found this in Mother’s room. There was a note beside it.”

The note contained just five words:

“The chapel holds the answer.”

William remembered Margaret’s warning.

Adrian must not enter the royal chapel before sunrise.

The commander ordered a carriage prepared immediately. William, Robert, Eleanor and Edward would travel to the capital before the coronation.

But as they prepared to leave, the captured adviser, Vane, began laughing.

“You are all too late.”

William turned toward him.

“What do you mean?”

Vane leaned closer.

“Adrian isn’t the only person who wants that crown. The royal council has already chosen its next ruler.”

“Who?” Eleanor demanded.

Vane’s smile widened.

“The person who signed the order for the King’s execution.”

He glanced toward the road leading out of the vineyard.

A royal carriage was approaching.

Its doors opened.

And the woman who stepped out wore the crown jewels.

It was Margaret.

William ran toward her, but she raised one hand to stop him.

“Forgive me, my son,” she whispered. “I never told you who your father really was.”

Robert stood frozen.

Then Margaret turned toward him.

“Because the man who raised you is not the man who fathered you.”

The golden ring slipped from William’s fingers.

Behind them, Adrian began to kneel.

“Your Majesty,” he whispered.

Margaret had not come to save the throne. She had come to claim it. 👑

text:
In 1952, a Black woman from Virginia traveled to France to give away an invention that the United States government had refused to embrace. She wanted nothing in return. She simply wanted wounded veterans to be able to feed themselves again.
Her name was Bessie Blount Griffin, and she was a physical therapist who had spent years helping soldiers who returned from World War II with devastating injuries.
Many had lost their arms. Others could no longer perform the simplest daily tasks without assistance. Blount believed that restoring independence was just as important as treating physical wounds.
Working in her own kitchen, she developed an extraordinary device: an electrically powered feeding apparatus that delivered food to a person's mouth through a tube. By biting down on a switch, someone without arms could control the delivery of each mouthful.
She patented her invention in 1951.
But when she offered it to the United States Veterans Administration, officials showed little interest. Blount refused to let her work disappear.
In 1952, she traveled to France and transferred the rights to her invention to the French government without payment.
Her achievement was remarkable in an era when Black women faced enormous barriers in medicine, engineering, and patent ownership.
Blount later pursued another extraordinary career in forensic science, becoming a pioneer in handwriting analysis.
She died in 2009 at the age of 95.
America had declined her invention. She gave it to another country rather than abandon the people it could help.

text:
I slept with my best friend's older brother, and the next morning my best friend called me asking if I'd seen him.

I'm 28M, and my best friend, Daniel, is 27. His older brother, Marcus, is 35, and I've known him for almost eight years.

I'd always thought Marcus was attractive, but he was the kind of man who seemed completely out of my league. Confident, successful, and annoyingly aware of the effect his smile had on people.

Nothing ever happened between us.

Until last Friday.

Daniel had invited me over for drinks, but he got called into work unexpectedly. I was about to leave when Marcus walked into the living room.

"Leaving already?"

"Your brother abandoned me."

Marcus laughed and offered to open another bottle of wine.

We ended up sitting on the couch, talking about relationships, embarrassing first dates, and the people we'd secretly found attractive over the years.

Then he asked, "Have you ever had a crush on someone you knew you shouldn't?"

I looked at him.

"Why?"

"Because I have."

Something in his expression made my stomach flip.

"Who?"

He held my gaze.

"You."

I genuinely thought he was joking.

Then he told me he'd noticed me years ago but had never acted on it because I was his brother's best friend.

I admitted I'd felt the same way.

The silence that followed was almost unbearable.

Finally, I asked, "So what happens now?"

Marcus moved closer but stopped just before our faces touched.

"That depends. Do you want me to kiss you?"

I'd wanted him to ask that question for years.

"Yes."

The kiss changed the entire evening.

We kept stopping to laugh at how ridiculous it was that we'd spent so long pretending there was nothing between us. Every time one of us suggested we should slow down, the other would admit they weren't ready to say goodnight.

We spent the night together, and by morning, I was lying beside the one man I'd never expected to wake up next to.

Then my phone rang.

Daniel.

I answered, trying to sound normal.

"Hey, have you seen my brother? He's not answering his phone."

I looked at Marcus.

He was already awake, trying desperately not to laugh.

"No," I told Daniel. "Haven't seen him."

The moment I hung up, Marcus buried his face in the pillow and started laughing.

"This is going to be a disaster," I said.

"Probably."

He reached for my hand.

"But are you sorry?"

I thought about it for a moment.

"Not even a little."

We eventually told Daniel the truth. He was shocked, mildly offended that we'd kept it from him, and spent an entire week calling us ridiculous.

Six months later, Marcus and I are still together.

Daniel has finally accepted it, although he insists he deserves credit for introducing us.

text:
Je veux parler au monde entier de ce qui se passe en France. S’il vous plaît, écoutez-moi.

Ils ont dit « importez le tiers-monde, devenez le tiers-monde ». Ils avaient tort. C’est pire que ça.

Aujourd’hui, la France brûle.

Des monuments historiques s’effondrent dans les flammes sous les regards, les cris et parfois les applaudissements de brutes.

À Limoges, ce 17 octobre 2026, l’hôtel de ville — ce magnifique édifice du XIXe siècle, inauguré en 1883, conçu dans un style néo-Renaissance, classé monument historique, qui avait traversé les deux guerres mondiales sans être détruit — a été pris d’assaut et incendié par des individus cagoulés.

La tour s’est effondrée. Une large partie de la toiture et de la façade a disparu. Les autorités parlent d’une « catastrophe patrimoniale » et d’un bâtiment « en grande partie perdu ».

Des siècles de pierre, de savoir-faire et de mémoire réduits en cendres en quelques heures.

« Devenir le tiers-monde » serait un euphémisme.

Le tiers-monde n’a jamais connu l’ascension que nous avons accomplie. Il n’a donc jamais rien eu à perdre de comparable.

Nous, peuples du monde civilisé, avons bâti le premier monde avec la sueur, le sang, l’ingéniosité et le sacrifice de nos ancêtres.

Ils se sont tués à la tâche, génération après génération, pour offrir un avenir digne à leurs descendants.

Chaque église, chaque mairie, chaque école, chaque pont porte encore la marque de leurs mains et de leur sang.

Aujourd’hui, les immigrationnistes crachent sur leurs tombes.

Ils importent en masse des populations issues de sociétés qui n’ont ni construit ni su préserver un ordre comparable — et qui, une fois installées, deviennent les acteurs de sa destruction.

Ce ne sont pas seulement des individus incapables de maintenir ce que nous avons élevé. Ils provoquent et applaudissent les effondrements, les pillages, les incendies.

Notre patrimoine n’est plus un héritage à transmettre, c'est devenu une cible prioritaire.

Voilà ce qui attend tout pays du monde civilisé qui ne stoppe pas net l’immigration en provenance du tiers-monde et qui ne met pas en œuvre, au plus vite, une remigration massive.

Sinon, la démographie fera le reste. Les taux de fécondité élevés dans ces communautés assurent le grand remplacement progressif.

Ce n’est pas une théorie. C’est de l’arithmétique.

Ce qui brûle aujourd’hui à Limoges brûlera demain chez vous si vous ne faites rien.

Peuples du monde civilisé — d’Europe, d’Amérique, d’Australie, du Japon, de Corée et partout où la raison, la science, le droit et la beauté ont élevé des sociétés d’exception, je vous en supplie : regardez ce qui se passe en France en ce moment.

Ne croyez pas que « ça n’arrivera pas chez nous ».

Les mêmes mécanismes sont à l’œuvre là où les frontières sont ouvertes et où les immigrationnistes sont au pouvoir.

Agissez tant qu’il en est encore temps.

Contrôlez vos frontières, exigez l’assimilation réelle ou le retour sans concession, protégez vos monuments, vos lois et vos enfants.

Ne sombrez pas dans le chaos sous les flammes et les applaudissements comme nous.

L’héritage de vos ancêtres mérite mieux que d’être livré à des brutes incendiaires.

A community like @searchfi_eth  which introduced  @deadstock_app to the community, an initiative that has generated profit by lucky pull and rather, if really unlucky a loss.

There’s more to this than just the numbers.
At first glance in the image below, you will acknowledge my consistency in the top leaderboard.
Whilst the second glance acknowledges the dark side of the pull, that one can also accrue loss.
But it doesn’t end there…!

Is Deadstock Legit? What Is the Deadstock App?

Collecting high-grade Pokémon cards has never been completely frictionless. You still have to find authentic PSA 10s, deal with shipping risks, wait for settlements, and navigate scattered marketplaces. 
Deadstock is designed to bring all of that into a single process. You open packs containing real graded cards, get a Digital Twin confirming ownership of the exact slab stored in a Japanese vault, trade it directly with another user, sell it back instantly, or request physical delivery whenever you choose.

The Problem It Solves and Why It Matters:

High-grade Pokémon cards make up a collectibles market worth multiple billions of dollars, but the supporting infrastructure is still fragmented. Buyers deal with uncertainty around authentication, shipping costs and delays, double-digit marketplace fees on some platforms, and no shared record showing what is genuine and securely vaulted. Selling can be a slow process: create a listing, wait, ship the card, and hope the buyer is happy.

Deadstock takes a different approach: it sources verified PSA 10 inventory, primarily through JTCC, and stores it in a professional vault.
It issue a corresponding Digital Twin, and give users three clear options after acquisition hold, trade on a low-fee marketplace, or redeem. For collectors who want the physical card eventually, the option exists. For those who prefer liquidity and the thrill of the pack open, the digital layer handles it. The platform positions itself as infrastructure that other collectibles businesses can eventually plug into.

How It Works: A Step-by-Step Breakdown:

1.  Create an account on  https://t.co/9kKkxppD4p (email, Google, or Apple).
2.  Fund it with USDC (Arbitrum or Solana routes have been available) or card (Visa/Mastercard). Recent updates made multi-chain top-ups easier via Unifold.
3.  Choose a pack (examples from public beta period: 30th Celebration Pack $10, Super $50, Hyper $200, 30th Celebration Box Pack $250, Master $1,000). Odds, rank tiers (SSS to C), FMV ranges, and expected value are published per pack.
4.  Open the pack. You receive a specific PSA 10 card (or unopened product in some packs) and its Digital Twin.
5.  Options:
a. Keep it in your collection.
b. Accept a time-limited company buyback offer (priced as a percentage of FMV).
c. List it on the peer-to-peer marketplace (fixed price; fees currently 0%).
d. Request redemption: the Digital Twin is burned and the physical card ships to you (you cover shipping, insurance, duties, and taxes).

Team,Background and Credibility:

ATH Labs Ltd. (ADGM free-zone, Abu Dhabi) is building liquidity infrastructure for tokenized collectibles (vault, oracle, tokenization, and application modules).
Dominic Jang is Co-Founder & Chief Business & Operations Officer (previously referenced as CSO) of ATH Labs / Deadstock. He posts under @domidom88 and has prior experience at Nexon, Layer1, and in investment banking. The full founding team is not fully detailed publicly.
Key markers: $2.5M seed round (Sept 2026) led by Bullish Capital plus angels; exclusive supply partnership with JTCC; global partnership with CGC for grading, vaulting, and products; public Terms of Service, registered address, and active X updates.

Conclusion:

If you collect PSA 10 Pokémon cards and want the option to open packs, trade instantly, or redeem physical slabs without the usual friction, Deadstock is one of the more transparent experiments currently live.

# The Critical Role of Market Resolution in Prediction Platforms

## Introduction

In the evolving landscape of prediction markets, platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi have emerged as leaders in transforming public sentiment into tradable outcomes. Yet, as discussions across X highlight on October 18, 2026, the true test of these platforms lies not in market creation but in resolution. Resolution is where trust gets decided. Ambiguous events can trigger volume fights or erode platform integrity, underscoring the need for clearer rules and more robust mechanisms. This article examines the mechanics of market resolution, drawing on current industry conversations to assess how credible sources and predefined criteria can safeguard the future of these platforms.

## Understanding Market Resolution

Market resolution refers to the process by which prediction platforms determine the final outcome of a contract once an event concludes. On Polymarket, this often involves community-driven or oracle-based verification, while Kalshi relies on regulatory oversight through its CFTC registration. Both approaches aim to deliver objective results, but they face inherent challenges when real-world events defy clean categorization.

Credible sources, including platform documentation and regulatory filings, emphasize that resolution criteria must be established before trading begins. Without this transparency, participants risk disputes that delay payouts and damage confidence. Recent X discussions reinforce this point, noting that hybrid oracles—combining on-chain data with off-chain verification—offer a promising path to reduce ambiguity.

## Resolution Trust and Ambiguity Risks

Trust forms the foundation of any prediction market. When resolution processes appear opaque, users quickly lose faith. Trending conversations on X warn that ambiguous events can spark volume fights or erode platforms entirely. For instance, poorly defined contracts around political or economic outcomes have historically led to extended dispute periods on Polymarket.

To mitigate these risks, analysts recommend stricter rules, such as enhanced moderation tools like Modra, which could automate initial reviews while preserving human oversight for edge cases. Kalshi’s regulatory framework provides an additional layer of accountability, requiring clear settlement standards that align with federal guidelines. Professional observers stress that platforms must publish detailed resolution protocols in advance, allowing traders to evaluate risk before committing capital. This proactive approach transforms potential liabilities into competitive advantages.

## Settlement Mechanics: A Guide to Transparency

Transparent settlement mechanics are essential for maintaining market integrity. A detailed X post from @USPredict outlines the need for predefined criteria, clear payout timelines, and structured dispute processes across platforms. These elements prevent the confusion that arises when outcomes hinge on subjective interpretation.

On Polymarket, resolution often begins with an oracle feed, followed by a dispute window where users can challenge results. Kalshi, by contrast, ties settlements to official government data or court rulings, offering greater predictability but slower finality. Hybrid models that blend both methods appear increasingly attractive. By integrating multiple data sources, platforms can minimize single points of failure while preserving auditability.

Industry best practices suggest that every market should include:
- Explicit outcome definitions
- Designated resolution sources
- Time-bound dispute windows
- Appeal mechanisms with independent review

Adopting these standards would align Polymarket and Kalshi more closely with traditional financial exchanges, where settlement certainty drives liquidity.

## Platform Survival and the Imperative of Robust Resolution

Beyond individual trades, robust resolution processes determine whether prediction markets can achieve long-term viability. Commentary on X from @shillnchillz highlights how poor handling of real-world events undermines confidence and drives liquidity away. Historical examples from earlier platforms demonstrate that unresolved or contested markets can trigger mass user exodus.

For Polymarket and Kalshi to thrive, resolution must evolve from a back-office function into a core product feature. This includes investing in better tooling, clearer communication with users, and partnerships with credible data providers. As prediction markets expand into new categories—such as climate events or corporate earnings—platforms that prioritize resolution excellence will attract institutional interest and retail volume alike.

## Conclusion

Market resolution remains the decisive factor in the success or failure of prediction platforms. By addressing ambiguity risks, implementing transparent settlement mechanics, and treating resolution as a survival imperative, Polymarket and Kalshi can strengthen user trust and sustain growth. As the industry matures, platforms that deliver credible, consistent outcomes will define the next chapter of this innovative sector.

text:
The Liberal government is handing extra Express Entry points to permanent residency applicants in so-called “high-wage” jobs while preparing to scrap the requirement that employers prove they can’t find a qualified Canadian for those positions. This is real confirmed by CBC and official IRCC announcements and it’s a disgusting way of tilting the system against Canadian workers.

Starting November 3, 2026, Immigration Minister Lena Diab’s changes will award additional Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for Canadian work experience or job offers in occupations whose median wage is at least 1.3 times the national median (roughly $46,300 annually, or higher thresholds for bigger point boosts). Job offers in these fields can score 50–100 points; Canadian experience can add 20–70. Employers no longer need a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) to make those offers count for points or program eligibility under key streams like the Federal Skilled Worker Program. 

Officials will still check that offers are “genuine,” but the core test of whether a Canadian could do the job is gone.
This comes after years of record immigration levels, rising youth and graduate unemployment, and housing and wage pressures. High-wage fields (engineering, certain trades, tech, health) are exactly where many Canadians are already competing or training. Removing the “no Canadian available” hurdle while giving foreign applicants a points advantage makes it easier to import labour instead of hiring or training locals. The government frames it as attracting “top talent,” but it effectively lowers the bar for employers to prefer non-Canadians in well-paid roles and accelerates permanent residency for those already here or with offers.
It’s not spin. The policy is on https://t.co/U4AbPceNwi and was reported by CBC on October 16, 2026. Canadians who spent years building skills or waiting in the labour market get no such express boost.

Bonne Mère (Good Mother), pray for us 🙏 

🎥 Basilica of Notre-Dame de la Garde, Marseille, France 🇫🇷  

It the city's most recognizable symbol and its most visited monument.  Located on the highest natural point in the city at an altitude of approximately 157 meters, it offers panoramic views of the Old Port and the Mediterranean Sea. 

Designed by architect Henri-Jacques Espérandieu in a Romano-Byzantine style, construction began in 1853 and the basilica was consecrated in 1864.  It is affectionately known by locals as "La Bonne Mère" (the Good Mother) due to its historical role as a guardian for sailors and fishermen.  The structure is crowned by a 11.2-meter-tall gilded copper statue of the Virgin Mary, visible from across the city.

text:
Chung Yeung Festival: history, traditions and how the Chinese holiday is celebrated
https://t.co/2re805VpWZ
From hiking and grave-sweeping to sharing a meal, the Double Ninth Festival brings families together to honour their roots and wish for longevity. October brings a significant cultural occasion to climb the hills: the annual Chung Yeung Festival, which falls on October 18 this year. The name of the festival, which translates to “double yang” in Chinese, originates from its occurrence on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month. This numerical alignment also gives the occasion its alternative title, the Double Ninth Festival. The festival’s origins trace back to Xu Qi Xie Ji, commonly translated as Continuation of Qi Xie’s Records, a compilation of strange tales by Southern Liang dynasty scholar Wu Jun (469-520).

Wu recorded that the alchemist Fei Changfang warned his disciple Huan Jing of an impending calamity threatening his household on the ninth day of the ninth month. He instructed Huan to prepare crimson fabric bags filled with cornelian cherries (dogwood), fasten them to his family members’ arms, ascend a high peak and consume chrysanthemum wine to avert disaster.

In modern Hong Kong, Chung Yeung is an essential occasion for family reunions and ancestral reverence. Furthermore, the pronunciation of “nine nine” – gau gau in Cantonese, jiu jiu in Mandarin – serves as a homophone for “longevity”, symbolising enduring health and prosperity.

Observances during the Chung Yeung Festival typically include tomb sweeping, ancestral worship and savouring seasonal delicacies. Families visit columbaria and hillside cemeteries, carrying incense, candles, joss paper, roast pork, fresh fruit and their ancestors’ favourite foods as tribute. Relatives clean the gravesites and burn paper offerings in a gesture of filial devotion.

After these sacred rituals, families traditionally gather at dim sum halls and restaurants for a celebratory feast, which occasionally features roast pork. In other regions across China, such as Huizhou in Guangdong province, flying kites is an integral Chung Yeung tradition – captured in a Huizhou folk song: “The ninth day of the ninth month brings Chung Yeung; fly your kite high and wish the string long.” Driven by autumn winds, this airborne ritual has endured for generations.

The Chung Yeung Festival stands alongside the Ching Ming Festival, which occurs on the 15th day following the spring equinox, as one of the two principal occasions dedicated to ancestral veneration. Yet while Chung Yeung is tied to autumn, Ching Ming – meaning “clear and bright” – marks the arrival of spring and typically occurs in early April.

The origins of the Ching Ming Festival stretch back more than 2,500 years to the Zhou dynasty (1046-256BC), when imperial courts offered sacrifices to ancestors to secure peace, prosperity and abundant harvests for the realm. Ching Ming also shares historical ties with another ancient observance, the Cold Food Festival, which dictated the consumption of unheated dishes. While rare in contemporary Hong Kong, some places still enjoy cold, green sweet rice dumplings known as qingtuan as a nod to custom. Whether scaling serene mountain trails or gathering for traditional dim sum feasts, the Double Ninth Festival continues to weave ancient folklore into the rhythm of modern city life.

text:
In Kambaramayanam, Kamban portrays Sita Maa as a beautiful, lovable, intelligent and strong willed woman till Aranya Kandam. Following her abduction by Ravana, however, the narrative increasingly brings out her sorrow, anguish and longing for Rama.

But when Hanuman meets Sita in Lanka and offers to carry her back to Rama, Kamban reveals an entirely different dimension of her character through a few extraordinary lines:

எல்லை நீத்த உலகங்கள் யாவும் என்
சொல்லினால் சுடுவேன்; அது தூயவன்
வில்லின் ஆற்றற்கு மாசு என்று வீசினேன்

“By the power of my word alone, I can burn all the worlds that stretch beyond the boundaries of the universe. But I refrained from doing so, for such an act would diminish the glory of the divine bow wielded by the pure and righteous Lord Rama.”

What a magnificent revelation of Sita’s character!

Here, Kamban establishes that Sita is no helpless woman awaiting rescue. She possesses the extraordinary power to destroy not merely Ravana but entire worlds. Yet she consciously chooses restraint, for she does not wish to diminish the glory of Rama and his bow.

That is the brilliance of Kamban’s characterisation. He does not need to place a sword in Sita’s hands to establish her strength. Her words alone reveal a power greater than any weapon.

Now compare this profound portrayal with the circus of a sword wielding Sita, an invention that has no basis in the original Ramayana. Creative liberty is one thing. Distorting the very essence of an established character for commercial spectacle is quite another.

Sita does not need a sword to become powerful. She was always powerful.
