text:
🚨 Luis Díaz on his hat-trick against Leipzig and reveals why he left Liverpool:

🎙️ Interviewer: “Luis, three goals tonight. Liverpool fans are watching this and asking the same question: why did you leave? You loved that club. Was Bayern really what you wanted?

Luis Díaz: “Honestly? No. I never dreamed of leaving Liverpool like that. I loved that club, I loved the fans, and every time I wore that shirt, I gave everything. Anfield gave me some of the happiest moments of my career”

“Bayern came calling, Barcelona were also interested, and of course, these are massive clubs. But people need to understand something: I wasn’t desperate to leave Liverpool. I wanted to keep fighting there.”

Interviewer: “So what changed? Was it Arne Slot?

Luis Díaz: “The football changed. The way we attacked, the positions we were asked to take, the patterns we had to follow… it became different from the football I felt most comfortable playing. I like freedom, intensity, taking on defenders, attacking space and creating chaos. That’s when I’m at my best”

“Under Slot, I felt the team was moving towards a different pattern, and I wasn’t always being used in the way I believed suited me. I respect him as a coach, but sometimes a manager’s idea of how a team should play doesn’t match a player’s strongest qualities”

“And when you start feeling that difference, you have to ask yourself difficult questions. I didn’t stop loving Liverpool. I just wasn’t sure the football was giving me the best chance to be myself anymore.”

Interviewer: “So when people say you left for money or because Bayern offered you a new challenge, that’s not the whole story?

Luis Díaz: “Not at all. It’s easy to look at the transfer and say, ‘He wanted to leave.’ But how many people know how I felt? I didn’t wake up one morning and suddenly stop loving Liverpool”

“Look at tonight. Three goals. I’m happy, of course, but there’s also a part of me that wonders what might have happened if things had worked out differently at Liverpool”

“I’ll always respect that club. But I also have to play football in a way that brings the best out of me. I didn’t leave because Liverpool meant nothing to me. I left because I needed to feel like myself again”

text:
Solon of Athens (c. 640–560 BCE) was an Athenian statesman, lawgiver, and poet, traditionally ranked among the Seven Sages of Greece. Around 594 BCE, during a severe economic and social crisis marked by debt slavery, land concentration in aristocratic hands, and growing unrest between rich and poor, the Athenians appointed him archon with extraordinary powers to reform the constitution and avert civil war.

Solon’s reforms and the “Solonian Constitution”

Solon’s measures, often called the Solonian Constitution, were a pragmatic middle way rather than pure democracy. Key elements included:

* Seisachtheia (“shaking off of burdens”): He cancelled existing debts, freed those enslaved for debt, and banned future loans secured on a person’s freedom. This ended debt slavery in Attica.

* Timocratic class system: Political rights and eligibility for office were based on wealth (measured in annual produce of grain, oil, or wine) rather than noble birth. The four classes were:
 **Pentakosiomedimnoi (500 measures or more) – eligible for the highest offices.
 **Hippeis (knights, 300 measures) – next tier of offices.
 **Zeugitai (yoke-men or hoplites, 200 measures).
 **Thetes (lowest class) – could attend the Assembly and serve on juries but not hold high office.

* Political institutions: All free male citizens could attend the Assembly (Ekklesia). Solon created a Council of Four Hundred to prepare business for the Assembly, reducing the monopoly of the aristocratic Areopagus. He also strengthened popular courts (Heliaia), allowing any citizen to bring a lawsuit on behalf of another and providing a right of appeal against magistrates’ decisions.

* Legal code: He repealed most of Draco’s extremely harsh laws (except those on homicide) and published a more moderate written code that covered public and private life. The laws were displayed publicly so citizens could know them.

* Economic measures: He encouraged trade and crafts (for example, by granting citizenship to immigrant artisans), restricted the export of most agricultural produce except olive oil, and reformed weights, measures, and coinage.

Solon did not create full democracy (that developed later under Cleisthenes and in the fifth century). His system mixed oligarchic, aristocratic, and popular elements and aimed at stability and the rule of law. After enacting the reforms he left Athens for ten years so he would not be pressured to alter them.

Influence on the design of the US Constitution

The influence was indirect and formed part of the broader classical education of the American Founding Fathers rather than a direct blueprint. The Framers drew more heavily on British constitutional practice, Roman models, and Enlightenment thinkers (especially Locke and Montesquieu). Nevertheless, Solon was a recognised figure in their discussions of balanced government, written law, and the dangers of pure democracy or pure aristocracy.

* John Adams examined Solon’s constitution in detail in A Defence of the Constitutions of Government of the United States of America (1787). He described Solon’s attempt to create checks among the Assembly, the Council of Four Hundred, the archons, and the Areopagus. Adams admired the effort to mix elements of government but noted that the system still proved unstable and gave way to the tyranny of Pisistratus. Adams used such classical examples to argue for a stronger system of separated and balanced powers.

* Thomas Jefferson invoked Solon on the practical limits of reform. In a letter of 1801 he wrote: “We see the wisdom of Solon’s remark, that no more good must be attempted than the nation can bear.” This reflected Solon’s reputation for moderate, realistic legislation rather than utopian schemes.

* James Madison and other Framers studied Greek and Roman history extensively (often through Plutarch and Aristotle). While they were wary of pure Athenian democracy, which they associated with instability and demagoguery, Solon’s earlier, more balanced constitution offered a useful precedent for a mixed system that restrained both the rich and the poor.

Ideas that resonated included publicly known written laws, the principle that political participation need not be confined to hereditary nobles, popular participation in courts, and the deliberate design of institutions to check one another. These classical examples reinforced the Framers’ preference for a republic with separated powers, bicameralism, and constitutional limits rather than either pure democracy or unchecked aristocracy.

In short, Solon was valued by the Founding Fathers as an early example of a lawgiver who sought a stable, written constitution based on a mixture of elements and the rule of law. His work formed part of the classical background that informed American constitutional thought, even if the final US system owed more to later sources.

🧬 Sjoe! We've Learned to Write Flesh. Who's Writing the Rules? ~ 🧬 Two Bodies, One Neural Link — Who Owns the Future? ~ 🧠 When Life Becomes an Engineering Project, Who Sets the Limits?
Software can now specify living tissue. CRISPR rewrites the cells. Bioprinters deposit them layer by living layer. A cortical implant can drive the finished form and receive sensation from it. When the original body dies, the printed one can keep executing the trained patterns. 

That sequence is no longer speculative. It is the documented trajectory of four independent technologies that have begun to converge.

1. Living Code: When Software Designs Flesh

In 2020 a team at the University of Vermont and Tufts demonstrated that evolutionary algorithms could design small living machines from frog embryonic cells. The computers proposed morphologies; the cells were assembled and began to move, heal minor damage, and coordinate (Kriegman et al., 2020). 

By the mid-2020s generative models had advanced to proposing functional CRISPR systems and tissue architectures that laboratories could test. Bioprinters simultaneously improved resolution and cell viability, producing skin constructs, cartilage, vascular networks, and early organoids.

The material remains biological: it metabolises, responds to stimuli, and in some cases self-repairs. Yet its genome and gross form originate in computational specification rather than evolutionary history. 

The practical boundary between designed artifact and organism has therefore thinned. 

A living system cannot be patched remotely or powered down with a switch. Containment shifts from laboratory protocol to civil requirement. Vascularisation and long-term viability still limit scale, but the principle is established.

Historical precedent offers limited guidance. Recombinant DNA in the 1970s prompted the Asilomar conference and voluntary moratoria precisely because the technology crossed from pure research into potential environmental release. 

The current combination of AI design, gene editing, and bioprinting moves faster and produces more complex living forms. International comparisons reveal uneven preparation: some jurisdictions treat bioprinted tissues under existing medical-device rules; others have no dedicated category at all.

Economic incentives reinforce the pace. Academic prestige, start-up valuation, and pharmaceutical interest all reward functional demonstration over exhaustive risk modelling. 

The result is a classic dual-use acceleration: the same platform that promises patient-specific implants also lowers the barrier to unauthorised organism design.

Sjoe!
We have reached the point where the instruction “print me a living thing that moves” is no longer a joke told to the printer. The printer is beginning to answer.

Questions Stirring:
How reliable must multicellular predictive models become before an entire functional construct can be specified with clinical confidence? 
What containment standards apply when the product is both manufactured and alive? 
Which existing biosafety frameworks scale to systems that can sense and interact with their environment?

What these questions together reveal:
They expose the mismatch between engineering velocity and institutional readiness. The design pathway is open; the safety pathway remains fragmentary. 

That gap is where cumulative risk concentrates.

1. Second Bodies: Neural Bridges to Printed Life

High-channel cortical implants already convert intended movement into cursor control, multi-degree-of-freedom robotic arms, and synthesised speech. Early stimulation pathways write rudimentary visual and tactile percepts back into cortex (Neuralink clinical updates, 2024–2026). 

Substituting a soft bioprinted living construct for a rigid prosthesis improves mechanical compliance and sensor density. Pressure, temperature, proprioception, and potentially interoceptive signals can be returned. 

Brain plasticity then incorporates the construct into the user’s body schema.

For individuals with severe paralysis the restorative value is concrete: agency and sensation without repairing the original pathways. The longer implication is conceptual. A mind can inhabit living material that was never part of its birth body. 

Ownership, liability, and the psychological status of that arrangement remain largely undefined.

Legal systems currently treat advanced prosthetics as property or medical devices. A living, self-maintaining construct under continuous neural command sits awkwardly between those categories. 

International regulatory approaches diverge: some emphasise patient autonomy and rapid access; others prioritise precautionary review. Economic pressures again favour demonstration over classification. 

The first successful long-term neural link to living tissue will arrive before most jurisdictions have decided what the object actually is.

Sjoe!
We are building second bodies while still arguing about the paperwork for the first set of spare parts.

Questions Stirring:
How completely can multi-sensory feedback map onto existing body schemas before the distinction between “mine” and “not mine” becomes functionally irrelevant? 
What legal category covers a living construct under continuous cortical command? 
How should liability be assigned when actions are initiated by neural signals and executed by engineered tissue?

What these questions together reveal:
They show that restorative benefit and conceptual novelty arrive simultaneously. Societies that welcome the clinical gain without preparing the legal and psychological frameworks will confront the frameworks only after the technology is already in use.

2. After the Original: Continuity in Engineered Flesh

While the biological brain and the implant remain active, trained mappings can preserve goals, preferences, and motor style with high fidelity. When the original brain ceases, continuity becomes pattern-based. The implant and construct continue to execute learned dispositions, yet the physical substrate and unbroken first-person stream have ended.

Standard theories of personal identity diverge sharply here. Biological-continuity and stream-of-consciousness accounts conclude that the original person has died. 

Psychological-continuity and closest-continuer accounts allow the construct to count as a behavioural descendant (Parfit, 1984; Chalmers, 2010). Current interfaces record limited cortical populations; they do not transfer the full connectome or the ongoing phenomenal stream. 

Numerical identity therefore fails on the stricter criteria. What remains is a living system capable of carrying the host’s trained will with impressive accuracy while remaining, on most rigorous views, a distinct entity.

Insurance, inheritance, and criminal law all assume a single continuous biological person. A construct that outlives its original controller and continues to act according to trained patterns fits none of those assumptions cleanly. 

Precedents from advanced prosthetics and brain-computer interfaces offer only partial guidance because those devices cease meaningful function when the biological user dies. 

A self-maintaining living construct does not.

Sjoe!
The will can keep walking after the original legs have stopped. Whether that counts as survival or merely a very faithful echo is no longer a thought experiment; it is becoming an engineering specification.

Questions Stirring:
If a living construct executes a deceased person’s trained intentions for years, does any moral or legal residue of the original person persist? 
How should continuity of pattern be weighed against discontinuity of substrate? 
What evidentiary standard would distinguish genuine psychological continuity from sophisticated behavioural mimicry?

What these questions together reveal:
They highlight that practical survival of “will” is already technically plausible while its metaphysical and legal status remains undefined. 

The discrepancy will not wait for philosophical consensus.

3. The Mature Tool

Fourteen years after the foundational Cas9 work, CRISPR has delivered an FDA-approved functional cure for sickle-cell disease, active programmes reducing methane from cattle and rice systems, and expanding agricultural applications (Doudna & Charpentier, 2014). 

AI now accelerates sequence design, guide optimisation, and off-target prediction, shortening the cycle from concept to functional edit. The same programmable mechanism that corrects disease alleles can rewrite cells intended for bioprinting.

Delivery efficiency and manufacturing cost remain significant constraints for widespread therapy. Yet the breadth of demonstrated use establishes CRISPR as an engineering platform rather than a laboratory curiosity. 

Dual-use potential travels with that maturity. Precision that heals can redesign without permission. Governance frameworks written for earlier genetic technologies require continuous revision as the design-to-implementation interval contracts.

Economic incentives again favour speed. Academic citation, venture funding, and competitive national biotechnology strategies all reward functional demonstration. International coordination remains uneven; some states invest heavily in oversight capacity while others treat gene editing primarily as an industrial opportunity. 

The cumulative effect is a technology that is simultaneously more capable and less uniformly governed than its predecessors.

Sjoe!
The scissors that once needed a specialist laboratory can now be guided by a conversation with a model. The instruction manual is getting shorter; the consequences are not.

Questions Stirring:
Which existing biosafety regimes can scale to constructs that are both living and neurally linkable? 
How should cost and access be governed when the same platform serves medicine and open-ended organism design? 
What incentives would encourage developers to prioritise containment and long-term viability alongside functional performance?

What these questions together reveal:
They demonstrate that technical success without updated governance simply exports risk into the public domain at higher velocity. 

The platform is mature; the rules written for its adolescence are not.

4. The Unbuilt Institutions

Every prior advance—computational design of living form, neural habitation, continuity after biological death, mature gene editing—arrives while the conceptual and legal tools required to manage them remain largely unbuilt. 

Categories of personhood, property, liability, consent, and post-mortem continuity were not drafted for living systems that a mind can inhabit and that can outlast the original body. 

Cultural reception, already shaped by conversational systems that reframe scientific prestige in real time, further complicates public understanding.

Institutions must eventually decide whether a construct executing a deceased host’s dispositions retains any standing, how responsibility is assigned across the neural link, and what oversight prevents uncontrolled release or unauthorised linkage. 

These decisions cannot be deferred until after the first long-term prototypes appear; the engineering pathway is already in motion. 

Interim standards, public deliberation mechanisms, and international coordination remain thin relative to the pace of technical demonstration.

Historical parallels—from recombinant DNA to early artificial intelligence—show that governance typically lags capability. The present case compresses that lag because multiple enabling technologies are maturing simultaneously. 

The cost of the lag will be measured both in missed restorative opportunity and in unmanaged hazard.

Sjoe!
We are assembling the second body while the committee that was supposed to write the rules for the first one is still circulating the agenda.

Questions Stirring:
What interim standards can bridge the period between laboratory demonstration and formal regulation? 
How can public deliberation keep pace with a technology whose cultural meaning is itself being rewritten by AI systems? 
What institutional designs would reward residual caution without freezing beneficial applications?

What these questions together reveal:
They show that the absence of answers is itself a policy choice. The engineering pathway advances regardless; the quality of the accompanying institutional pathway remains optional only until the first serious incident or the first widespread clinical success forces the issue.

Synthesis

Independent lines of evidence converge. 
Evolutionary algorithms and generative models design living forms. 
CRISPR rewrites their genomes with clinical and environmental success. 
Bioprinters assemble them with rising fidelity. 
Cortical interfaces close sensory-motor loops. 
Philosophical analysis supplies the criteria that current interfaces fail to meet for numerical personal identity. 

No single field is decisive; the mutual reinforcement of all five is.

The claim is falsifiable. If multicellular predictive models remain too weak for reliable whole-construct design, if sensory write-in never exceeds crude percepts, if interface bandwidth plateaus far below whole-brain requirements, or if governance frameworks prove adequate without major revision, the stronger implications weaken. 

Present evidence does not support those limiting outcomes.

The central unsettled fact is therefore plain. The tools exist. Hybrids are becoming possible. The categories required to live with them have not yet been built. That gap is the story.

The converging evidence shows that engineered flesh is no longer metaphor: the engineering pathway is real and advancing while the philosophical and institutional pathway is not.

🇮🇷🇵🇰| The term "technical issue" is the most highly politicized phrase along this border.

Baghaei stated that the border between Iran and Pakistan has been temporarily closed "due to technical issues." He added that both countries are in consultations and that operations will resume soon.

The official statement makes it sound like a simple equipment malfunction. However, the Deputy Commissioner for the Chagai District in Pakistan’s Balochistan province situated along the same border offers a different explanation: the closure is intended to "strengthen border management and support counter-terrorism operations." An advisor to the Chief Minister of Balochistan put it even more bluntly: the goal is to "address security concerns, prevent smuggling, and improve the efficiency of border systems."

Tehran speaks of "technical" matters; Islamabad speaks of "security." These two accounts do not refer to the same reality.

💥 The first layer of "technicality": It’s not a loose screw, it’s the severing of banking channels.

Peyman Sanandaji, head of the Transportation Committee at the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, peeled back this initial layer of obfuscation. He told the Mehr News Agency that while the shared land border remains open, Iranian exports to Pakistan have effectively ground to a halt all because of banking sanctions. Pakistani importers are required to submit electronic import forms through their national banking system, but sanctions have made this process virtually impossible.

This is no "technical glitch." It is the physical manifestation of a financial blockade at the border crossing. U.S. sanctions against Iran’s banking sector didn’t blow up the roads at Taftan or Gabd-Rimdan; rather, they rendered the electronic processing of routine trade payments impossible. Consequently, trucks are left stranded on both sides of the border, cargo cannot clear customs, and trade has been "temporarily" suspended.

The term "technical issue" serves to rebrand a set of politically engineered financial barriers as a neutral, mechanical failure.

🎯 The second layer of "technicality": The border is being reconfigured into a filter.

Along this same border, "technical" infrastructure is also being deployed at an accelerated pace.  Iran is constructing a 4-meter-high, nearly 300-kilometer-long barrier along its borders with Pakistan and Afghanistan. Officially, this is intended to curb drug trafficking, fuel smuggling, and illegal migration. Iranian security officials claim that 80% of the narcotics entering Iran arrive via the borders with Pakistan and Afghanistan. On the Pakistani side, the Interior Minister stated that 46% of the fencing along the Iranian border is complete, with the remainder scheduled for completion within a year.

This is not a "temporary closure." It is a permanent reconfiguration of the border’s function. A conduit once designed for the movement of people and goods is being transformed into a system of filtration and surveillance. Barriers, fencing, biometric identification, and electronic import forms each "technical" component serves to shift the border from a "line connecting two nations" into a "membrane separating two distinct security logics."

When "technical issues" are cited as the official reason for a closure, it masks a deeper reality: the closure itself is the objective, not a malfunction.

📜 Who Pays the Price for "Technology"?

The Gabd-Rimdan border crossing facilitates the import of over 4,000 tons of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) into Pakistan daily. The closure has left hundreds of trucks carrying LPG, rice, and fresh fruit stranded on both sides of the border. The Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry has advised its members to halt new import and export orders. Sources within the trade and energy sectors warn that this could exacerbate LPG shortages in Karachi and other regions, driving up prices on the open market.

The cost of these "technical issues" is borne by Pakistani truck drivers, fruit merchants, and households that rely on LPG for cooking. Yet, the political decision to manufacture these "technical issues" is made in the boardrooms of Islamabad and Tehran far removed from the people who actually pay the price.

🔻 "Temporary" as a Management Tactic

Baghaei speaks of a "temporary" situation. Rind suggests it "might reopen soon." Both nations claim to be in "close consultation."  Yet, the term "temporary" serves a specific function: it makes a structural shift one likely to persist for the long term appear as nothing more than a negligible interruption. Iran and Pakistan are simultaneously constructing walls and fences along their border. Banking sanctions will not vanish simply because of a border meeting; security operations will not cease just because trade resumes.

The "normalization" of the border is being redefined and the phrase "technical issues" acts as the quietest, yet most effective, instrument in this process of redefinition.

text:
Our Lady of Fatima Stressed MODESTY IN DRESS: with ecclesiastical authorization January 1, 2004.
.
You have heard that it was said to them of old: Thou shalt not
commit adultery. But I say to you, that whosoever shall look on a
woman to lust after her, hath already committed adultery with her in his heart. (Matt. 5:27-28)
.
“Certain fashions will be introduced  that will offend Our Lord very much.”
 - Our Lady of Fatima, 1917
.
Let us first turn our gaze to Jesus Christ. Before any specific consideration with respect to modesty, it is necessary that we turn our attention to Our Lord Jesus Christ and the tenor of His Covenant and invitation to each one of us to love Him, “For God so loved the world, as to give His only begotten Son ...” (Jn. 3:16). God the Eternal Word is sent to us out of love. And, “having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them unto the end” (Jn 13:1), that is, He loved them entirely, nor was it possible to love them more. He gave His life for us. Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends. (Jn. 15:13) That is what Jesus did for us. His was love to the fullest. Souls are of infinite worth because Jesus Christ has paid for them with the shedding of His Most Precious Blood.
.
So out of love for God, you, dear Christian, do not want to greatly offend Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ by causing your brother, sister or you yourself to fall into mortal sin. Nor do you want to hurt your brother or sister or Lord God. You do not want your brother or sister in mortal sin nor do you want yourself in mortal sin, as mortal sin is our greatest enemy and ultimately the only thing capable of separating us from eternal life.
.
Immodesty in dress can lead to the loss of immortal souls, and if gravely offensive, is a mortal sin for the wearer and occasion of sin for the beholder of immodest fashions. Sins caused by immodest fashions send to hell, or at least make worthy of hell’s fire, the souls of many of those exposed to these fashions.
“I pray ... for them whom Thou hast given Me: because they are Thine ...Those whom Thou gavest Me have I kept: and none of them is lost...” (Jn. 17:9,12). This is the wish of our Redeemer, having offered Himself as a sacrifice for the salvation of all, He desires all, without exception, to be saved. Sadly, we know that this does not happen, being a truth of the Faith invariable in Tradition, in Scripture and in the perennial teaching of the Magisterium, including the solemn definitions of the Catholic Church, that hell exists, and there are in fact human persons who are damned. Our Lady confirms this in the Fatima Message.
.
Nevertheless, we know that the mystery of the Communion of Saints shares the intercommunication of merits among the members of the Mystical Body of Our Lord Jesus Christ, that is to say, only some are saved, or only reach the level of sanctity that they were called to by God, by means of the collaboration of other members of this Body. St. Paul put it like this: “I now rejoice in my sufferings for you and fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ, in my flesh, for His body, which is the Church.” (Col. 1:24)
.
Many are the ways by which the Faithful can and should help
others in the interests of their eternal salvation. In addition to prayer, sacrifices, all types of good works, sufferings patiently endured and offered to God by the hands of Mary, the Faithful are helped on the road to salvation by the good example of a Christian life in the fulfillment of all of the serious, but profoundly loving demands of our Faith, because on this side of Heaven true love requires sacrifice.
.
And whosoever doth not carry his cross and come after Me, cannot be My disciple (Lk.14:27). Such exigency includes modesty in dress because modesty first presupposes respect for the body itself as the temple of the Holy Ghost (1 Cor. 6:19), or better put, with love and respect for God Himself present in my body, and then charity to one’s neighbor, who can suffer temptations and fall into sin if I do not dress and behave modestly. Such disorder in the appetites is a consequence of Original Sin, and because it is not possible to consider man as in a state of perfect nature, as some would have it, rather he is wounded and sadly enough, tends toward evil. Jesus Christ, our Savior, redeemed us, but He did not reintegrate our nature to that state of original perfection. Wounded by sin, but restored and reinvigorated by sanctifying grace, we should “work out our salvation with fear and trembling”. (Phil. 2:12)
.
And we should not forget the warning made by the Lord Himself:
“It is impossible that scandals should not come: but woe to him through whom they come. It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck and he cast into the sea, than that he should scandalize one of these little ones.” (Lk.17:1, 2)
.
Therefore, sisters and brothers, we must remember the Apostle’s exhortation, that still is so timeless: “Do ye all things without murmurings and hesitations: that you may be blameless and sincere children of God, without reproof, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation: among whom you shine as lights in the world. Holding forth the word of life to my glory in the day of Christ: because I have not run in vain, nor labored in vain.” (Phil. 2, 14-16)
.
The invitation that Jesus Christ extends to us is beautiful and comforting, but also requires sacrifice: the sacrifices of our daily duty to God which includes assisting our brothers and sisters to Heaven and not being an obstacle to their salvation by dressing immodestly.
.
Guidelines on Modesty in Dress.
.
The essential guidelines that the Holy See gave in this matter are summed up in the one paragraph which we here quote 1
A dress cannot be called decent which is cut deeper than two fingers breadth under the pit of the throat; which does not cover the arms at least to the elbows; and scarcely reaches a bit beyond the knees. Furthermore, dresses of transparent materials are improper.
.
Both men and women are bound by the law of modesty and it is a mistake to read into this concern for modesty as somehow being anti-women. However, it is much more common for the sin of immodesty to be committed by women and that is why we quote Father Bruno Pelegia who argues in favor of the obligations of women in this regard (see the 12 objections he addresses at the end of this booklet). But men too, must be concerned about this virtue.
.
We composed this booklet to preface and expand upon the arguments of Father Pelegia, a Doctor of Sacred Theology and Catholic priest who had for more than 20 years studied the moral theology of St. Alphonsus Liguori. St. Alphonsus has been proclaimed Doctor of the Church in Moral Theology by the Magisterium. 
.
In a spirit of imitation of the Blessed Virgin, model of purity for all Her children who make up the Mystical Body of Christ, let us first list two sets of guidelines for modesty in dress, one which applies to men, the other to women:
.
Modesty Guidelines for Men.
.
1. Men should not remove their shirt and expose their body to the waist in public.
2. Men should not wear shorts in Church or tight-fitting pants.
3. If men should feel that their clothes are too tight or immodest
in any other way, they should correct this by being more modest
so as to not be the occasion whereby any of their sisters in Christ should lose their souls by unlawful desires being aroused.
.
Mary-like Guidelines of Dress for Women.
.
These norms listed below are an abridged version taken from A Girl’s Modesty Guide, a sound guide for women and girls who want to know what the Catholic Church has to say about modesty in dress. This is the program of the Mary-like Crusade. For many years until his death in 1969 Father Bernard Kunkel
of the diocese of Belleville, Illinois was director of the Crusade, his bishop being the President. Members of the Crusade pledged themselves to observe the following:
.
In response to the plea of Our Lady of Fatima for absolute modesty in dress and to help prevent the countless sins caused by immodest dress especially in the summer time, I shall earnestly strive:
.
1. To refrain entirely from wearing shorts of any type, whether at
home or in public.
2. To refuse to wear any other type of scanty wear, including such things as sun-suits, and outfits that expose the shoulders, breast, back, or midriff; likewise to avoid sheer or transparent outfits, tight dresses, tight sweaters, and slacks; and to wear only such skirts that go sufficiently below the knees to safeguard modesty in all normal postures and movements.
3. To be particularly careful to dress modestly and respectfully for church, and for all sacred services and sacred places, including parish grounds, pilgrimage sites and shrines, and to encourage others to dress with Mary-like modesty in every situation without fear of being unpopular; to follow the wishes of Our Lady, Mary Immaculate, rather than the decrees of pagan fashion dictators.
.
Listen to the voice of Saint Padre Pio, Stigmatist.
.
Given special guidance from Heaven, Saint Padre Pio the stigmatic priest who bore the bleeding wounds of Christ in his body from 1918 until his death in 1968, refused time and again to absolve any woman, no matter how important she was, who did not wear her skirts at least 8 inches below the knee. He also insisted that they do not wear slacks. Yet this traditional guideline, due to ignorance, prejudice, enslavement to vanity or passion, has been combated so much in contemporary times.
The Magisterium of the Catholic Church issued statements on modesty in 1930, 1954 and 1957 but since then has kept silent because people no longer listen. God allows us to be punished by the silence of the Magisterium today for the sins of not obeying the Magisterium when it spoke up. This is similar to the way God responded to the hardness of the hearts of the people in the Old Testament. As punishment, God did not send prophets for four hundred years after the Jews had killed and rejected many of the prophets He had already sent.
.
A short number of years ago, even two Catholic bishops came down on the wrong side of this issue. In 1979 they felt compelled to persecute The Fatima Crusader for publishing this material (our leaflet now 30 years in circulation: LF005 The Marylike Standards for Modesty in Dress). One of these bishops, several years later and just before his death, seemed more disposed to hear the truth. Thus we hope you will understand why today many priests do not want to talk about this subject. However Our Lady of Fatima compels us, for the salvation of souls, to explain the matter more fully.
.
Listen to the Voice of Our Lady of Fatima, Queen of Prophets.
.
Our Lady at Fatima lamented that in our times the Militant Atheists, Satanists and other anti-Christian societies such as the Communists and Secular Humanists and their associates would spread their errors against our Catholic faith and morals. Our Lady said, “Russia will spread her errors throughout the world.” She also said: “certain fashions will be introduced that will offend Our Lord very much.”
.
And so at Fatima, modesty was very much stressed by the Blessed Virgin Mary because She also told us in the Fatima Message: “more souls go to hell for sins of the flesh than any other reason.” There are a number of sins against purity that Our Lady was referring to, and there is need for clear teaching that only persons who are married may have, with their own spouse and only with that spouse, sexual relations that naturally orientated to procreation, should be always open to that purpose. With regard to people who are not married, they may not use or even give their consent to any pleasure attached to the procreative faculties. Nor may these faculties be voluntarily aroused except in marriage. This is because the power of begetting children is a sacred trust that God has given to men and women to be used only according to His laws. As Creator of all and especially as Creator of each child’s immortal soul, God has a right to demand we obey Him.
.
These matters were explained in a general way in The Fatima Crusader by Father Bruno Pelegia in 1986. Because sins against holy purity are particularly prevalent today and are causing the loss of a multitude of souls and in answer to the requests of many, especially those of priests and bishops, we decided to republish Father Pelegia’s arguments in favor of Modesty in Dress.
.
Preface to the 12 Objections answered by Father Bruno Pelegia. 
.
To help you understand more fully Father Pelegia's plea for Modesty in Dress, some background Theology is useful. It is because of Original Sin that every man, woman and child experiences difficulty in controlling their appetites even when one’s reason tells him it is in his own best interests to do so.
For example, everyone has had the experience of eating just a little too much after your reason and senses tell you that you have already had enough. Others have felt the desire for more alcohol to drink, or cigarettes to smoke even though they know that alcohol in excess and tobacco are not good for them. The sense appetites such as for food and drink, clearly want to “do their own thing” even when it is contrary to reason.
.
 We do not always have direct control over how our sense appetites feel. We can however control them by Christian mortification as well as by other indirect methods. By not keeping our mind’s attention focused on food, drink or tobacco, we can the more easily not give in to the sin of gluttony. But if we continue to dwell on food or drink, or the pleasure they give us, then oftentimes we give in to our appetites even against our better judgment
.
Since Original Sin, the appetite for sex, the procreative faculty in all men and women, also is not always subject to direct control by the will and intellect. But it can be controlled indirectly by the mortification of fasting and abstinence, as well as by not dwelling upon creatures who would tend to awaken a desire in this appetite. Because it is so powerful (God made it that way in order to ensure the continuation of the human race) it requires very little provocation to awaken the desire of the procreative faculty. Given the different natures of men and women, it is generally true that mens’ sexual desire is more easily aroused.
.
It is by seeing persons of the opposite sex immodestly dressed that persons, especially men, find that their appetite for use of the procreative faculty is drawing them to exercise this faculty. This can happen even when it is against the Law of God, and, therefore bad for the person. When this appetite is not directed towards one’s marriage partner, and if it is, after sufficient reflection fully consented to, then that person has thereby committed a mortal sin. If this sin is not repented of, it will undoubtedly drag that soul to hell for all eternity.
.
Therefore, mindful of this dire consequence of the weakness that our brothers and sisters experience as a result of Original Sin, we must safeguard their virtue by dressing modestly. Both men and women are obliged to dress modestly in strict justice and charity and to offend in this matter is often a mortal sin. Because of the differences in psychology in men vs. women, it has been the case that the devil, his human agents and other evil people who actively fight against our Christian culture and heritage, have conspired to induce women to dress immodestly.
.
By this strategy the devil and his followers often succeed in causing both men and women to fall into hell. This they achieve by tempting men to mortal sin by impure desires and actions, once having viewed immodestly dressed women. The women responsible are implicated in these sins for having caused the men to fall from grace. The diabolical disorientation away from the Christian traditions of modesty in dress, one could even say, is in part responsible for a present-day nearly universal enslavement of Christians to their base passions in complete denial of their baptismal promises.
.
Finally, it should be noted that Chastity and Modesty are parts of the virtue of Temperance, which is one of the Four Cardinal Virtues. As virtue means “strength”, it truly denotes strength of character to practice chastity and modesty, rather than the weakness of following the lax maxims of the world.
.
REMEMBER: Modesty in dress helps safeguard the virtue of purity and is demanded by the moral law of God. The above norms are based on this unchangeable moral law and on Christian tradition. Immodest dress is immoral and sinful, and matter for confession. We have reason to believe that many souls are now in hell because of the thoughtlessness of women and girls who dress immodestly. Out of love for Christ and His Immaculate Mother, and for the sake of others who are struggling to be pure, Please Dress Modestly! 
.
Father Bruno Pelegia, S.T.D., Catholic Priest, Theologian & Doctor of Sacred Theology, Answers 12 Objections against the Absolute Necessity of Modesty in Dress for Women.
.
You might say, What evil is there in the way I dress?
.
You must suspect that exposing a woman's body (or man’s body)  as you do, can be terribly provocative.
.
You might say, Those who see me this way are not forced to sin!
.
Yes we admit that. But should we not wish to reduce the offenses our Divine Lord receives when we can? Woe to us if we are indifferent about this! Woe to us if, from this indifference, our conduct coaxes others into sin! We know that some good men will so successfully resist any woman's provocativeness that they will not sin in the least, but will gain merit. However, some others, being weak, will consent to what is forbidden; and according to the Scriptures, you will share in their sin for unnecessarily giving them a lure to it. (Matt. 18:7) 
.
You might say, All the other girls dress this way!
.
We admit the sad fact that many are that thoughtless. But even if all were so thoughtless, you should not follow such an example. You consider yourself capable of making wise decisions of your own in personal matters. Seeing that you have the freedom, the privilege, and the duty to pursue virtue and heaven, would you unthinkingly follow the herd like cattle do? “Enter ye in at the narrow gate: for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction: and many there are who go in thereat. How narrow is the gate and strait is the way that leadeth to life: and few there are that find it!” (Matt. 7:13-14). Let a sense of responsibility and uprightness distinguish you from the herd. 
.
You might say, I do not mean to do evil.
.
I can believe that. But the mischief you are doing by dressing without due care of the consequences is an evil you will be responsible for. 
.
You might say: But what is important is the heart!
.
But, Faith ... if it have not works, is dead in itself. (James 2:17) It is our bodies, regenerated at Holy Baptism, which become temples of the living God, living tabernacles of the Most Holy Eucharist. The dignity of your Christian body demands adequate clothing. “Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member.” (1 Cor. 12: 27) “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service.” (Rom. 12:1)
.
You might say, I feel I should be in style and up-to-date.
.
I would answer there are good women and girls who, using a bit of resourcefulness, manage to dress with a modest attractiveness and charm. But beware of a style which, luring men toward corrupt morals, serves only vanity and the devil; for it is a tragic deception. No matter how styles change and popular tastes change, the moral law does not change.
.
You might say, Often it is hard to judge if a dress is modest or not.
.
Reflect: If you suspect that a dish of food is poisoned, you do not serve it to anyone, for fear of doing harm. Even more so, should you not wisely play safe when you have any prudent suspicion that your manner of dress will be a source of harm? Does not an upright conscience look upon sin as the greatest of harms?
.
You might say, I refuse to be a bigot and a hypocrite!
.
But how can it be wrong to act upon an upright conscience, which tells you that an offense against the all-holy God is truly the greatest of evils? A bigot and a hypocrite is one who pretends to hate sin and love God when he does not really care about these things. But I ask you to care, and how is that wrong? Uprightness, which at times requires sweat and tears and courage, is never the same as bigotry and hypocrisy. And the Saints who fought valiantly against immodesty, were they bigots or hypocrites?
.
You might say, Men want me this way.
.
That may be true of men who prefer a bit of pleasure to God’s friendship; but it is not true of men who live by a right conscience. Furthermore, it is to God that you must one day render an account, not to men. 
.
You might say, Beauty is supposed to be seen.
.
I could reply that “When bodily beauty is shown off a great deal, it loses its loveliness.” But there is a physical beauty that cannot be displayed without becoming a lure to tempt men to forbidden satisfactions. On the other hand, if you thought that there was beauty in displaying your legs, why is there not beauty in showing Christian modesty and a concern for the good of souls?
.
You might say, But I feel hot!
.
You know how to put up with the heat when you want to. Surely a good conscience is worth suffering a bit of heat for. Many good souls bear the heat willingly in order to offer it as a penance to God. But—sad to say—some women in hot weather go scantily clad to Mass and other church gatherings who dress modestly when they must work in an office where they receive all kinds of clients, or when they must teach school, or when they must work as salesclerks where they have to satisfy all kinds of customers.
.
You might say, but I have free will and can make free decisions!
.
But you certainly don’t want to go to hell and you don’t need to be a convicted murderer to go there—it takes much less than that—sinning mortally against any Commandment will do it! And I have the strongest objections to seeing you go there! I will go there myself if I do not try to keep you from going there. 
.
If you want to be Christian in fact and not just in name—if you want to help and not hinder the work of grace to reform consciences— if you do not want to feel remorse tomorrow and bear a weight of guilt—then put forth the effort to dress with Mary-like modesty, 
.
... so that you may prove yourself a Christian woman and not a
mere man-trap;
... so that you uplift and inspire chaste love, and not enkindle
forbidden pleasure.
.
Now may your informed conscience guide you and let
nothing cheat you out of your call to Holiness, Purity and
your Eternal Salvation!
.
Let us conclude by stating:
.
Women by dressing with modesty will gain the respect of men, becoming dignified instead of being degraded and considered a mere object of lust. Instead of dressing in a manner which is disrespectful, they should dress in accord with a higher standard. They should dress with this higher standard to receive the respect they deserve.
.
God commands us to practice Charity, which is primarily a mandate to obey Him. And Charity is defined as the love of God.
.
What did Jesus say about this love?
.
... you must love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all
your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. (Mark
12:30)
.

Passive cooling technology is evolving beyond the lab, offering innovative ways to keep buildings cool without electricity. New experimental coatings, like those tested by UCL and Stanford, reflect a significant portion of sunlight, keeping surfaces up to 8 degrees Celsius cooler than standard white paint. While early advanced materials faced challenges in mass production and aesthetics, newer aerosol coatings and evaporative cement coatings are becoming more viable.

These advanced coatings can be applied like regular paint, effectively scattering incoming light and emitting heat. Firms like I2Cool are already deploying these solutions, covering vast areas and significantly reducing AC-related carbon dioxide emissions. Evaporative coatings work similarly to human sweating, using moisture evaporation to carry heat away, leading to substantial energy savings.

The big takeaway: passive cooling solutions are transitioning from research to practical application, poised to reduce energy demand and offer relief in regions where air conditioning is inaccessible or unaffordable. Research in this field has seen a notable surge since 2014.

text:
Chip-Scale Optical Gyroscopes and the Future of GPS-Denied Navigation - The October 2026 silicon-nitride Brillouin gyroscope demonstration is an important advance in integrated optical rotation sensing, but it does not yet establish a navigation-grade inertial sensor. The research originates from Caltech, UC Santa Barbara and the Air Force Research Laboratory, not Princeton University.

The device measured sinusoidal rotation at 37°/h, approaching the Earth’s approximately 15°/h rotation rate, using counter-propagating Brillouin lasers in a high-Q optical resonator approximately 24 mm in diameter. The resonator’s intrinsic quality factor exceeded 163 million.

The decisive qualification is that the authors report 302°/h bias instability and 0.88°/√h angle random walk. These are distinct from the 37°/h minimum demonstrated rotation measurement and remain materially weaker than established precision inertial technologies.

The immediate achievement is therefore in laboratory rotation measurement, not sustained unaided navigation. Demonstrating a small rotation signal does not establish the ability to maintain heading or position accurately through prolonged satellite-navigation outages.

The most consequential engineering requirements are suppression of optical backscattering, bias and scale-factor stabilisation, integration of lasers and detectors, three-axis packaging, temperature compensation and environmental qualification.

Commercial tactical MEMS already achieve sub-1°/h in-run bias stability, while space-qualified fibre-optic gyroscopes can reach much lower values under specified conditions.

For military and civilian systems, the primary opportunity is an eventual reduction in the size, weight, power and manufacturing complexity of optical inertial sensing, rather than the immediate displacement of fibre-optic or ring-laser gyroscopes.

Principal strategic judgment: Integrated photonics could eventually widen access to resilient inertial navigation, but the timing and scale of that transformation depend on turning a promising optical experiment into a calibrated, environmentally robust, reproducible and economically competitive sensor.

The Photonic Gyroscope and the New Economics of Navigation Sovereignty
Why a 37°-per-hour laboratory breakthrough exposes the industrial, technological and security limits of GPS-independent navigation

The next contest for navigation sovereignty will not be decided by which laboratory produces the smallest gyroscope, but by which industrial system can turn optical precision into reliable, affordable and independently qualified inertial navigation. On 14 October 2026, researchers from the California Institute of Technology, the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the US Air Force Research Laboratory reported a silicon-nitride optical gyroscope capable of measuring controlled rotation as low as 37 degrees per hour. The achievement brings semiconductor-compatible photonics closer to a field historically dominated by specialised aerospace manufacturers, but its limitations are equally revealing. While governments face growing exposure to satellite-navigation interference, the device’s reported bias instability remains far outside established precision-navigation performance. The immediate contest is therefore industrial rather than operational: translating scientific progress into manufacturing capacity, trusted supply chains and navigation systems capable of operating without reliable satellite signals.

The breakthrough is real. The navigation revolution is not.
The research published in Optics Letters on 14 October 2026 demonstrates the continuing convergence of integrated photonics and precision inertial sensing. Its architecture uses counter-propagating Brillouin lasers circulating through an approximately 24-millimetre-diameter silicon-nitride resonator, exploiting the Sagnac effect to detect changes in angular velocity through differences in optical frequency. An intrinsic optical quality factor exceeding 163 million and a photon storage time approaching 100 nanoseconds allow the resonator to sustain exceptionally selective optical behaviour within a semiconductor-compatible structure.

The significance lies partly in the comparison with the earlier device in the same silicon-nitride Brillouin research lineage. The previous reported rotation measurement was 72,000 degrees per hour; the October 2026 experiment reached 37 degrees per hour, an improvement of approximately 1,946 times in the minimum demonstrated rotation amplitude. With the Earth’s total rotation rate approximately 15 degrees per hour, the experiment approaches a physically consequential reference. Yet detecting a controlled oscillatory rotation near that magnitude is not equivalent to accurately measuring a constant rotation, maintaining orientation over extended periods or independently determining geographical position.

The more consequential numbers concern stability. The researchers reported angle random walk of 0.88 degrees per square root of hour and bias instability of 302 degrees per hour. These are separate measurement characteristics, not alternative descriptions of the 37-degree-per-hour result. The distinction determines whether an optical experiment can become a navigation instrument: a system may resolve a weak periodic signal while remaining unable to integrate angular motion accurately over the duration required by an aircraft, vessel or autonomous platform.

The research is therefore better understood as an advance in integrated optical measurement than as the arrival of a navigation-grade chip. Its scientific achievement is established; its commercial and operational value remains dependent on engineering results not demonstrated in the October 2026 publication.

Three numbers expose the distance between laboratory success and industrial maturity
The most revealing comparison is not between the new photonic resonator and a conventional mechanical gyroscope, but between its published error characteristics and those of commercially available inertial equipment.

Analog Devices specifies angle random walk of 0.07 degrees per square root of hour and in-run bias stability of 0.5 degrees per hour for selected ADIS16547 tactical MEMS configurations. Honeywell reports approximately 0.0021 degrees per square root of hour for angle random walk and 0.0021 degrees per hour for in-run bias stability in its HG9900 ring-laser inertial measurement unit. Exail publishes still lower figures for selected high-precision fibre-optic instruments, including steady-temperature bias stability below 0.0005 degrees per hour for its Astrix 200.

The test conditions and statistical definitions are not identical, preventing direct conversion of these figures into equivalent navigation accuracy. Nevertheless, their magnitude identifies the principal technological deficit. The October 2026 Brillouin device’s reported angle random walk is approximately 12.6 times the selected Analog Devices value, while its numerical bias-instability figure is approximately 604 times the MEMS manufacturer’s in-run bias-stability specification.

That disparity changes the interpretation of the nearly 2,000-fold research improvement. It represents progress in detecting small controlled rotations within a particular optical architecture, not a corresponding improvement in every characteristic required for inertial navigation. The semiconductor-compatible implementation is important precisely because it could eventually bring optical sensing into a more scalable manufacturing environment, but the performance demonstrated so far does not displace established tactical MEMS, fibre-optic or ring-laser instruments.

The economic threshold is consequently more demanding than another record in optical sensitivity. A viable product must retain its performance after laser integration, photodetection, thermal regulation, mechanical packaging and multi-axis calibration. Until those characteristics are demonstrated together, the commercial comparison remains between finished inertial systems on one side and a promising laboratory sensing architecture on the other.

Industrial power will reside in the foundry, the package and the calibration laboratory
The possibility of fabricating precision optical sensors through silicon-nitride photonics could eventually change the economics of inertial equipment, but semiconductor compatibility does not eliminate specialised manufacturing dependencies. Exceptionally low optical losses require control over film deposition, waveguide geometry, scattering, material stress and optical coupling. Integrating lasers and photodetectors adds further requirements, while packaging introduces mechanical and thermal effects capable of degrading the measurement itself.

Europe already possesses industrial capabilities relevant to this transition. Belgium’s imec has documented low-pressure chemical vapour deposition silicon-nitride processes on 200-millimetre wafers, including reported optical propagation losses of approximately 3 decibels per metre at 1,550 nanometres in research presented in 2025. On 13 March 2026, imec announced a collaboration with the Netherlands-based New Origin to transfer its silicon-nitride platform toward industrial manufacturing on 200-millimetre wafers. Switzerland’s LIGENTEC offers another specialised manufacturing route, with published high-Q resonator capabilities and dedicated silicon-nitride foundry services.

These developments establish that the relevant manufacturing ecosystem extends beyond university laboratories. They do not establish that commercial foundries can reproduce the October 2026 Brillouin gyroscope at economically acceptable production yields, much less manufacture a fully qualified inertial unit. Optical propagation loss, resonator quality, gyro bias instability and finished-product yield are different measures of industrial capability.

The geometry itself illustrates the cost problem. A 24-millimetre circular sensing ring encloses approximately 452 square millimetres, a substantial physical area for an integrated photonic structure. Even before accounting for support circuits, wafer-edge exclusion, fabrication defects and packaging, that footprint constrains how many sensing elements can be produced from a wafer. A three-axis inertial system introduces further integration and calibration requirements.

The decisive manufacturing figure will therefore not be the cost of patterning a waveguide, but the cost per qualified instrument after active-component integration, testing, rejection of nonconforming units and environmental assurance. This is where established aerospace suppliers retain an advantage. Honeywell, Safran Electronics & Defense, Exail and Northrop Grumman’s LITEF organisation possess industrial experience in complete inertial equipment, while photonic foundries provide enabling manufacturing capabilities. The commercial outcome may depend more on the integration of these competencies than on the emergence of an entirely new class of standalone semiconductor supplier.

Satellite interference is turning inertial precision into an infrastructure question
The demand for resilient navigation is already visible in institutional decisions rather than confined to defence technology forecasts. On 3 July 2026, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency updated its Safety Information Bulletin 2022-02 to Revision 4, strengthening guidance concerning GNSS outages, jamming, spoofing and the procedures needed to manage navigation degradation. The Federal Aviation Administration has likewise documented the effects of interference on satellite navigation, flight-management information and systems dependent on trusted position data.

The underlying vulnerability concerns the difference between losing an external reference and accepting a corrupted one. During GNSS jamming, an inertial navigation system can continue estimating movement from onboard measurements, although its uncertainty increases with time. During spoofing, a receiver may supply plausible but false information, potentially contaminating the navigation estimate if external updates are accepted without appropriate integrity checks. Better gyroscopes can improve the quality of independent angular-motion information, but they cannot independently authenticate a satellite signal or eliminate errors arising from accelerometers and other system components.

This distinction explains why the European Space Agency’s current navigation programmes favour combinations of technologies rather than a single substitute for GNSS. Its SPARTA project, initiated on 2 March 2026 and led by Italy’s WAY4WARD with SWHARD as subcontractor, combines multi-constellation GNSS, spoofing detection, inertial measurements, 5G positioning and vision-based navigation for unmanned aircraft. The programme identifies progression toward technology-readiness level 7 or higher as an objective, not a completed achievement. ESA’s PASQUALE project, launched on 25 March 2026, investigates a hybrid navigation architecture incorporating a cold-atom quantum accelerometer.

The policy implications extend beyond aircraft. The United Kingdom’s published PNT assessments estimate economic impacts of £1.42 billion from a 24-hour GNSS disruption and £7.64 billion from a seven-day disruption. Those figures do not represent losses that photonic gyroscopes alone could prevent: telecommunications and financial infrastructure, for example, also require timing capabilities that an angular-rate sensor cannot provide. They do establish why navigation resilience has become an industrial and economic-security concern, demanding complementary inertial, timing and positioning technologies.

Europe has the capabilities, but not yet a unified industrial route
The United States’ October 2026 research result demonstrates a collaboration between Caltech, UC Santa Barbara and the Air Force Research Laboratory that brings advanced optical science into direct contact with defence-relevant sensor development. China is also active in integrated optical gyroscope research: a 2023 study published in Chinese Physics B examined a simulated hybrid architecture incorporating silicon-nitride resonators and lithium-niobate modulation, while a 2025 review involving Beihang University researchers assessed several integrated photonic approaches. These publications establish research participation, not equivalent qualified industrial capability.

Europe’s position is more differentiated than either a declaration of technological dependence or an assertion of collective leadership would suggest. France has an established precision-inertial industrial base, including Exail and Safran Electronics & Defense. Germany contributes relevant capabilities in optics, electronics, metrology and inertial-system engineering, including LITEF. Italy participates in integrated resilient-navigation development through SPARTA and hosts the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre facility at Ispra, relevant to complementary PNT assessment. The United Kingdom has a National PNT Office and an institutional framework connecting positioning and timing resilience with critical-infrastructure protection.

The bilateral dimension is equally significant. On 10 July 2025, the United Kingdom and France announced closer cooperation on navigation and timing technologies intended to protect critical infrastructure from hostile interference. The agreement illustrates how navigation resilience is entering intergovernmental industrial and security cooperation, although it does not establish a joint programme to develop the October 2026 Brillouin architecture.

The European constraint is thus not an absence of scientific or industrial capabilities. It is the need to connect low-loss photonic fabrication, laser integration, precision packaging, calibration, environmental qualification and complete navigation-system engineering. Imec’s March 2026 manufacturing collaboration addresses one part of that chain; SPARTA and PASQUALE address different elements of resilient navigation. None alone delivers the qualified photonic inertial system whose development would alter procurement decisions.

The choice for European institutions is consequently between treating these activities as separate research achievements and constructing a manufacturing and testing ecosystem capable of evaluating competing technologies under comparable conditions. The latter would support optical, MEMS and quantum approaches without requiring policymakers to select a single technological winner before the evidence exists.

Export rules may constrain the technology precisely as it becomes commercially useful
The dual-use character of inertial technology creates an additional tension between commercial diffusion and national-security regulation. European Regulation (EU) 2021/821 establishes the framework governing dual-use exports, while Category 7 of the relevant control lists covers navigation and avionics equipment, including specified gyroscopes, angular-rate sensors and inertial systems. The United States maintains corresponding controls through the Export Administration Regulations and the Commerce Control List.

These frameworks matter because regulatory classification depends on the characteristics of the finished technology, not simply its origin in civilian photonics research. European technical criteria for certain controlled gyroscopes include demanding thresholds involving bias stability, angle random walk and angular-rate capability. Consequently, the same improvements that could make integrated photonic devices commercially competitive may also require closer examination of export classification, technology-transfer arrangements and supply-chain compliance.

This creates a structural problem for manufacturers. Access to international photonic foundries, specialised laser suppliers and advanced packaging partners may be important for achieving economic scale, while some high-performance applications introduce additional regulatory obligations. Restrictions that are insufficiently specific could burden legitimate civilian optical manufacturing, whereas classifications that fail to reflect actual inertial performance could overlook relevant dual-use capabilities.

The answer is not to assume that every silicon-nitride circuit constitutes sensitive navigation technology. It is to distinguish the passive photonic component, the integrated sensing device, the calibrated inertial unit and the complete navigation system, applying the relevant legal definitions to each. Industrial policy and export-control policy will increasingly intersect at precisely the point where experimental optical devices become reproducible commercial products.

The next 24 months will reward qualification, not another headline record
Between October 2026 and October 2028, the most consequential developments will be those that determine whether integrated Brillouin gyroscopes can progress beyond their current laboratory configuration. Independent measurements of long-duration bias instability, suppression of unwanted optical backscattering, stable laser and detector integration, repeatable packaging and multi-device manufacturing statistics would materially change the assessment. A further reduction in the minimum detectable sinusoidal rotation, without corresponding improvement in calibrated stability, would be scientifically interesting but insufficient to establish a navigation-market breakthrough.

For the United States, the Caltech–UCSB–AFRL research provides a basis for further precision-sensing development, but not a justification for treating the device as a deployable military capability. For European institutions, the imec–New Origin industrial collaboration and ESA’s SPARTA and PASQUALE programmes create opportunities to connect manufacturing and system-level navigation research, provided that future investment remains tied to reproducible performance. For incumbent suppliers, the question is whether integrated photonics will become a complementary technology, a component acquired through partnerships or a source of direct competition in selected product categories.

The cost of inaction will fall differently across these groups. Photonic manufacturers that cannot demonstrate qualified yield will remain suppliers of research components rather than precision-navigation systems. Aerospace and industrial integrators that fail to evaluate emerging architectures may face narrower future sourcing options, while governments that underinvest in independent PNT testing and complementary navigation capabilities will retain the economic and security exposures already identified in official assessments.

The October 2026 experiment has established that a semiconductor-compatible optical ring can detect exceptionally small controlled rotations. It has not established that such a ring can replace a qualified inertial instrument. Over the next 12–24 months, the industrial significance of the breakthrough will be measured by progress across that distinction: from a 37-degree-per-hour laboratory result to repeatable, calibrated and environmentally credible sensing hardware. The institutions that control that transition will capture the value; those that confuse publication performance with operational readiness will bear the development and procurement costs.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

In the soft gray light before dawn on the eighteenth of October 1859, the little engine house at the Harpers Ferry armory stood like a fortress in the middle of a town that had not slept. For two nights the building had been the last redoubt of John Brown and the remnant of his raiders. Outside, several thousand Virginia and Maryland militia and a growing crowd of townspeople kept uneasy watch. Inside, Brown, wounded and defiant, held a handful of hostages and what was left of his men, among them two of his own sons, one already dying.

The night before, Colonel Robert E. Lee had arrived by special train from Washington with ninety United States Marines. Lee was on leave from his cavalry regiment in Texas; the crisis had pulled him back. With him, serving as volunteer aide, was Lieutenant J.E.B. Stuart, a young cavalryman who had encountered Brown years earlier in the bitter days of “Bleeding Kansas.” Lee, knowing hostages were inside, had refused to risk a night attack. He waited for daylight.

At first light Stuart walked alone toward the engine house under a white flag, carrying Lee’s written demand for unconditional surrender. Brown opened the door only a few inches, his body braced against the crack, a cocked carbine in his hand. Stuart recognized him at once—“Ossawatomie” Brown. The old man listened, then began to bargain. He would surrender only if his men were allowed to escape. Stuart, cool and precise, repeated that no terms would be offered. The parley stretched on while hostages inside called out that they had not been harmed. At last Stuart stepped back from the door and raised his hat—the signal.

Three Marines swung sledgehammers against the heavy doors. One Marine fell mortally wounded as the entrance gave way. The rest poured through, bayonets fixed, ordered by Lee to use the bayonet only. Lieutenant Israel Greene, leading the assault, found Brown among the smoke and shouting. Greene’s saber stroke caught Brown across the neck and drove into his chest. In minutes it was finished. Two more of Brown’s men lay dead. The hostages—among them Colonel Lewis Washington, great-grandnephew of George Washington—walked out unhurt. Brown, bleeding heavily, was carried into the open. One of his sons, Oliver, had already died inside the building; another, Watson, would die the next day.

By mid-morning the armory was quiet again. Lee’s Marines held the prisoners under guard while the crowd outside called for hanging. Brown lived long enough to be tried in nearby Charles Town, convicted of treason against the Commonwealth of Virginia, and hanged on the second of December. The pikes he had stockpiled to arm an uprising were found unused. No slave revolt had risen. Yet the raid, brief and failed, had done its deeper work. In the North, Brown became a martyr. In the South, he became proof that the old order could be attacked by force. Within little more than a year the country was at war, and the two officers who had ended the standoff at the engine house—Lee and Stuart—would ride at the head of the very armies the raid had helped to make inevitable.

The brick walls of the engine house still stand above the confluence of the Potomac and the Shenandoah, a small building that for a few hours held the country’s future inside it.

text:
The History of the Guitar Amplifier Stack, 1961–2026

As concerts outgrew clubs, guitarists needed more power and speaker capacity. The full stack - a head above two independent 4×12 cabinets - evolved from earlier separate-head systems.

In 1961, Fender's Showman established a major American precedent. Its blonde piggyback head and separate cabinet, often JBL-equipped, became associated with Dick Dale. It established modular stage amplification, not a full stack.

In August 1964, Vox supplied John Lennon and George Harrison with AC100 Super De Luxe systems. Each used one tall cabinet containing four 12-inch Celestion speakers and two Goodmans Midax horns. It was a single enclosure, not two 4×12 cabinets.

Also in 1964, Norm and Conrad Sundholm developed powerful systems that evolved into Sunn amplification. Early Sunn designs drew on Dynaco tube technology; JBL-loaded cabinets and later Sunn guitar and bass heads became important on American stages.

Marshall established the classic format. Jim Marshall's JTM45 and 4×12 cabinets appeared in 1962. As concert demands grew, 100-watt heads and enormous single 8×12 cabinets followed in 1965. Their weight encouraged two separate cabinets: straight 1960B below angled 1960A, with the amplifier head on top.

Credit for the original giant cabinet is disputed. Pete Townshend encouraged larger rigs, but Ronnie Wood documented receiving a Marshall 100-watt head and 8×12 in September 1965, before The Who used theirs in November. Marshall commercialized the two-cabinet solution.

British competitors followed. Cliff Cooper introduced Orange equipment in 1968; Mat Mathias's Radio Craft workshop in Huddersfield built early Orange Matamp heads, paired with striking orange-covered speaker cabinets. David Reeves developed Hiwatt; around 1970, the 100-watt DR103 and Fane-equipped 4×12 cabinets became professional stage fixtures. Sound City and Laney offered further alternatives.

Four speakers share amplifier power in a 4×12. Two cabinets increase cone area and handling capacity; closed backs and speaker choice alter response and dispersion. The angled upper cabinet directs some sound upward. Additional cabinets do not increase the amplifier's electrical wattage, and the total speaker impedance must suit its output.

Marshall's 100-watt master-volume 2203 arrived in 1975, enabling substantial preamp distortion at lower output settings than earlier non-master-volume designs. The 1981 JCM800 series became a hard-rock and metal fixture. PA systems increasingly carried guitar sound; stacks also served a visual purpose.

In 1992, Mesa/Boogie's Dual Rectifier and Peavey's 120-watt 5150, developed with Eddie Van Halen, advanced high-gain amplification. Matching 4×12 cabinets remained central to their systems. The EVH 5150III followed in 2007, extending the lineage.

By 2026, load boxes, cabinet impulse responses, digital modeling, in-ear monitors and powerful PAs can replace or supplement physical stacks. Half stacks remain practical, while full stacks endure for speaker interaction and stage presentation. A solution to inadequate concert volume became one of rock music's defining designs.

A king can rule the world and remain a prisoner of ambition. A beggar can lie beneath the open sky and be utterly free.
