text:
🔴 The Second Testimony: His Job Was to “Keep Secrets” Until the Bombs Fell on the Office

The second installment in the series “Men Who Were True to Their Word” focuses on Seyyed Majid Tabatabaian.

https://t.co/wmOl5JzSz7 titles his story “The Fusion of Duty and Devotion.” This is no mere rhetorical flourish; it describes the work he performed for thirty-seven years serving in secrecy, remaining loyal in silence, and upholding his commitments far from the public eye.

💥 “Keeping Secrets” as a Profession (Beginning in 1989)

In 1989, he joined the security detail for the Supreme Leader, serving in a senior capacity. The term used in the accounts is not “security” or “guarding,” but rather “keeping secrets” (*ketman-e asrar*). In the context of Persian political life, this refers to individuals who possess the discernment to know what should be said, what should remain unsaid, and what must never be spoken of at all.

Thirty-seven years that is how long he held this post. While Abbas Sa’adabadi the driver held the steering wheel and followed a visible route, Tabatabaian’s work took place in the shadows. He remained unseen, unrecorded, and undiscussed. For thirty-seven years, his name was virtually absent from the public record, a testament to the success of his work.

For a senior official on a protection detail, the true measure of professional achievement is the extent of one’s absence from the historical record.

🎯 Why “Duty” and “Devotion” Must “Fuse”

The title employs a precise term: *emtezaj* a fusion, a blending, a synthesis. It is not merely “coexistence” or “balancing” two things; it is the merging of two distinct elements into a single, unified whole.

“Duty” (*vajeb*) implies a religious or legal obligation, a requirement to be fulfilled, for which one receives a reward. “Devotion” (*eshq* love/passion) is something irrational, incalculable, and offered without expectation of return.

The fusion of these two concepts describes a state where his work was simultaneously his professional obligation and his deepest personal desire. He remained at his post for thirty-seven years not because he was bound by a contract, but because he had no wish to leave.  The records state that he spent his life on a path defined by "secrecy, sacrifice, and loyalty." None of these three qualities can be forged through a mere employment relationship. Secrecy can be purchased, and sacrifice can be bought but loyalty cannot. Loyalty can only be given.

📜 February 28, 2026,  The Office

He met his martyrdom in the Leader’s office. The date was February 28, 2026, the first day of what the Americans and Israelis termed the "third imposed war."

On that same day, a girls' school in Minab was bombed, claiming the lives of at least 160 students and teachers. That same day, the war began. That same day, the first of 87 hospitals and clinics began to collapse.

He died in an office, not on the front lines. His post was not a combat position; his duty was to protect an individual. When the bombs fell near the office, he did not flee not because he was armed, and not because he had received orders to stay, but because for thirty-seven years, his place of work had been by that person’s side.

The records use a specific term: *barfiqatihi* (برفقته) "in his company." It is said that he "attained the medal of martyrdom while by the Leader’s side." In Persian, this term carries the dual meaning of "companionship" and "journeying together." He was not killed while trying to escape; he was at his post, at his workplace the very place he had gone to every single day for thirty-seven years.

⚔️ Why this series is being released now

https://t.co/wmOl5JzSz7 has brought the stories of these two men together in a single series: the first installment focuses on a driver, the second on an official tasked with maintaining secrecy. Two men, two different roles, yet the same ultimate fate.

The series is titled "Rijal Sadaqu" (رجال صدقوا)"Men who spoke the truth," or "Men who remained faithful to their pledge." The name is drawn from the Quran (Surah Al-Ahzab, 33:23): "Among the believers are men who have been true to the covenant they made with Allah."

The release of this series serves a single purpose: to strip away the cold, statistical nature of "martyrdom" as it appears in military reports, and to restore the reality of the human beings behind the numbers. It is not merely a matter of "4,000 dead."  He was “a driver who had spent thirty-seven years behind the wheel” and “an official who had kept a secret for thirty-seven years.” Numbers can be filed away; names cannot.

🔻 What was that “secret”?

The records do not state what secret he kept which is, by definition, the very nature of a secret.

Yet, one thing is certain: he knew the leader’s itinerary, the layout of the offices, the deployment of the security detail, and the identity of every individual who had entered that inner circle over the course of thirty-seven years. Had this information fallen into the hands of the enemy, it could have altered the course of the war. He did not let that happen. When the bombs fell, he remained in the office along with those secrets.

His life’s work consisted of all that he never spoke aloud. His martyrdom ensured that those things would remain with him, forever.

Long live the memory of the martyrs. Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
SHE THOUGHT SHE HAD WON A HOLIDAY. SHE ENDED UP WITH A LIFE SENTENCE IN CHINA.

In 2014, Dawn Michelle Hunt, an American woman and former flight attendant from Chicago, believed she had been offered an opportunity to travel to Hong Kong, mainland China and Australia. The trip was presented as a prize, with the organisers covering her expenses.

She had reservations about the offer, but after checking the company behind it, she believed it was legitimate.

For days, she enjoyed what appeared to be a generous holiday. Then came the designer handbags.

Her luggage was already full, so she accepted additional luggage from the organisers and packed the handbags inside. She had no reason to believe, according to her family’s account, that she was being drawn into a criminal operation.

At an airport in China, as she prepared to continue her journey to Australia, authorities searched her luggage. They discovered methamphetamine concealed inside the linings of the handbags.

Dawn was arrested.

In an instant, what she believed was a holiday became a nightmare that would consume more than a decade of her life.

Her family maintains that she was deceived and did not knowingly transport drugs. Chinese authorities convicted her of drug smuggling. After spending three years in detention awaiting trial, she was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve. Her sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment.

She has remained in Chinese custody ever since.

But the most heartbreaking part of this story is not only what happened to Dawn. It is what happened to the family she left behind.

A FATHER’S FINAL WISH

Dawn’s father, Gene Hunt, was a United States Army veteran and a retired Chicago Police sergeant who served for 32 years. He had spent his life working, serving others and taking care of his family.

Then came the ordeal of watching his daughter remain imprisoned thousands of miles away.

As the years passed, Gene’s health deteriorated. He battled prostate cancer and other medical problems while holding on to the hope that he would see Dawn return home.

Imagine being an ageing father who knows his daughter is alive but cannot reach her. Imagine celebrating another family occasion without her, wondering whether the next year will finally bring the reunion you have prayed for.

For Gene, this was not an abstract diplomatic dispute. It was personal. It was his daughter.

His final wish was to see her freed.

On January 25, 2026, Gene died at the age of 92.

Dawn was still in prison.

He never got to welcome his daughter home. She never got the chance to embrace him again, sit beside him in his final days or say goodbye in person.

A man who had served his country and spent decades protecting others died without the reunion he had longed for.

There is something profoundly painful about that ending. While governments exchange communications and legal processes continue, time does not stand still for families. Parents grow old. Health fails. People die.

And sometimes, the person they have spent years waiting for never arrives.

THE BROTHER WHO REFUSED TO LET THE WORLD FORGET

Dawn’s brother, Tim Hunt, has spent years fighting to bring her home.

He has written hundreds of letters to officials and lawyers, appealed to the American government, spoken to the media and continued to pursue diplomatic intervention.

In September 2024, he testified before the U.S. Congressional-Executive Commission on China, describing his sister’s case and the toll it had taken on their family.

He has also travelled to China to visit Dawn. In a September 2026 interview with NBC Chicago, Tim described the deterioration he had witnessed in her physical appearance and health.

Behind every public appeal is a brother who has had to watch his sister’s life slip away, year after year, while searching for the right person or institution capable of changing her circumstances.

And after their father’s death, the fight became even more personal.

My advice; find it in your heart, to reconsider your decision to contest the January 2027 presidential election, but instead let Nigerians chose someone who can help restore peace, security and stability that will help save this country from sliding into a failed state.

You have failed and I dare say it’s evil and wicked of you to ask Nigerians to give you another chance, when the one that produced you under questionable circumstances have put the country in dire circumstances than ever imagined. 

In case the sycophants surrounding you have not told you; Nigerians have made up their mind to stand against any attempt to subvert their will this time and will go to any lengths to defend their votes and confront headlong any attempt to have a repeat of the 2023 elections, especially the presidency. Going by the people’s reaction and events witnessed so far; it won’t be wrong to assume that even the gods have rejected you.

October 16 Feast of the Purity of Our Lady: What the Virgin Mother Has Said About Sexual Sin.
.
God has sent His leading Ambassadress, Mary, the Mother of His Son, Jesus Christ, time and time again to beg the world to come back to the values of life. These values once protected us from the evils now at hand. This is especially true concerning the sins of the flesh and fornication.
.
At Fatima in Portugal nearly a hundred years ago, Mary spoke to Blessed Jacinta and said:
.
More souls go to hell because of sins of the flesh than for any other reason.
Certain fashions will be introduced that will offend Our Lord very much.
.
Many marriages are not good; they do not please Our Lord and are not of God.
.
But it was years later in an apparition that is little known in the United States, that Mary was at her most revealing concerning purity of body and heart. It was then when she came as Our Lady of America to a young nun in the 1950's to proclaim the United States as God's instrument in bringing a revival of purity and love to the world.
.
I wish it to be the country dedicated to my purity. I desire that they be the children of my pure Heart. I desire through my children of America to further the cause of faith and purity among people and nations. Cleanse your souls in the precious Blood of My Son. Be my army of chaste soldiers, ready to fight to the death to preserve the purity of your souls." (Our Lady Of America)
.
It's hard to believe that Mary would choose the United States as her vessel for purity, considering that America is responsible for the spread of sexually transmitted diseases, abortion, fornication, pornography and other evils that have so captured the imaginations of the world. But God is calling the USA to come back to the roots of Biblical holiness that used to mark us as a nation:
Let them come with confidence and simplicity, and I, their Mother, will teach them to become pure like to my Heart that their own hearts may be more pleasing to the Heart of my Son." (Our Lady of America)
.
To bring this needed revival, we must do three things:
.
1) Pray the Rosary every day, along with the special Nine Days Prayer to the Holy Martyrs for our people to turn in disgust from sins of the flesh to purity of heart.
.
2) Wear the Brown Scapular as a sign of our consecration to the Precious Blood of Jesus for purity of heart, soul and body.
.
3) Offer up to God, in the view of the Cross, all of our sufferings no matter how large or small. We are especially called to do this through fasting and almsgiving.
.
How Can Such Small Actions Save the Body of Christ ?
.
Many times it is the little things we do that make all the difference.
.
Remember the story of Naaman the Syrian Leper?
.
2 Kings 5:
.
[1] Naaman, general of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable: for by him the Lord gave deliverance to Syria: and he was a valiant man and rich, but a leper. [2] Now there had gone out robbers from Syria, and had led away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid, and she waited upon Naaman's wife. [3] And she said to her mistress: I wish my master had been with the prophet, that is in Samaria: he would certainly have healed him of the leprosy which he hath. [4] Then Naaman went in to his lord, and told him, saying: Thus and thus said tile girl from the land of Israel. [5] And the king of Syria sad to him: Go, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel. And he departed, and took with him ten talents of silver, and six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of raiment, [6] And brought the letter to the king of Israel, in these words: When thou shalt receive this letter, know that I have sent to thee Naaman my servant, that thou mayest heal him of his leprosy. [7] And when the king of Israel had read the letter, he rent his garments, and said: Am I God, to be able to kill and give life, that this man hath sent to me, to heal a man of his leprosy? mark, and see how he seeketh occasions against me. [8] And when Eliseus the man of God had heard this, to wit, that the king of Israel had rent his garments, he sent to him, saying: Why hast thou rent thy garments? let him come to me, and let him know that there is a prophet in Israel. [9] So Naaman came with his horses and chariots, and stood at the door of the house of Eliseus: [10] And Eliseus sent a messenger to him, saying: Go, and wash seven times in the Jordan, and thy flesh shall recover health, and thou shalt be clean.[11] Naaman was angry and went away, saying: I thought he would have come out to me, and standing would hare invoked the name of the Lord his God, and touched with his hand the place of the leprosy, and healed me. [12] Are not the Abana, and the Pharphar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel, that I may wash in them, and be made clean? So as he turned, and was going away with indignation, [13] His servants came to him, and said to him: Father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, surely thou shouldst have done it: how much rather what he now hath said to thee: Wash, and thou shalt he clean? [14] Then he went down, and washed in the Jordan seven times: according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored, like the flesh of a little child, and he was made clean.
.
Mary is saying the same thing to us: Come to the Blood of Jesus. Wear the sign of it's power on your bodies in the Scapular. Let the Word of the Blood wash your minds and emotions clean through the Holy Rosary. Give your spirits to God through the sacrifice of your daily lives on the Cross with Jesus.
.
If everyone were willing to do these things in faith, the entire country would be transformed. Why? Because faith works by love and the sacrificial love that is willing to do little things prepares us for the bigger things we can do in this life and the next.

🇬🇧 WHO PROTECTS THE MEN WHO PROTECT BRITAIN?

🚨 Five SAS soldiers. One mission against ISIS. Three years under suspicion of murder. Not a single charge.

In July 2022, Britain’s elite Special Air Service deployed into the darkness of Syria to capture an ISIS terrorist leader.

They came under fire. They made split-second decisions. Two men were killed.

An initial review found the soldiers had acted in self-defence.

What happened next is a national disgrace.

Five SAS operators were arrested on suspicion of murder. Their homes were raided. They faced the possibility of life imprisonment.

And just 48 hours after questioning, these same soldiers were sent straight back into the Syrian warzone to continue fighting ISIS.

Apparently, they were trusted enough to risk their lives for Britain — but not enough to be spared years of legal uncertainty.

For three years, the threat of prosecution hung over them. Eventually, no charges were brought. Yet the possibility of reopening the investigation remained.

All five have since left the Army.

Let that sink in.

Britain trains some of the finest Special Forces operators in the world. We send them into places most politicians would never dare set foot. We expect them to confront terrorists, make impossible decisions in seconds and protect our national security.

And when they come home, what do we offer them?

Police investigations. Legal uncertainty. Financial burdens. And years of their lives spent defending decisions made under enemy fire.

Accountability is essential. But accountability must never become persecution by process.

From Syria to the investigations involving Northern Ireland veterans, Britain must ask itself a deeply uncomfortable question:

Why are we so willing to send our soldiers into danger, yet so reluctant to stand behind them afterwards?

Our enemies are watching. So are the next generation of men and women considering military service.

The SAS motto is Who Dares Wins.

Perhaps Westminster should remember another principle:

THOSE WHO SERVE BRITAIN DESERVE JUSTICE, FAIRNESS AND THE FULL SUPPORT OF THE NATION THEY DEFEND.

🇬🇧 Stand with your soldiers. Stand with your veterans. Stand with the SAS.

An extraordinary investigation by The Sunday Times today. Every British citizen should read it.

Nicole Amor’s unit was moved to Port Shuaiba, a potential Iranian target identified by Army intelligence. The unit’s commander had been briefed on that threat and rejected alternative locations.

Survivors said the site lacked effective drone defenses. Concrete barriers offered some protection from the sides, but their workspace had a tin roof and no protection from above. 

An Iranian drone struck on March 1, killing six soldiers, including Nicole, and wounding more than 20.

Hegseth described a weapon slipping through defenses and hitting a fortified position. 

Survivors directly disputed that account: “It was not a fortified position.”

That’s why her husband is demanding accountability. He wants to know why those soldiers were placed there despite the warnings, and who will answer for the failures that left them exposed.

text:
It was the first time she could remember him being genuinely angry with her over something she had believed would make him proud.
She hadn't understood it then.
Even after Voldemort returned, when the family's old allegiances became dangerous obligations once more, she struggled to reconcile that conversation with the father who had spent her childhood indulging nearly every request she made. Perhaps Lucius had recognized something in her behavior that she herself had not yet understood. Perhaps he had simply been frightened of what might happen if the Dark Lord learned that his most famous enemy had become important to a Malfoy.
Whatever the reason, that afternoon marked the beginning of a distance between them that neither seemed to know how to close.
The following months had only made matters more complicated.
Draceana remembered the Second Task of the Triwizard Tournament with particular embarrassment. One moment, she had been going about her ordinary business at Hogwarts; the next thing she clearly remembered was waking near the shore of the Black Lake, soaking wet and shivering beneath a blanket while several people fussed over her. Professor McGonagall had subsequently explained that the champions' loved ones had been placed under an enchantment and taken beneath the lake as part of the competition.
And somehow, among all the people Harry Potter might have been expected to rescue, the organizers had chosen her.
Draceana had been furious when she learned about it.
Surely there had been some mistake. Potter had friends, after all. He had that Weasley boy practically attached to his side, not to mention Granger, who seemed incapable of allowing him to make a decision without first expressing her opinion. Why in Merlin's name would anyone decide that she was someone precious enough to Potter to be used in such a task?
Naturally, she had demanded an explanation.
Harry hadn't been able to give her one.
He had looked nearly as bewildered as she felt, which was hardly reassuring. The whole affair became even more intolerable when students began whispering about the Yule Ball and the Black Lake as though the two events proved something neither of them was willing to acknowledge.
Draceana had responded in the only manner she knew. She insulted Potter, accused the tournament officials of incompetence, and insisted that the entire situation was a ridiculous misunderstanding.
Yet she remembered something else from that day.
Harry had emerged from the water holding her, despite the exhaustion written across his face, and had remained nearby until he was certain she was all right. Even after she began complaining, he had seemed more relieved than offended.
That memory had troubled her far longer than she cared to admit.
Then came the Third Task.
Cedric Diggory died, and the Dark Lord returned.
Draceana remembered the fear that spread through Hogwarts as the news slowly became known, the arguments that followed, and the uncomfortable atmosphere that settled over the school. Her father's warnings, once so difficult to understand, suddenly acquired a terrible meaning. Lucius had spoken of the Dark Lord's return for years, and now the man whose name had once been whispered only in private was gathering his followers again.
Harry Potter stood at the center of it all.
She remembered seeing him after Cedric's death, sitting alone with his shoulders hunched and his eyes red from crying. He looked nothing like the infuriating boy who had argued with her during their dance rehearsals, nor the determined Seeker who always seemed capable of finding some way to win. For a while, Draceana had simply stood there, uncertain whether she should approach him. She had never been particularly skilled at comforting people, especially someone who had spent years giving her every reason to dislike him.
Nevertheless, she sat beside him.
When Harry finally broke down, she had drawn him into her arms and allowed him to cry against her shoulder. She remembered his hands clutching the fabric of her robes and the way his breathing gradually settled as the minutes passed. She said very little. There was nothing she could think of saying that would make Cedric Diggory's death any less terrible.
So she held him until he was ready to let go.
Looking back, Draceana wondered what her father would have said if he had seen them together that night.
By their fifth year, the distance between her and Harry had grown considerably. Hogwarts was no longer the familiar place where their greatest concerns involved Quidditch, examinations, and embarrassing each other in front of their classmates. The Ministry refused to acknowledge Voldemort's return, Dolores Umbridge tightened her control over the school, and students increasingly found themselves choosing sides in arguments that extended far beyond the castle walls.
Draceana joined the Inquisitorial Squad.
It was what everyone expected of her, and she had initially taken some satisfaction in the authority it gave her. She could scarcely imagine a more convenient opportunity to make Potter's life difficult.
Yet whenever Umbridge discussed ways to discover where his secret organization was meeting, Draceana found herself listening with considerably more attention than necessary. Occasionally, Harry would encounter her in a corridor and receive some cutting remark about the foolishness of wandering near a particular staircase after curfew. At other times, she would loudly inform him that even an idiot ought to know which passages were being watched.
Harry generally responded with suspicion or irritation.
She considered that preferable to gratitude.
Her little warnings had never been enough to prevent the eventual discovery of Dumbledore's Army. As the year drew toward its conclusion, events moved with a speed that left Draceana increasingly uncertain of what was happening beyond Hogwarts.
Then her father was arrested.
The Ministry finally acknowledged that Voldemort had returned, and Lucius Malfoy's position among the Dark Lord's followers could no longer be concealed.
Draceana remembered very little about the confusion surrounding those final days. There had been hurried conversations, frightened servants, and her mother's attempts to learn precisely what had happened at the Department of Mysteries. For the first time in her life, she saw people who had once treated the Malfoy family with great respect suddenly become reluctant to associate with them.
But none of those memories troubled her as much as the last confrontation with her father.
She could still see Lucius's face.
The same father who had bought her everything she pointed toward in Diagon Alley, who had watched her first attempts at flying with barely concealed pride, and who had affectionately called her his little princess whenever she came running into his study.
He had always seemed so certain of himself.
So proud of his family.
And now, faced with the collapse of everything he had worked to preserve, he looked at his own daughter with an anger she had never imagined him directing toward her.
He spoke of the disgrace brought upon their name, of the danger facing Narcissa and Draceana, and of Harry Potter's growing influence over her. His words came faster than she could answer, each accusation cutting into the confidence she had spent her entire life building.
She remembered trying to explain herself.
Trying to remind him that she was still his daughter.
That she had never intended to disappoint him.
But he was no longer listening.
And then he said it.
"I wish you had been born a son instead."
Draceana had never forgotten those words.
She remembered staring at her father, waiting for him to take them back, waiting for the familiar expression of affection to return to his face. Surely he hadn't meant it. Surely the man who had always called her his precious daughter would realize what he had just said.
But there had been no time for another conversation.
Lucius Malfoy was taken away, and those became the last words she heard from him before his imprisonment.
In the quiet of her bedroom, Draceana continued staring toward the darkened windows. Her expression remained unchanged, although the tear that had slipped down her cheek earlier had long since dried.
She had spent most of her life trying to become the daughter her father wanted.
And when she finally began to understand what she wanted for herself, everything seemed to fall apart.
Draceana slowly raised her right arm, allowing the loose sleeve of her nightdress to slip toward her elbow. There, etched into her pale skin, was the hideous image of a skull with a serpent emerging from its mouth. She stared at it for a moment before giving her arm a sudden, irritated shake, as though the movement alone might be enough to dislodge the mark and send it tumbling to the floor.
Of course, it remained exactly where it was.
She remembered the day it had appeared with a clarity that made her fingers tremble.
It was during the summer before her sixth year, when Malfoy Manor was still struggling to recover from the disgrace of her father's imprisonment. Lucius had barely been taken away when the Dark Lord himself arrived at the estate, accompanied by several of his followers. The servants had been ordered to disappear, the doors to the drawing room were shut, and Narcissa had hurried her daughter downstairs without offering much explanation.
Draceana had heard stories about Lord Voldemort all her life. Her father had spoken of him with reverence, describing a wizard of extraordinary power who would one day restore the proper order of the magical world. To her younger self, those stories had sounded almost magnificent, particularly when Lucius spoke of the influence their family would possess once the Dark Lord returned to power.
The creature seated before her that evening bore little resemblance to the figure she had imagined.
He occupied her father's favorite chair as though the entire manor already belonged to him, his long, pale fingers resting upon its armrests while his red eyes examined the two witches kneeling at his feet. His face was unnaturally white, with narrow slits where his nose should have been, and whenever he spoke, his voice seemed to creep into every corner of the room. Draceana had never known silence could feel so oppressive. She could hear her own heartbeat, the faint movement of her mother's robes beside her, and the occasional delighted breathing of her Aunt Bellatrix, who stood near the Dark Lord's chair.
"Lucius has disappointed me."
Voldemort spoke quietly, yet Draceana felt the words settle over her like a weight.
"After everything I entrusted to him, after all the opportunities I so generously provided, he managed to accomplish nothing. Worse still, his incompetence has cost me several valuable servants."
Draceana kept her head lowered. Her mother had instructed her not to speak unless addressed, and for once in her life, she had no intention of disobeying.
"I wonder," Voldemort continued, examining his pale fingers, "what punishment would be appropriate for such a failure."
Narcissa moved beside her.
"My Lord," she began carefully, "my husband has always been devoted to your cause. Whatever punishment you deem necessary, I beg you to allow me to bear it in his place."
Voldemort turned his head toward her.
"How touching."
Narcissa bowed lower.
"Please, my Lord. My daughter has done nothing to deserve your displeasure. She is still young. If you require someone to answer for Lucius's failure, then let it be me."
Draceana remembered glancing toward her mother in astonishment. Narcissa Malfoy, the woman who had taught her never to lower her head before anyone unworthy of her respect, was kneeling upon the drawing-room floor and begging.
And the Dark Lord seemed amused.
"Your devotion to your family is admirable, Narcissa. Unfortunately, I have little interest in punishing you."
His gaze shifted toward Draceana.
"Your daughter, however..."
Draceana felt herself grow cold.
Me?
Voldemort rose from the chair. His movements were almost leisurely as he approached, and Draceana found herself shrinking beneath the shadow that fell across her. She wanted to look away, to close her eyes, to do anything that might remove her from the attention of those terrible red pupils, but her body refused to move.
"Look at me, child."
She obeyed.
"Yes," he murmured, studying her face. "The daughter of Lucius Malfoy. The heiress to one of the oldest and most distinguished families in our world."
A thin smile crossed his face.
"Perhaps you will prove more useful than your father."
Draceana could scarcely breathe.
So this is him...
Harry had stood before this man.
Harry had faced him in the graveyard where Cedric Diggory died, and somehow he had returned to Hogwarts alive. Until that moment, Draceana had never truly understood what that meant. She had heard the rumors, listened to the arguments, and watched Potter insist that the Dark Lord had returned, but none of those things had prepared her for the being standing before her now.
She couldn't imagine raising her wand against him.
She couldn't even imagine standing.
"My Lord, please," Narcissa pleaded again. "Draceana is only sixteen. She—"
"Enough."
Narcissa fell silent.
Voldemort extended one hand.
"Your arm."
Draceana hesitated.
Bellatrix's delighted laughter came from somewhere behind him.
"Go on, dear niece. The Dark Lord has given you an order."
Draceana slowly offered her right arm. Her hand was trembling so badly that she could barely keep it raised.
Voldemort took hold of her wrist.
Then came the pain.
It began beneath her skin, a terrible heat that spread from her forearm toward her shoulder. Draceana screamed and tried to pull away, but his grip remained firm. She could feel something moving through her flesh, twisting and burning as though a red-hot iron were being pressed directly against her bones. Her free hand clawed at the carpet while tears streamed down her cheeks.
Beside her, Narcissa cried out.
"Please! My Lord, please stop!"
Bellatrix laughed louder.
And when Voldemort finally released her wrist, Draceana collapsed forward, clutching her arm against her chest. Through her tears, she saw the black image slowly settling into her skin.
A skull.
A serpent.
The Dark Mark.
Voldemort returned to his chair while Draceana struggled to regain her breath.
"There," he said pleasantly. "A proper servant of the Dark Lord."
Narcissa immediately gathered her daughter into her arms, holding her trembling body close. Draceana could feel her mother's fingers brushing through her hair, could hear her whispering reassurances against the side of her head, but the words scarcely registered.
She kept staring at her arm.
Her father had always spoken of serving the Dark Lord as an honor.
Draceana had never felt less honored in her life.
"Now," Voldemort continued, "let us discuss how you will redeem your family's unfortunate reputation."
Draceana slowly lifted her head.
"You will return to Hogwarts as usual. There, you will complete two tasks for me. First, you will find a means of admitting my followers into the castle without attracting the attention of its defenders."
He paused, apparently enjoying the uncertainty spreading across her face.
"And when the opportunity presents itself, you will kill Albus Dumbledore."
Draceana stared at him.
What?
Dumbledore?
The headmaster of Hogwarts? The wizard whom even her father had spoken about with grudging respect? The man widely regarded as one of the most powerful wizards alive?
How could a sixth-year student possibly kill someone like him?
For one fleeting moment, she wondered whether the Dark Lord had made some terrible mistake.
Voldemort's smile widened.
"By any means necessary, of course."
Draceana lowered her eyes.
There was no point asking whether he was serious. The mark still burning upon her arm answered that question well enough.
"Fortunately," Voldemort continued, "you will not be entirely without assistance."
He gestured toward a figure standing quietly beside the fireplace.
The man stepped forward and lowered his hood.
Draceana recognized him immediately.
"Professor Snape...?"
Severus Snape regarded her with the same unreadable expression he wore during his lessons at Hogwarts. His black eyes briefly settled upon her trembling form before he inclined his head toward the Dark Lord.
"Severus has proven himself most useful to me," Voldemort explained. "You would do well to heed his guidance."
Snape said nothing.
Draceana couldn't bring herself to ask why one of her professors was standing in her family's drawing room beside Lord Voldemort, nor why he seemed perfectly comfortable in the company of Death Eaters. Her thoughts were too scattered, her arm still burned, and her mother's grip around her shoulders had grown painfully tight.
All she understood was that her life no longer belonged to her.
The Dark Lord had given her an impossible task, and whether she succeeded or failed, she doubted that she would ever be free of him.
Draceana lowered her arm.
The memory faded, leaving her once again in the quiet of her bedroom, where the Dark Mark rested against her skin as though it had always been there. She stared at it for another moment before pulling her sleeve back into place.
What followed that summer had been a miserable collection of failed plans, sleepless nights, and increasingly desperate attempts to accomplish the task she had been given. The cursed necklace, the poisoned mead, the endless hours spent trying to repair the Vanishing Cabinet. With every failure, she imagined the Dark Lord returning to the manor, imagined her mother kneeling before him again, and wondered how much longer he would tolerate her incompetence.
She had wanted to tell someone.
There had been nights when she nearly approached Professor Snape, although she couldn't bring herself to trust him completely. On other occasions, she considered speaking to Professor Dumbledore, only to remember the order hanging over her head and the punishment her family would face if she failed.
And sometimes, when she happened to see a certain untidy-haired Gryffindor passing through the corridors, she found herself wanting to call his name.
Harry Potter.
The boy who had faced the Dark Lord and survived.
The boy who had once offered her his coat during a cold winter evening.
Surely, if anyone could understand how frightened she was, it would be him.
But what would he think if he discovered the mark on her arm? What would he say if she confessed that she had been ordered to murder Dumbledore? She had spent years insulting his friends and mocking the very things he believed in. Even if he listened, what reason would he have to trust her?
Draceana had never found the courage to ask.
And then, one morning, he appeared in the girls' bathroom.
She remembered his voice, the accusation in his eyes, and the terrible instant when he noticed her sleeve slipping down her arm. She remembered raising her wand, frightened and furious, and the unfamiliar word that escaped his lips a moment later.
After that, there was only pain.
Draceana remained seated against her pillows, staring at the fading sunlight. She wondered which part of her life had become the most unbearable. Perhaps it was the knowledge that her childhood home was no longer truly hers. The halls where she had once run freely, the drawing room where her father used to entertain his guests, even the gardens beyond her window had all fallen beneath the Dark Lord's shadow. His presence seemed to linger everywhere, suffocating and oppressive, until the enormous manor felt little different from a beautifully furnished cage.
Or perhaps it was the impossible task he had forced upon her, one she had been expected to accomplish under the threat of death to herself and her family. She had spent nearly an entire school year trying to find some way out, only to discover that every failure brought her closer to the punishment she feared. Then there was her father, the man she had adored since childhood, who had once bought her everything she wanted and called her his precious daughter. She could still hear his final words, spoken with such bitterness that she sometimes wondered whether he had meant them all along. How could she forget being told that the father she loved would have preferred a son?
But perhaps the cruelest thing of all was… The boy…
The boy she had spent years chasing through school corridors, arguing over the smallest things, and secretly looking forward to seeing every morning. The boy who had danced with her beneath the glittering chandeliers, lent her his coat on a cold winter night, and allowed her to hold him when he could no longer contain his grief. Somewhere along the way, those countless little moments had become precious to her. She understood that now, when remembering them was all she could do.
I fell in lo—
Draceana lowered her gaze.
Even now, she couldn't bring herself to finish it.
The very same boy had raised his wand against her and struck her down.
She slowly looked toward the window, where her faint reflection stared back at her in the dying sunlight. The girl she saw looked nothing like the proud young heiress who used to announce her family name as though it were the most important thing in the world. She had spent her childhood believing that a Malfoy could endure anything, yet after everything that had happened, she could scarcely remember what that confidence had felt like. Her father had rejected her, the Dark Lord held her family's lives in his hands, and the one person she had secretly hoped might understand her had nearly killed her.
Now, after everything that had happened, she could scarcely remember what that pride had felt like. Even the anger that had once come so naturally whenever someone dared insult her seemed to have deserted her. She had no desire to argue, no strength left to fight, and nothing she could think of that might return her life to the way it had been.
For the first time, Draceana Malfoy felt as though she had lost everything.
Draceana slowly pushed aside the blanket.
Her bare feet touched the cool floor as she rose from the bed, steadying herself against one of the carved wooden posts. The healers had advised her to avoid unnecessary exertion, but she found herself unwilling to spend another evening staring at the same view from her pillows. She crossed the room in slow, measured steps, one hand resting lightly against her abdomen whenever the movement pulled at the scars beneath her nightdress.
By the time she reached the windows, the last remnants of sunlight were disappearing beyond the distant woods.
She placed her fingertips against the glass.
It was cold.
From here, she could see the gardens where she had played as a child, the paths she used to follow while her father accompanied her on evening walks, and the distant gates beyond which the rest of the world continued without her. Everything looked exactly as she remembered. The hedgerows were neatly trimmed, the fountains continued flowing, and the great iron gates stood proudly at the edge of the estate.
Draceana wondered how much longer any of it would remain.
Her father's words returned to her, followed by the Dark Lord's terrible smile and the sight of Harry raising his wand.
If I could go back...
She had heard of Time-Turners, of course. There had been rumors about the Ministry possessing devices capable of allowing a witch or wizard to revisit the past, although she knew that such magic was dangerous and heavily restricted.
Still, she couldn't help wondering.
If she could return to that morning, would she have found the courage to tell Harry everything? Would she have lowered her wand and asked him to listen? Perhaps he would have believed

Our #NavratriAcrossBharat series now takes us to Konkan, the beautiful coastal region of western Bharat, where Navratri is celebrated through distinctive traditions that honour the Divine Mother, womanhood and the blessings of nature.

One of Konkan's cherished traditions is Suvasini Puja, in which married women are honoured as embodiments of Sumangali. Women invite other married women into their homes, offer Haldi Kumkum, bangles, betel nuts, garments and other auspicious gifts, and come together for a traditional meal. This beautiful custom reflects the importance of honouring feminine divinity in everyday life.

In Goa, at the heart of the Konkan region, temples celebrate the fascinating Makharotsav. The deity is placed on an elaborately decorated ceremonial swing and gently rocked amid devotional music, prayers and aarti. Another meaningful tradition in Konkani households is Nave Jevan, when food prepared from the newly harvested grain is first offered to the Divine before being shared by the family.

@anuradhagoyal  explores how Konkan's Navratri traditions bring together reverence for women, temple rituals, community bonds and gratitude for nature's abundance. Stay tuned as we continue discovering the remarkable Navratri traditions across Bharat!

text:
Daf Yomi Bekhorot 26b: Laws the Torah Entrusted to the Sages

The Mishnah in Bekhorot (26b) discusses the obligation of an Israelite who owns a firstborn kosher animal to care for it before giving it to a Kohen. The Mishnah distinguishes between smaller animals, such as sheep and goats, which must be cared for for thirty days, and larger animals, such as cattle, which require fifty days.

The Talmud seeks the biblical basis for these requirements, drawing upon the verses that address the treatment of firstborn animals (Ex. 22:28–29). The discussion establishes that an additional period of care is required for cattle, but then asks why this period should be fifty days rather than sixty. The Talmud answers, Lo mesaran hakatuv ela laChakhamim—the Torah entrusted the matter to the Sages.

This formulation raises a question about the relationship between biblical and rabbinic law. Ordinarily, Jewish law distinguishes between obligations imposed by the Torah and those established by the Rabbis. Here, however, the Talmud describes a third possibility: the Torah itself mandates a requirement but leaves its precise definition to the Sages. Understanding the nature of this authority has implications for the status of the resulting laws, their application in difficult circumstances, and the ability of later authorities to reconsider earlier determinations.

The Torah’s Delegation of Authority

The principle appears explicitly in the discussion of work during Chol HaMoed, the intermediate days of Passover and Sukkot.

The Talmud (Chagigah 18a) derives from biblical verses that Chol HaMoed is subject to restrictions on work, although the restrictions are not identical to those of the festival days themselves. The Talmud then confronts the question of which activities are prohibited and which are permitted. Its answer is that the Torah entrusted these distinctions to the Sages.

Rashi explains that the Torah indicates that restrictions apply without specifying their complete scope. The Sages, entrusted with understanding the Torah’s intention, determine which forms of work are prohibited and which are permitted.

Accordingly, work that would otherwise be prohibited may be permitted when necessary to prevent financial loss, known as davar ha’aved. Other activities are permitted because they serve the needs of the festival, while work undertaken for ordinary purposes may remain prohibited.

The status of these restrictions is disputed among the Rishonim. The Ritva (Moed Katan 2a) maintains that the fundamental prohibition is biblical and that the Torah authorized the Sages to identify its limits. Tosafot (Chagigah 18a, s.v. Cholo Shel Moed), by contrast, incline toward the view that the restrictions are rabbinic, and the Rosh (Moed Katan 1:1) concludes that the biblical derivations are asmakhtot, scriptural supports for rabbinic law.

Maimonides’ formulation (Hilchot Yom Tov 7:1) also generated disagreement about his position. He explains that Chol HaMoed is distinguished from ordinary weekdays by its sanctity and association with the festival, and that work is restricted so these days will not be treated as entirely ordinary. He describes the prohibited activities as violations of divrei sofrim, a designation commonly understood in this context as indicating rabbinic law. However, some authorities understand his position differently.

The Beit Yosef (Orach Chaim 530) argues that the prohibition is biblical, but that the Torah authorized the Sages to determine which activities should be prohibited and which permitted.

The disagreement reflects different understandings of what it means for the Torah to entrust a legal question to the Sages.

Three Understandings of the Delegated Rabbinic Authority

R. Hershel Schachter explains that the disagreement about Chol HaMoed may be understood as a disagreement about the nature of the Torah’s delegation of authority. The Torah may have authorized the Sages to determine the details of an existing biblical prohibition, or it may have assigned them responsibility for creating rabbinic restrictions.

R. Schachter further observes that a third possibility must be considered, in which the Sages are not exercising legislative authority but interpreting the Torah itself. Accordingly, there are three possible understandings of the principle.

According to the first, the Torah establishes a biblical obligation but grants the Sages authority to determine its specific requirements. Once they make those determinations, the requirements acquire the status of biblical law. The Rabbis are not merely creating additional restrictions; they are supplying details that the Torah itself authorized them to establish.

According to the second, the Torah delegates legislative responsibility to the Sages. It expects them to establish the necessary rules, but those rules retain the status of rabbinic legislation. Their authority derives from the Torah’s mandate, but the resulting prohibitions and obligations are rabbinic.

A third approach understands the Sages’ role as interpretive rather than legislative. The Torah has an intended meaning, and the Sages are responsible for discovering it through the methods of the Oral Torah. Their determinations are authoritative interpretations of biblical law, rather than independently chosen requirements.

The distinctions have significant practical consequences.

R. Yosef Engel, in Beit HaOtzar (I, principle 87), raises the question of whether a subsequent rabbinic court could change an earlier determination in an area entrusted by the Torah to the Sages.

Ordinarily, a rabbinic court cannot simply repeal the enactments of its predecessors. Under the relevant conditions, a later court that is greater in wisdom and number may have the authority to reverse certain earlier rabbinic enactments. The application of this principle to decisions concerning biblical laws whose details were entrusted to the Sages, however, depends upon the precise nature of the authority exercised in the original determination.

If the Sages’ determination becomes the binding content of biblical law, it may be impossible for a subsequent court to change it, even if that court possesses greater authority. Once established, the requirement may be treated as part of the biblical obligation itself.

If, however, the original decision was an act of rabbinic legislation, a later court might be able to change it under the ordinary rules governing rabbinic enactments.

The third possibility introduces another distinction. If the original ruling represents an interpretation of the Torah, it may be subject to the principles governing disagreements over biblical interpretation. Under the appropriate circumstances, a later court may reach a different understanding without requiring the greater institutional authority needed to repeal an earlier legislative enactment.

Thus, the formula that the Torah entrusted a matter to the Sages does not necessarily tell us whether their role is to interpret, legislate, or permanently define a biblical requirement. Those possibilities must themselves be examined.

Aesthetic Excellence and the Four Species

The requirement of hadar, or aesthetic excellence, in the four species used on Sukkot offers another application.

The Torah requires taking the fruit of a beautiful tree, understood to refer to the etrog (Lev. 23:40). Yet the biblical text does not supply an exhaustive definition of hadar or specify all the defects that would render an etrog unsuitable.

The Ran explains that the Torah left the standards of hadar to the Sages. This helps explain why certain disqualifications apply differently on the first day of Sukkot and on subsequent days, when the obligation outside the Temple is rabbinic. Although the Sages generally modeled rabbinic observances upon biblical requirements, they did not necessarily reproduce every detail when the Torah had itself left those details to their determination.

The Rosh (Sukkah 3:14) develops a related principle concerning the use of a dry lulav under circumstances of pressing necessity. He maintains that certain disqualifications were entrusted to the Sages, who could insist upon appropriate standards in ordinary circumstances while permitting an otherwise unacceptable specimen when no alternative was available.

This position was challenged by the Chacham Tzvi (Responsa 9). The Torah’s requirement of hadar raises the question of whether the Sages’ authority to interpret an undefined biblical standard includes authority to permit an item that fails to satisfy that standard.

The issue is whether the Sages are suspending a biblical requirement or determining that its application legitimately varies according to the circumstances.

The Or Sameach (Hilchot Lulav 8:1) suggests an approach grounded in the nature of aesthetic excellence itself. Such judgments are partly dependent upon human standards and conventions. What is regarded as appropriately distinguished in one place or circumstance may not be understood identically elsewhere.

If the Torah requires hadar, but this is not an entirely fixed physical characteristic, the Sages must determine how that requirement is to be applied.

The possibility that an otherwise unsuitable specimen may be accepted when nothing better is available can then be understood differently. Rather than suspending the Torah’s requirement, the Sages may be determining how that requirement should be fulfilled under the circumstances.

This is not a general license to relax biblical standards when observance becomes difficult. Rather, it suggests that the meaning of certain biblical requirements may depend upon contextual judgments that the Torah has entrusted to the Sages.

Yom Kippur and the Definition of Affliction

A further example emerges from the additional restrictions of Yom Kippur.

Beyond the prohibitions of eating and drinking, Jewish law requires abstention from activities including washing and anointing. The Mishnah and Talmud recognize exceptions, such as washing to remove dirt rather than for pleasure, or anointing for a medical purpose.

The Ran explains that these additional forms of affliction have a biblical basis, but that the Torah entrusted their precise application to the Sages. Accordingly, the Sages were authorized to distinguish between activities undertaken for enjoyment and those performed for other purposes.

A person who washes to remove dirt is not engaged in the same kind of activity as someone washing for pleasure, even when the physical action is similar. Likewise, applying oil for a medical purpose may differ substantially from anointing oneself for enjoyment.

These distinctions raise the question of whether the Sages are establishing exceptions to a preexisting prohibition or defining the prohibition according to the purpose and character of the activity.

If the additional restrictions are fundamentally rabbinic, the availability of leniencies may follow from the broader rules governing rabbinic law. If they are biblical prohibitions whose details were entrusted to the Sages, however, the permissibility of a particular activity must be grounded in their authority to define the biblical requirement.

The Sages may thus distinguish among different categories of conduct, identifying which forms of washing or anointing constitute the affliction-related activities the Torah intended to prohibit.

Does Entrusted Authority Permit Leniency?

This distinction also arises in the prohibition against following the practices of other nations.

Maimonides (Hilchot Avodat Kochavim 11:3), drawing upon the Talmud (Bava Kamma 83a), permits certain Jews who have close relationships with governmental authorities to adopt otherwise prohibited forms of dress or appearance when doing so is necessary for their position.

The Kesef Mishneh asks how the Sages could permit a biblical prohibition. His first explanation is that the exception was justified by the need to save Jewish lives. Jews serving in positions close to governmental authorities could use their influence to protect other Jews from danger. He further invokes the example of David’s four hundred men, whose distinctive appearance helped intimidate enemies and thereby contributed to the protection of the Jewish people.

The Kesef Mishneh then offers another explanation. The Torah did not specify every prohibited practice but instead declared, “You shall not follow their customs” (Lev. 18:3), entrusting the precise parameters to the Sages. They determined that the prohibition would not extend to those who needed to adopt such practices because of their governmental responsibilities.

R. Elchanan Wasserman challenges this explanation (Kovetz Shiurim, Bava Kamma 98). The Torah’s delegation, he argues, grants the Sages authority to identify which practices fall under the prohibition. It does not necessarily empower them to permit conduct that is already prohibited.

This disagreement illustrates two possible conceptions of delegated authority. One grants the Sages a measure of flexibility in determining the operative rules, taking account of the broader circumstances and purposes of the law. The other limits their authority to interpreting the Torah’s prohibition and determining which practices fall within it.

A related issue concerns the treatment of uncertainty in these areas. Rabbinic law is generally subject to a principle of leniency in cases of uncertainty, while biblical law ordinarily requires greater stringency. The legal status of a requirement whose details were determined by the Sages under biblical authorization therefore has practical consequences for the resolution of uncertain cases.

If the Sages’ determinations acquire biblical status, uncertainty may require stringency. If the Torah authorized them to establish the operative standards, however, those standards may themselves include leniencies for particular circumstances. Such leniencies would reflect the definition of the law rather than its suspension.

Why Does the Torah Leave Certain Matters to the Sages?

The preceding examples invite a further question: Why would the Torah choose to leave the details of some commandments to the Sages while specifying the requirements of others?

One possible explanation lies in the distinction between commandments directed toward particular actions and commandments directed toward broader objectives.

In many commandments, the Torah’s concern is with the performance or avoidance of defined conduct. The prohibition of particular forms of labor on Shabbat, for example, establishes restrictions on activities that constitute melachah. These activities remain prohibited regardless of whether their performance in a particular situation would interfere with the individual’s enjoyment of Shabbat.

Other commandments, however, may be structured primarily around an intended value or condition. Their detailed rules serve to bring about that objective, and determining the appropriate rules requires judgment concerning what will most effectively realize it.

The Torah’s purpose in restricting work during Chol HaMoed, for example, is not necessarily that particular activities should never be performed on those days. Rather, the objective is to preserve the days for the celebration of the festival, preventing ordinary work from overwhelming the religious experience of the occasion.

The Ritva (Moed Katan 13a) explains that the restrictions are concerned with exertion and with preventing activities that diminish festival joy. Accordingly, work needed for the festival may be permitted, as may work undertaken to prevent financial loss. The latter permission is especially instructive: someone who must remain preoccupied with an impending loss may be unable to enjoy the festival.

An allowance for preventing financial loss can therefore serve the same objective as a prohibition against ordinary work. Both are intended to preserve the distinctive character and joy of the festival.

The Yerushalmi (Moed Katan 2:3) similarly connects the restrictions on work with the expectation that the festival days should be devoted to the activities appropriate to their celebration.

The Keren Orah, in his introduction to Moed Katan, develops this understanding of the restrictions on work. The Torah leaves their precise definition to the Sages because the objective is to preserve the sanctity and celebration of the festival. The Sages determine which activities interfere with that objective and which can coexist with it.

A fixed list of activities, applied without regard to their circumstances, might sometimes undermine the very purpose the law was intended to accomplish.

The requirements of hadar present a parallel example. If the Torah’s objective is aesthetic excellence and dignified performance of the mitzvah, the relevant standards involve judgments concerning appearance, accepted conventions, and circumstances.

Likewise, in the restrictions of Yom Kippur, defining an activity as pleasurable washing or anointing requires consideration of its purpose. The action itself may not fully determine whether it falls within the intended prohibition.

Interpretation, Judgment, and Human Circumstances

This approach may also illuminate other applications of the principle.

Rashi (Kiddushin 11b) invokes the Torah’s delegation to the Sages in connection with the monetary threshold for a judicial oath. The Torah’s requirement concerns a monetary claim, but the precise amount sufficient to establish the relevant obligation requires definition.

If the concern is with what constitutes a meaningful monetary claim, that assessment may involve a standard that requires human judgment rather than one explicitly specified in the biblical text.

Another application appears in the discussion of accepting evidence that a missing husband has died, thereby allowing his wife to remarry.

The Nimukei Yosef (Yevamot 31b in the Rif’s pagination), citing the Ritva’s presentation of his teacher’s explanation, discusses how the Sages could rely upon evidence in this context despite the Torah’s ordinary requirements for testimony.

The explanation is that, under circumstances in which falsehood is unlikely to remain concealed and the surrounding considerations provide substantial assurance of reliability, the Sages may recognize the evidence as sufficiently credible. The Torah entrusted them with determining what forms of public knowledge and recognizable truth can constitute reliable testimony.

The point is not that the Sages can disregard the biblical requirement for evidence out of sympathy for the woman. Rather, they may possess authority to determine that particular forms of evidence satisfy the underlying standard of reliability in the relevant circumstances.

At the same time, the principle should not be extended without qualification. The Yereim (274) invokes a similar formulation concerning the identification of prohibited labor on Shabbat. R. Yosef Engel, in Gilyonei HaShas (Shabbat 49b), observes that the idea of the Torah entrusting matters to the Sages has been applied to Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Chol HaMoed.

It is therefore not possible to distinguish all such cases simply by asserting that Shabbat concerns defined actions while Chol HaMoed concerns broader purposes.

The expression may encompass several kinds of authority. In some cases, the Sages interpret the meaning of a biblical category; in others, they determine the practical details needed to realize a broader objective. These applications do not necessarily involve identical forms of authority.

The Ritva and the Development of Rabbinic Law

The implications of this principle extend beyond the particular examples in which the Talmud explicitly invokes it. The Ritva suggests a broader understanding of the relationship between the Torah’s intentions and the development of rabbinic law.

In his commentary to Rosh Hashanah (12b), the Ritva discusses why the Sages established the new year for trees in Shevat and the new year for agricultural produce in Tishrei. These distinctions reflect differences in their natural development. Trees have absorbed much of the year’s rainfall by Shevat, whereas crops depend upon the rains of the agricultural season until their maturation.

The Sages’ determinations thus reflect their understanding of the relevant agricultural realities and the distinctions appropriate to the Torah’s requirements. The Ritva concludes that the Torah entrusted such matters to the Sages, adding the significant phrase k’rov dinei Torah, like “most” of the laws of the Torah.

That final phrase suggests that the process under discussion is not an exceptional form of legislative delegation. It may instead be understood as an expression of the general responsibility of the Sages to interpret the Torah and determine how its requirements apply to the realities of the world.

This understanding relates to the third possibility identified above, in which the Sages are not creating obligations independently but determining the meaning and application of biblical law through the Oral Torah.

The Ritva develops a related concept in his discussion of asmakhta (Rosh Hashanah 16a).

The term is commonly understood to refer to a biblical verse cited in support of a rabbinic enactment, without treating that verse as establishing an actual biblical obligation. This could suggest that the Rabbis first developed their enactments and subsequently associated them with biblical language as an aid to memory or an expression of support.

The Ritva strongly rejects the understanding that an asmakhta is merely an incidental association invented by the Rabbis. He explains that when a rabbinic enactment has a biblical asmakhta, the Torah itself has indicated that the practice is appropriate, although it has not established the practice as a binding obligation.

Instead, the Torah entrusted the Sages with the decision whether to make the practice obligatory.

Accordingly, the biblical text may express approval of an observance, or indicate that it would be desirable, without requiring its performance as a matter of biblical law. The Rabbis then exercise their authority in determining whether the practice should be established as a binding obligation.

This formulation suggests a relationship between biblical and rabbinic law that is not exhausted by the distinction between direct biblical commandments and independent rabbinic enactments. Some rabbinic laws may give obligatory expression to practices that the Torah itself contemplated and encouraged but did not mandate.

It also places the principle of mesaran hakatuv laChakhamim within the larger process by which the Oral Torah gives practical form to the Written Torah. The Sages may interpret obligations whose details were left unspecified, determine the standards necessary to realize particular biblical objectives, or establish enactments that give binding force to values and practices suggested by the biblical text.

These functions differ in their legal character and may produce obligations of different statuses, but each reflects a way in which the Torah incorporates the work of the Sages into the development and application of Jewish law.

The Torah’s Intention and the Authority of the Sages

The Ritva’s approach suggests that the distinction between the Torah’s delegation of specific legal details to the Sages and their broader authority to enact rabbinic legislation may not be as sharp as it initially appears. Even when the Rabbis establish obligations that are not themselves biblical commandments, they may be giving binding expression to practices that the Torah contemplated and encouraged, leaving their implementation to rabbinic judgment.

The principle of the Torah entrusting matters to the Sages can thus be understood as part of a broader relationship between the Written and Oral Torah. In some instances, the Sages are authorized to define the details of biblical obligations; in others, they establish rabbinic legislation that gives practical expression to the Torah’s intentions. In both capacities, the Sages serve as a crucial link in the chain of tradition, reflecting the ongoing partnership between God and His human partners in the interpretation, development, and application of Jewish law.

text:
The Quiet Iconoclasm: Icons of the Interior

We usually picture iconoclasm as physical violence: marble smashed, monuments pulled down, church walls whitewashed by zealous reformers. Historically, these outbreaks marked the arrival of a new faith determined to burn away the remains of the old. But the most radical iconoclasm carries no hammer. It works quietly, dissolving the images a person carries within, and in doing so it wears away what sustains speech, the soul, and an independent mind.

In the late phase of a civilization, as Spengler argued, the spiritual fire that once animated its culture cools and sets into technique and administration. As the fire cools, a people’s relationship to its symbols changes. Where there was once instinctive reverence for myth, honor, and destiny, only the cold utility of the intellect remains. This iconoclasm does not destroy icons in religious fervor; it dissolves them through the steady pressure of abstraction, starving the soul of the images and language it needs to stay awake.

The transformation is most visible in our centers of power, run by a managerial class that governs through metrics and models. To these administrators, a people’s historical symbols, traditional ways of life, and spiritual expressions are not sacred anchors but sources of friction. Their iconoclasm is clinical rather than fanatical. They clear the public square of inherited memory, not to make room for a higher truth, but to leave a blank surface that can be organized and optimized without resistance.

The final target of this iconoclasm is the human interior itself. When language loses its transcendent weight, speech stops carrying truth, conviction, or historical identity, it flattens into a sterile vocabulary designed to manage reactions rather than express experience. Words that once tied the human spirit to a larger cosmic order fall out of use, replaced by institutional terms that treat consciousness as one more variable to be measured and steered.

The shift is audible in the way the builders of our technical utopia describe their own tools. In a recent interview with Louis Robson, who leads Palantir’s sovereignty work, Palantir CEO Alex Karp reflected on what happens when predictive models built for the battlefield are turned on a country’s own citizens. Such systems, he said, may end up predicting not only people’s behavior but “their actual thoughts,” and he called this a capability that must be brought under control.

Karp offered this as a warning, and it should be taken as one. But the warning reveals more than it intends. It treats a person’s future thoughts as, at least in principle, forecastable, and leaves open only the question of who should govern the forecast. 

That is the decisive break of our era. The iconoclasts of the past broke images because they served a rival god. The technical order needs no rival god, because the soul has no place in its model at all. It replaces the icon with the spreadsheet, the temple with the data center, and the tragic destiny of man with an optimization problem. Seen through that lens, thought is no longer a sanctuary but raw material, something to be anticipated and managed before it is ever spoken.

Yet this total disenchantment is no lasting victory for the engineers. It is the signature of a closing cycle. By reducing the mind to data and draining speech of its fire, the technical order builds a monument of perfect artificial coldness, a structure that cannot bear its own weight. It does not halt history; it hollows it out. And in the cyclical view of history, a hollow is never an ending. 

A civilization that has optimized the soul out of its equations has lost its last reason to exist. Suppressing the inner life does not hold back collapse; it hastens the turning of the wheel, until this long post-heroic winter gives way to a raw, organic dawn rising from the ruins of the machine.

text:
Mary's Chastity: from the Glories of Mary by Saint Alphonsus Liguori, with Nihil Obstat and Imprimatur, 1931.
.
Since the fall of Adam, the senses being rebellious to reason, chastity is of all virtues the one that is the most difficult to practise. St. Augustine says: "Of all the combats in which we are engaged, the most severe are those of chastity; its battles are of daily occurrence, but victory is rare." May God be ever praised, however, Who in Mary has given us a great example of this virtue. 
.
"With reason," says Blessed Albertus Magnus, "is Mary called the Virgin of virgins; for she, without the counselor example of others, was the first who offered her virginity to God." Thus did she bring all virgins who imitate her to God, as David had already foretold: After her shall virgins be brought ... into the temple of the King. [Ps. 44:15] Without counsel and without example. Yes; for St. Bernard says: "O Virgin, who taught thee to please God by virginity, and to lead an Angel's life on earth?" "Ah," replies St. Sophronius, "God chose this most pure virgin for His Mother, that she might be an example of chastity to all." Therefore does St. Ambrose call Mary "the standard-bearer of virginity."
.
By reason of her purity the Blessed Virgin was also declared by the Holy Ghost to be beautiful as the turtle dove: Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtle-dove's. [Cant. 1:9] "Mary," says Aponius, "was a most pure turtle dove." For the same reason she was also called a lily: As the lily among the thorns, so is my love among the daughters. [Cant. 2:2] On this passage Denis the Carthusian remarks, that "Mary was compared to a lily amongst thorns, because all other virgins were thorns, either to themselves or to others; but that the Blessed Virgin was so neither to herself nor to others;" for she inspired all who looked at her with chaste thoughts. This is confirmed by St. Thomas, who says, that the beauty of the Blessed Virgin was an incentive to chastity in all who beheld her. St. Jerome declared that it was his opinion that St. Joseph remained a virgin by living with Mary; for, writing against the heretic Helvidius, who denied Mary's virginity, he says, "Thou sayest that Mary did not remain a virgin. I say that not only she remained a virgin, but even that Joseph preserved his virginity through Mary." 
.
St. Gregory of Nyssa, says, that so much did the Blessed Virgin love this virtue, that, to preserve it, she would have been willing to renounce even the dignity of Mother of God. This we may conclude from her answer to the Archangel, How shall this be done, because I know not man? [Luke 1:34] and from the words she afterwards added, Be it done to me according to thy Word, [Ibid., 38] signifying that she gave her consent on the condition that as the Angel had assured her, she should become a Mother only by the overshadowing of the Holy Ghost. 
.
St. Ambrose says, that "whoever has preserved chastity is an Angel, and that he who has lost it is a devil." "Our Lord assures us that those who are chaste become Angels, They shall be as the Angels of God in Heaven. [Matt. 22:30] But the impure becomes as devils, hateful in the sight of God. St. Remigius used to say that the greater part of adults are lost by this vice. Seldom, as we have already said with St. Augustine, is a victory gained over this vice. But why? It is because the means by which it may be gained are seldom made use of. 
.
These means are three, according to Bellarmine and the masters of a spiritual life: fasting, the avoidance of dangerous occasions, and prayer.
.
1. By fasting, is to be understood especially mortification of the eyes and of the appetite. Although our Blessed Lady was full of Divine grace, yet she was so mortified in her eyes, that, according to St. Epiphanius and St. John Damascene, she always kept them cast down, and never fixed them on anyone; and they say that from her very childhood her modesty was such, that it filled everyone who saw her with astonishment. Hence St. Luke remarks, that, in going to visit St. Elizabeth, she went with haste, that she might be less seen in public. Philibert relates, that, as to her food, it was revealed to a hermit named Felix, that when a baby she only took milk once a day. St. Gregory of Tours affirms that throughout her life she fasted; and St. Bonaventure adds, "that Mary would never have found so much grace, had she not been most moderate in her food; for grace and gluttony cannot subsist together." In fine, Mary was mortified in all, so that of her it was said my hands dropped with myrrh. [Cant. 5:5]
. 
2, The second means is to fly the occasions of sin: He that is aware of the snares shall be secure. [Prov. 11:15] Hence St. Philip Neri says, that, "in the war of the senses, cowards conquer:" that is to say those who fly from dangerous occasions. Mary fled as much as possible from the sight of men; and therefore St. Luke remarks; that in going to visit St. Elizabeth, she went with haste into the hill country. An author observes, that the Blessed Virgin left St. Elizabeth before St. John was born, as we learn from the same Gospel, where it is said, that Mary abode with her about three months, and she returned to her own house. Now Elizabeth's full time of being delivered was come, and she brought forth a son. [Luke 1:56] And why did she not wait for this event? It was that she might avoid the conversations and visits which would accompany it.
. 
3. The third means is prayer. And as I knew, said the wise man, that I could not otherwise be continent except God gave it ... I went to the Lord and besought Him. [Wisd. 8:21] The Blessed Virgin revealed to St. Elizabeth of Hungary, that she acquired no virtue without effort and continual prayer. St. John Damascene says, that Mary "is pure, and a lover of purity." Hence she cannot endure those who are unchaste. But whoever has recourse to her will certainly be delivered from this vice, if he only pronounces her name with confidence. The Venerable John d' Avila' used to say, "that many have conquered impure temptations by only having devotion to her Immaculate Conception." 
.
O Mary, O most pure Dove, how many are now in Hell on account of this vice! Sovereign Lady, obtain us the grace always to have recourse to thee in our temptations, and always to invoke thee, saying, "Mary, Mary, help us." Amen.
