text:
ஸ்ரீ காளஹஸ்தி ஈஸ்வரன் 

பட்டினத்தார் பாடல் 

https://t.co/qIJUrH6L1G via @YouTube 

ஸ்ரீ காளஹஸ்தி ஈஸ்வரன் பட்டினத்தார் பாடல்

In these verses, Saint Pattinathar deeply expresses the temporary nature of human life and his detachment from worldly pleasures. 

He points out that people waste their entire lives just eating three meals a day, sleeping, and chasing physical desires, only to cry in fear when death finally approaches.

He prays to Lord Shiva, saying: 

"I am wandering day and night just to survive, caught in the endless illusion of this human body, which is nothing but blood and flesh. You alone must save me."

He earnestly begs Lord Shiva of Srikalahasti—who sits under the sacred banyan tree on the banks of the Swarnamukhi river—to remove these cheap worldly desires from his mind and grant him eternal liberation (Mukthi).

The Temple: 

In this song, Pattinathar is referring to the famous Srikalahasti temple located in Andhra Pradesh.

The Deity: 

Lord Kalathi Eswaran (Srikalahasteeswara) is a powerful form of Lord Shiva. 

He is worshipped here as the Vayu lingam (representing the wind). 

It is one of the highly revered Pancha Bhoota Sthalams (temples of the five elements).

The River: 

The temple is located on the banks of the Swarnamukhi river. 

Pattinathar beautifully calls this river "Ponmugali" in his song.

Historical Significance: 

Srikalahasti is a very important place in Shaivite history because it is where the famous hunter-saint Kannappa Nayanar offered his own eyes to Lord Shiva and attained instant salvation.

Dakshinamurthy: 

The phrase "Kallal Nizharkeezh" in the poem refers to Lord Shiva sitting in the form of Lord Dakshinamurthy under the sacred banyan tree.

முப்போது அன்னம் புசிக்கவும், 
தூங்கவும், மோகத்தினால்
செப்போது இளமுலையாருடன் 
சேரவும், சீவன்விடும்
அப்போது கண்கலக்கப்படவும் 
வைத்தாய், ஐயனே!
எப்போது காணவல்லேன்? 
திருக்காளத்தி ஈச்சுரனே!

இரைக்கே இரவும் பகலும்
 திரித்து இங்கு இளைத்து, மின்னார்
அரைக்கே அவலக் குழியருகே 
அசும்பு ஆர்த்தொழுகும்
புரைக்கே உழலும் தமியேனை 
ஆண்டருள், பொன்முகலிக்
கரைக்கே கல்லால் நிழற்கீழ் 
அமர்ந்தருள் காளத்தியே!

இந்த பாடல்களில் பட்டினத்தார் மனித வாழ்வின் நிலையாமையையும், சிற்றின்பத்தின் மீதான வெறுப்பையும் ஆழமாக வெளிப்படுத்துகிறார். 

மனிதர்கள் ஒரு நாளைக்கு மூன்று வேளை உண்பது, உறங்குவது, சிற்றின்ப ஆசையில் மூழ்குவது, பின்னர் உயிர் பிரியும் அந்த இறுதி வேளையில் மரண பயத்தால் கண்கலங்கி நிற்பதுமாகவே தங்கள் முழு வாழ்க்கையையும் வீணாக்குகிறார்கள். 

வயிற்றுப் பிழைப்புக்காக இரவும் பகலும் அலைந்து திரிந்தும், ரத்தமும் சீழும் மாமிசமுமாகிய இந்த மனித உடலின் மீது தீராத ஆசை கொண்டும் உழலும் என்னை நீதான் காத்தருள வேண்டும் என்று பொன்முகலி (சுவர்ணமுகி) ஆற்றங்கரையில் கல்லால மரத்தின் கீழ் வீற்றிருக்கும் திருக்காளத்தி சிவபெருமானிடம் பட்டினத்தார் மனமுருகி வேண்டுகிறார்.

ஆந்திரப் பிரதேசத்தில் உள்ள காளஹஸ்தி (திருக்காளத்தி) திருத்தலத்தையே பட்டினத்தார் இப்பாடலில் குறிப்பிடுகிறார்.

காளத்தி ஈஸ்வரன் (ஸ்ரீகாளஹஸ்தீஸ்வரர்) சிவபெருமானின் சக்திவாய்ந்த திருவுருவமாகும்.

இங்கு சிவபெருமான் பஞ்சபூதங்களில் ஒன்றான 'காற்றைக்' குறிக்கும் வாயு லிங்கமாக வழிபடப்படுகிறார்.

இது மிகவும் புகழ்பெற்ற பஞ்சபூதத் தலங்களில் ஒன்றாகும்.

இக்கோயில் சுவர்ணமுகி ஆற்றங்கரையில் அமைந்துள்ளது.

இதையே பட்டினத்தார் தனது பாடலில் "பொன்முகலிக் கரை" (பொன்முகலி என்பது சுவர்ணமுகி ஆற்றைக் குறிக்கிறது) என்று அழகாகக் குறிப்பிட்டுள்ளார்.

சிவபெருமானுக்காகத் தன் கண்களையே பெயர்த்து அளித்த வேடனான கண்ணப்ப நாயனார் முக்தி அடைந்த தலம் திருக்காளத்தி ஆகும்.

சைவ வரலாற்றில் இது மிகவும் சிறப்பு வாய்ந்ததாகும்.

மேலும், இப்பாடலில் வரும் "கல்லால் நிழற்கீழ்" என்ற வரி, சிவபெருமான் கல்லால மரத்தின் (ஆலமரம்) கீழ் தட்சிணாமூர்த்தியாக அமர்ந்திருக்கும் கோலத்தைக் குறிக்கிறது.

text:
From Breadwinner to Broke: How Foreign Labor and Corporate Greed Stole the American Dream

Post #8: L-1 and B-1: The Visa Loopholes You Never Heard About No Ads. No Locals. No Chance.

In 2015, Southern California Edison laid off hundreds of American tech workers. Many were told to train their replacements, foreign workers flown in under the L-1 visa. One employee described the day as a funeral procession- Americans packing up their desks as foreign workers shadowed their every move.

They had no chance to apply. No way to compete.

They were cheaper. More compliant. And thanks to our visa system, perfectly legal.

The H-1B visa gets all the headlines, but L-1 and B-1 are the quiet saboteurs. They don’t just replace workers, they erase the entire hiring process.

L-1 visas allow multinational companies to transfer employees from a foreign office to a U.S. site. No labor market test. No wage protections. No requirement to even advertise the job to Americans.

B-1 visas are for short business visits, but they’ve been abused as shadow work visas. Infosys paid $34 million for exploiting B-1s to fly in low-wage workers under the guise of training. The abuse didn’t stop there.

How it works:

Entire teams are shifted into U.S. offices under L-1s. No postings, no offers to locals.

B-1 visa holders perform full-time duties while labeled as “meeting attendees.”

Workers rotate every 11-18 months to avoid scrutiny.

One former whistleblower called it “outsourcing without the flight.”

Americans aren’t just losing jobs. They’re being denied the right to compete.

Unlike H-1B, these visas have no numerical caps and almost zero oversight. No wage floors. No transparency. And no accountability when Americans are sidelined.

If H-1B is controlled offshoring, L-1 and B-1 are the black market versions, hidden in plain sight.

This isn’t about global talent. It’s about corporate shortcuts and complicit policies that erase Americans from their own economy.

Who uses it?

Disney

Southern California Edison

Facebook

IBM

Accenture

Tata

Infosys

These aren’t loopholes. They’re the foundation of the new corporate playbook, built to erase you, quietly and legally.

Quote from whistleblower:

"They didn’t offshore the jobs. They onshored the foreign labor. We were just obstacles."

Maria Taylor is a singer-songwriter celebrated for her hushed vocals, cinematic atmospheres, and emotionally resonant storytelling — both as a solo artist and as a founding member of Azure Ray. Her forthcoming album, Story’s End, unfolds like a hazy, widescreen narrative, with each song acting as a chapter tracing love, loss, fracture, and the quiet search for solace in the aftermath. Written over several years and shaped by profound personal upheaval, the record finds Taylor expanding the signature elements of her work — bell-like piano, sweeping strings, and intimate lyricism — into something more nuanced, expansive, and ultimately life-affirming. Recorded between her California home studio and ARC Studios in Omaha, Story’s End features collaborations with Mike Mogis, Ben Brodin, Brad Armstrong, Conor Oberst, Nate Walcott, and others. The album gradually arrives at a fragile but powerful sense of transformation and hope. At once journal-like and cinematic, Story’s End offers listeners a space for reflection and consolation, paying close attention to the fleeting moments that quietly give life its meaning.

text:
Zack Polanski, "What I see over and over again is politicians say they support a two state solution, and that's fine, other than, Benjamin Netanyahu has made it very clear that he doesn't support a two state solution"

Laura Kuenssberg, "Do you support a two state solution?"

Zack Polanski, "I support whatever the Israelis and Palestinians need to be able to live side by side with equal rights"

"But I think the idea of a two state solution is for the birds, when we've got so many people running to be prime minister of Israel in the October election, who are saying that they don't support that either"

"So if this Labour government want a two state solution, my question is, what are you doing to make that happen?"

"Because the status quo right now is a one state apartheid state where Palestinians do not have the same freedoms as Israelis"

"And to come back to your first question, that's racist"

My view:

Polanski is right to challenge the gap between the promise and the reality. Netanyahu has explicitly rejected the creation of a Palestinian state, and the main Israeli opposition has not offered a clear commitment to one either. 

The question is not merely whether foreign politicians endorse a two-state solution in theory, but how they respond when influential Israeli leaders reject it and settlement expansion continues to make it harder to achieve.

That does not mean a two-state solution is meaningless or should be abandoned. It remains one possible way for Israelis and Palestinians to live with self-determination and security. 

But invoking it while doing nothing about the conditions that undermine it risks turning a peace plan into a slogan. 

If this is the government’s policy, it should say what steps it will take to protect the possibility of a Palestinian state and what consequences will follow if that possibility is further eroded.

Polanski calls the current system apartheid. 

Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Israeli human-rights organisation B’Tselem have each concluded that Israeli authorities’ treatment of Palestinians meets the definition of apartheid. 

Israel rejects that characterisation. 

The underlying question still demands an answer: how can there be lasting peace while Palestinians live under restrictions and unequal rights, without the freedom and security Israelis expect for themselves?

Any vision of peace must include safety for both peoples. Israeli civilians must be able to live without the threat of attacks, rockets or hostage-taking. Palestinians must be able to live without occupation, displacement, bombardment or being denied equal rights and a political future. 

Neither people’s safety can be built on the permanent insecurity of the other.

So the question for Labour is a fair one: if you support two states, what are you doing to make them possible?

text:
Amazing true story:

On a pouring Sunday morning in Georgia in 2014, TunDe Hector hit rock bottom on the shoulder of a slick highway. Enduring a painful divorce and severe financial hardship, she watched helplessly as her fuel gauge dropped to empty and her car sputtered to a halt. She had a single $5 bill in her pocket, an empty gas can in her hand, and miles of cold rain between her and the nearest filling station.

Minutes later, Chris Wright drove past on his way to church with his family. Spotting the solitary woman trudging through the downpour with a gas can, he felt an unmistakable tug on his conscience. After dropping his wife and children off at the church doors, he looked at his wife, Carmen, and said, "I have to go back. I have to help her."

Chris turned his vehicle around, pulled onto the shoulder, and offered TunDe a dry seat. He drove her to the nearest gas station and paid to fill her container. As they pulled back up to her stranded car, Chris felt another quiet prompting inside his chest telling him to empty his wallet. He reached into his pocket, pulled out $40, every dollar he had on him, and pressed the folded bills into her hand. TunDe wept right there in the passenger seat, thanking a man whose name she did not even know before they parted ways.

Three years later, in the summer of 2017, tragedy struck the Wright family. Chris’s mother, Judy Wright, entered the final, devastating stages of Parkinson’s disease. Doctors informed the family that she had only weeks left to live and required immediate, round-the-clock hospice care at home. The family arranged for a private nursing aide, only for the scheduled caregiver to cancel at the very last minute.

In her place, the agency sent a replacement certified nursing assistant: TunDe Hector.

Neither TunDe nor the Wright family recognized one another when she walked through the front door. Over the following days, the family watched in awe as TunDe cared for their dying matriarch with extraordinary gentleness, dignity, and warmth. She spoke softly to Judy, prayed over her bed, and treated her with the devotion of a daughter. During quiet hours beside Judy’s bed, the family learned that TunDe dreamed of finishing nursing school, though she was currently locked out of registering for classes because she owed tuition money she could not afford.

One afternoon during a shift change, the conversation turned to how faith carries people through impossible seasons. TunDe began telling the family about the lowest day of her life three years prior, describing how she had run out of gas in the pouring rain with only five dollars to her name, and how a kind stranger had circled back from church, bought her fuel, and handed her every dollar in his wallet.

Across the room, Chris Wright froze. His jaw dropped, and tears immediately welled in his eyes.

"TunDe," Chris whispered, his voice breaking. "That was me."

They both removed their hats, looked closely at one another, and broke down crying in the middle of the living room. The woman Chris had rescued on the side of a lonely highway had been sent back into his life three years later to comfort his mother in her final days on earth.

Two weeks later, on July 9, Judy passed away peacefully. It happened to be TunDe’s birthday. Even though she was off duty and celebrating with her own loved ones, the second TunDe received the phone call, she left her birthday party and rushed straight to the Wright home to comfort Judy’s widowed husband and prepare her friend one last time with dignity.

Overwhelmed by her selflessness, the Wright family decided that simple thank-you notes were nowhere near enough. When they wrote Judy’s obituary, they included a special request: in lieu of funeral flowers, please donate toward TunDe Hector’s nursing school tuition.

They set up an online fundraiser hoping to gather $1,000 to clear her past-due class balance. Within 45 minutes of going live, the fund surpassed its goal. Within days, the story of their full-circle encounter spread across the country, and strangers donated over $34,000, enough to pay for TunDe’s entire nursing degree. A single forty-dollar bill given in the rain had returned years later as priceless grace when a family needed it most.

text:
After a long time asking for changes, explaining the problems, and waiting for improvements, I have reached the point where I cannot justify putting more money into breeding under the current conditions.

I care about this game. That is why I have spent so much time talking about it. But caring about it does not mean I have to keep paying into systems that no longer make sense to me.

These are the reasons I am sitting this season out.

1. I have not seen the growth or betting experience I expected

Since the Kentucky Derby partnership ended, I have not seen the onboarding momentum I expected. My understanding from earlier communications was that other partnerships were waiting in the wings. I am still waiting to see that translate into visible growth and new players.

The same goes for the broader gambling experience I understood was coming. A Pick Three experiment does not, by itself, fulfill that expectation for me.

A Pick Three is an established betting product. It is not an innovation unique to Photo Finish Live. I can already bet on real-world racing through established platforms with much larger pools. After everything we were told about how big this could be, a roughly $150 pot does not give me much to get excited about.

Then there is the experience itself. This was supposed to involve the new Open Tote system, yet I cannot cancel my betting transactions, and the way my bets are displayed is confusing. From my experience, the system still feels unfinished, but players are already being asked to put money into it.

Where are the incentives? Where are the promotions that give customers a reason to try it? A qualifying amount spent could earn a bonus bet or even a breeding credit. Those are examples of offers that could make participation more appealing. Promotions are a familiar part of the betting market, so why does the pitch here seem to depend so heavily on existing players wanting to help the game?

I am the customer. I am the client. I am the stable deciding whether this experience is worth my money.

Attracting new players, securing sponsors, and delivering a compelling product are responsibilities of the business. Existing players cannot keep being asked to make up the difference with their own spending.

2. The schedule is still too complicated

In my view, there are still too many races competing for entries, and finding the right opportunities remains unnecessarily confusing.

Think about a new player trying to understand the schedule. A racing game needs a schedule that players can understand and fields that are worth entering. More races do not automatically create more meaningful opportunities.

3. Breeding costs need to reflect the market

The breeding economics are the biggest reason I am stepping back.

From what I am seeing, horse prices and breeding activity have declined, while the cost of producing a horse has not adjusted enough to make the proposition attractive.

Consider a hypothetical $500 breeding expense for a chance at producing a horse worth $800. That $800 is uncertain. It is als before considering other costs and the time involved.

Then add months of waiting before you can properly evaluate what you have.

I do not expect guaranteed profits. I do expect the pricing to reflect the market players are actually participating in. Breeding fees need to come down again if the value of the resulting horses cannot support them.

Players declining to breed is feedback about that calculation.

4. Training reports do not give me actionable guidance

Training sessions have been a major disappointment for me. The “early contender” label, in particular, has not matched what I understood it to mean from the horses I have seen.

Advice to “plan around a horse’s peak period” only helps if the report gives me enough information to identify that period. Otherwise, I am paying for guidance that sends me back to guessing.

Continued in the comments below @photofinishgame — Part 2 of 2. 👇

text:
My take: Mr. Musk has identified a real political obstacle, but his proposed technological escape deserves skepticism.
The report matches advance coverage of Isaacson’s interview, scheduled for October 20. Musk acknowledges that Washington distracted him from his companies and argues that AI and robotics offer the route out of the debt problem. 
I would separate three things:
He has a point about spending resistance. Every expenditure has someone who depends on it, profits from it, or wins votes by protecting it. Identifying waste is easier than assembling the votes to eliminate it.
His explanation also serves his reputation. “The system resisted me” may explain part of the failure, but leadership also means choosing workable methods, demonstrating savings, and building support. Resistance alone doesn’t establish that every proposed cut was sound.
AI could increase prosperity without fixing the budget. Greater production could expand taxable income and make debt more manageable. But if Washington spends the additional revenue—and borrows more besides—the debt problem remains. A robot cannot supply fiscal discipline, but if Mr. Musk plan had Congressional teeth...all saving going to reduce our debt...then Musk hits a home run!
I would also distinguish courts enforcing legal limits from politicians refusing cuts. Government has to exercise authority within the law, even when the objective is worthwhile.
I find his admission that he stayed too long more persuasive than his claim that technology is the only solution. Engineering talent and political judgment are different skills, and Mr Musk makes for great target practice by fools pretending to be Parliament.
My investment-banking instincts apply here: when a businessman says the nation’s salvation depends on the industry in which he has enormous investments, examine the proposition carefully. He may see a real opportunity; he also has something to sell.

Second, if these threats “shift from rhetoric to action,” the consequences “will be palpable.”

Third, he delivered a direct message to Trump: “Focus your attention on how to safely withdraw US forces from the region.”

💥 “Already Completed” Means More Than “Still Being Prepared”

Rezaei stated that “operational plans have been drafted.” Akhlaghi said that “preventive measures have been completed.”

In military terminology, preventive measures are not limited to counterattack plans. They can include preparations made before a strike occurs, such as reorganizing air defense systems, reinforcing critical infrastructure, decentralizing command structures, dispersing mobile missile launchers, and raising combat readiness.

The word “completed” is significant. It suggests that these preparations were not started only after the threat became immediate, but had already been put in place while the threat was still being discussed.

🎯 Why “Withdrawal” Instead of “Retaliation”?

Akhlaghi did not say, “We will strike your bases,” or “We will close the Strait of Hormuz.” Instead, he said, “Focus your attention on how to safely withdraw US forces from the region.”

This is a different kind of warning. It makes no specific promise about the nature of a potential strike and offers no list of targets that an adversary could analyze or prepare to defend. Instead, it raises one central question: would US forces in the region remain safe if the conflict escalated?

US military deployments in the Middle East include Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, Al Dhafra Air Base in the UAE, Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, and military personnel and facilities in Iraq and Syria. The defense of these installations relies on systems that include Patriot and THAAD missile batteries, alongside regional early-warning networks.

Akhlaghi did not explicitly claim that these defenses would fail. His message was that Washington should begin considering the possibility of withdrawing its forces.

The statement introduces a factor that US military planners cannot simply dismiss. Any decision about future deployments must account for the possibility that a conflict could become more dangerous and difficult to control than expected.

 📜 A Missile Engineer on “Preventive Measures”

Akhlaghi is presented as a key figure in Iran’s solid-fuel ballistic missile program. His name has been associated with systems including the Fateh series, Kheibar Shekan, Haj Qasem, and Fattah. He has also been linked to the development of Iran’s aerospace launch infrastructure and has faced international sanctions.

When a figure associated with missile development says that “preventive measures have been completed,” the statement carries implications beyond battlefield tactics. It raises questions about industrial capacity, missile production, stockpiles, and the ability to sustain military operations.

It suggests that preparations may extend beyond replenishing weapons after a conflict begins. They may also involve the dispersal of mobile launchers, the production of solid fuel, and maintaining the capacity to continue operations under pressure.

The central point is that Akhlaghi is presenting these preparations as already completed, rather than as measures that still need to be initiated.

 ⚔️ How Akhlaghi’s Statement Connects to Rezaei’s Warning

Rezaei stated that Iran’s new operational plans would not follow the conventional rules and standards on which its adversaries rely.

Akhlaghi said that preventive measures were complete and urged the United States to consider how it would withdraw its forces.

Rezaei’s message was that Iran would not follow the adversary’s expected script. Akhlaghi’s message was that Washington should consider the risks of remaining in the region if that script no longer holds.

The two statements address different aspects of the same security message. One concerns operational planning. The other concerns defense preparations and the potential consequences for US forces.

Together, they indicate that Iranian officials want Washington to reconsider the assumptions behind its military planning.

🔻 Who Is the Intended Audience?

Akhlaghi delivered his remarks in parliament, but the message was directed beyond the lawmakers present.

It was also aimed at the Pentagon and US Central Command, whose responsibilities include planning and overseeing American military operations in the region.

For officers responsible for deployments at Al Udeid, Camp Arifjan, Al Dhafra, and Prince Sultan Air Base, the warning raises a practical question: are their plans sufficient if a future conflict escalates beyond the limits they currently anticipate?

The message was also directed at Trump. The argument is that whether Washington chooses confrontation now or later, it must consider the risks to American personnel and the practical challenges of withdrawing them if the situation deteriorates.

This is not simply a warning about retaliation. It is a challenge to the assumptions behind US military planning.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

Tim has spoken about the pain of not getting Dawn home before their father died. He is left carrying the hope that sustained Gene for so long: that one day, his sister will walk free.

Think about the emotional weight of that responsibility. He is grieving his father while worrying about his sister, continuing a campaign that has already consumed more than a decade of his family’s life.

Yet he has refused to give up.

THE APPEALS THAT REACHED WASHINGTON

Tim’s efforts have drawn the attention of American lawmakers and diplomatic officials.

In 2025, the family continued pressing the U.S. government for humanitarian intervention. According to Tim, the American government made a humanitarian request for Dawn’s release in May of that year.

Congressman Chris Smith has also advocated for her freedom. Legislation bearing the names of Dawn Michelle Hunt and another detained American, Nelson Wells Jr., was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives to draw attention to their cases.

By 2026, the families were renewing their appeals to President Donald Trump, urging him to raise the cases directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

American diplomatic engagement and consular assistance have helped keep the case before the authorities, but these efforts have not yet secured Dawn’s release.

Her family continues to wait.

A STORY THAT SHOULD MAKE EVERY TRAVELLER THINK TWICE

Dawn’s case is also a warning about accepting luggage, parcels or gifts from people whose intentions you cannot independently verify. Never assume that a generous offer is harmless simply because the organisers appear professional or the trip seems legitimate.

International drug-smuggling convictions can carry extraordinarily severe penalties, and being unfamiliar with a country’s legal system offers little protection once an arrest occurs.

At the same time, it is important to distinguish the family’s account of deception from the conviction handed down by the Chinese authorities. Her relatives maintain that she did not knowingly carry drugs; that position should be understood as their account of the case.

But whatever one’s view of the legal proceedings, the human cost is impossible to ignore.

More than 12 years have passed. A father died without seeing his daughter again. A brother continues to fight. And a woman whose family says she was deceived remains behind bars, with serious concerns about her health.

Dawn Michelle Hunt is no longer simply a name in a drug-trafficking case. She is a daughter who could not say goodbye to her father, a sister whose family is still fighting for her, and a woman whose future remains uncertain.

Her story reminds us that while governments negotiate and courts pronounce sentences, families live with the consequences every single day.

Gene Hunt’s final wish went unfulfilled. His daughter remains in prison. His son continues the fight.

The question now is whether the next chapter will finally bring the reunion this family has waited more than a decade to see.

May Dawn return home, and may her family’s long struggle finally find a resolution.

💡 This week showed us how a physical supply shock can spread through politics, inflation, debt markets and asset prices

🚨And the biggest change wasn't simply that oil became more expensive

🧱 GOVERNMENTS ARE STARTING TO RECONSIDER POLICIES THAT BECOME TOO EXPENSIVE TO MAINTAIN

1) 🛢️ THE WEEK STARTED WITH A BOTTLENECK 
- AND ENDED WITH POLICY BENDING AROUND IT

📅 MONDAY: 
THE MARKET WAS STILL PRICING THE POSSIBILITY OF AN ENERGY TRUCE

🏛️Washington spoke about stopping attacks on energy infrastructure

🛑 But a political announcement does not repair a refinery
🛑 It does not reopen a shipping route
🛑 And it does not put missing fuel into storage

🚨Meanwhile, the risks around Hormuz, attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries continued to threaten physical supply

📈 By Friday, Brent had touched $110 per barrel for the first time since May
It settled at $109.86

🔍 FOLLOW THE CHAIN:
⚔️ Conflict threatens production and transport
↓
🚢 Fewer reliable routes and higher delivery risks
↓
⛽ Fuel becomes more expensive and harder to secure
↓
🚛 Transport and production costs rise
↓
🔥 Inflation becomes harder to contain
↓
🏦 Central banks have less room to make financing cheaper

⚠️ THIS IS WHY THE ENERGY STORY IS ALSO A CAPITAL STORY

🏭 Businesses need working capital to pay for more expensive inputs
🏛️ Governments need to protect supply and infrastructure
🛒 Households have less room to spend elsewhere when fuel and transport cost more
💵 And money committed to solving one urgent problem cannot simultaneously finance every other ambition

🧱 THE BOTTLENECK CREATES THE BILL
THE BILL CREATES THE CAPITAL COMPETITION

💡 But there is another layer

⚖️ When the physical system cannot deliver enough supply on acceptable terms, governments start reconsidering what they are willing to permit

🎯 And that brings us to the biggest political shift of the week

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
2) 🇺🇸🇷🇺 WASHINGTON IS NOW CHANGING THE RULES TO GET MORE ENERGY INTO THE MARKET

🏛️ Earlier in the week, the Russian diesel agreement was already creating a conflict inside Washington

⛽ The administration wanted additional fuel supply

📜 Lawmakers from both parties objected to easing restrictions on Russian energy exports

📢 THEN THE SITUATION MOVED FURTHER

🇺🇸 On October 16, Trump signed an executive order waiving major provisions of the new Graham Act sanctions framework, citing US national interests

⚖️ This does not mean every existing Russia-related sanction has been lifted

🇷🇺 By October 17, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first tanker carrying Russian diesel had departed from Dikson for the world market

⚠️ That is a reported shipment into the global market 
- not confirmation that this particular tanker is delivering diesel to the United States
🇺🇸The US deal is a separate channel

💡 WHY DOES THIS MATTER?
🧱 Because we have moved beyond politicians discussing possible relief

🔄 The policy framework itself is being adjusted to make additional supply possible

🔄 The chain:
⛽ Fuel prices create economic and political pressure
↓
🏛️ Washington seeks additional supply
↓
📜 Restrictions are relaxed or waived
↓
🚢 Russian fuel can reach more buyers
↓
💰 Russia gains a potential export-revenue channel
↓
⚖️ The US faces a trade-off between energy affordability and its strategy toward Russia

🧱 WHEN THE COST OF A POLICY RISES, THE POLICY ITSELF CAN BECOME NEGOTIABLE.

🛑 But do not confuse a change in policy with a solution to the shortage

🏗️ The new shipments do not instantly repair damaged infrastructure, eliminate shipping risks or guarantee a lasting decline in fuel prices

🏛️ And the political backlash in Washington means the deal remains a source of conflict, not a settled consensus

🎯 RUSSIAN DIESEL IS AN ADDITIONAL SUPPLY CHANNEL
❌ IT IS NOT A REPAIRED ENERGY SYSTEM

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
3) 🇪🇺 AND NOW THE SAME LOGIC IS REACHING EUROPE - THROUGH GAS

💡 This is where the week's story becomes much bigger than a diesel deal

📅 On October 8, US and Russian officials were exploring arrangements involving Nord Stream and potential US investment in Russian energy assets

🇺🇸 On October 17, Trump's envoys had raised the possibility of Europe resuming Russian gas purchases as part of a potential Ukraine peace settlement

🇪🇺 European officials reportedly reacted skeptically

⚠️ THIS IS A PROPOSAL - NOT AN AGREED RETURN OF RUSSIAN GAS TO EUROPE

🧱 And the distinction matters

📜 The EU has already adopted a legal framework to phase out Russian natural gas imports, with the remaining long-term LNG contracts scheduled to be prohibited from January 2027 and long-term pipeline contracts from late 2027, subject to specified exceptions

❓ So the question is not simply whether Russian gas is cheaper

⚖️ The question is whether Europe would reconsider a strategic decision because the cost of energy, industrial competitiveness and security is becoming harder to manage

🔄 FOLLOW THE CHAIN:
🇪🇺 Europe seeks to reduce dependence on Russian energy
↓
⚡ Alternative supply and infrastructure must cover the gap
↓
💸 Energy security requires investment and long-term contracts
↓
🏭 High energy costs pressure energy-intensive industries
↓
🏛️ Governments face a choice between maintaining the existing strategy and reconsidering the cost

🏛️Now Washington is reportedly suggesting that renewed gas purchases could become part of a peace arrangement

That introduces a new conflict:
- 🇺🇸 The US administration is exploring whether energy and commercial arrangements could help produce a political settlement
- 🇪🇺 European governments must weigh energy affordability against security, sanctions and the risk of renewed dependence on Russia
- 🇷🇺 Moscow has an incentive to restore access to European buyers and the revenue that comes with it

💡 THIS IS NOT PROOF THAT EUROPE WILL RETURN TO RUSSIAN GAS

⚖️ It is evidence that energy supply is becoming part of the negotiation over how the war might end 
- and that Washington and Europe may not agree on the economic price of that settlement

🎯 THE CAPITAL QUESTION: 
WHO WOULD FINANCE THE INFRASTRUCTURE, WHO WOULD CONTROL IT, AND WHO WOULD RECEIVE THE REVENUE?

🏢 Because reopening a pipeline is not just a commodity decision
🧱 It can reshape contracts, investment, ownership and political leverage for years

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
4) 📜 THE ENERGY SHOCK IS COLLIDING WITH EXPENSIVE CAPITAL - AND AI IS FEELING IT

📊 This is where the market data connect the geopolitical story to financial assets

🇺🇸 US producer-price inflation came in much hotter than expected.

🏛️ At the same time, the federal fiscal 2026 deficit reached $1.99 trillion

📉 Meanwhile, the market was reassessing how much more financing AI infrastructure would require 
- and whether the expected returns justified the bill

🤖 LOOK AT COREWEAVE
📉 Its shares fell nearly 25% over the week
💳 The company's debt came under pressure, and credit-default swap costs reached record levels as investors focused on its heavy borrowing

🛑 This does not prove that AI demand has collapsed

💡 It shows that investors are separating two questions that were often treated as one:

1️⃣ DOES THE WORLD NEED MORE AI INFRASTRUCTURE?
🔌 Chips, data centres, networking, electricity and cooling remain essential to the buildout

2️⃣ CAN EVERY COMPANY FINANCE THAT BUILDOUT AND EARN ENOUGH TO JUSTIFY THE COST?
⚖️ That is a different question

🔄 The chain:
🤖 AI demand
↓
🏗️ Data-centre investment
↓
💳 Debt and other financing
↓
⚡ Power, equipment and operating costs
↓
💰 Future revenue must cover the investment and its financing cost

💳 If a company borrows heavily today, its future returns must justify both the assets it builds and the cost of financing them

⚠️ REAL DEMAND DOES NOT GUARANTEE GOOD RETURNS FOR EVERY INVESTOR

🔥 And when inflation remains stubborn, that calculation becomes even more important

📉 A company can have strong demand and still be vulnerable if it has borrowed too much, overpaid for capacity or depends on refinancing under favourable conditions

🎯 THE AI BUILDOUT CAN CONTINUE WHILE AI INVESTMENTS GET REPRICED

💡 That distinction is one of the most important lessons of this week

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
5) 📊 THE MARKET DIDN'T SELL EVERYTHING 
- IT BECAME MORE SELECTIVE

💡 This is where we need to correct a common interpretation

❌ The week was not a simple story of every risky asset falling and all capital moving into cash

📉 The technology sector was hit especially hard
🚫The Nasdaq lost about 4.5% over the week, and technology shares fell sharply

📈 Energy and several defensive sectors performed better
🗓️The Dow, meanwhile, finished the week higher

💡 THE IMPORTANT SIGNAL IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SECTORS

🔄 Investors were reassessing companies whose valuations and financing needs depended heavily on future AI growth, 
while energy benefited from rising prices and supply concerns

🛑 But we should not claim that every dollar leaving technology went directly into energy 
🌊Market performance alone cannot establish that exact flow

📜 The bond market gives us another part of the picture

📉 The US 10-year Treasury yield fell toward 5.1% by the end of the week, even as inflation data strengthened concerns about the cost of money

🛡️ Government bonds attracted defensive demand during the equity selloff

💡 That matters because capital has alternatives:
💵 It can earn income while waiting
📜 It can seek protection in government bonds
⚡ It can pursue companies exposed to essential energy supply
🤖 It can keep funding AI - but demand more evidence of returns
✴️ It can enter crypto - but it does not have to

⚖️ THIS IS NOT A CLAIM THAT CAPITAL HAS ABANDONED GROWTH

🧱 It is a reminder that when safe assets offer meaningful yields and financing costs remain high, investors can become more demanding about what they are willing to fund

📊 The early third-quarter earnings data reinforce that nuance

📅 As of October 16, only 9% of S&P 500 companies had reported

📈 Of those, 84% beat EPS expectations 
(above historical averages), 
while 67% beat revenue expectations (below the five- and ten-year averages)

⚖️ That is an early, mixed picture 
- not enough evidence to declare a broad corporate earnings collapse

🎯 THE MARKET IS NOT SAYING THAT EVERYTHING IS BAD
🗣️IT IS ASKING WHICH BUSINESSES CAN STILL JUSTIFY THE CAPITAL THEY REQUIRE

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
6) ✴️ CRYPTO: MORE FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY MEAN MORE BUYING

🏦 This week's crypto headlines included tokenization, stablecoins, the digital euro and growing institutional interest in blockchain-based financial infrastructure

💡 Those developments matter 
- but we have to distinguish changes in the financial system from immediate demand for volatile crypto assets

📊 US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded net outflows of about $228 million across the week, through October 16

📅 October's cumulative outflow had reached roughly $617 million by that date

🛑 That does not mean nobody is buying BTC

🧱 It means the available ETF-flow data do not support the claim that a broad new wave of external capital is entering the market

💡 AND THE BIS ADDED AN IMPORTANT PIECE TO THE BIGGER PICTURE

📜 Its October 13 working paper found evidence that stablecoins and bank deposits can act as partial substitutes: changes in the rates banks offer on deposits are associated with changes in stablecoin growth

⚖️ The study does not prove that every dollar entering stablecoins leaves the banking system, nor does it establish that stablecoin growth automatically benefits BTC or ETH

This is the distinction:
🏦 Stablecoins can compete with traditional deposits for users' funds
↓
💵 They can provide digital payment and liquidity services
↓
📜 Their reserves can connect the crypto ecosystem to traditional financial assets
↓
⚖️ But that does not mean the same money must flow into speculative tokens

🔗 Tokenization can also make securities easier to issue, transfer or settle...
🧱 without necessarily creating a new buyer for every token connected to the infrastructure

🧱 BETTER RAILS ≠ AUTOMATIC TOKEN DEMAND

🗣️The same question we have been asking since mid-August still applies:
💰 Who is providing the next dollar?
📊 Is that money entering consistently?
🔄 Is it new capital, or existing capital changing hands?
⏳ Can demand continue after a short squeeze or a temporary rally ends?

🎯 INFRASTRUCTURE CAN GROW WHILE TOKEN PRICES STRUGGLE TO ATTRACT SUSTAINED NEW CAPITAL

⚠️That is why we cannot use adoption headlines as a substitute for actual flow data

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🍊 THE BIG PICTURE - OCTOBER 12–18

🗓️Now connect the week

🛢️ Energy disruption pushed prices higher
↓
🏛️ Governments faced greater pressure to secure supply
↓
📜 Washington adjusted its sanctions framework and opened a channel for Russian diesel
↓
🇪🇺 US envoys reportedly raised renewed Russian gas purchases as part of a possible peace arrangement
↓
⚖️ The economic cost of existing geopolitical policies became more visible
↓
🔥 Inflation and energy costs continued to complicate the path toward cheaper financing
↓
🤖 Investors questioned the financing risk behind parts of the AI buildout
↓
📜 Government bonds attracted defensive demand as technology shares sold off
↓
✴️ Crypto still needed sustained fresh inflows to demonstrate broader demand

❌ THESE ARE NOT SEPARATE STORIES

⛓️They are connected by a common constraint:

💰 THE WORLD HAS MORE THINGS IT NEEDS TO FINANCE — AND NOT EVERY INVESTMENT WILL RECEIVE CAPITAL ON THE SAME TERMS

🏛️ Governments need energy and security
🏭 Businesses need working capital and infrastructure
🤖 AI companies need financing for capacity they expect to monetise in the future
📜 Investors can earn income from government debt while waiting for better opportunities
✴️ Crypto can keep building financial infrastructure without guaranteeing that fresh money will buy its tokens

🔄 And when energy becomes expensive enough, governments may reconsider policies they previously treated as fixed

⚠️ BUT WE MUST NOT GO TOO FAR

❌ The evidence does not prove that all capital is leaving AI for energy, that Europe has agreed to restore Russian gas imports, or that the US has abandoned every Russia-related sanction

💡 It shows a more specific and important change:
🧱 THE COST OF MAINTAINING THE EXISTING SYSTEM IS STARTING TO CHANGE POLITICAL DECISIONS — WHILE FINANCING RISK IS CHANGING WHAT INVESTORS ARE WILLING TO PAY FOR

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
💰 WHAT CHANGED IN THE CAPITAL MAP THIS WEEK?

🛢️ 1) ENERGY - THE PHYSICAL BOTTLENECK IS DICTATING POLICY

⛽ The cost of securing supply is becoming difficult to ignore
🏛️ Governments are reconsidering restrictions and exploring alternative supply channels
🏗️ But additional shipments and political announcements do not mean the underlying energy system has been repaired

🇺🇸🇪🇺 2) GEOPOLITICS - WESTERN POLICY IS BECOMING LESS UNIFIED

🇺🇸 Washington is exploring energy arrangements that European governments may oppose
🧱 That creates uncertainty around sanctions, energy contracts, infrastructure ownership and future investment

🤖 3) AI - REAL DEMAND, MORE SCRUTINY OF FINANCING

🤖 AI infrastructure remains strategically important
💳 But investors are paying closer attention to leverage, borrowing costs and whether future cash flows justify capital committed today

📜 4) GOVERNMENT BONDS - DEFENSIVE DEMAND STILL MATTERS

📉 Treasuries attracted buyers during the equity selloff
⚠️ That does not eliminate inflation or fiscal risks
📜 It shows that capital has alternatives to chasing growth assets

✴️ 5) CRYPTO - INFRASTRUCTURE IS ADVANCING, BUT FLOWS REMAIN THE TEST

🔗 Tokenization and stablecoin adoption can change financial infrastructure
❌ They do not automatically create sustained demand for BTC, ETH or every other token

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚨 THE WEEKLY CONCLUSION

⚖️ The week began with an energy shock

🔄 It ended with that shock influencing sanctions policy, negotiations over Russian gas, the financing of AI infrastructure and the way investors priced risk

🧱 THE MOST IMPORTANT CHANGE WAS NOT JUST THE PRICE OF OIL

💡 It was the growing evidence that the cost of keeping the physical economy running can force governments to reconsider political decisions 
- while expensive financing forces investors to reconsider financial ones

⚖️ TWO DIFFERENT QUESTIONS
💸 ONE CAPITAL CONSTRAINT

🏛️ Governments must decide what they can no longer afford to restrict, delay or leave unfunded
💰 Investors must decide which assets still justify the price and risk of owning them

❌ Do not confuse a government changing policy with the energy crisis being solved
❌ Do not confuse real AI demand with guaranteed investment returns
❌ Do not confuse better crypto infrastructure with fresh money buying tokens

🛑 And do not assume that a selloff in one sector proves capital has moved into another

💡 THE BIGGER PICTURE IS BECOMING CLEARER:
🏗️ The world is spending more to secure energy, infrastructure and strategic independence.
💳 At the same time, the cost of financing those commitments remains significant, and investors have alternatives to taking additional risk

💵 CAPITAL IS NOT SIMPLY CHASING THE BIGGEST STORY
🔒 It is weighing necessity, financing costs, future returns and the risks of being wrong

🗣️So stop asking only:
🚀 WHAT IS THE NEXT BULLISH NARRATIVE?

🗣️Start asking:
💰 WHO MUST SPEND?
🏛️ WHO HAS THE POWER TO CHANGE THE RULES?
💳 WHO CAN AFFORD TO FINANCE THE NEXT PROJECT?
👀 WHO IS ACTUALLY PROVIDING FRESH CAPITAL?
⚠️ AND WHO IS LEFT CARRYING THE BILL?

⚖️ Because the energy crisis, the AI buildout, government borrowing and crypto adoption are not equal claims on capital

🎯 THEY ARE COMPETING FOR MONEY UNDER DIFFERENT CONDITIONS

🔍 FIRST SEE WHERE MONEY IS FORCED TO GO
🔄 THEN SEE WHERE IT CHOOSES TO GO

🙈 SURVIVE FIRST
🙊 PROFIT LATER
💰 FOLLOW THE CAPITAL

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran’s proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz remains on the table, adding that Iran is reviewing comments from the United States.

“Our conditions are completely clear and were presented to the United States in the form of a seven-day plan,” Araghchi said. “They have offered comments that we are reviewing, but from our perspective the plan remains on the table.”

He said that if Washington met Iran’s conditions, the strait would reopen on the sixth day and negotiations would begin on the seventh.

"Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online

A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago, as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.

The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.

In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.

She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.

A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.

The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.

No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.

Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.

“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.

“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”

The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.

New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.

Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.

Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

text:
For three winters, a retired bus driver named Walter Reed left a small lamp burning in the window of his apartment every night.

His building stood on a quiet street in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Most of the tenants barely knew one another, but everyone knew Walter.

He was the man who shoveled snow from the entrance before sunrise, fixed broken stairwell lights, and held the door open for anyone carrying groceries.

But there was one thing nobody understood.

Every evening at exactly 8:15, Walter would place a yellow lamp beside his window, turn it on, and pull a chair close to the glass.

Then he would sit there until midnight.

Sometimes, he would wave at passing cars.

Other nights, he would simply stare at the empty street.

His next-door neighbor, a college student named Rachel, once joked that he must be expecting a secret admirer.

Walter smiled but said nothing.

One November evening, Rachel noticed that the lamp was missing.

Concerned, she knocked on his door.

Walter answered wearing his usual gray sweater, but his eyes looked swollen.

"Mr. Reed, are you all right?" she asked.

He nodded toward the empty window.

"The bulb finally burned out."

Rachel offered to buy him another one, but he gently declined.

"It's not the bulb," he explained. "It's the waiting."

She sat down across from him.

After a long silence, Walter opened a drawer and removed a faded photograph.

It showed a little boy standing beside a yellow school bus, holding a lunchbox almost as big as his chest.

"That was my son, Daniel," Walter said. "His mother left when he was six. After that, it was just the two of us."

He explained that he had driven a city bus for thirty-one years. Every afternoon, he would finish his shift, park near Daniel's school, and wait for him to climb aboard.

Daniel grew up believing his father could fix anything.

But when Daniel turned nineteen, they had an argument that neither man knew how to end.

Daniel wanted to leave Pittsburgh and become a musician.

Walter wanted him to stay, find steady work, and build a secure life.

Their final conversation ended with Daniel shouting, "You don't get to decide my future!"

Walter replied with words he would spend the rest of his life regretting.

"Then don't come back asking me for anything."

Daniel left the following morning.

For years, neither of them called.

Then, one winter night, Walter received a letter from an unfamiliar address.

Inside was a photograph of Daniel standing outside a small music studio in Chicago.

On the back, Daniel had written:

"Dad, I finally found my own way. I hope someday you'll be proud of me."

Walter had read that letter hundreds of times.

He never replied.

He told himself he would call when he had the right words. Then a week passed, then a month, then a year.

Eventually, the letters stopped coming.

Walter placed the photograph back in the drawer.

"I used to leave that lamp on because I thought if Daniel ever came home, he'd know I was still here."

Rachel wiped her eyes.

"Have you tried looking for him?"

Walter lowered his head.

"Every day for the last three years. I just never knew where to begin."

The following morning, Rachel helped him search for Daniel online.

They found an old music page, a few photographs, and eventually a social media account that had not been updated in months.

There was no telephone number.

No address.

Nothing that could tell them where Daniel was now.

But Rachel noticed something Walter had overlooked.

One of Daniel's old posts mentioned a charity concert he had organized for families experiencing homelessness.

The event's website listed an email address.

Walter stared at the screen for nearly twenty minutes before asking Rachel to help him write a message.

He typed only three sentences.

"Daniel, I was wrong. You deserved a father who listened instead of someone who always believed he knew best. If you can forgive me, my door is still open."

He sent it.

Then he waited.

One week passed.

text:
A Slight Demonstration

 Decatur, Alabama, October 1864

[Author’s Notes: I am writing this piece in mid-October, well ahead of the campaign it introduces. Hood’s Tennessee Campaign will not start in earnest until late November, and the posts I plan on Franklin and Nashville will need room to run in detail. Before that, I want the reader to see how the campaign began. The dread was already in the army before it crossed into Tennessee. It came from small things: a railroad that wasn’t mended, a plan changed on the road, a general who would not answer his superior’s questions. Decatur is a good place to see all of that at once. It is a minor affair, a few days of rifle pits and a small garrison, and it is worth a piece of its own. I am putting it up now because it belongs at the front of what follows, and because this weekend is the time I have to write it.]

****************************
On the ninth of October, from a place in north Georgia called Van Wert, John Bell Hood sent off a telegram asking that a railroad be mended. He wanted the Memphis & Charleston repaired “at once to Decatur, if possible,” so that it could serve his army as a line of supply and also, if matters went badly, as a line of retreat.

Retreat. It is not a word a general commonly has in mind at the opening of an invasion, and it was an odd one to find in the head of Hood, who had left the use of an arm at Gettysburg and a leg at Chickamauga and had never in anyone’s hearing been accused of timidity. But he had his reasons, and they were the sort a man accumulates one at a time. Atlanta was more than a month gone. He had struck north of the Chattahoochee at Sherman’s railroad and drawn Sherman after him through Allatoona and Resaca and Dalton, and none of it had brought the great collision he wanted. Allatoona in particular had gone wrong in the way that stays with a commander: a prepared position, a costly assault, a failure. Nothing so far was bad enough to be called a disaster. That was the trouble with it. It was a string of small misfortunes, each reasonable by itself, and a man who looks at enough of them in a row begins to feel that he is being told something.

There was also, now, a man above him, though what that meant depended on whom you asked. Jefferson Davis had come out to the army at Palmetto in the last days of September to talk over the move against Sherman’s communications, and had gone away deciding that the western armies needed someone senior to look after them, and that Hood should keep the one he had. The someone was Beauregard. Davis met him at Augusta, and on or about the second of October handed him the Military Division of the West, everything east of the Mississippi, with Hood’s department and Richard Taylor’s under it. Beauregard took hold on the seventeenth at Jacksonville, Alabama, and his General Orders No. 1 said that Hood and Taylor “will retain command of their respective Departments.” Davis’s instructions added that Beauregard was to coordinate supply and cooperation, and that he was to command an army directly only when he stood personally with it. It was an arrangement that satisfied the letter of every regulation and settled nothing. It would work for exactly as long as Hood chose to tell him things.

They had talked around the ninth at Cave Spring, and they talked again at Gadsden on the twenty-first. There Hood laid out his plan. He would cross the Tennessee near Guntersville, break the bridges and the railroad at Bridgeport and Stevenson, and either pull Sherman after him into Middle Tennessee or fall on Thomas’s scattered detachments. Beauregard had misgivings about the execution of it, and about the change of base, and about the timing. He talked it over with Hood and with the corps commanders, Lee and Stewart and Cheatham, and on the evening of the twenty-first he approved it. Hood marched for the river. That was the plan Beauregard had approved. It was not the one Hood carried out.

On the road he learned that Guntersville was more strongly held than he had supposed, and Forrest, whose cavalry he wanted for eyes, was off to the west, and the railroad he had asked for was not repaired. What remained was Decatur, which the information at hand (some of it, apparently, from Roddey’s cavalry) described as lightly held, and which offered a pontoon bridge and a rail junction besides. It looked like a door. Hood went to it, and Beauregard was not promptly told. He would put it in his report with the flatness of a man who has been through it: Hood, he wrote, “suddenly changed his line of march.” Whether Hood meant to keep it to himself the record does not say. It does say that twelve days before he laid Guntersville before Beauregard at Gadsden, he had asked for rails to Decatur.

He reached the town on the twenty-sixth. His headquarters on the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth were at the house of General Garth, near Decatur, and Beauregard caught up with him there, six days after approving a crossing at Guntersville, which is a thing to hold in mind: the two of them under one roof while the army felt its way up to the town. Beauregard afterward recorded that he cautioned Hood about the irregular reporting of his movements. Pickets were driven in; rifle pits were scraped out; artillery was shifted about. Elements of Cheatham’s corps, and Stewart’s, and Lee’s, took up the ground in front of the Union works. Hood would write that the army “turned Decatur” while he ordered “a slight demonstration” against the town until the rest had passed safely beyond.

Across the line it did not look slight at all. Colonel Charles Doolittle of the 18th Michigan had perhaps twelve hundred to eighteen hundred men when the month began, and now General Granger had come down from Huntsville to take command, and Thomas had sent what reinforcement he could, new regiments from Michigan and Ohio and, on the twenty-seventh, the 14th United States Colored Infantry under Colonel Thomas J. Morgan. The Union count came to something between three thousand and five thousand. Before them lay extensive works and a line along the river front, and in the river lay two gunboats. One was the USS Stone River. The other was the USS General Thomas. A man given to omens might have made something of that; the record does not say that anyone did. Prisoners and deserters came in and told the Union officers that much of Hood’s army was out there and that an assault was meant, and the reports that went up from Granger said as much.

On the twenty-eighth, Morgan took about four hundred men, eight companies of the 14th, out of the lines and went at an earthwork near the river on the Confederate right. They took it. They spiked the guns, gathered up prisoners, and walked back. Granger’s reports, and Morgan’s own, dwelt on how little the thing had cost. Other actions drove Confederate troops from advanced positions and brought in more prisoners, many of them from Cheatham’s command, and the guns on the boats raked what they could reach. The Confederate artillery was moved and moved again, and it silenced neither the works nor the bridge.

The decision, when it came, came at headquarters. A Union report, drawn from the word of a servant who had escaped from Hood’s camp, has Hood wishing to go on and Beauregard judging an assault impracticable. It is secondhand, and it is the only account of that conversation anyone left. It is also entirely believable. By the twenty-ninth and thirtieth the army was not going forward. It was the sound decision, and it came late, because the mistake had been made on the road to Decatur, where a report that the place was weak had been taken for a fact.

Hood had asked for a lightly held town, been told he had one, and believed it. The belief cost him nothing. The days did.

The army drew off westward by way of Courtland. Stephen Lee’s corps was on the Tennessee near Florence by the thirtieth, Johnson’s division across and into the town, and on that day Colonel George William Brent, writing for Beauregard, asked Hood for two things to send on to the War Department: “a brief summary of the operations of your army from the date of its departure from Jonesboro’, Ga., to the present time; also a concise statement of your plans of future operations.” 

It was not a great deal to ask. Hood, who reached Tuscumbia on the thirty-first, was slow to answer, and when he did he pleaded that he was too busy and too ill. What he sent were copies of earlier telegrams to the government. Some of what he had to say to Richmond, and to Taylor, had been going to them direct, without passing through the headquarters of the man the President had put over him, and Beauregard would note in the end that no full report of the campaign from Hood or from any of his subordinates ever came through those headquarters as regulations required.

Beauregard sent Richmond what he had on the sixth of November, along with his own summary of the plan as amended in talk on the third: Lawrenceburg first, then Pulaski or Columbia as events indicated, and Forrest to come up after a demonstration. He pressed Hood on his flanks, on crossings above Savannah or Clifton beyond the reach of the gunboats, on the safety of Corinth and the Mobile & Ohio. He ordered the base changed to Tuscumbia and told Taylor to put the railroads in running order. He urged speed, over and over, once the army was together. 

The railroads were what they were, and it rained, and Forrest was awaited, and the army did not move out of Tuscumbia and Florence until about the twenty-first of November. The want of supplies, Beauregard wrote, “delayed his advance for nearly three weeks, whereby Sherman was given time to repair the damage done to the Chattanooga and Atlanta Railroad and to collect sufficient supplies for his march across Georgia.” 

Hood, in his own account, would lean on the authority he had been given and the difficulties he met, and some of the difficulties were real. The weather could be blamed for the mud. It could not be blamed for the silence.

The Union loss at Decatur ran to the low hundreds, killed and wounded and missing. The Confederate loss was larger, put at several hundred, and no report tallied it fully. Neither figure was the real expense. George Thomas, in Nashville, used the interval the way a patient man uses all his intervals. He gathered in his troops. He dug.

The road Hood was leaving Decatur to find led to Franklin, and after Franklin to Nashville; he would reach the first on the thirtieth of November and the second in the middle of December. Beauregard would come to believe that after Franklin an attack on Nashville was unwise, and that Murfreesboro would have been the better target. Neither man knew that yet. What Hood knew was that the bridge at Decatur had not been taken, that the stores in the town had not been touched, and that he had called the whole affair a demonstration.

The pontoon bridge stayed where it was. So did the gunboats. So, in Nashville, did Thomas.

text:
What Muscle Remembers: Movement, Insulin and the Cells Beneath the Skin

A biopsy from the thigh
There is a muscle on the outer thigh, the vastus lateralis, that researchers favor when they want to know what is happening inside a person. It is large, it is accessible, and it does the ordinary work of standing up, climbing stairs, and carrying things home. In a study published this month in iScience, a team from the University of Michigan, the National Institutes of Health and several Finnish universities took a small piece of this muscle from 263 Finnish adults, most of them around sixty years old, and read it the way one might read a diary: cell by cell, nucleus by nucleus, looking at which genes were switched on and which were quiet.

What made this cohort unusual was not the biopsy itself but what the researchers already knew about each person.

Every participant had sat through an oral glucose tolerance test with fasting insulin measured, which allowed the team to calculate HOMA-IR, the standard estimate of insulin resistance. Every participant had also filled out a twelve-month questionnaire describing their leisure-time physical activity, from gentle walks to the kind of effort that leaves you breathless.

About a quarter had newly diagnosed, untreated type 2 diabetes.

About a third had normal glucose tolerance.

The rest lived somewhere in between.

The question the researchers asked was simple to state and difficult to answer. When we look inside the muscle of someone who moves a great deal, and inside the muscle of someone whose body has grown deaf to insulin, do we see the same story told in opposite directions?

…and if we do, is it one story or two?

What the muscle said
Muscle is not one tissue but a chorus of fiber types. Type 1 fibers are slow, oxidative, and patient; they are dense with mitochondria and burn fat for fuel across long hours. Type 2x fibers are fast and glycolytic, built for brief, powerful efforts and quick to fatigue. Type 2a fibers sit between the two. Roughly seventy percent of the nuclei in these biopsies belonged to muscle fibers, and the proportions shifted in a pattern that will not surprise anyone who has spent time with the literature, though it has rarely been shown at this resolution. People with lower insulin resistance carried more Type 1 nuclei and fewer Type 2x. People who reported more total physical activity carried the same signature. The effect sizes were modest, on the order of four to eight percent, but they were consistent across two independent sequencing methods, and they held in men and in women alike.

The more interesting finding came when the researchers looked beneath fiber type to the genes themselves. Across every fiber type, and in the tissue as a whole, higher physical activity was associated with greater expression of genes governing aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis: the machinery by which a cell converts oxygen and fuel into usable energy. Higher insulin resistance was associated with the opposite, a quieting of those same energy pathways. And the mirror image extended further. Genes in the MAPK signaling cascade, a stress-responsive pathway whose dysregulation has been linked to both diabetes and cancer, were more active in the insulin-resistant and less active in the physically active. Genes for breaking down branched-chain amino acids followed the metabolic pattern: more expression with movement and insulin sensitivity, less with resistance.

When the team plotted the two traits against each other, gene by gene, the correlation was negative in every fiber type, and nearly every gene that reached significance for both traits pointed in opposite directions. Within the energy-metabolism pathways, the shifts were small and coordinated across many genes rather than dramatic in any single one, which is how living tissue tends to adapt: not by flipping a switch but by leaning, gently and collectively, one way or the other.

Then came the question that gives the paper its weight. Is this one story or two?

The researchers put both traits into the same statistical model so that each could be tested while holding the other constant. If physical activity protects muscle only by lowering insulin resistance, the activity signal should have dissolved once insulin resistance was accounted for. It did not. The associations were attenuated, as one would expect of two traits that share biology, but each remained. Insulin resistance appears to shape the muscle's gene expression partly on its own terms, and physical activity appears to counter it partly on its own terms, with the two converging on a shared set of pathways and even a shared subset of genes. The authors put it carefully: the two traits have inverse and partially independent directions of association. In plainer words, movement and insulin sensitivity are allies that arrive at the same destination by overlapping but not identical roads.

What this study can and cannot tell us
I want to be honest about the shape of this evidence, because the temptation with a beautiful dataset is to let it say more than it does. This is an observational study. The biopsies were taken once, at one moment in each person's life, and the physical activity was self-reported over the preceding year. No one was assigned to train or to rest. The researchers can describe how muscle looks in people who move more and people who resist insulin more; they cannot prove that moving caused the muscle to look that way, nor that the muscle changes caused the insulin resistance. The authors say this themselves, and they add that they could not run a formal mediation analysis because, in this cohort, vigorous activity and HOMA-IR were not even significantly correlated with each other once age and sex were accounted for. That is a real limitation, and it means the partial independence they found should be read as a strong hint rather than a settled fact.

The participants were older Finns, mean age sixty, almost all over forty-five, and a quarter of them had untreated type 2 diabetes. The findings may not transfer cleanly to a thirty-year-old in Santo Domingo. Gene expression is also not the same as protein, and protein is not the same as function; a gene switched on more brightly in a nucleus does not guarantee a stronger mitochondrion in the cell.

What the study does well is considerable.

It is the largest single-nucleus atlas of human skeletal muscle with insulin resistance, diabetes status, and physical activity measured in the same people. Its findings agree with smaller interventional studies in which people were actually trained, and with decades of histology showing that slow fibers accompany better metabolic health.

The most defensible reading is this: the muscle of a person who moves regularly carries a molecular signature of energy competence, and the muscle of a person who has drifted into insulin resistance carries the inverse, and these two signatures are largely mirror images drawn on the same page.

What we have been handed is a map rather than a mechanism, and it is a good map.

How I would train in light of this
The study measured two things about movement: the total amount of it, across a year, and the share of it that was vigorous, meaning six METs or more, the kind of effort you cannot hold a conversation through. Both mattered, and they mattered differently. Total activity was what tracked the shift toward slow, oxidative fibers. Vigorous activity was what produced the sharpest signal in the energy-metabolism genes. I read this as support for something I have believed for a long time and tried to build into every program I write: the base and the peak are not competitors, and the easy hours are what make the hard ones possible.

So the first recommendation is also the least glamorous.

Accumulate volume at low intensity:
Most days, in whatever form your joints and your life will allow. For most of the people I work with this means walking, and increasingly it means rucking, a loaded pack on the back and a long unhurried pace, because it builds aerobic durability, trunk strength, and bone loading with less impact than running. The study's Type 1 fiber signal rewards exactly this kind of patient repetition. If you are building from nothing, begin with the body's own weight and add load only when distance has become comfortable; the injury risk of load carriage climbs with the weight on your back, and it climbs faster for lighter frames.

The second recommendation is to earn and then spend, your intensity:
Once the base is in place, one or two sessions a week of hard, breathless work appear to do something the easy hours do not, and the aerobic respiration genes in this study are the molecular face of that something. Boxing is my preferred vehicle because it demands coordination and reaction alongside the cardiovascular load, but intervals on a bike, hill repeats, or a rower will serve. What matters is that the effort is real, that it is brief, and that it is rare enough to recover from.

The third recommendation concerns strength:
The paper does not test resistance training directly, but it cites the interventional literature showing that strength training shifts fibers away from the fast glycolytic Type 2x toward more oxidative types, and the Type 2x fibers were the ones that accumulated in people with higher insulin resistance and higher BMI. Keep lifting. Muscle is the body's largest reservoir for glucose disposal, and a muscle that is trained is a muscle that listens to insulin. Two or three sessions a week built around the major movement patterns is enough for most people who are not competing.

A last note, because the data invite it. 

The signal for sex was far larger than the signal for any lifestyle trait, by an order of magnitude in gene expression and more in chromatin. Men and women do not share identical muscle, and the programs I write for them are not identical either. I take it as an invitation to watch closely how your own body answers, and to let that answer shape the work.

How I would eat in light of this
The paper is not a nutrition study, and I will not pretend otherwise. But two of its findings open a door to the kitchen, and I would be remiss to walk past it.

The first is the behavior of the branched-chain amino acid catabolism genes. These are the enzymes that break down leucine, isoleucine, and valine, the amino acids most abundant in muscle protein and most responsible for triggering muscle growth after a meal. In this cohort, people with lower insulin resistance and higher vigorous activity expressed these genes more strongly.

This fits a pattern that has been building in the literature for a decade: insulin-resistant muscle tends to lose its ability to clear branched-chain amino acids, and they accumulate in the blood as a marker, and possibly a contributor, of metabolic dysfunction.

The practical lesson is not to eat less protein.

Older adults in particular need more of it than the minimums suggest, somewhere in the range of 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight each day, spread across meals so that each one carries enough leucine to wake the muscle. The lesson is that protein does its best work in a muscle that is trained and insulin-sensitive, and that eating well and moving well are the same project seen from two angles.

The second finding is the direction of the energy-metabolism genes with respect to two-hour glucose. People whose blood sugar rose less after the glucose challenge had muscle that burned fuel more readily. The glucose tolerance test is, in a sense, the body's report on what happens after every carbohydrate-rich meal, and muscle is where most of that glucose should go. I would take from this what I already counsel: build each meal around protein and fiber, place carbohydrates where they will be used, which usually means around the training you did or the training you are about to do, and avoid the long stretches of liquid sugar and refined starch that ask the muscle to absorb what it cannot. For those who measure, a fingerstick before and ninety minutes after a meal is a humble and honest teacher.

Beyond these two threads the study is silent, and so I will be brief. Eat food that was recently alive. Favor fish from clean, cold water and know whether it was wild or farmed. Let olive oil, nuts, legumes, and vegetables carry the bulk of your plate. Drink less alcohol than you think is harmless. None of this comes from the Finnish biopsies. It comes from the broader weight of evidence that the biopsies now quietly support, which is that the muscle of a well-fed, well-moved body looks different at the level of the nucleus, and that difference is the kind you want.

What I keep returning to
There is a humility in this paper that I admire. The authors had the richest muscle dataset of its kind in the world, and they resisted every opportunity to announce a cause. What they offered instead was a careful description of two forces leaning on the same tissue from opposite sides, overlapping where they meet and separate where they do not. I think that is the right posture before a body. We observe carefully, we learn what the evidence will bear and no more, and we adjust the work without attachment to being right.

If I take one image from these 263 thighs, it is the small coordinated shift: hundreds of genes each moving a little, in the same direction, under the influence of how a person spent the previous year. Nothing dramatic happened in any one of them. The muscle simply leaned, over months, toward competence or away from it. That is how the body keeps its records, and it is how I would ask you to keep yours.

LAVV

Sources: Ciotlos DL, Hanks SC, Varshney A, et al. Inverse directions of association of higher physical activity and higher insulin resistance with human skeletal muscle fiber-type gene expression. iScience. 2026;29:117293. https://t.co/JI367SySQS. Open access, CC BY-NC-ND. Protein intake range cited for older adults draws on the ESPEN and PROT-AGE consensus positions rather than on this paper.
