text:
Why do I refer to myself as infamous in the post? It’s not because the nipple pierced pink hair members of the Konrad Haters Club™️ over on bluesky.

Senior year at the greatest nautical college in the world, you get custom coveralls with the training ship embroidered on the back and your nickname on the front.

My nickname was “Infamous.”

Partly because I’d accumulated the most demerits in recent school history. My record was eventually broken by a kid who took TEN YEARS to graduate, which frankly feels like cheating. If you spend a decade collecting demerits at a four-year college, that’s not a record. That’s a career.

But what made me infamous wasn’t the number of demerits. It was how I escaped the consequences.

Maritime academies have a threshold of demerits beyond which you’re expelled so most of my competitors were gone before coming close.

But I found a loophole… if you successfully appeal, convince someone to “lose” the triplicate paperwork, obtain a pardon from the Admiral, or perform some sufficiently noble act to offset your crimes, those demerits no longer count toward expulsion.

By the end of freshman year, I’d accumulated enough demerits to qualify for a dishonorable discharge from several third world navies, but through begging, borrowing, stealing, creative paperwork management, and occasional acts of conspicuous virtue, I’d somehow remained enrolled.

My other survival strategy was avoiding Commander Kenny, the school’s deputy commandant, at all cost.

Kenny was a grizzled Vietnam-era Army NCO who had somehow gotten himself commissioned as an O-5 in the Merchant Marine, a miracle I never dared investigate. He had the disposition of an inebriated & rabid German shepherd.

This worked until the end of freshman year, when everyone boarded our 565-foot training ship for the summer voyage to Europe.

It’s relatively easy to avoid someone on a college campus. It’s considerably harder aboard a ship, where the only reliable escape routes involve swimming.

Shortly after getting underway, the regiment assembled in a massive cargo hold for uniform inspection. The captain gave a speech. The commandant gave another. Then Kenny stepped forward.

“I only have one question,” he announced.

“Where is the INFAMOUS Cadet Konrad, AND HOW THE HELL HAS HE MANAGED TO AVOID DETENTION?”

Every head turned toward me.

“THE CRACKDOWN BEGINS NOW, KONRAD.”

He made my summer a living hell.

If something needed scraping, chipping, painting, cleaning, or extracting from a compartment that smelled like Satan’s septic tank after a swingers convention hosted by the Golden Corral, Kenny made certain I was the first to be voluntold.

But he’d overlooked one important detail.

I loved being at sea.

I loved ships, hard work, foreign ports, and practically everything about the profession. So while he was attempting to break my spirit through manual labor, I was mostly having a wonderful time.

I also may or may not have discovered that certain particularly unpleasant jobs required specialized tools, and that those tools had a mysterious tendency to relocate themselves to Davy Jones’ locker.

An old salt aboard once offered me some wisdom:

“Shit rolls downhill, kid. But ever since they invented the block and tackle, we’ve been able to haul it right back up.”

Words to live by.

Eventually, Kenny and I reached a truce, partly because he couldn’t figure out how to punish someone who genuinely enjoyed working aboard ship.

And partly because even the most disciplined ship occasionally needs something unusual accomplished in a foreign port.

Special provisions. Impossible favors. Bureaucratic obstacles that need to disappear.

And who better for the captain to call than the cadet with a demonstrated talent for accomplishing things without leaving behind a paper trail?

Which brings me back to the coveralls. 1/2

This past Monday I was out on the trails at Guana in NE Florida. While on the orange trail I encountered another hiker at a cross point and offered him water since he was not carrying any. We ended up heading the same direction so we struck up some small talk about where we were from and how long we had been in the area, and during the conversation learned we had both been at the Phish concert in Jacksonville the Friday before. I also learned he had never seen an alligator in the wild, so I showed him one of my observation spots and he got to see a baby that was out. We went our separate ways, but about 30 minutes later, crossed paths again and chatted a little more. We started talking about Goose and he mentioned he was trying to go to their shows in Nashville next month. I’m going to those shows myself and am trying to connect with this hiking trail stranger again. He seemed like a really cool, kind, jam band dude, so I want to try and find him and connect again- like bromance serendipity, I guess? 🤣

His name was either Brayden or Bryson. I’m horrible with names. So, if you’re out there and see this… let’s connect.

These are distinct from the larger number of states that have passed laws requiring parental notification or clarifying that not affirming a gender identity is not abuse.
Here are the most prominent examples:
Washington: SB 5599 (2023, signed by Gov. Jay Inslee)
This law changes notification rules for licensed shelters, host homes, and programs serving runaway or homeless youth. If a minor is seeking or receiving “gender-affirming treatment” (or reproductive health care), the facility can notify the state Department of Children, Youth & Families instead of the parents. The state is then supposed to offer family reunification services. 
Critics (including lawsuits and amicus briefs from other states) argue it allows children to be sheltered without parental knowledge or involvement when they are seeking gender-related medical interventions. Supporters say it protects runaway youth from potential abuse or neglect and does not change medical consent laws or authorize the state to permanently remove children. The law has faced legal challenges that reached higher courts.
California: AB 1955 / SAFETY Act (2024, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom)
This law prohibits school districts from requiring employees or contractors to disclose a student’s sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression to anyone (including parents) without the student’s consent. It also bars districts from enforcing “forced outing” policies. 
It was passed in response to several local school districts that had adopted policies requiring parental notification if a student requested different names, pronouns, or use of opposite-sex facilities. Critics say it allows schools to facilitate social transitions without parents’ knowledge. California officials have stated it does not prohibit staff from disclosing information if they choose to, and parents retain access to official education records under FERPA. The law has been the subject of ongoing federal and state court challenges.
Colorado: Kelly Loving Act (HB 25-1312, 2025)
As originally introduced, this bill would have required courts in custody cases to treat “deadnaming,” “misgendering,” or threats related to gender-affirming care as forms of “coercive control.” That would have been a mandatory factor when determining parenting time and the best interests of the child. 
Those specific custody provisions were stripped out before the bill passed and was signed into law. A similar provision in a 2026 bill was also removed. The final version of the Kelly Loving Act focuses on other anti-discrimination measures.
Other Related Cases and Context
There are documented cases (not always tied to a single new statute) of child protective services investigations or temporary removals in states including California, Oregon, Indiana, Maryland, and Virginia involving parents who refused to use preferred names/pronouns or consent to social or medical transition. Outcomes vary: some parents were later cleared, some cases involved co-occurring mental health or medical issues (e.g., eating disorders), and some parents allege non-affirmation was treated as a key factor. In 2026, the federal Administration for Children and Families issued guidance reminding states that declining to affirm a child’s gender identity is not, by itself, abuse under federal child welfare law.
In contrast, states such as Indiana, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee, West Virginia, Alabama, and others have enacted laws requiring schools to notify parents of requests for name/pronoun changes or social transition. Several states (including Texas, North Carolina, and Indiana) have also clarified that raising a child consistent with biological sex does not constitute abuse.

text:
When a Service Dog Retires, Honoring a Working Life
Sunday, Oct 18, 2026

Every working dog eventually hangs up the harness. Retirement is one of the hardest and most loving decisions a service dog team makes, and there is no single right age.

Guide Dogs for the Blind says retirement comes at different times in life. Dogs with heavier workloads, busier lifestyles or health concerns may retire younger, while others work into their senior years. A dog may lose the usual pep in its step or its enthusiasm for the work, and the handler, who knows the dog best, is often the first to notice the work losing its normal sharpness.

Canadian Guide Dogs for the Blind retires its guides at a maximum age of eleven, and earlier if a dog develops health issues, slows down or shows guiding behavior that could become a safety issue. Guide Dogs, the UK sight loss charity, starts discussing retirement when a dog is around eight years old, though the dog may keep working a few more years. It recommends vet checkups every six months until age nine, then every three months.

Where does a retired dog go? Many stay home as a beloved pet. Guide Dogs for the Blind gives handlers who have worked with their dog for twelve months or longer the first option to keep their guide or place the dog with a trusted family member or friend. Otherwise it offers the dog to its puppy raisers, then finds another loving home.

Feelings of grief and loss are normal when a partnership ends, Guide Dogs notes, and talking with friends, family or fellow handlers can help. Here at home, our own Odin is 8 1/2 and went almost blind this past year, adapting with his nose and ears. Every dog ages on its own timeline, and every one of them has earned a soft landing.

Watch Dogs of Service from Iowa PBS on YouTube

Sources: Guide Dogs for the Blind client guidance on retirement, Canadian Guide Dogs for the Blind FAQ via @CDNGuideDogs, Guide Dogs UK retirement guidance via @guidedogs, photos via Wikimedia Commons by DASGAK zzo Hoamiie, CC0, Whispyhistory, CC0, and Atlas815, CC BY SA 4.0.

text:
The Nature of Sin: A Biblical, Lexical, and Confessional Analysis

Jack Kettler

Abstract

This paper offers a concise theological examination of the nature of sin according to Scripture and the Reformed confessional tradition. Sin is defined as any want of conformity to or active transgression of the moral law of God, encompassing both sins of commission and sins of omission. The study draws on key biblical texts, the Westminster Shorter Catechism, lexical analysis of the principal New Testament terms for sin, and Charles Hodge’s systematic exposition. It further situates the doctrine of sin in relation to original sin, total depravity, and the Fall, before concluding with the biblical and confessional resolution of human sin in the person and work of Christ.

Keywords: sin, law of God, commission, omission, original sin, total depravity, imputation, Reformed theology

1. Introduction

The doctrine of sin holds a foundational place in Christian theology, especially in the Reformed tradition. A precise understanding of sin is indispensable to a coherent account of the human condition, the necessity of redemption, and the work of Christ. This paper examines the nature of sin by integrating biblical testimony, confessional standards, lexical evidence, and classical systematic theology. The aim is to set forth a clear, historically grounded definition of sin and to show how it is resolved through the satisfaction and imputation accomplished by Jesus Christ.

2. Definition of Sin

“Sin may be defined as any lack of conformity, whether active or passive, to the moral law of God. This deficiency may appear in an act, a thought, or an inward disposition or state

Two complementary aspects are customarily distinguished. A sin of “commission” consists in the deliberate transgression of the revealed will of God—the explicit breaking of divine law. A sin of “omission” consists in the ethical failure to perform that which one is able and obliged to perform—the absence of conformity to what the law requires. In an active sense, the doing of what God forbids constitutes a sin of commission. In a negative sense, the failure to do what God commands constitutes a sin of omission.

Illustrative sins of commission include blasphemy, fornication, adultery, homosexuality, lying, drunkenness, murder, and slander. Illustrative sins of omission include remaining silent in the face of falsehood, withholding the truth, refusing to do good to those who require it when one has the power to assist, leaving necessary duties unfinished until opportunity has passed, and remaining silent in the face of evil.” (Erickson 578).

3. Biblical Foundations

Scripture confirms these definitions:

“Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law” (1 John 3:4).

This text from 1 John addresses the sin of commission.

“Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin” (James 4:17).

This text from James addresses the sin of omission.

Additional passages establish the universality of sin and the necessity of repentance and union with Christ:

·         “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3).

·         “My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

·         “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).

·         “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

·         “All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death” (1 John 5:17).

·         “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death” (James 1:15).

4. Confessional Definition

The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Question 14) supplies a precise formulation:

Q. What is sin?

A. Sin is any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, the law of God.

The Catechism’s proof texts are 1 John 3:4, James 4:17, and Romans 3:23 (“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God”).

5. Lexical Analysis of the New Testament Vocabulary

“W. E. Vine’s “Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words” offers a detailed treatment of the principal terms for sin. The noun “hamartia” (literally “a missing of the mark”) is the most comprehensive term for moral obliquity. It is employed (a) of sin as a principle or source of action (e.g., Rom. 3:9; 5:12, 13, 20; 6:1–2; 7:7–13); (b) of sin as a governing power personified (e.g., Rom. 5:21; 6:12, 14; 7:11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 25; 8:2); (c) as a generic term sometimes inclusive of concrete wrongdoing (e.g., John 8:21, 34, 46; 9:41; 15:22, 24; 1 John 1:7–8; 3:4, 8–9); and (d) of a specific sinful deed (e.g., Matt. 12:31; Acts 7:60; Jas. 1:15; 2:9; 4:17; 5:15, 20; 1 John 5:16).

The related noun “hamartēma” denotes an act of disobedience to divine law (e.g., Mark 3:28; Rom. 3:25; 1 Cor. 6:18). The verb “hamartanō” (“to miss the mark”) is used of sinning against God, Christ, man, one’s own body, or earthly masters (e.g., Matt. 27:4; Luke 15:18, 21; John 5:14; 8:11; Rom. 2:12; 3:23; 5:12; 6:15; 1 Cor. 6:18; 7:28; 1 John 1:10; 2:1; 3:6, 8–9). Christ is uniformly predicated as without sin in every respect (2 Cor. 5:21; 1 John 3:5; John 14:30; John 8:46; Heb. 4:15; 1 Pet. 2:22) (Vine 1045–1047).”

6. The Protestant Doctrine of Sin (Charles Hodge)

“Charles Hodge summarizes the consensus of the Protestant churches at the time of the Reformation. Founding their doctrine upon moral and religious consciousness and upon the Word of God, they defined sin as the transgression of, or want of conformity to, the divine law. Melanchthon, Gerhard, Baier, and Vitringa all employ formulations that identify sin as “anomia”—a discrepancy from, or non-congruence with, the law of God that obliges the sinner to punishment under the order of divine justice.

Hodge extracts five propositions from these definitions: (1) sin is a specific evil, differing from all other forms of evil; (2) sin stands in necessary relation to law, so that where there is no law there can be no sin; (3) the law in view is the law of God, not merely the law of reason, conscience, or expediency; (4) sin consists essentially in the want of conformity of a rational creature to the nature or law of God; and (5) sin includes both guilt and moral pollution.

Consciousness itself discloses that sin is a specific evil known immediately by moral beings. It further discloses that sin is related to law: the word “ought” implies obligation under authority. The law that binds the conscience is that which has been revealed in the constitution of human nature, the Decalogue, the Mosaic institutions, and the whole of Scripture. Sin is neither a mere limitation of being, nor a subjective state without character before God, nor merely something unwise or inexpedient; it possesses a distinct character that includes both guilt and pollution.” (Hodge, Vol. 2, 180–182).

7. Related Doctrinal Categories

·         “Original sin” denotes the sinful state and condition into which all human beings are born, comprising both imputed guilt (the guilt of Adam’s first sin reckoned to their account) and inherited corruption (a disposition toward sin).

·         “Total depravity” affirms that the inherent corruption of humankind “extends to every part of our nature, to all the faculties and powers of both soul and body; and that there is no spiritual good, that is, good in relation to God, in the sinner at all, but only perversion.”

·         The “Fall of man” refers to the disobedience of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, whereby they transgressed the divine prohibition against eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, resulting in God’s curse upon them and all their posterity.

8. The Resolution of Sin in Christ

The Heidelberg Catechism (Question and Answer 56) articulates the believer’s confession concerning the forgiveness of sins:

·         Q. What believest thou concerning “the forgiveness of sins”?

·         A. That God, for the sake of Christ’s satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, neither my corrupt nature, against which I have to struggle all my life long; but will graciously impute to me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never be condemned before the tribunal of God.

The apostle Paul writes:

“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Matthew Poole comments:

“Christ knew no sin, as he was guilty of no sin… but God made him to be sin for us. He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). Our sins were reckoned to him… He was made a sacrifice for our sins, a sin offering… That we might be made the righteousness of God in him; that so his righteousness might be imputed to us… As Christ was not made sin by any sin inherent in him, so neither are we made righteous by any righteousness inherent in us, but by the righteousness of Christ imputed to us” (Poole 616).

9. Conclusion

Sin is any want of conformity to, or transgression of, the law of God—whether by commission or omission, whether as principle, power, or particular act. Scripture, confessional standards, lexical data, and classical Reformed theology converge upon this definition. The universal guilt and corruption of humanity find their sole remedy in the substitutionary work of Christ, who was made sin for us that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

Notes

1.      Millard Erickson, “Christian Theology” (Grand Rapids, MI: Baker), 578.

2.      W. E. Vine, “An Expository Dictionary of New Testament Words” (Iowa Falls, IA: Riverside Book and Bible House), 1045–1047.

3.      Charles Hodge, “Systematic Theology”, vol. 2 (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans), 180–182.

4.      Matthew Poole, “Matthew Poole’s Commentary on the Holy Bible”, vol. 3 (Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 1985), 616.

Further Resources

·         Herman Bavinck, “The Origin of Sin,” https://t.co/5oytCJuR6g.

·         J. C. Ryle, “A True Understanding of Sin,” https://t.co/5oytCJuR6g.

·         Rebecca Writes, “Theological Terms in A–Z,” https://t.co/WYdiMx76FD.

Selected Quotations

·         “Here is a beautiful antithesis. In ourselves we are scattered, in Christ we are gathered together… Our sins overwhelm us, but they are laid on Christ by whom we are unburdened.” — John Calvin, “Sermons on Isaiah’s Prophecy of the Death and Passion of Christ”, 66–67.

·         “No one knows the one-hundredth part of the sin that clings to his soul.” — John Calvin.

·         “Sin consists in doing, saying, thinking, or imagining anything that is not in perfect conformity with the mind and law of God.” — J. C. Ryle, “Holiness”, 2.

·         “Sin is a disease which pervades and runs through every part of our moral constitution and every faculty of our minds.” — J. C. Ryle, “Holiness”, 3.

·         “Any sin is more or less heinous depending upon the honor and majesty of the one whom we had offended. Since God is of infinite honor, infinite majesty, and infinite holiness, the slightest sin is of infinite consequence.” — Jonathan Edwards.

Declaration

“For transparency, I note that I used Grok, an AI tool developed by xAI, and Grammarly AI for editorial assistance in drafting, organizing, and refining the manuscript’s clarity and grammar, as indicated in the article’s attribution. All theological arguments, exegesis, and interpretations are my own, and I take full responsibility for the content.” –  Jack Kettler

text:
Tanner McKee has a Super Bowl ring and two career starts.

Both of those starts came in the final game of a season, when nothing was on the line.

Today Jalen Hurts has a blood clot in his calf, so McKee starts for the Eagles against the Panthers.

It is the first start of his life that actually matters.

Here is the whole thing.

McKee grew up in Corona, California, and he was a big deal. Four star quarterback. Elite 11 finalist. More than 30 scholarship offers.

Then at 16 a mole on his forehead came back positive for melanoma.

Here is the scene. A 16 year old sitting in a pre op room in a surgical gown. Purple X marks drawn on his forehead and his neck. Phone in his hand, scrolling messages from college coaches offering him scholarships.

He looked at his mom and said this.

"If they only knew."

They cut it out. No chemotherapy. No radiation.

Here is his father on that week.

"Is his football career done? Are our lives going to totally change?"

Then he signed with Stanford. And then he left.

McKee belongs to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter day Saints, and he decided when he was eight years old that he would serve a mission. So at 18, with 30 offers sitting behind him, he got on a plane to Curitiba, Brazil for 21 months.

Nick Saban told him Alabama would wait.

He packed a football. For the first ten months it basically sat there.

"I remember throwing the ball over power lines and little kids being all excited."

The kids could not figure out why the ball was not round.

He lost about 15 pounds of muscle. His weight room was makeshift weights and walking.

Somebody asked if he could play right then.

"If I had to play a game right now, it would be tough. I'd get crushed."

"I'm 100 percent missionary. I'm not too worried about how I'm going to come back as an athlete."

Then one of his mission leaders tracked down a local semi pro team called the Coritiba Crocodiles and asked if they would practice with him. The players were anywhere from 14 to 40 years old. Before anybody could start they had to shoo chickens and roosters off the field, which had no lines on it.

He spent the day teaching a receiver named Athos how to high point a football.

Here is what Athos said about him.

"I identified with him because I also used to have heart issues when I was young."

McKee enrolled at Stanford at 20. In his fourth college start he beat Oregon, the number three team in the country, in overtime.

He went in the sixth round, 188th pick.

Now the honest part. He is 1 and 1 as a starter and he has under 600 passing yards in his entire NFL career. This could be one afternoon and then back to the clipboard.

But nobody else in that building put two football years down on purpose and then went and got them back.

He learned Portuguese out there. His teammates call him the Mormon Missile.

Today he gets a start that counts.

text:
They Built the World’s Largest Vineyard. We Built Over It.

The story of Rancho Cucamonga...

Before the warehouses, vineyards stood.

Before the loading docks, harvests took place.

East of Los Angeles, an Italian immigrant helped build a wine empire most Americans have never heard of.

His name was Secondo Guasti.

Around 1900, he and his investors began transforming Cucamonga’s dry, rocky land into an enormous vineyard. His Italian Vineyard Company eventually controlled roughly 5,000 acres—an operation promoted as the world’s largest vineyard.

He built a community around it: workers’ homes, a school, a store, a firehouse, a church.

Families planted roots alongside the vines.

The wider Cucamonga district became a giant of American wine. Before World War II, vineyards covered more than 27,000 acres around Rancho Cucamonga.

Then Southern California’s expansion reached the rows.

Housing. Roads. Commercial development. Eventually, immense warehouses.

The arithmetic overwhelmed the agriculture: land could bring a family far more money as a development site than as a lifetime of grape harvests.

Imagine spending decades farming—and receiving an offer that could finally secure your children’s future.

That is how a landscape disappears. One understandable decision at a time.

But another outcome was possible.

In 1968, Napa County established an agricultural preserve, restricting subdivision and prioritizing agriculture across thousands of acres.

Cucamonga’s vineyards largely gave way to the growing metropolis.

This was a working wine country. Affordable bottles. Immigrant families. Generations of knowledge carried from distant villages into California soil.

Today, surviving vineyards and preservation efforts still defend pieces of that inheritance.

They deserve our attention before the next piece disappears.

Because a century-old vine cannot be replaced by putting a grape cluster on a shopping-center sign.

We know how to calculate land value.

We are much worse at calculating the cost of losing what grows there.

text:
Yes, it is generally legal, appropriate, and common for someone to pick up food from a food bank or pantry on behalf of a disabled person who cannot go themselves.
Legality
There is no general law against helping someone obtain food assistance this way. Food banks and pantries are private nonprofits (often distributing USDA commodities under programs like TEFAP or CSFP), and they set their own rules. Most explicitly allow proxies or authorized representatives for people who are disabled, homebound, ill, or have transportation barriers.
The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act protects good-faith food donations and distribution by nonprofits, but that is about liability for the food itself, not about proxy pickups. Proxy arrangements are a standard, accepted operational practice.
Appropriateness
It is appropriate and often encouraged. Food banks exist to help people who need food; disability or mobility issues are among the most common reasons they create proxy policies. Doing this with the person’s clear permission respects their autonomy and dignity. Many organizations also offer home delivery or other accommodations for homebound clients when available.
How Common It Is
Very common. Numerous food banks, pantries, and federal commodity programs (such as CSFP for seniors) maintain official proxy forms specifically for disability, health concerns, or transportation limitations. Examples include state CSFP programs (California, Washington, and others), regional food banks, and local pantries that require a signed authorization, household information, and sometimes ID from the proxy.
Typical requirements include:
•A signed proxy/authorization form from the client naming the person picking up.
•Basic household details (size, sometimes ages).
•The proxy presenting ID.
•Periodic renewal of the form (often annually).
Policies vary by organization—some are flexible for one-time or emergency pickups; others want the form in advance. Always check with the specific food bank or pantry beforehand.
Practical tip: Contact the food bank, explain the disability situation, and ask about their proxy process. Many will provide the form or walk you through it. Some also coordinate deliveries or other help for people who cannot leave home.
(Note: You are in British Columbia, Canada. Canadian food banks generally operate similarly and commonly allow authorized pickups or deliveries for clients who cannot attend in person, though exact rules depend on the local organization. The principles of legality and appropriateness are the same.)
In short: With the disabled person’s authorization and following the food bank’s process, this is a normal and helpful thing to do.

text:
In 1891, Billy Sunday walked away from about $400 a month (roughly $14,000 today) to take a job that paid $83.

He was one of the fastest players in baseball, and Philadelphia had just signed him to a three-year deal. He had a new baby at home and an invalid brother to support.

But four years earlier, he had been drinking with teammates outside a Chicago saloon when a gospel band marched by. 

He followed them into the Pacific Garden Mission and walked out a Bible-believing Christian. He could not shake the feeling that he was being called to preach full time.

He told his wife, Nell. She told him that if the Lord was talking to him, he had better listen.

So, he asked for his release. When word got out, Cincinnati offered him even more money. He said no to them too and went to work for the Chicago YMCA.

He never stopped playing ball, though. He just brought it to the pulpit. Sunday sprinted across the stage, slid into imaginary bases, stood on chairs, and pounded the furniture. He preached like a man trying to beat out a throw to first.

Twenty years later he was the most famous preacher in America. Cities had to build wooden tabernacles to hold his crowds.

By some estimates he preached to 100 million people without a microphone.

Quoted after: Students For Liberty ( on Facebook)
>>>
Once Upon a Time in Sweden

Astrid Lindgren had spent three decades as the country's most loved storyteller. Pippi Longstocking, the strongest girl in the world, made her one of the best-selling children's authors on earth, and she had backed the ruling Social Democrats for most of her life. 

Then She Did the Arithmetic

In early 1976 Lindgren worked through her own taxes. As a self-employed writer she owed state and municipal income tax, plus the social fees an employer would normally pay on a worker's wages. At the top of her income they added up to 102%: for every extra krona her books brought in, the state took the whole krona and billed her two öre more. 

"Now I Will Tell You a Fairy Tale"

Lindgren turned her tax bill into a fairy tale, and the Stockholm evening paper Expressen ran it on March 10, 1976. Its heroine, a writer named Pomperipossa, lived in a land called Monismania, where wise men had governed for more than 40 years. She handed over 80 to 83% of every extra krona without complaint, because the kingdom's tax master was "reasonable." 

"Did You Know Your Marginal Tax This Year Is 102%?"

Pomperipossa worked out that on two million kronor of income she would keep 5,000. That was not much in a country where salted herring, "once the poor man's food," had become terribly expensive. 

In Monismania, Welfare Paid Better Than Writing Books

Then a wonderful thought struck her: she could go on welfare. "And so the welfare-supported Pomperipossa lived happily ever after." She also had a message for the rulers: "Tremble, wise men, and tighten the night watch around your treasure chests!" 

The Finance Minister Answered From Parliament

Gunnar Sträng had run Sweden's treasury since 1955, and he was in parliament that same day for a debate on the economy. From the floor, he called the fable "an interesting combination of stimulating literary ability and deep ignorance" of tax policy, and the line Swedes remember is his dismissal that Mrs. Lindgren could tell stories but couldn't count. 

She Offered Him a Trade

Lindgren turned his line back on him: "Gunnar Sträng has always been good at telling stories, but he has never learned to count." Then she suggested the two of them switch jobs. Prime Minister Olof Palme later conceded on television that her numbers were right. 

Six Months Later, Sweden Voted

On September 19, 1976, the Social Democrats were voted out of government for the first time in 44 years, and Sträng's 21 years at the Finance Ministry ended with them. Nuclear power also shaped the race, and so did the January arrest of Ingmar Bergman, Sweden's most celebrated film director, on tax evasion charges that prosecutors dropped two months later. Pomperipossa is still credited with helping turn the vote. 

Swedes Still Call It the Pomperipossa Effect

A marginal tax rate above 100% has carried her character's name ever since. Swedish lawmakers were still invoking Pomperipossa in parliamentary debates more than forty years later.

text:
BETRAYAL
/An Elegy for Ukraine - and a Lament for the Free World/
.
A tsunami of decisions from the USA
sweeps over Ukraine, deepening its pain.
Promises dissolve like mist at dawn,
while trust lies shattered beneath the rain.
Just promises and lies! Nothing else, for how long yet!
.
Sanctions unfortunately remain unfulfilled,
Starshield's support is cast in doubt.
The victim bears the blame for war,
while truth struggles to cry out.
Treason hanging in the air!
.
An energy truce was promised,
yet Russia strikes the grid again and again.
Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Odesa
are scarred by missiles, fire, and pain.
Do not you see it, Donald Trump?
.
Tens of thousands lose their light;
repair crews battle through the night.
Drones and ballistic missiles descend,
while homes are shattered, lives come to an end.
Defend the skies, the endless cry!
.
Ukraine has offered peace before,
a ceasefire without demands.
Even elections were put on the table,
if silence could return to the land.
Yet Russia answers with renewed attacks.
Ukraine's pleas falling on deaf ears in the Kremlin.
.
Europe shoulders freedom's burden,
while questions haunt the halls of power:
why ease the pressure on the aggressor
as Ukraine endures its darkest hour?
Solidarity it is that counts.
.
Sikorski speaks of Europe's burden,
of aid sustained by European hands,
while broken promises cast their shadows
across a continent that still stands.
“The USA haven’t spent
a single cent on Ukraine
since January 2025,
so more than 1.5 years.
We in Europe are doing it.” - He said.
.
Just matter factly...
And it could not be worse...
It is always... promises and lies.
First saying yes
and then striking with saying no,
devastating one,
The Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act
waived by president Donald Trump.
The Starshield system cancelled for Ukraine.
The diesel deal with Russia.
Blaming president Zhelenskyy
By Donald Trump,
instead of Putin for the war.
Numerous other facts, promises and lies, indeed.
.
Divine Choir:
Let truth be thunder, justice flame,
Let peace rise higher than revenge.
No peace can grow from wishful blindness,
no justice rise where lies prevail.
If freedom is betrayed for profit,
the free world's conscience, too, will fail.
So let us all stand triumphantly up
for freedom and peace Ukraine fully deserves.
.

text:
The key insight here is not socialism va capitalism. That’s been known and articulately expressed countless times. The buried lede here is that storytelling is what determines the outcome. Pro-liberty capitalists and constitutionalists have had the facts and arguments for a hundred years, but they gave up storytelling because they thought it was cheap, childish, or manipulative. They thought facts and arguments were enough, because they should be enough.

But people are made of story. They follow story. They participate in story. Its truthfulness is not a factor in whether or not they so do. Marx and the Frankfurt School spun a story. It was a poorly written story and obviously unfactual, but it was the only story. The opposition (their parents) were not offering a story. The capitalists weren’t weaving tales of heroism and derring do for their children. They were much too practical for such things. So in the absence of anything better, the children followed and participated in the only story they were offered. Off they went after the pied piper. His piping wasn’t even that good, but it was the only song in their lives.

And the capitalists and constitutionalists and libertarians all got to the debate and found no one there but each other, so they debated. And any some point they looked out at the audience chamber and found it empty. Their children were off following the storytellers, burning and ransacking what their parents had built and calling it victory.

text:
🇺🇸 LEU: From $464 to $115. What Drove the Selloff and What It Would Take to Bring the Bulls Back
Today I'm taking a closer look at LEU: Centrus Energy Corp.

LEU hit an intraday high of $464.25 on October 16, 2025. A year later, the stock closed at $114.94, down 75.24% from that peak. Measured from the last closing price before the period began, $436 on October 15, 2025, the return over the full period was -73.64%. Calculations are my own, based on historical price data. [1]

My take: this selloff reflects a combination of sky-high expectations for nuclear power, uneven near-term results, the cost of scaling up production, and shareholder dilution. Centrus is moving the project forward, but the cash has to go out the door now, while most of the payoff from new capacity is still years away. The market has started putting more weight on that timing gap. [6][12][14][23]

What Investors Are Really Buying With Centrus

Today's business and tomorrow's business have different economics. Currently, most revenue comes from supplying fuel and enrichment services sourced from third parties, primarily to existing nuclear power plants. Revenue depends on the execution of long-term contracts, delivery schedules, and the spread between purchase and sale prices. A separative work unit, or SWU, measures the work involved in enriching uranium; its price is not the price of uranium coming out of a mine. [3]

What investors were willing to pay up for was the prospect of large-scale enrichment using Centrus's own production capacity. LEU, or low-enriched uranium, fuels today's nuclear power plants. HALEU, a more highly enriched fuel, serves some next-generation reactor designs. Centrus is developing both, so its business opportunity also extends to the existing reactor fleet. [12][13]

The key valuation question, then, is how much future profit and cash flow the business will generate per share once the plants are built, the costs are covered, and the financing is in place. Rising demand for fuel alone does not answer that question.

The Selloff Started Long Before September's Offering

The stock was already taking hits on October 22, 2025, when it fell about 16.5% to $314.83. The entire decline to $115 therefore cannot be pinned on an event that happened almost a year later. Further sharp legs down came around earnings releases and financing decisions. [1]

November's third-quarter report showed why revenue alone can give a misleading picture. Revenue was $74.9 million, but the company posted a gross loss of $4.3 million. The LEU segment alone recorded a gross loss of $7.8 million. Positive net income of $3.9 million therefore did not mean the core business was generating healthy margins. The company pointed to the mix of contracts being fulfilled and the timing of deliveries. One quarter was not enough to conclude that demand had suffered a lasting collapse. [4]

On November 6, Centrus also announced an at-the-market, or ATM, equity offering program of up to $1 billion. The program allowed Centrus to raise capital over time; the company did not issue $1 billion worth of stock in a single day. LEU fell about 14.7% during the November 6 session. Investors were digesting weak margins alongside the prospect of a rising share count. [1][5]

The biggest earnings shock came in February. After the company released its report following the close on February 10, 2026, the stock fell from $264.99 to $185.20 over the February 11 and 12 sessions, a decline of 30.1%. Fourth-quarter net income dropped from $53.7 million to $17.8 million, while diluted earnings per share fell from $3.20 to $0.79. Initial revenue guidance for 2026 was $425 million to $475 million, with a midpoint that was essentially flat versus 2025. [1][6]

For full-year 2025, Centrus reported revenue of $448.7 million and net income of $77.8 million, compared with $442.0 million and $73.2 million, respectively, a year earlier. Yet diluted earnings per share, or EPS, fell from $4.47 to $3.90. The company earned more, but those earnings were spread across a larger share count. The diluted calculation also includes potential shares from convertible instruments. [3][6]

On the February earnings call, management also explained that part of the margin deterioration reflected a shipment of Russian material slipping into the following quarter. That lower-cost material would have reduced the average cost of inventory. During the Q&A, management pointed to a transportation issue without attributing that particular delay to a lack of permits.

The point to keep in mind: delivery timing can swing results significantly even when end demand has not changed. [7]

Revenue Is Growing, but Earnings per Share Remain Under Pressure

After the first quarter, management raised revenue guidance to $450 million to $500 million. That was a meaningful improvement over the February outlook and pushed back against the idea that the business was falling apart. The range was reaffirmed in August. [8][9]

First-half revenue reached $252.8 million, up 11.1% from a year earlier. Reported net income, however, fell from $56.1 million to $26.8 million, a decline of 52.2%. On the company's adjusted basis, which excludes expansion preparation costs and stock-based compensation, net income was much steadier: $62.2 million versus $63.1 million. Even so, adjusted diluted EPS fell from $3.63 to $2.81, down 22.6%. Percentage changes are my calculations. [9]

Adjusted earnings help assess business performance before those charges. Reported earnings also capture the expansion costs the company is incurring. Stock-based compensation carries an economic cost even when it does not trigger an immediate cash outflow.

Spending is also set to accelerate. On the August earnings call, management said it expected the pace of spending to pick up in the coming months. The full-year plan of $350 million to $500 million covered broader capital deployment, including certain prepayments and preparatory costs.

Important: this entire figure should not be treated as accounting CapEx alone or as the final price tag for the whole project. [7][27]

The Spending Comes Now, With New Capacity Still Targeted for 2029

On December 19, 2025, Centrus announced the start of centrifuge manufacturing for commercial enrichment. The first new capacity is expected to come online in 2029. As of the end of the period covered here, that still left several years of project execution ahead. [12]

In January, the company was selected for a $900 million U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) award to expand HALEU capacity; on July 1, it announced that it had signed a fixed-price contract. Including additional fuel purchase options, the total value reaches $1.07 billion. [13] Payments are tied to milestones: about 40% of the base funding is scheduled for 2028 and 30% for 2031. Most of the money is therefore due to arrive in later years. [10]

The industrial progress is real, but it comes with deadlines, costs, and responsibility for delivering the project. Savings announcements deserve the same careful reading. In March, Centrus and Palantir said they had identified nearly $300 million in potential savings on the expansion. Those are potential savings that still have to be borne out in the project's budget and execution. [22]

The stock could begin a sustained rally before 2029 if investors gain a firmer basis for assessing costs, timing, and future profitability. What matters for valuation is growing confidence that the buildout will create sufficient value per share.

Why a $4.5 Billion Backlog Doesn't Settle the Investment Case

At the end of June, reported backlog, meaning future orders and commitments, totaled $4.5 billion. The LEU portion included about $700 million tied to the existing supply business and $3 billion in sales linked to future production. Of that $3 billion, approximately $2.4 billion was covered by definitive agreements. [11]

In August, the company said future orders were no longer subject to additional conditions related to financing the expansion. That is meaningful progress, but operational conditions tied to bringing production online remain, and some arrangements still require definitive agreements. Revenue will be recognized as deliveries take place over many years. Backlog therefore shows the scale of future sales, but on its own it does not tell us how much the company will earn or when the cash will arrive. [11]

A separate concern involves roughly $800 million of Technical Solutions backlog. In its August 5 release, Centrus said the DOE's proposed FY2027 budget did not provide for continued funding of the existing HALEU cascade's operation. At the time, the DOE had also indicated that it did not intend to exercise further options under the legacy operating contract. That backlog included unexercised options and funding that had not yet been awarded. [9]

The new $900 million expansion contract and the future of the existing facility therefore need to be assessed separately. As management explained during the August Q&A, the increase in commercial backlog did not include the new DOE contract. [27]

The most recently disclosed extension of the legacy agreement covered facility maintenance and storage through September 30, with no further production under that option. Centrus was working toward commercial use of the cascade. In the sources I reviewed, I found no confirmation that its future status had been resolved by October 16. That is not proof of a permanent shutdown, but it remains a material question that needs an answer. [10][13]

September's Financing: More Flexibility for the Company, More Dilution for Shareholders

Centrus had already raised $390.4 million in gross proceeds during 2025 through the November ATM program, at an average price of $269.21 per share, according to the CFO on the February earnings call. [7]

In September, the company completed another offering with gross proceeds of $500 million and estimated net proceeds of about $489 million. The September 11 filings confirm that the securities were issued. The offering included 500,000 shares and pre-funded warrants covering approximately 2.01 million additional shares, with just $0.10 per share left to pay upon exercise. Economically, these are almost fully paid shares. [15][16]

Together, that amounts to approximately 2.51 million new shares or their economic equivalents. Using the most recently disclosed base of about 19.95 million Class A and Class B shares, this simplified calculation implies an approximately 11.2% reduction in an existing shareholder's ownership percentage. This is a pro forma estimate that does not account for other potential changes in the share count. [10][16]

The offering also included conventional warrants covering approximately 6.99 million shares. They give holders the right to buy shares at specified prices; they do not mean that all of those shares were issued upfront. The four series have exercise prices of approximately $226.86, $272.24, $317.61, and $362.98. The potential additional $2 billion in proceeds would require full cash exercise of the warrants. With the stock at $115, those proceeds cannot be treated as guaranteed financing. [14][16]

Likewise, the $199.64 offering price is not proof that the stock itself "has to be worth that much": the price included both a share and an allocation of accompanying warrants. Over the two trading sessions after September 9, the stock fell from $181.49 to $152.31, down 16.1%. The offering was a specific event associated with that leg of the selloff. It does not explain the preceding months. [2][14]

Russia: A Strategic Opportunity for Tomorrow, a Supply Dependency Today

Reducing Russian supplies increases the strategic value of new U.S. capacity. At the same time, according to the latest filing, more than half of the fuel scheduled for delivery to customers through 2027 was sourced under the TENEX agreement. Other sources were insufficient to fully replace that supplier. Deliveries require the relevant import approvals, Russian licenses for individual shipments, and workable transportation arrangements. [10]

The August presentation puts several key dates side by side: the end of the main TENEX supply period in 2027, the Orano agreement running through 2030, and the first new cascade in 2029. The full U.S. ban on Russian LEU imports beginning in 2028 makes securing supply during the transition especially important. It does not automatically mean a fuel shortage; it means inventories, alternative supplies, and the timing of customer commitments need to be examined carefully. [12][17]

The Case for a Rebound: Customer Commitments Are Firming Up

June brought a letter of intent with Oklo for multiyear fuel supplies to as many as five Aurora units, with deliveries planned to begin in 2029. It called for a definitive agreement to be negotiated later, with prepayments a possibility. Turning that document into a binding contract would be another test. [18]

On August 6, Centrus announced a definitive LEU/HALEU supply agreement with X-energy that included prepayments to support the expansion. A contract with Radiant followed on September 9, then another with Antares on September 17, both also including prepayments. The announcements for the latter two companies called for deliveries to begin before the end of the decade. Full contract values and schedules were not disclosed, leaving too little information to calculate their impact on earnings over the next few quarters. [19][20][21]

Customer prepayments matter for two reasons: they show that customers have more skin in the game, and they can reduce the need to fund construction through additional stock offerings. The questions are how much, when the cash arrives, and on what terms. An offtake agreement reduces some demand risk, but its economic value still depends on production starting and the customer's own project moving forward.

Why Positive Headlines Failed to Stop the Slide

The available excerpt from a September analysis in The Wall Street Journal cited Citi's Vikram Bagri, who argued that the nuclear sector faces a growing number of publicly traded companies and more new share issuance, while higher interest rates reduce the present value of capital-intensive projects whose returns lie far in the future. That is Bagri's interpretation of sector conditions, and it fits the challenges facing Centrus. It does not allow us to assign specific portions of the 75% selloff to individual factors. [23]

On October 14, the BLS reported that U.S. CPI rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year. That backdrop makes it harder to rebuild lofty valuations based on distant cash flows. LEU lost 19.3% in the final week of the period covered here, measured from the October 9 close. In the sources I reviewed, I found no new negative company announcement that could, on its own, explain the declines on October 14 and 16. [2][24]

Analysts Are Pricing In Different Degrees of Success

On September 3, Jefferies initiated coverage of Centrus with a Hold rating and a $169 price target. According to Investing. com's account, the bank believed the stock's price at the time already reflected a successful scale-up around 2030. Further upside would depend, among other things, on how tight the fuel market remains through the 2030s. That is a useful lens for examining the assumptions behind the valuation. [25]

Benzinga's summary also shows Stifel cutting its price target from $246 to $216 on August 25 while maintaining a Buy rating, and Guggenheim initiating coverage on October 8 with a Buy rating and a $167 target. These are not my price targets or forecasts for the next few weeks. I do not have the full original research reports, so I cannot supply the missing rationale or time horizons. For additional context, Guggenheim was the lead underwriter of the September offering. [14][26]

What Would Bring the Bulls Back

First, the buildout would need to move more clearly from plans to execution: finished equipment, construction documentation, suppliers lined up, and credible cost estimates. It would be especially useful to know how much capital is needed to reach a meaningful initial level of production and how much funding still needs to be secured.

Second, new agreements should make deliveries and financing more predictable. Confirmed prepayments, letters of intent becoming definitive contracts, and a resolution of the existing HALEU cascade's status would all matter. The number of customer names tells us less than the terms of their contracts.

Third, Centrus needs margins, deliveries, and cash flows that can bridge the period before 2029. At the end of June, the company had about $1.87 billion in unrestricted cash and approximately $1.21 billion in debt principal. First-half operating cash flow was negative $16.7 million, while cash capital expenditures, or CapEx, totaled $94.8 million. These are historical figures that predate the September offering. [10]

Fourth, the improvement would need to translate into value per share. Persistently rising capital needs alongside a weak stock price would make new equity offerings increasingly costly for existing shareholders. Delivering the project with less dilution, on the other hand, would strengthen the case for a higher valuation.

The Next Catalysts to Watch

Third-quarter results and updated guidance. The key items will be margins, cash flow, the pace of spending, the share count, and whether the company is on track for $450 million to $500 million in revenue and $350 million to $500 million in capital deployment. As of the cutoff for this analysis, I had not found an earnings release date confirmed by the company, so I am not assigning a specific day. [11]

Q4 2026: construction documentation and the first new centrifuge. The August plan called for completing the first new centrifuge in Oak Ridge by year-end, finishing the Certified-for-Construction documentation needed to proceed with construction, and signing agreements with all critical partners. Agreements were in place with about 75% of those partners at the time. The first centrifuge is a test of execution; the first new production cascade remains scheduled for 2029. [11][17]

December 2026: the planned Investor Day in Piketon. The CEO announced it on the August earnings call. It could be an important opportunity for updates on strategy, timing, costs, and the outlook. No specific date was given in that announcement. What would matter for valuation is new, measurable information about the project's economics. [27]

Decisions on the existing HALEU facility. Clarity on the terms of its commercial use and its relationship with the DOE could reduce the current uncertainty. Actual payments and milestone completion under the new expansion contract will also matter. [13][27]

Customer contracts and prepayments. I would pay particular attention to developments with Oklo and disclosures of payment amounts and timing under new contracts. Customer project schedules matter too, because fuel orders ultimately have to line up with actual demand. [18][19][20][21]

A possible $115 million to $125 million acquisition. In its September filings, Centrus disclosed advanced talks to acquire a U.S. manufacturing supplier. It cited approximately $160 million in 2025 revenue at the target company, but no definitive agreement was in place. A signed deal, the target's profitability, and the acquisition's effect on construction costs could all move the stock. The target's revenue should not be added to the Centrus forecast at this stage. [15]

2027 deliveries and logistics. The latest filing identified March 2027 as the expiration date of the Canadian carrier's permit. Ahead of that, the focus is on individual shipments, licenses, and securing supply through the transition. [10]

What the Chart Is Telling Us

The $112 to $115 area marks the recent lows, including $112.61 on October 16. It has not yet been confirmed as a lasting bottom. The first signs of improvement would be for the stock to stop falling, establish a higher low, and reclaim the $127 to $135 area. The next test would be whether the stock could hold the $140 to $150 area, where it traded previously. This is my conditional interpretation of recent price action. [2]

One strong session does not make a trend: LEU rose 5.9% on October 15, then fell 9.5% the next day. Whether buying holds up after good news and how the stock behaves on the next pullback will tell us more than a sharp one-day pop. [2]

The Outlook for the Next Few Months

In the bullish scenario, Centrus meets this year's milestones, demonstrates better cost control, secures customer prepayments, and clarifies the status of the existing cascade. Investors could then start pricing in a higher probability of profitable production before that production actually begins. A calmer financial backdrop would help.

My working scenario for the next three to six months sits in the middle: continued construction progress and more contracts, alongside heavy spending and uneven earnings. The stock could remain highly volatile, with enthusiasm over a new contract alternating with concern about the cost of fulfilling it. That assessment reflects the long lead time for new capacity and the company's current funding needs; it does not predict the direction of the next few trading sessions.

In the bearish scenario, delays, higher construction costs, supply problems, or a slower pace of customer investment enter the picture. Further financing at lower share prices would increase dilution, while future profits would be pushed further out. The size of the decline so far offers no protection against that outcome.

Getting from $114.94 back to $464.25 would require a gain of roughly 304%. That is arithmetic, not a forecast. The old high is a poor price target on its own. [1]

Over the next few months, what matters most is delivering the milestones promised for year-end, clarifying the economics of the expansion, and assessing how new customer commitments stack up against funding needs. A sustained bull run would become more credible if those developments improved the outlook for future cash flow per share and the market continued to reflect that improvement in the stock price.

have now finished @NadiaWBeard's wonderful "The Melody of Things", published a few weeks ago. The book elegantly brings together various strands, like a remarkable composition of its own. 

First for ppl who follow Georgia, a story of coming to Tbilisi to learn from inspiring Georgian teachers in its great Conservatory. Incredibly refreshing to read this perspective, exceptional in books on Georgia. (Tbilisi is not big on the book's cover, which is more geared to international readers.) 

At its core, The Melody of Things is a story about returning to the piano with a full commitment, after years away from it. It's also about struggling to get better (who isn't?) when the patience and discipline require genuine sacrifice (in Nadia's case: early mornings, long commutes, dramatically less time with friends). 

Nadia also tells a story of mentorship ("Manana") and being in a long tradition of mentors, each passing along art -- and that requiring a relationship & honesty, a laying bare how far the best effort you can muster takes you, and where not, that far transcends the technical. 

In another strand, Nadia offers a reflection on whether and how excellence needs to be heard or seen to truly manifest, and this part, too, is told so captivatingly as if it was a lightly played sonata. 

Greatly enjoyed the bit about being forced into an even closer engagement with what you play and the essence of a piece precisely because it's so hard to hit all the notes.

Knowing Nadia, some friends (@antelava ) & acquaintances ( @GidorRan) in book,  and always curious about Tbilisi, of course I had an extra interest --but think many of you out there may also enjoy, or know someone who would, if any of these themes (and there is a lot more!) appeal. 

A gem of a piece.
