text:
Policeman W. F. Anderson: The First Responder Who Entered the Basement Where Mary Phagan Was Found

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Telephone Rings at Police Headquarters

At approximately 3:20 a.m. on Sunday, April 27, 1913, a telephone call reported a killing at the National Pencil Company factory on South Forsyth Street in Atlanta. The officer who answered the call was W. F. Anderson.

Anderson did not know what awaited him at the factory. He was responding to an emergency report, and he had to act quickly. The Atlanta Constitution later described the moment in a July 20 article about the discovery of Mary Phagan's body. Its reportage portrayed Anderson dropping the telephone receiver and calling to the desk sergeant:

“I'm no mind-reader,” retorted Anderson, diving for the door.

The newspaper then quoted him shouting:

“Killing up on Forsyth street!”

The article was written by Britt Craig and published nearly three months after the murder. It is a dramatic newspaper reconstruction, not a verbatim police transcript. Nevertheless, it identifies Anderson as the officer who received the initial call and set the response in motion (The Atlanta Constitution, Sunday, July 20, 1913).

The police officers traveled to the factory in an automobile driven by Woods White Rogers AKA W. W. “Boots” Rogers, a former county policeman. Sergeant L. S. Dobbs and other officers joined the response. When they reached the factory, they encountered Newt Lee, the night watchman toting a smoky lantern, who had reported finding a young girl's body in the basement.

Anderson was one of the officers who entered the building and examined the scene. His testimony would become important because he could describe what the responding officers encountered during the first hours of the investigation, before the case developed into the highly publicized prosecution of factory superintendent Leo M. Frank.

What Anderson found in the basement

The National Pencil Company building stood on South Forsyth Street, between Alabama and Hunter Streets. The building had four floors, with manufacturing and office areas above a basement.

Lee led the officers toward the basement entrance. The officers descended by a ladder through a scuttle opening. They encountered a dark area where the available light came from lanterns and police lights.

Mary's body lay on the basement floor near a partition. Anderson described her position, clothing, injuries, and the objects nearby. His account became part of the evidence used to reconstruct the discovery.

The precise location of each object deserves attention. Newspaper reports do not always agree about where the shoe, hat, handkerchief, pencil, and papers lay. A careful account should preserve those differences rather than combine them into one description.

Anderson also described the condition of the basement door and its fastening. The newspapers reported a staple that had been pulled from the fastening. This was relevant to the investigation of access to the building, but the observation alone could not establish when the staple had been disturbed or who had disturbed it.

Anderson was a first responder, not a forensic scientist. He could tell the coroner what he saw. His testimony could not, by itself, identify the killer or establish the time and manner of every act inside the factory.

Wednesday, April 30, 1913: Anderson testifies at the coroner's inquest

Three days after the discovery, the coroner's inquest resumed at Atlanta police headquarters. Coroner Paul Donehoo presided, and the jury examined the evidence surrounding Mary's death.

Anderson was the first witness examined during the resumed proceedings. The Atlanta Journal reported his account of the discovery, the condition of the basement, Mary's body, and the questions raised by Lee's story.

One of the central questions concerned the lantern Lee said he had used. Lee's account placed him at a distance from the body when he first noticed something on the basement floor. Anderson questioned whether the smoky lantern could have provided enough light for Lee to recognize what he was seeing.

The Atlanta Journal reported Anderson estimating that the lantern would illuminate roughly twelve to fifteen feet. The Atlanta Georgian gave a similar estimate of approximately ten to twelve feet.

The surviving trial record preserves Anderson's earlier statement as Defendant's Exhibit 93, printed page 307 of the Brief of Evidence. It records his words:

“With the lantern that he had I could see about ten or twelve feet, something like that.”

The exhibit is relevant because it preserves a portion of Anderson's original inquest testimony, allowing it to be compared with his later testimony at Frank's trial (The Atlanta Journal, Wednesday, April 30, 1913; The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, April 30, 1913; Brief of Evidence, Defendant's Exhibit 93, p. 307).

The lantern question was not a small detail. If Lee could not clearly identify the body from where he said he stood, the jury had reason to examine how he discovered it and what he actually saw. At the same time, Anderson's estimate was not a controlled scientific test. Visibility depended on the condition of the lantern, the darkness, the angle of view, and the objects between the light and the body.

The disagreement over the body's position

Another issue concerned Mary's position when the officers arrived.

The Atlanta Journal reported that Anderson and the responding officers found Mary lying face downward, with her head toward the front of the building. Lee was reported as giving a different description of the body's position when he first discovered it.

This raised an obvious question: had Lee described the scene incorrectly, or had the body been moved between discovery and the officers' examination?

The testimony alone did not answer that question. A difference between two descriptions is a reason to investigate, not proof that someone moved the body.

The testimony of Rogers adds another layer. At the May 8 inquest session, Rogers described Lee's account of finding Mary and said the officers found her face downward. His recollection did not match every version of Lee's initial description printed in the newspapers.

These differences are important because the early accounts were later used to reconstruct the crime scene. They should be examined individually, with the speaker and date identified, rather than treated as if every report repeated exactly the same words.

What Anderson said about the objects near Mary

The newspapers also discussed a pencil, writing paper, notes, and a handkerchief found in the basement.

The Atlanta Georgian reported Anderson describing a note and other objects, but its account also indicates uncertainty about who found particular items. Anderson saw Sergeant Dobbs pick up a note. He was not necessarily the person who collected every object mentioned in the investigation.

At trial, Anderson was questioned about a pencil found near the body. The Atlanta Journal reported him estimating that the pencil was eight or ten feet away. He also acknowledged that pencils were common throughout the factory.

That qualification is important. A pencil found in a pencil factory was not, by itself, evidence identifying the person who had handled it. The same principle applies to paper and other ordinary factory materials. Their location could be relevant, but their importance depended on additional evidence connecting them to the crime.

The prosecution's case included the notes found near Mary's body. Anderson's testimony helped establish what officers encountered at the scene, but it did not establish who wrote the notes. Other witnesses and exhibits were needed to address that question.

Anderson's attempts to reach Leo Frank

Anderson's testimony was relevant to the investigation of Frank because the officers attempted to contact the factory superintendent after finding Mary's body.

According to the later trial testimony, Anderson tried to reach Frank by telephone at approximately 3:30 a.m. He continued trying for several minutes and made another attempt around 4 a.m. The calls were unsuccessful.

Rogers corroborated the setting. At trial, he testified that Anderson was in the factory office with Lee at approximately 3:45 a.m. and was trying to telephone someone. Rogers did not know whom Anderson was attempting to reach.

The Atlanta Constitution published Rogers's testimony on Thursday, July 31, 1913. The report states:

“Officer Anderson was in the factory office with Newt Lee about 3:45 o'clock that morning and he tried to call someone over the phone. I don't know who he tried to get.”

This is useful independent testimony about Anderson's actions. It places him in the office with Lee during the early investigation and confirms that he was attempting to make a call.

The unanswered calls were relevant because Frank was the superintendent of the factory. But the evidence must be described accurately. An unanswered telephone call does not prove that the person being called heard it, knew who was calling, or deliberately refused to answer.

Rogers later testified about the trip to Frank's home and the subsequent journey to the undertaking establishment and factory. Those events belong to the larger investigation, but they should not be attributed to Anderson. Anderson's role was the initial police response and the effort to contact people associated with the factory.

Friday, August 1, 1913: Anderson takes the stand for the State

Anderson testified for the prosecution on Friday, August 1, during the trial of Leo Frank. Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey questioned him, and defense attorney Luther Z. Rosser cross-examined him.

His testimony returned to the discovery of the body, the basement, Lee's lantern, the objects found nearby, and the early telephone calls. The defense had a clear reason to examine these details closely. If the State relied on the officers' observations to establish the circumstances of the discovery, the defense was entitled to test how reliable those observations were.

Anderson's testimony also concerned the tracks near the body and the question of whether the scene showed signs of movement or disturbance. Such observations could help reconstruct the scene, but they did not independently establish who made the tracks or when they appeared.

The most revealing part of the later examination concerned the lantern. Anderson's testimony was not simply that nothing could be seen from twenty-five feet away. He acknowledged that a large object might be visible without being recognizable as a person.

The Brief of Evidence records his answer:

“You could see the bulk of anything that far, but you couldn't tell that far whether it was a person.”

This qualification is central to understanding his testimony. Anderson was distinguishing between seeing a shape and recognizing what the shape was. His earlier estimate of the lantern's range and his later answer should be read together.

What the three newspapers emphasized

The Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Journal, and Atlanta Georgian covered the trial from different angles. Their accounts overlap, but they do not offer identical presentations of Anderson's evidence.

The Atlanta Constitution published a dedicated report on Saturday, August 2, titled “Policeman W. F. Anderson Tells of Newt Lee's Telephone Call.” Its coverage placed Anderson's role in the early response near the center of the story. The report connected the call from Lee, the officers' arrival, the attempts to reach Frank, and the question of what could be seen with the lantern.

The Atlanta Journal published an extensive account on August 2 under the headline “Dr. Harris Collapses on Stand as He Gives Sensational Evidence.” Although the headline emphasized Dr. Harris, the article also included detailed questioning of Anderson. It discussed the lantern, the tracks, the telephone calls, and Anderson's earlier inquest testimony. The report is useful because it shows how the defense tested his memory and earlier statements during cross-examination.

The Atlanta Georgian also reported the first investigation and the coroner's inquest. Its April 30 account included additional details about the body, the objects near it, and the basement. It also contains a discrepancy in Anderson's initials, printing W. T. Anderson where other reports identify him as W. F. Anderson. The matching role and testimony strongly suggest a newspaper error, but the discrepancy should be noted rather than silently corrected.

The newspapers also differ in their descriptions of the shoe, hat, and other objects. These differences are a reminder that a newspaper account is not the same thing as a complete sworn transcript. The original Brief of Evidence should take priority when it records Anderson's exact words.

The evidence that was incriminating to Frank

Anderson's testimony was relevant to the State's case in several ways.

First, he helped establish the timing and circumstances of the initial police response. His testimony placed the officers at the factory shortly after Lee's call and established that the body was discovered during the early hours of April 27.

Second, he testified about attempts to reach Frank. These calls were part of the chronology of the investigation, although they did not prove that Frank deliberately ignored them.

Third, Anderson's description of the basement, the body, and the objects nearby helped establish the scene the officers encountered. This evidence could be compared with the accounts of Lee and other witnesses.

Fourth, his testimony about the lantern challenged Lee's ability to identify the body from the position he described. That question was important to the credibility of the discovery account, even though Anderson's estimate did not conclusively establish what Lee could or could not see.

Finally, Anderson's evidence became part of the record that the prosecution and defense used to test competing explanations of the crime. The State could rely on his firsthand observations, while the defense could challenge the accuracy of his recollection and the conclusions drawn from it.

What Anderson did not provide was a direct identification of Frank as Mary's killer. He did not testify that he saw Frank attack Mary, move her body, or write the notes. His evidence was circumstantial and concerned the discovery and investigation. Its weight depended on how it fit with the rest of the case.

The surviving inquest record and Defendant's Exhibit 93

One of the most valuable records for researchers is Defendant's Exhibit 93, printed page 307 of the Brief of Evidence. It preserves part of Anderson's April 30 testimony about Lee's position and the lantern.

The exhibit matters because Anderson's complete coroner's inquest transcript has not been located in the material examined here. The surviving passage gives researchers a direct source for comparing his inquest statement with his August 1 trial testimony.

During the trial, the defense also questioned whether Anderson's earlier testimony had been recorded. Stenographer H. L. Parry said he had not personally recorded Anderson's testimony. That statement does not prove no transcript existed, because the surviving exhibit demonstrates that at least part of the testimony was preserved.

On Monday, August 18, 1913, Rosser read a portion of Anderson's earlier inquest testimony into the trial record. The exchange shows that the defense considered the earlier statement useful for testing Anderson's recollection.

Anderson and the Georgia Supreme Court record

The principal Georgia Supreme Court decisions in the Frank case include Frank v. State, 141 Ga. 243 (1914), and the later proceedings reported at 142 Ga. 617 and 142 Ga. 741. These records are important for understanding the legal challenges to the conviction.

The material examined for this article establishes Anderson's testimony in the trial record and the survival of the inquest excerpt as Defendant's Exhibit 93. I have not verified a separate substantive discussion of Anderson in the published Supreme Court opinions. It would be misleading to claim that the Court specifically endorsed or rejected his testimony without locating the relevant passage.

The next step is to examine the complete appellate record and the original Brief of Evidence for references to Anderson, his exhibits, and any arguments concerning his testimony. The search should include variations such as “W. F. Anderson,” “Policeman Anderson,” and “Defendant's Exhibit 93.” The absence of a direct mention in a published opinion would not mean his testimony was absent from the underlying trial record.

Conclusion: Why Anderson deserves a closer look

W. F. Anderson was one of the first police officers to respond to the report of Mary Phagan's death. He entered the factory basement, examined the scene, participated in the early effort to contact Frank, and testified at the coroner's inquest and the murder trial.

His evidence is important because it comes from the first hours of the investigation. It records what the officers saw, what they questioned, and what they could not establish. His testimony about the lantern raised a question about Lee's account. His evidence about the body and the objects nearby helped reconstruct the scene. His telephone testimony helped establish the chronology of the police response.

The strongest historical account of Anderson is one that preserves both the value and the limits of his testimony. He was a first responder with firsthand observations. Those observations deserve careful study, especially where the newspapers differ. But his evidence should not be stretched into claims he did not make.

The record leaves a clear research path: compare the three newspapers dated August 1–2, 1913, line by line with Anderson's sworn testimony; examine Defendant's Exhibit 93; and search the complete Georgia Supreme Court materials for any direct reference to him. That work can give readers a clearer picture of what Anderson actually saw and how his testimony fit into the prosecution of Leo Frank.

text:
Key themes to watch in energy heading into the week

1. Middle East Geopolitical Risk - Still the Dominant Driver

The Strait of Hormuz disruption remains the central market narrative. Some estimates put Gulf crude flows back at 80-90% of prewar levels, although tracking remains highly uncertain and refined-product flows are recovering much more slowly.

Fresh escalation over the weekend also warrants attention: a Saudi reconnaissance helicopter crashed near the Yemen border, killing two crew members, while Riyadh continues to deal with severe disruption following Houthi attacks. Tanker attacks around Hormuz also intensified last week, keeping a substantial geopolitical premium in Brent.

2. Ukraine Strikes on Russian Refineries Resume

Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian oil infrastructure after the proposed US-brokered “energy ceasefire” unraveled, with the Ryazan refinery targeted last week.

That adds another layer of refinery supply risk on top of disruption in the Middle East. Russian refining has already been badly affected by Ukrainian strikes, adding to the global shortage of diesel and other middle distillates.

3. Diesel/Distillate Tightness

Diesel remains arguably the most stressed part of the oil market.

The IEA says more than 20 million barrels of diesel could be released from emergency stocks as soon as possible. Around 330 million barrels of the original 400 million barrel March commitment have already been released, with roughly another 100 million barrels expected.

US distillate inventories remain exceptionally low and are expected to stay below historical norms through 2027, while diesel cracks remain extremely elevated.

Washington is also easing pressure on Russian energy exports as it tries to bring more diesel supply onto the market ahead of the midterms - a move facing significant opposition in Congress.

4. Supply/Demand Balance - Deficit Narrowing but Intact

Our balance still points to a roughly 2.4 mb/d deficit in 3Q, narrowing toward 0.5 mb/d in 4Q.

But the important distinction is that this remains heavily conflict-driven. Excluding disruption and demand destruction, the underlying market would look considerably looser.

5. Emergency Buffers Are Being Drawn Down

Governments continue to lean heavily on strategic stocks to contain the price shock.

The US has offered additional SPR barrels, while IEA members have pledged to accelerate the roughly 100 million barrels still outstanding from the March emergency release.

Those releases can soften near-term tightness, but they also leave less protection if geopolitical disruption intensifies again.

text:
BOX FOUR: THE IRANIAN HORMUZ OFFER

What Tehran believes it is selecting:

Coercive negotiation. Iran imposes economic pain, then offers partial relief in exchange for sanctions reduction, an end to the blockade and recognition of its security role.

What the box may contain:

A negotiated reopening, continued informal Iranian control, or miscalculation producing direct US–Iranian naval combat.

Why the choice is being made:

Iran cannot match US conventional naval power. It can make commercial passage expensive, ambiguous and politically conditional. Insurance markets and shipowners then transmit Iranian pressure farther than its weapons can reach.

Potential outcome:

Even a partial agreement may legitimise the proposition that Iran can close and reopen the strait for political payment. Rejection preserves the blockade but prolongs global economic damage.

BOX FIVE: THE US BLOCKADE

What Washington believes it is selecting:

Economic strangulation without occupation cutting Iranian revenue until Tehran accepts nuclear and regional concessions.

What the box may contain:

Iranian adaptation, covert cargo movements, attacks on commercial shipping and growing costs for US allies and consumers.

Why the choice is being made:

A blockade appears controllable and less destructive than another major bombing campaign. It offers measurable outputs: vessels inspected, redirected or seized.

Potential outcome:

Iran loses substantial revenue but gains asymmetric opportunities. The longer the blockade continues, the more naval assets, intelligence coverage and diplomatic capital Washington must commit.

BOX SIX: KINETIC DETERRENCE

What the United States, Israel and the Gulf coalition believe they are selecting:

Punishment of launch sites, commanders, depots and logistics until the adversary calculates that further attacks are too costly.

What the box actually contains:

A learning contest. Fixed infrastructure is destroyed; mobile systems disperse. Senior personnel are killed; replacements adopt tighter security. Supply chains are interrupted; smaller networks and commercial cover emerge.

Why the choice is repeatedly made:

Kinetic action is visible, immediate and politically communicable. Governments can show aircraft launching and targets destroyed. Negotiations, institutional reform and local political settlements are slower and appear less decisive.

Potential outcome:

Operational success without strategic termination.

WHY THE WAR WILL NOT END THROUGH KINETIC RECIPROCITY

The present model is circular:

1. A Houthi, Hezbollah or Iranian-aligned attack produces retaliation.
2. Retaliation destroys identifiable targets but causes new political grievance.
3. Surviving networks disperse and modify tactics.
4. Iran supplies knowledge, components or finance while limiting direct exposure.
5. Another attack occurs from a different location or through a different actor.
6. The coalition retaliates again.

Every cycle validates both narratives. The coalition claims that continued attacks prove force is necessary. Iran and its aligned actors claim that continued strikes prove armed resistance is necessary.

Kinetic action can suppress capability. It cannot alone settle:

Who governs Yemen.

Whether southern Yemen remains united with the north.

Who monopolises force in Lebanon.

Who legitimately governs Gaza.

How Iran’s nuclear and missile programmes are constrained.

Who guarantees navigation through Hormuz.

How regional states obtain security without depending entirely on external military protection.

Without answers to those questions, destroyed launchers are replaced and ceasefires become rearming intervals.

text:
Rubio rebukes Zelensky over Starlink claims
The US secretary of state has denied that Washington ordered restrictions on satellite services used by Ukrainian drones
Published 18 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/qPoeNvazR6
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected Vladimir Zelensky’s claim that Washington ordered restrictions on satellite services used by Ukraine to carry out drone strikes deep inside Russia. The dispute comes amid a public spat between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump over sanctions and strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Earlier this week, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX’s Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Zelensky told journalists on Saturday that tests on Starlink equipment in EU countries indicated that the restrictions imposed in Ukraine were “a planned operation.”
When asked to comment on Zelensky’s remarks later that day, Rubio offered a different account.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate,” he told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
“We had nothing to do with it. Nobody in the United States ordered that Starlink speed be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before,” the US diplomat said.
Rubio confirmed that Ukraine currently had no access to Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade sister service, but had requested it.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk similarly denied restricting Starlink in Ukraine but clarified that the service must be used for civilian and defensive purposes only, not offensive operations.
The Telegraph, however, reported on Friday that Musk had personally asked Trump to cap Starlink speeds for Ukraine, while Reuters reported that the White House had instructed the Pentagon to slow down Starshield. Trump has denied any involvement and said he did not believe Musk was responsible either.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the Starlink restrictions remained in place. A Ukrainian official told Axios that SpaceX had blamed the cap on “a technical problem.”
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he went further, suspending new sanctions on Russian oil and gas trade on national security grounds. Trump also sought to pressure Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, which he blamed for contributing to high energy prices.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed by Trump, who, in turn, argued that the Ukrainian leader was “not a good guy for us to deal with” and should be replaced.

text:
Trump eyes reopening Europe to Russian gas – NYT
US negotiators have reportedly proposed restarting pipeline supplies via Ukraine as part of a peace deal with Moscow
Published 18 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/NbRZzvrrCd
The US plan for securing peace in Ukraine calls for Europe to increase its purchase of Russian gas, while Ukraine would consider reopening pipelines that once carried it to the EU, The New York Times reported on Saturday, citing people familiar with the talks.
The proposal is the latest in a series of steps by US President Donald Trump to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev. It follows an agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and the waiving of sanctions and tariffs mandated by the late American Senator Lindsey Graham.
Washington has reportedly pitched restoring Russian gas exports to Europe as part of a longer-term plan to offer Moscow economic incentives under a broader settlement. The proposed deal would also address relations between Russia and NATO, security guarantees for Ukraine and territorial issues, the sources told the newspaper.
US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly raised the idea of restoring Russian gas flows to Europe via Ukraine in talks with European and Ukrainian officials, including Vladimir Zelensky during a visit to Kiev in September.
Russian gas exports through neighboring Ukraine were only halted in January 2025, after authorities in Kiev opted not to extend the transit deal with Moscow.
Russia supplied around 45% of the EU’s gas imports before the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, but sanctions and damage to key infrastructure, such as Nord Stream 1, had cut its share to about 12% by 2025. The bloc nevertheless bought 36 billion cubic meters (bcm) of Russian gas last year, including pipeline supplies and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The latest estimates put the value of EU purchases of Russian LNG at €7.2 billion, nearly €1 billion more than in 2024.
Since the halt of gas transit through Ukraine, TurkStream has been the only remaining route for Russian pipeline gas to the bloc.
Brussels began phasing out gas imports from Russia under some short-term pipeline contracts in June 2026 and plans to ban Russian LNG imports from January 2027 and pipeline gas imports by September, with a complete phaseout targeted by the end of that year.
Meanwhile, Russia has shifted more energy exports to Asia, with deliveries of Russian natural gas to China reaching 38.8 bcm in 2025, up 24.8% from a year earlier. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow is ready to supply fuel to EU countries but needs a signal from Brussels. He said Russia would assess the feasibility and commercial viability of such exports rather than wait for Europe to “slam the door” on energy ties.

Sunday Futures Open Outlook
October 18, 2026

Tonight’s open enters a heavily recalibrated market landscape following a sharp Friday multi-asset realignment. Conversely, energy and metals surged hard to end the week. November WTI crude oil (/CL) exploded 3.5% higher on Friday, re-igniting structural energy shock risks as crude moves back to the $100 benchmark. Over on the metals floor, December gold (/GC) held firm near $4,181.10/oz, retaining underlying safe-haven support despite broader paper liquidation. text:
$GME @gamestop When structuring a transaction under Section 251 of the Delaware General Corporation Law (DGCL)—which governs merger agreements and details how constituent shares or securities are converted—a holding company or acquiring entity can indeed address, buy out, or acquire both a target company's stock and its outstanding warrants.
Villanova University Charles Widger School of Law
Section 251(b)(5) explicitly allows merger consideration to consist of cash, property, rights, or securities of the surviving or parent holding company. How the holding company handles the warrants depends on the merger structure and the specific terms of the target's existing warrant agreements.
Fox Rothschild LLP
Typically, outstanding warrants are dealt with through one of three mechanisms in a Section 251 merger:
1. Cash-Out (Acquisition/Buyout)
The holding company can offer to "buy out" the warrant holders by paying them cash. This is usually equal to the "spread" or intrinsic value of the warrant—meaning the merger consideration per share minus the warrant's exercise (strike) price. If the merger price is below the strike price (i.e., the warrants are "out of the money"), they may be canceled for little to no consideration unless negotiated otherwise.
2. Assumption and Conversion
The holding company can assume the warrants. Under this approach, the warrants are converted into replacement warrants to purchase the holding company's stock instead of the target's stock. The exercise price and the number of shares purchasable are mathematically adjusted to reflect the exchange ratio of the merger.
3. Accelerated Exercise or Expiration
Most warrant agreements contain change-of-control or reorganization clauses. These clauses often require the company to give advance notice of a merger, giving warrant holders a window to exercise their warrants and receive common stock so they can participate in the merger as standard stockholders. If they choose not to exercise within that window, the warrants typically expire upon the closing of the merger.
CreditSights
Key Considerations
Warrant Agreement Terms: The exact options available are constrained by the governing law and the contractual language inside the target's original warrant agreements.
Section 251(g) Distinction: If you are referring strictly to a holding company reorganization (often done under DGCL Section 251(g) to insert a parent holding company above an existing operating company without a shareholder vote), existing warrants of the operating company are routinely converted into equivalent warrants of the new holding company to preserve the holders' rights.

text:
Let's talk about $GME and the 251(g). 

What is it and what would it actually do?

A 251(g) is a Delaware holding company reorganization. 

GameStop becomes a subsidiary of a new parent company (Teddy) and every share converts 1 for 1 into the new holdco.

Same rights, same board, same everything. That's why it doesn't need a shareholder vote. It's non material because nothing changes for shareholders on day one.

The 251(g) is the plumbing, not the event.

Under a holdco, GameStop and anything it acquires can sit side by side as separate subsidiaries. 

Think about what that means with the $EBAY bid.

It allows PE money to come in easily. 

Outside money can invest directly into a subsidiary without diluting the parent. 

This is how you finance big moves without touching the common stock.

The reporting segment breakdown already happened. 

Each piece can get valued on its own. 

That's how you get a sum of its parts rerating.

I have been saying for a long time the best time for a 251(g) is right after all the insiders have bought. 

Cohen, Cheng, Grube and Attal have all bought this year.

But watch what comes through the structure. 

A financing. A tender offer. An acquisition.

That's the potential catalyst….

text:
Do you think 5.3% today is high? How about 36% in 1861?

The secretary of the treasury had authority to issue ten millions of treasury-notes at par, to creditors or others, at the rates of interest offered by the lowest bidder after public advertisement of not less than ten days. On the 18th of December he invited proposals for $5,000,000 of these notes. Offers at twelve per cent, or less, were made for $1,831,000. The remaining offers were for $465,000, at rates ranging from fifteen to thirty-six per cent. He did succeed in raising the small sum of $5,000,000 at twelve per cent interest. When Secretary Chase entered the treasury department he must have speedily learned two things, the imperative need of borrowing money, and the great difficulty in obtaining it, even at high rates of interest.

Letter on Condition of the Treasury, Jan. 18, 1861. Mis. Doc, No. 20, 36 Cong., second session.

When the loan was advertised Harper's Weekly remarked: “The money is required to pay soldiers, sailors and others whose claims on the government have accumulated to this large amount, and have been left unpaid for some time. It is not supposed that the negotiation will be an advantageous one for the government. It was proposed to obtain for the bonds the endorsement of the States of New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Massachusetts; and, thus fortified, it is supposed that they might have commanded par.” This proposal, however, was defeated. Feb. 23, 1861.

Bolles, Albert S. The Financial History of the United States, from 1861 to 1885. D. Appleton and Company, 1886.

text:
Here are the names where the record actually supports it — NC first.

**North Carolina — the clearest call-out is State Sen. Brent Jackson**
Jackson was the primary sponsor of the 2022 Farm Act (SB 762), which started with a farm right-to-repair section. In committee he replaced that section with a study after dealer and manufacturer opposition, saying: “At the end of the day, we might change something or we might do nothing.” That is documented in [WRAL](https://t.co/1Y5iqAKWSd) and [News & Observer coverage](https://t.co/hl0a1OTEoP), and the final study-only law is [SL 2022-55](https://t.co/tZazsNXkgN).
The Senate Agriculture, Energy, and Environment Committee adopted the removal by voice vote, so there is no roll call to blame other members individually — Jackson is the documented driver. **Gov. Roy Cooper** signed the weakened bill on July 8, 2022. Fair to say he signed it; the record does not show he authored the removal. The 43 senators and 99 House members who voted yes voted for the whole Farm Act after repair was already out, so I won't call them out for the removal itself.
Later NC: HB 938 (2025, electronics repair) was filed and sent to House Rules with no further action. No named holder is documented.

**Federal — Rep. Brett Guthrie**
Guthrie (R-KY), chair of House Energy and Commerce and sponsor of H.R.7389, offered the substitute whose Section 202 codifies the old industry agreements instead of the REPAIR Act's telematics access, and sends telematics to a study due by 2030. That is his bill, his amendment, his committee — [https://t.co/s8idXd2sKD record](https://t.co/Oxym0Wd8JO).
The REPAIR Act and FARM Act sit stalled in Guthrie's House committee and Sen. Ted Cruz's Senate Commerce Committee with no hearing. That's chair-jurisdiction inaction, not a documented personal hold, and I'll label it that way.
Two people **not** to call out: Rep. Jake Auchincloss was the lone “no” vote on H.R.7389 because it didn't protect Massachusetts' stronger law — a pro-repair objection. Rep. Neal Dunn, the REPAIR Act sponsor, protested the narrowing publicly. And on the military repair provisions stripped from the defense bill, no individual remover is named in the official record; reporting points to conference leaders, so I'd label that an allegation, not a record.

**Other states**
Maine: Sen. Chip Curry sponsored and Gov. Janet Mills signed the 2026 law delaying telematics compliance to Sept. 1, 2027 — recorded. text:
In 1974, a chance meeting in a Memphis parking lot led to one of the quieter, more personal chapters of Elvis Presley’s final years.

Magnolia “Maggie” Smith was a college student majoring in biology. She had lost her father a few years earlier, she and her mother were struggling financially, and she had no reliable way to get to and from classes. 

Elvis struck up a conversation with her, learned the situation, and offered her a job at Graceland. His main condition was that school come first. He wanted her focused on her studies and her grades.

He followed through on that in practical ways. He bought her a car so she could get to campus. He covered her tuition. He arranged regular pay and gave her a quiet place at Graceland where she could study without interruption. 

Her official title from 1974 to 1977 was Executive Assistant. 
The role was not limited to household work; she helped with whatever was needed around the house, spent time with Lisa Marie, answered phones, and traveled with the family on both Memphis and West Coast trips. A large staff kept Elvis’s life running, and she was part of that team in his last three years.

Maggie later described Elvis as a father figure. He would call to check on her grades and ask for full reports on her classes. He cried with her, prayed with her, and read to her. 

One book he returned to was The Prophet by Kahlil Gibran, which he gave her. She recalled his humor as well as those more emotional moments, and she spoke of feeling closer to him than many people realized.

Accounts of the relationship appear in later writings that quote Maggie directly and in the wider oral history of Graceland staff. 

Elvis’s well-known pattern of generosity toward people around him—cars, support for education, personal attention—makes the outline of the story consistent with how he treated others in his circle, even if the full details remain less documented than his public career. 

Maggie’s role, as she and others described it, was both practical and personal: a job that prioritized her education while placing her inside the daily life of Graceland and the Presley family.🌹

text:
Without post-70 AD, rabbinic Judaism, the Protestant church does not have a Bible.
First, the manuscript tradition that all of our modern translations are based on is the Masoretic text. The Masoretes were the rabbis that followed after the Tannaim and the Amoraim. They worked from the 7th to the 10thcentury AD and their main focus was the preserving of the Hebrew text of the Old Testament and developing the vowel and accent system that we use today when we read the Hebrew text. Delete the work of the Masoretes and you delete the text that we use for our Old Testament. No rabbis, no Bible.
Second, the Protestant recovery of the ability to read the Old Testament in the original Hebrew language was made possible by relying on the work of late medieval rabbis, primarily the grammarians, along with the assistance of 16thcentury Jews who either were willing to teach Hebrew to their Christian neighbors or who actually converted to the Christian faith themselves and brought their rabbinic knowledge of the Hebrew text with them. For instance, in the early thirteenth century, David Kimhi composed the Miklohl, a basic grammar of the Hebrew language, and the Hashorashim, a Hebrew dictionary. When sixteenth century Christians began returning to the Hebrew language, these texts provided their entrance into Hebrew fluency.
Additionally, the grammarians produced a series of commentaries on the text of the Old Testament, commentaries which developed something very similar to what we now refer to as the historical-grammatical method. These commentaries served as tutors to early protestant exegetes, trying to make their way through the Hebrew text for the first time. For instance, from 1517-1519, the Christian publisher Daniel Bomberg, working in Venice, published what we now refer to as the Bomberg Rabbinic Bible. It contained the Masoretic text of the Old Testament, surrounded by the corresponding Targum (Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew text), and commentaries by grammarians such as Rashi, Kimhi, Ibn Ezra, etc.
Bomberg’s Rabbinic Bible became an essential tool in the libraries of Reformed exegetes. If you have spent any time in Bucer’s commentary on the Psalms, you know how heavily he relied on Bomberg’s sources for his own understanding of the text. What is harder to notice, but which is equally true, is how much weight Calvin himself gave to these sources. At one point Calvin singles out Kimhi as the best of the Jewish exegetes. This reliance on the assistance of the grammarians permeates the works of sixteenth and seventeenth century, Protestant exegesis. Delete the Rabbis, and you delete the Protestant ability to read and translate the Hebrew text.
This reliance on Jewish sources was not without its pitfalls. The anti-trinitarian controversies that plagued the Reformed church in the 16th century were largely a result of Protestant reliance on Jewish commentaries. For instance, Kimhi’s commentary on the Psalms included critiques of the Christian reading of the messianic Psalms. Some young exegetes were not ready to go up against Kimhi’s work and found themselves succumbing to heterodox views on the deity of Christ, etc.
Nevertheless, the vast majority of the Reformed church figured out how to make good use of Jewish sources without losing their minds. For instance, it is not a coincidence that many of the contributors to the formation of the Reformed political tradition, men like Franciscus Junius and John Selden, were also great Hebraists, steeped deeply in the works of medieval rabbis. They drew from that tradition for much of their work. There were movements to burn all the Jewish sources that rose up at various moments, but these movements were primarily driven by the Papists, not the Reformed, who generally opposed this mania.
To repeat my opening claim - without post-70 AD, rabbinic Judaism, the Protestant church does not have a Bible. The Jews were still wrong about Jesus. But without them, you don’t have Bible.

text:
To President Obama, Sir,

You write to the public of a "basic principle of American democracy" , that a government shall not single out a man for his political opinions. I read your words twice, and then a third time, in the manner of a man who cannot believe his own ears. For of all the men who have walked the halls of that house, there is scarce one who trampled that principle more thoroughly than yourself.

You speak of the full weight of the federal government brought down upon a critic. Very well. Let us weigh it. ⚖️

When you sat in the chair, you turned the secret engines of your own intelligence upon the man who would succeed you. Warrants obtained upon a dossier your own faction purchased, whispered into the ear of a tribunal as though it were revelation. Your officers swore to facts they had never troubled themselves to verify. And when the President was cleared, when the special counsel hunted two full years and returned with no collusion, did any man of your party offer apology? Not one. Your faction pronounced the absence of a crime to be itself a crime, and went on hunting.

So mark this, Sir: when you now cry "foul" at the raiding of a congresswoman's house, know that you taught the raiding.

And while your intelligence watched the President-elect, your Secretary, the man your own Vice President raised to guard the southern door, threw it wide open and called the throwing of it policy. Millions entered unrecorded, unvetted, unaccounted for; towns were remade overnight by men who never asked leave. Washington would call it dereliction. A plainer age would call it treason, and not be far wrong.

And when the assassin's ball passed through the President's ear at Butler, Providence stayed its hand and spared us a civil war. Had he fallen, your faction, which speaks of half the nation as a basket of deplorables, which sneers that we "cling to our guns and religion" , would have had no man left to answer to. Your people spoke openly of his death as though it were a remedy. It was not a remedy. It was a near miss of the whole republic.

Now comes Senator Slotkin of Michigan, a woman schooled in the craft of the Central Intelligence, trained in the art of unseating governments abroad, and says aloud what your faction has long intended: that they shall prosecute Republican leaders, and by prosecuting them frighten the young conservatives off the field before they ever reach it. She would have the rising generation believe that to stand with a president is to stand in a dock.

Sir, I warned you of factions. In my Farewell Address I wrote that the spirit of party "agitates the community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms; kindles the animosity of one part against another." That was 1796. You have spent two centuries proving me a prophet.

You complain that a principle is being broken. Sir, you did not break it first, but you broke it well. And a principle broken in your house does not mend itself in another's.

Your most humble and obedient servant, G. Washington

I didn’t commit anywhere until June AFTER my senior year.

Completely random. Completely lucky.

I went to junior college, suffered a knee injury that required surgery, and eventually had to move from catcher to the outfield.

But something good happened.

I became a pretty damn good JUCO baseball player.

About halfway through my freshman year, I earned the starting right field job and never gave it back.

Then came recruiting. Again.

And once again, it was a pain in the ass.

I had interest from some really good programs. Michigan State, Western Michigan, Grand Valley State, University of Tampa.

But the offers just wouldn’t come.

I was 6’2”, 205 pounds. Ran a 6.6 sixty. Threw 94 mph from the outfield. Had proven I could produce at the college level.

I couldn’t understand why nobody would offer me.

My sophomore season came and went without a Division I offer.

FINALLY, with the help of my coaches, I got two.

University of Rhode Island and Western Illinois.

Rhode Island had THREE scholarships for its entire roster. They offered me $3,000.

Out-of-state tuition was $29,000. This was 2006.

Western Illinois somehow had even less scholarship money, but offered me in-state tuition.

So off I went to Macomb, Illinois.

📊 THE NUMBERS
• Full 4:43 video posted by El-Sayed's campaign account: 5.6M+ views
• 45-second clip captioned "I haven't seen you disavow them": 405K+ views (@DSA_Watch), reshared as "again refused to disavow"
• X posts on El-Sayed or the Muslim Brotherhood: 7,900+ in one hour Sunday morning, up from about 2,500 an hour overnight (X post counts)
• US terror designations of Muslim Brotherhood branches in 2026: 4 (Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon in January; Sudan in March), per Newsweek's summary of State Dept actions
• Election Day: Nov 3, 16 days out. El-Sayed (D) vs. Mike Rogers (R) for the open Peters seat

🗣️ WHAT PEOPLE ARE SAYING
• Critics, including Steve Cortes: El-Sayed "again refused to disavow" a group "his family is linked to"
• President Trump this week called him "a member of the Muslim Brotherhood"
• El-Sayed: the question assumes "because I am Muslim" he'd have "allegiance to something that is not our Constitution," and he compared it to the questions JFK faced as a Catholic
• Supporters cheered the answer; UK site The Poke said he "politely bodied" the questioner. Critics say the pushback dodged the family questions

✅ THE FACTS
• Asked "Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?", El-Sayed answered "Yes, absolutely," then asked why the voter assumed he wouldn't (full video; CNN; Newsweek)
• The viral caption quotes a later line: "Have you disavowed them? I haven't heard you disavow them yet."
• The voter, who gave his name as Tommy, walked out as the crowd cheered (CNN)
• The family angle traces to a 2012 post by his half-sister about their mother's Muslim Brotherhood "activism" in the early 1970s. El-Sayed says he was 3 when his parents divorced and doesn't know what his mother did in Egypt then (CNN)
• CNN: https://t.co/DkVrHA0aod
• Newsweek: https://t.co/qFkKiKyF9l

❓ CHECKING THE VIRAL CLAIMS
• "He refused to disavow": ❌ False. He said "Yes, absolutely" before the back-and-forth.
• "He turned it back on the voter": ✅ True. "Have you disavowed them?" came after his yes.
• "He's a member of the Muslim Brotherhood": ❓ Unproven. No evidence has been offered publicly, and he denies any ties.
• "Tommy is a former GOP Senate staffer": ❓ Reported by one outlet (The Handbasket). Not independently confirmed.

🤔 NUANCE
Both clips are real. A 45-second cut can't carry a 4-minute exchange, so check which line a caption is quoting. A single 2012 post about a parent's college activism 50 years ago isn't evidence about the candidate himself, but it's also fair game for voters to ask. The US designates certain branches as terrorist groups, not the global movement as a whole, which is why "disavow the Brotherhood" can mean different things to different people.

Watch the full exchange, then decide: tough question, or loaded one?

text:
As October shadows lengthen across the 
prairie, autumn moving steadily through the 
fields with cooler mornings in its wake, and 
the soul senses that repair is not enough — something deeper must change, 
consider a new way of being.

Ezekiel heard the Lord promise more 
than rebuilt cities. He would sprinkle clean water, remove 
the heart of stone, and give a new heart and a new spirit. 
His own Spirit would be placed within 
them so they would walk in His statutes. 
Then the prophet stood in a valley of 
dry bones and watched them rattle, come together, receive breath, and stand 
as a vast army. 
Two divided sticks became one in 
the Lord’s hand. 
This was not renovation. It was resurrection 
and a new covenant of peace.

In Revelation a mighty voice cried, 

“Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” 
The system that traded in luxury, power, 
and the souls of people collapsed in a 
single hour. 
Those who had grown rich from her 
mourned, while heaven called the people 
of God to come out of her. 
The corrupt order could not be redeemed 
on its own terms. It had to be left behind.

Job finally heard the Lord answer out 
of the whirlwind. 
“Where were you when I laid the 
foundation of the earth?” 
The God who set boundaries for the 
sea is the same God who creates a new 
heart where none existed.

In these ordinary days we actually live, a new way of being is the difference 
between trying harder in the old pattern and receiving the inner change only 
God can give. 
New habits help. New environments help. 
But the deeper need is a new heart 
and the Spirit who makes obedience possible. 
Babylon still offers its glittering alternatives. 
The call remains the same: 
come out, and live from the life 
God Himself places within.

So today, stop settling for surface repair. 
Ask for the new heart. Receive the breath that raises 
what has been dry. 
Walk as one who belongs to the 
covenant of peace.

The old way ends. 
The new way begins with Him.

🧡 🌙

Ezekiel 36:1–37:28 Revelation 18:1–24 Job 38:1–11

text:
THE DARK ONES — THE LAST SHOCK

At the end of The Dark Ones, there is no further door waiting.

No new degree.

No new symbol.

No new voice promising:

There is more.

The two protagonists have been through everything.

The Veil.
The False Light.
The Brotherhood.
The Royal Art.
Solve / Coagula.
The Will.
The Beast.
The Chaos.
The Coming Savior.
They tried to understand.
They looked behind every curtain.
They learned how easily power can look like knowledge, how easily desire can be called freedom, and how quickly fear can make a human being trade his own humanity for security.
And eventually comes the realization:
You do not have to understand Hell completely in order to leave it.
We had seen enough of Hell.
We did not need to understand it all.
We only needed to leave.
That is the moment in which The Dark Ones ends.
ALTIYAN CHILDS — THE LAST SHOCK

Altiyan Childs spends a large part of his public testimony warning about what he understands as a hidden occult and spiritual system.

But near the end, he places the emphasis somewhere unexpected.

After all the symbols, rituals, claims, warnings, and dark images, he does not describe the greatest shock as yet another revelation about Satanism, Freemasonry, or hidden knowledge.

Instead, he says in essence:

The greatest shock of all is Jesus Christ.

For Childs, that realization changes everything. In his personal testimony, he describes salvation not as another initiation or the acquisition of still more secret knowledge, but as a break with his former life and a return to Christ.
That is exactly why the final song is called:
THE LAST SHOCK

Not because something even darker waits at the end.

But because the protagonist discovers that the truth he spent the entire journey searching for behind closed doors

was never hidden at all.

WAKE UP

Childs begins and ends his story with a deeply personal image.

A car ride at night.

Speed.

Sleep.

A concrete wall ahead.

And then:

no thunder.

No grand vision.

Only a whisper that wakes him.

For Childs, this “Wake up” becomes a turning point in his own story.

That is why the central hook of THE LAST SHOCK is not a theological lecture.

It is an awakening:

I WAAAAKE UUUUP—
’TIL I’M HEEEEERE—
AWAAAAAKE NOW—
FOR THE LAAAAST SHOOOOOCK—
I WON’T EEEEEEVER—
BREAK DOWWWWWN.

This is no longer the person from THE VEIL.

That person still wanted to open another door.

The person in THE LAST SHOCK finally walks out.

THE FINAL PRISON IS HATRED

But even after the protagonist recognizes the deception, one final trap remains.

He can see through the entire system —

and still remain shaped by it internally.

He can learn everything about darkness —

and end up hating everyone.

Then he may have left the room,

but carried the room inside himself.

That is why the song asks:
What is the point of recognizing every monster if you eventually begin to think like one?
The protagonist now knows every language of accusation.
He knows how to identify enemies.
How to distribute blame.
How to divide people into sides.

But suddenly he hears his own voice —

and recognizes the same hunger:

Someone has to pay.

That frightens him more than the Beast.

“LOVE YOUR ENEMY”

This is where the song connects directly with Childs’ actual conclusion.

Near the end of his testimony, Childs says in essence that finding the road to life is harder than achieving success, wealth, or even reaching the highest levels of an initiatory system.

Then he names something that seems almost impossible:

loving your greatest enemy.

If you can learn to do that, he says, then in his view you have found the road to life.

His conclusion comes down to three words:

God.
Love.
Jesus wins.

That is the real liberation inside THE LAST SHOCK.

Not:

Destroy your enemy.

But:

Do not allow your enemy to decide what you become.

Love does not mean blindness.

It does not mean submission.

It does not mean calling evil good.

It means:

I will not give you the power to turn me into your reflection.

The circle breaks at the moment

hatred no longer decides

who we are.

NO MORE SECRETS

Throughout the album, the protagonist assumed that truth had to be hidden.

Behind a veil.

Inside a lodge.

Within a ritual.

Inside an ancient text.
Behind another door.
But at the end, Christ is not standing behind one final secret curtain.

He stands:

in the open.

No initiation.

No password.

No special degree.

No elite deciding who may enter.

The protagonist says:

I thought
the truth would make me powerful.
Instead—
it asked me
to forgive.

That reverses the entire journey.

He searched for truth as power.

At the end, he encounters truth as responsibility.

AND THE WOMAN IS STILL THERE

Alongside all these enormous ideas, there is another much smaller story.

The woman.

She is still there.

After everything.

After every dark room.

After every deception.

After every promise.

After every attempt to pull them away from each other, from themselves, or from their humanity.

Her hand is still inside his.

And suddenly that simple human image becomes more important than every piece of hidden knowledge in the album.

No throne.

No power.

No perfect system.

Only:

a hand that asks for nothing.

The woman says:

Come home.

The protagonist answers:
We’re coming.
THE ARTWORK
That is why Christ stands between the protagonists and the darkness in the final artwork.
The dark figures still exist behind them.

They have not vanished.

They are still reaching toward them.

But Christ stands between them.

Not as another occult master.

Not as another initiator.

Not as another figure selling a secret.

But as the end of the entire principle.

The darkness does not have to be completely analyzed first.

The protagonists only have to stop

following it.

Christ outshines it.

Not because the past never happened.

But because the past no longer owns

what now stands before it.

THE ENTIRE JOURNEY

THE VEIL said:

There is more.

FALSE LIGHT said:

Come closer.

THE INNER BROTHERHOOD said:

We have you.

THE ROYAL ART said:

Pay the price.

SOLVE / COAGULA dissolved the human being.

DO WHAT THOU WILT taught him to call desire freedom.

THE BEAST 666 said:

You are mine.

ORDO AB CHAO revealed the machine.

THE COMING ONE offered false salvation.

And finally THE LAST SHOCK asks:

What remains

when you stop opening doors?

The answer is surprisingly small.

My name.
My conscience.
Her hand.
Love.

And finally:

Jesus Christ.

The last shock was never

that an even greater monster was waiting behind everything.

The last shock was

that the way out had been open the entire time.

You did not always have to go deeper.

Eventually, you only had to stop

confusing darkness with knowledge.

Stand up.

Take the other person’s hand.

Forgive.

Refuse to become your own enemy.

And leave.

The last shock
was never another secret. It was Jesus Christ.

God.
Love.
Jesus wins.

The light is still on.

We’re home.

THE DARK ONES

THE LAST SHOCK

I'm only going to tell you once: the market is seriously underestimating $RKLB.

The stock closed Friday at $50.84, roughly 66% below its $151 high, yet the company's fundamentals continue to strengthen, and the bullish developments keep piling up.

Rocket Lab just secured the largest commercial Electron launch contract in its history: 20 additional missions for Japan's Synspective, bringing the customer's total to 47 launches. The company also reported a backlog of more than 90 launches across its vehicles before this latest deal.

And the financial performance is impressive. Q2 revenue surged 62% YoY to a record $234M, while backlog jumped 137% to $2.36 BILLION. Space Systems alone generated $189.5M, up 94% YoY, accounting for 81% of total revenue. Launch Services contributed just $44.6M. This is no longer simply a rocket launch company.

Meanwhile, $RKLB continues to expand aggressively into national security and defense. The company secured a U.S. Space Force contract worth up to $397M for spacecraft and launch services, plus more than $160M in contracts to build three geostationary satellites.

And here's another major development: Rocket Lab has fully financed its pending acquisition of Iridium Communications, completing a $1.94 BILLION equity offering. If completed, the acquisition would give Rocket Lab its own global satellite communications network, transforming it into a company capable of building, launching, and operating satellite constellations.

Through its acquisitions, Rocket Lab also owns technology already proven on NASA's Perseverance rover on Mars. Its expanding Space Systems business now supplies critical satellite components, robotics, and communications technologies across the industry.

Yes, Neutron's inaugural launch has been delayed until 2027. But management has identified the manufacturing issue involving its carbon-composite structures and successfully tested a revised manufacturing process on one of the rocket's domes. Further testing remains, but the delay doesn't erase the progress across the rest of the business.

Think about the setup: revenue growing 62%, Space Systems growing 94%, a $2.36B backlog, record commercial launch contracts, expanding government business, and a major satellite communications acquisition in the works.

Yet $RKLB is trading around $51.

The space economy isn't just about launching rockets. It needs satellites, communications networks, spacecraft components, and the infrastructure that keeps everything operating. Rocket Lab is positioning itself to become a major provider of that critical infrastructure.

At around $51, I strongly believe $RKLB offers one of the most compelling long-term opportunities in the space sector for investors willing to look beyond short term setbacks and accept the execution risks.

text:
Weston, West Virginia. Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum, opened to patients in October 1864.

Virginia authorized the asylum in 1858, and construction began with prison labor and blue sandstone quarried at nearby Mount Clare. The Civil War interrupted the work, and the 7th Ohio Volunteer Infantry seized the unused building fund from a local bank and delivered it to Wheeling, where it became a start-up treasury for what would become the new state of West Virginia. Designed by Richard Snowden Andrews on the Kirkbride Plan, the main building is said to be one of the largest hand-cut stone buildings in the United States, and it is a National Historic Landmark.

It was built for 250 patients. It held 717 by 1880 and about 2,600 at its peak in the 1950s. People were admitted for reasons that included asthma, laziness, egotism, domestic troubles and greediness. A 1949 Charleston Gazette series found poor sanitation and too little furniture, lighting and heat. Patients underwent insulin shock, electroshock, hydrotherapy and lobotomies, and in the early 1950s the hospital was home to the West Virginia Lobotomy Project with Walter Freeman. There is no official count of the patients who died there; research is underway, and estimates could reach five figures. It closed in May 1994.

That is the documented part. The legend took over after Morgantown contractor Joe Jordan bought the 242,000-square-foot building at a 2007 auction for 1.5 million dollars. Since 2008 it has offered historic tours, paranormal tours, overnight ghost hunts and an autumn haunted house, with guides dressed as 19th-century nurses. Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures, Paranormal Lockdown and Portals to Hell have all featured it as a haunted location.

text:
Siemens Says: Harvest, Markets and Winter Preparations
By Harry Siemens
 
October 18, 2026
Prairie farmers enter another week balancing unfinished harvest, changing markets and preparations for winter. Progress is real, but provincial totals hide sharp differences between farms that have finished and neighbours still waiting for fields and crops to dry.
Manitoba’s October 14 report puts harvest at 79 per cent complete. Canola reaches 86 per cent, soybeans 61 per cent and grain corn 12 per cent. Spring wheat, barley and oats each stand at 97 per cent, leaving later crops to carry much of the remaining workload.
Quality deserves attention alongside yield. Manitoba reports sprouting and weathering in later-harvested cereals, while some canola fields face lodging, pod shatter and regrowth. Soybean yields generally range from average to above average. Early corn results offer encouragement, although the province needs more harvested acres before drawing firm conclusions.
Saskatchewan’s October 6 to 12 report lists canola at 89 per cent harvested and spring wheat at 96 per cent. Rain and snow interrupt remaining combining and fieldwork. Alberta reaches 88 per cent completion of major crops as of October 13, gaining ten percentage points despite weather delays.
Grain markets reward careful comparisons. October 16 average spot canola bids range from $16.60 to $17.18 per bushel across the listed Prairie regions. Manitoba averages stand at $17.01 in the west and $17.08 in the east, in Canadian dollars.
Deferred delivery offers higher posted values. Eastern Manitoba’s May canola bid averages $17.66 per bushel, compared with $17.08 for spot delivery. That difference must cover storage, interest, handling and quality risk before it represents extra profit.
For wheat, October 16 bids for No. 1 Canada Western Red Spring with 13.5 per cent protein average $304.27 per tonne in western Manitoba and $320.79 in eastern Manitoba. Those benchmarks underline why farmers need actual grades, protein results and local delivery terms when comparing offers.
Cattle trade brings both opportunity and caution. Winnipeg Livestock Sales reports increased feeder demand on October 16 as feeder futures improve. Steers weighing 500 to 600 pounds trade from $580 to $665 per hundredweight, while comparable heifers bring $500 to $602.
Butcher cows move the other way, falling $4 to $5 per hundredweight into a reported $188 to $214 range. Alberta dressed cattle sales reach $500 per hundredweight delivered. American dressed sales in Iowa and Nebraska rise $5 to US$345 to US$355, showing the importance of watching both sides of the border.
Fall work continues wherever conditions permit. Saskatchewan producers apply fertilizer, control weeds, harrow and service equipment. Manitoba farmers haul straw, spread manure and prepare winter feed. Wet ground and unfinished harvest restrict how much gets done.
The practical focus now is protecting value: finish harvest when conditions allow, monitor stored grain, compare realistic net bids and match cattle purchases with feed costs. Every decision should account for the crop’s condition and the farm’s cash requirements.
For Canadian and American farmers alike, headline prices tell only part of the story. Drying bills, freight, grade discounts and winter feeding costs determine what remains on each individual operation.

text:
When the Questioner Becomes the Accused: ABDUL EL-SAYED and the POLITICS of DARVO 

How denial, counterattack, obfuscation, and the reversal of scrutiny threaten political accountability.

A peculiar phenomenon is unfolding in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race: When Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed faces an uncomfortable question, the ensuing exchange can become less about the answer than about the supposed moral failings of the person who dared to ask.

It is a remarkable exercise in political misdirection. And psychology offers a framework for examining it.

DARVO: The Psychology of Reversing Accountability

In 1997, psychologist Jennifer J. Freyd introduced the concept of DARVO: Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender.¹

Originally developed to describe defensive responses to allegations of abuse and wrongdoing,

DARVO identifies three interconnected behaviors:

1. Deny: Reject or minimize the allegation.

2. Attack: Challenge the credibility, motives, or character of the person raising it.

3. Reverse Victim and Offender: Recast the person facing scrutiny as the injured party and the questioner as the aggressor.

Applying this framework to political rhetoric is not a clinical diagnosis, nor does it establish that an allegation is true. But it can expose how a public figure redirects scrutiny through accusation and moral reversal. And El-Sayed’s recent exchanges warrant precisely that examination.

The Tommy Exchange: From Candidate to Prosecutor

At a Michigan town hall, an attendee named Tommy asked whether El-Sayed would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. What followed was a revealing reversal. Instead of unequivocally disavowing it, El-Sayed asked whether Tommy himself had repudiated the organization. He then questioned Tommy’s assumptions, religious beliefs, and understanding of the Constitution.²

Tommy acknowledged that he suspected El-Sayed might hold competing allegiances. Such an assumption deserves scrutiny, especially when it targets someone because of his religion. But the broader political maneuver remains striking: a candidate who had just answered a question turned the exchange into an interrogation of the citizen.

The questioner became the defendant. The candidate became the prosecutor. It was an effective display of rhetorical control. Whether it demonstrated a comparable commitment to transparency is another question entirely.

The NBC Interview: When Evidence Becomes an Offense

The pattern becomes more consequential in El-Sayed’s October interview with NBC’s Tom Llamas. When confronted with historical social media posts from his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, describing their mother’s alleged involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood during the 1970s, El-Sayed dismissed the material as hearsay and challenged the questioning’s seriousness.³

He denied personal and family ties while explaining that he had never discussed the matter with his biological mother. Here, the distinction between allegation and evidence is essential.

A relative’s historical political affiliation does not establish El-Sayed’s own affiliation, ideology, or wrongdoing. The Associated Press has reported no evidence connecting him personally to the Muslim Brotherhood.⁴ Nevertheless, journalists are entitled to ask a candidate to reconcile apparently conflicting public statements. And rather than simply distinguish what he knew, what he disputed, and what remained uncertain, El-Sayed questioned the legitimacy of the inquiry and suggested Llamas was insinuating dishonesty.

As a result, the journalist’s attempt to clarify the record became the controversy. That is the troubling hallmark of political reversal: the demand for an explanation is reframed as an offense that requires its own explanation.

Israel, Iran, and the Art of Rejecting the Question

The October 8 Senate debate offered another example of El-Sayed’s confrontational approach to unwelcome scrutiny. When asked repeatedly whether Israel or Iran posed the greater threat to the United States, he dismissed the comparison as ridiculous and ultimately maintained that both countries presented dangers of different kinds.⁵

A candidate is entitled to reject a false choice. He is also obligated to explain his foreign-policy judgment. Yet insulting the question does not resolve the underlying issue. Nor does redirecting attention to an opponent automatically answer what voters were trying to determine.

This exchange does not, by itself, demonstrate the full DARVO sequence. It does illustrate a related tendency: discredit the premise, challenge the inquiry, and regain control of the political narrative.

Religious Liberty Is Not Political Immunity

Let us establish two principles without equivocation. No American should be presumed disloyal because of religious identity. Equally, no candidate should be insulated from legitimate scrutiny by the suggestion that uncomfortable questions are inherently discriminatory.

Religious freedom protects a candidate’s right to seek public office. It does not extinguish the public’s right to scrutinize that candidate. The distinction is fundamental to constitutional democracy. Freyd herself cautions that DARVO-like behavior cannot establish the truth of an underlying accusation. That warning must be respected.¹ But the repeated use of counterquestions, attacks on an inquiry’s legitimacy, and reversals of moral responsibility deserves examination regardless of political affiliation.

The Final Verdict: Accountability Cannot Be Reversed

The most revealing feature of El-Sayed’s confrontational style is not necessarily what he denies. It is how rapidly he can move from answering a question to questioning the person asking it.

A citizen seeks clarification. A journalist seeks consistency. A moderator seeks a policy judgment. Suddenly, the person conducting the inquiry must defend their intelligence, motives, or moral integrity. And the original subject risks disappearing beneath the spectacle.

That is the political danger of DARVO-style rhetoric. It turns accountability into an accusation and scrutiny into a supposed act of aggression. Abdul El-Sayed may be an accomplished debater. But rhetorical agility and political accountability are not interchangeable virtues.

The United States Senate is not a courtroom in which elected officials prosecute citizens for questioning them.
— Isaac Halevi

The U.S. government is an institution whose members are answerable to the citizens they represent, which includes every American citizen—not only the constituents in their respective state.

And when a politician becomes more determined to discredit the questioner than to clarify the answer, the public should pay very close attention.

SMITHFIELD FOODS $SFD IS BUYING THE HOT DOG IT ALREADY MAKES. THE VOTE LANDS FOUR DAYS BEFORE ITS WEAK QUARTER DOES:

Smithfield Foods (SFD) at $18.64, +$0.16 / +0.87% on Friday, is #3 on the Income Len5, which hunts cash paid to owners that a business can keep paying. Its 6.7% yield is the richest of the Len5's top three, and it comes from a falling stock, not a stretched payout. The verdict: the dividend rests on bacon, sausage and hot dogs, a business still forecast to earn more than twice what the dividend costs, while the hogs and fresh pork that dragged the stock down are not what covers it. The weak spot is timing, because the dividend goes out evenly and the cash to pay it arrives late in the year. The first test is its cash purchase of Nathan's Famous (NATH) at $101.90, +$0.02 / +0.02% on Friday. Nathan's shareholders vote on the sale this Friday, October 23. On Tuesday, October 27, Smithfield reports a July-September quarter it has already warned will be weak.

On September 8, Smithfield reaffirmed its 2026 forecast for packaged meats at $1,075M-$1,150M of operating profit, before interest and taxes. The dividend costs about $492M a year, under half of that. The same update put fresh pork at a July-September loss of $70M-$90M as the gap between hog costs and wholesale pork prices narrowed. For Nathan's, Smithfield is paying $102 a share from cash on hand. With Nathan's debt repaid, the deal needs about $485M, more than a third of the cash Smithfield held at June 28. It has made Nathan's grocery-store hot dogs under license since March 2014, so it is buying a brand it already sells, not more hogs. Trading within cents of the offer, Nathan's is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value & Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5 watchlists; its price now tracks the deal.

The timing shows in January-June: operating cash, the money the business brings in, was $204M against $246M of dividends paid. That gap is the calendar, not a crack, since about nine-tenths of 2025's operating cash arrived in July-December. On October 14 Smithfield also lined up a $600M bank loan to repay bonds due in 2027, so that debt does not draw on the same cash. What would knock Smithfield off the Income Len5: packaged meats profit sliding toward what the dividend costs, with a forecast below $1,075M on Tuesday as the first sign, or a quarterly dividend under $0.3125. Last year's November dividend was declared October 30, so the board's next decision may come within days of the report. Results arrive before the open Tuesday, with a call at 9am ET. Friday commits the cash; Tuesday shows whether the business that refills it is still on forecast.
