GLOBAL SHIP LEASE $GSL EARNS A YEAR OF DIVIDENDS IN ONE QUARTER. ITS SHIP ORDER COSTS ABOUT WHAT THE WHOLE COMPANY IS WORTH:

Global Ship Lease (GSL) at $41.32, -$0.68 / -1.62% on Friday, sits #2 on the Income Len5. It owns 71 container ships and rents them to shipping lines on fixed contracts, called charters, so its income is set years ahead instead of by this month's freight prices. The verdict: today's dividend is covered with room to spare, but the profit behind it is slipping just as the bill for a new fleet arrives. In April-June it earned $89.3M for common shareholders, the profit left after its preferred stock is paid. A full year of the $0.625 quarterly dividend costs about $90M (arithmetic), so one quarter nearly pays the year. The $2.50 a year is a 6.05% yield. That cover is what the Income Len5 hunts: cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying. Charters already fill all of 2026 and 90% of 2027. Counting the rent already signed for its new ships, $3.2B of revenue is under contract, about twice the company's $1.49B stock market value (arithmetic).

The fact against is direction. April-June profit was $2.48 a share, from $2.61 a year earlier. Revenue rose 3.5% over the same year. The ships, weighted by size, average 18.4 years old, and their replacements cost about $1.5B: 15 ordered in June with charters attached, two more on October 6 without one. That is roughly what the whole company is worth at Friday's close (arithmetic). On October 12 it signed a $1B loan, drawn as those 15 arrive from late 2028. That covers about three-quarters of their $1.33B price (arithmetic); the two October ships, about $163M, sit outside it. It has already agreed to sell four older ships for $65.5M, handed over through late 2027. What would knock Global Ship Lease off the Income Len5: profit falling far enough that the dividend has to compete with the shipyard payments, with the first sign being the tenth of 2027 still open renting at rates well below the contracts it replaces.

July-September results are expected in mid-November, on a date the company has not set; last year's came November 10. Read first whether the $0.625 is declared again, then what rates the open part of 2027 is renting at. The ships paying this dividend are 18 years old. The ones meant to carry it after 2028 are still a bill to pay.

#1 ON THE INCOME LEN5, T. ROWE PRICE $TROW HAS THE CASH FOR ITS 5% YIELD. THE RISK SITS IN ITS RETIREMENT FUNDS:

#1 of the 30 names the Income Len5 watches: T. Rowe Price Group (TROW) at $100.97, -$0.40 / -0.39% on Friday. The Baltimore fund manager pays $1.30 a share each quarter, a 5.15% yield (arithmetic). The verdict: the cash to pay it is there, and the risk is savers leaving its retirement funds. In January-June, adjusted profit, which sets some one-time items aside, was $5.09 a share against $2.60 of dividends. That covers the payout about twice (arithmetic). It also spent $501M on buybacks, the company purchasing its own shares, in those six months. It has no borrowings of its own and ended June with $4.19B in cash and money invested in its own funds. That is exactly what the Income Len5 hunts: cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying.

The strongest fact against it is who is leaving. Clients took out $28.3B more than they put in during July-September, from $6.5B in April-June. That is about 1.5% of the money it runs (arithmetic). It still matters: T. Rowe earns a small yearly slice of every dollar it manages, so money that leaves stops paying fees. September alone lost $12.2B, including a large exit by a workplace retirement plan from T. Rowe's target-date funds, the all-in-one funds that shift from stocks to bonds as savers near retirement. Those funds hold about a third of all the money it runs (arithmetic). Management had warned in July that the second half would be harder. Part of the high yield is simply a lower price: Friday's close sat 17.0% under July 28's (arithmetic).

What would knock T. Rowe Price off the Income Len5: outflows heavy enough to drag quarterly adjusted profit down toward the dividend, or a cut to the dividend itself. It reports Thursday, October 29, at 7am ET, when analysts expect $2.64 a share of adjusted profit, from $2.81 a year earlier. The cash for the $1.30 is in hand. The open question is whether the savers leaving its retirement funds have started to show up in its profit.

text:
Hayne's Response on Feb 7th, 1861

"Your reply, through your Secretary of the War Department, to my communication of the 31st of January, covering the demand of the Governor of South Carolina for the delivery of Fort Sumter, was received yesterday. Although the very distinct and emphatic refusal of that demand closes my mission, I feel constrained to correct some strange misapprehensions into which your Secretary has fallen.There has been no modification of the demand authorized to be made, and no change whatever in its character, and of this you were distinctly informed in my communication of the 31st of January. You have the original demand as delivered to me by Governor Pickens on the 12th of January, and you have an extract from the further instructions received by me, expressly stating that he, the Governor, was “confirmed” in the views he entertained on the 12th of January by that very correspondence which you assign as the cause of the alleged modification. You assume that the character of the demand has been modified, yet you have from me but one communication, and that asserts the contrary, and you have nothing from the Governor but the very demand itself, which you say has been modified. What purpose of peace or conciliation your Secretary could have had in view in the introduction of this point at all, it is difficult to perceive.

You next attempt to ridicule the proposal presented “as simply an offer on the part of South Carolina to buy Fort Sumter and contents as property of the United States, sustained by a declaration in effect that if she is not permitted to make the purchase, she will seize the fort by force of arms.” It is difficult to consider this as other than intentional misconstruction. You were told that South Carolina, as a separate, independent sovereignty, would not tolerate the occupation, by foreign troops, of a military post within her limits, but, that inasmuch as you, in repeated messages and in your correspondence, had “laid much stress” upon the character of your duties, arising from considering forts as property, South Carolina, so far as this matter of property, suggested by yourself, was concerned, would make compensation for all injury done the property, in the exercise of her sovereign right of eminent domain. And this your Secretary calls a proposal to purchase! The idea of purchase is entirely inconsistent with the assertion of paramount right in the purchaser. I had supposed that an “interest in property,” as such, could be no other than “purely proprietary,” and if I confined myself to this narrow view of your “relations” to Fort Sumter, you, at least, should not consider it the subject of criticism. Until your letter of yesterday, you chose so to consider your relations, in everything which you have written, or which has been written under your direction. It was precisely because you had yourself chosen to place your action upon the ground of “purely proprietary” right that the proposal of compensation was made, and you now admit that in this view “it (Fort Sumter) would probably be subjected to the exercise of the right of eminent domain.”In your letter of yesterday (through your Secretary) you shift your position. You claim that your Government bears to Fort Sumter “political relations of a much higher and more imposing character.” It was no part of my mission to discuss the “political relations” of the United States Government to anything within the territorial limits of South Carolina. South Carolina claims to have dissolved all political connection with your Government, and to have destroyed all “political relations” of your Government with everything within her borders. She is unquestionably at this moment de facto a separate and independent Government, exercising complete sovereignty over every foot of her soil except Fort Sumter. Now, that the intention is avowed to hold this place as a military post, with a claim of exclusive jurisdiction on the part of a Government foreign to South Carolina, it will be for the authorities to determine what is the course proper to be pursued. It is vain to ignore the fact that South Carolina is, to yours, a foreign Government, and how with this patent fact before you, you can consider the continued occupation of a fort in her harbor a pacific measure, and parcel of a peaceful policy, passes certainly my comprehension.

You say that the fort was garrisoned for our protection, and is held for the same purposes for which it has been ever held, since its construction. Are you not aware, that to hold, in the territory of a foreign power, a fortress against her will, avowedly for the purpose of protecting her citizens, is, perhaps, the highest insult which one government can offer to another? But Fort Sumter was never garrisoned at all until South Carolina had dissolved her connection with your Government. This garrison entered it in the night, with every circumstance of secrecy, after spiking the guns, and burning the gun carriages, and cutting down the flag-staff of an adjacent fort, which was then abandoned. South Carolina had not taken Fort Sumter into her own possession, only, because of her misplaced confidence in a Government which deceived her. A fortress occupied under the circumstances above stated, is considered by you, not only as no cause of irritation, but you represent it as held for our protection!Your Excellency’s Secretary has indulged in irony on a very grave subject. As to the responsibility for consequences, if, indeed, it does rest on us, I can assure your Excellency we are happily unconscious of the fact.I return to Charleston to-morrow. 

With considerations of high regard, I am, very respectfully,

I. W. HAYNE,
Special Envoy.

text:
**TRUMP’S FALL: A LESSON FOR THE ENTIRE WORLD**

Donald Trump is a political hurricane, swinging like a pendulum between supporting Ukraine and serving Putin. And the entire world swings with him, unable to escape the consequences of what happens in the White House. This hurricane has already inflicted enormous damage on one of America’s two major political parties: the Republicans.

The November congressional elections could become a historic turning point. Polling suggests Republicans might even lose a Senate seat in Texas for the first time since 1988. That alone would be an extraordinary political earthquake.

Unlike members of the House, senators enjoy greater independence from the White House. Not every Republican senator has surrendered to Trump, and some may eventually turn against him. With Democrats potentially regaining control of Congress, impeachment is no longer an unimaginable scenario.

But impeachment may not even be necessary. Congressional investigations into Trump's inner circle, particularly his family, could create devastating political and legal consequences. Even figures like Marco Rubio may discover that loyalty to Trump has destroyed their presidential ambitions.

The Republican Party could spend years recovering from the wreckage.

And perhaps Trump understands this better than anyone. His disgraceful decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel looks increasingly like a desperate attempt to rescue himself politically, regardless of the consequences for Ukraine.

The aggressor state stands to benefit financially while Putin continues his war. Meanwhile, Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism sounds increasingly measured, confident and presidential. Trump, who once publicly humiliated Ukraine's leader, now seems unable to offer a convincing response.

But perhaps there is an even uglier explanation. Could Trump, sensing his political future collapsing, simply be trying to extract whatever financial benefit remains from his presidency?

Some commentators have speculated about possible arrangements involving investments in Russian companies. These allegations remain unproven, but the very fact that such questions are being raised illustrates the extraordinary collapse of trust surrounding the American president.

For the leader of the United States, such suspicions are deeply humiliating. But this president is not Reagan, Bush or Ford. His name is Donald Trump.

What interests me even more is the reaction of Ukrainian Trump supporters, both at home and among the American diaspora. How will they justify their former idol now? Will they insist they never supported him? Will they pretend they never defended his decisions?

For years, they portrayed Trump as a powerful leader who would bring peace through strength. Yet when Ukraine needed principled leadership, he chose accommodation with the Kremlin.

History will judge those choices.

Trump's political decline offers a warning far beyond America. Never surrender your judgment to politicians who recognize no principles beyond personal advantage. Never confuse arrogance with strength, cruelty with leadership, or empty promises with genuine convictions.

Because when leaders abandon their principles, ordinary people pay the price. Sometimes with their freedom. Sometimes with their future.

And sometimes with their lives.

Iran offers US deal to reopen Hormuz within a week
Tehran says normal shipping through the vital oil route could resume within seven days if Washington accepts its peace terms
Published 17 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/LTqyuHJ1Oc
Iran could restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington accepts a peace plan proposed by Tehran last month, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said. The terms were previously rejected by US President Donald Trump.
The Islamic Republic remains “committed to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” Araghchi told a ministerial meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation on Saturday, blaming disruptions to shipping through the key waterway on the “aggressive actions” of the US and Israel.
”Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” the minister said. “The choice now rests with the United States.”
“This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation,” Araghchi added.
Tehran has offered to restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its naval blockade, easing restrictions on the Islamic Republic’s oil exports and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also demanding an end to hostilities “on all fronts,” including Israel’s military operations in Gaza and Lebanon.
Last month, Trump rejected Iran’s terms as “unacceptable.” He argued that the US retained full control over the strait and held a stronger negotiating position, while Iran was desperate to reach an agreement because it was “losing so badly.”
The US president has hinted that he could resume strikes, while American media outlets have reported that Pentagon officials and national security advisers briefed him on options involving the use of a massive conventional explosive nicknamed the “Mother of All Bombs.” However, Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have ruled out attacks on Iran before the US midterms on November 3 and Israel’s parliamentary elections on October 27, respectively.
Iran closed the waterway, which handles around a quarter of global seaborne oil and LNG trade, shortly after the US and Israel launched their bombing campaign on February 28. Iranian forces have since fired on vessels traveling along routes designated by the US Navy, which Tehran considers illegal.
Two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said. The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride also sank after striking a mine earlier this week, while another cargo vessel hit a mine but managed to reach port safely.
The prolonged disruption of shipping through Hormuz has driven up global energy prices and fueled inflation concerns. Brent crude surged to a five-month high on Friday, settling at $109.86 per barrel, up 3.7%, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate climbed above $100. Analysts have warned that uncertainty over Middle Eastern supplies is keeping a significant risk premium in oil prices, which could ease if Washington and Tehran reach an agreement restoring normal shipping.

On October 18, 1944, Field Marshal Erwin #Rommel was given a state funeral in Ulm. The official story was that he had died from injuries sustained in a car accident.

The truth was very different. Because of his links to the July 20 conspirators, he was supposed to face the People’s Court. Even #Hitler, however, hesitated. With the Allies pressing the Reich’s borders from every direction, he feared the public reaction if Germany’s most popular general were put on trial and executed.

A quieter solution was chosen. Rommel was offered a deal: if he took his own life, his family would be spared Sippenhaft (collective punishment of relatives) and the widow and children would continue to receive financial support. Rommel accepted. He said goodbye to his family and swallowed a cyanide capsule on October 14, 1944.

The state funeral, with Gerd von #Rundstedt delivering the eulogy, was a cynical farce. The regime once again rolled out the pomp and theatrical pathos that had defined its public image since 1933. Ulm itself was reduced to ruins two months later. Another few months after that, Hitler and the Nazi state were finished.

Erwin Rommel was 52 years old. R.I.P.

text:
Your argument here is an incoherent assemblage of assertions, simultaneously detached from historical and empirical reality and founded upon a premise that is fundamentally false.

The Palestinian people do not lack freedom because Israel exists.

They never possessed a sovereign state of their own to begin with.

When the territory they now claim as Palestine was under Jordanian occupation, which was itself illegal under international law, they advanced no demand for the establishment of a Palestinian state upon that land.

Most crucially, the absence of a Palestinian state is neither the cause of the absence of peace between Jews and Palestinians nor the motive for so-called Palestinian resistance.

No person of sound reason would assert that the Palestinians will somehow undergo a sudden transformation into peaceful pacifists and allies of Jews the moment a sovereign Palestinian state is established.

Palestinian public opinion, as measured by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, has demonstrated unyielding support for armed struggle against Israel, with no meaningful distinction drawn between combatants and noncombatants.

This stance has remained consistent throughout Palestinian history. Support for lethal attacks against random, innocent Jewish civilians, commonly referred to as terrorist attacks, has consistently constituted a majority position in both the West Bank and Gaza.

Large majorities have likewise opposed the disarming of Hamas as a precondition for ending hostilities.

This reality is compounded by the still more troubling fact of the Palestinian response to the atrocities of October 7. The majority either denied that Hamas had committed the documented atrocities against civilians, or celebrated and justified them.

Only a small minority accepted that the atrocities had occurred and objected to them.

Post-October 7 polling recorded majority approval of the decision to launch the attack itself.

The near-total refusal to attribute basic humanity to the other side is vast and systemic.

Dehumanization of Israelis among the Palestinian population is overwhelming and extreme.

The vast majority of Palestinians, both in Gaza and in the West Bank (though to a somewhat lesser degree in the latter), assign near-zero humanity to Jews living in Israel.

It is precisely this unyielding support for terrorist acts against Jewish civilians, this uncompromising exaltation of violent jihad against Jewish civilians, and this total dehumanization that perpetuates the conflict. The barrier to peace is emphatically NOT Israel’s supposed unwillingness to allow them the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state.

This is precisely the reason why a terrorist attack by a Palestinian against random, innocent Jewish civilians almost never elicits condemnation from Palestinian voices, whereas the extremely rare instance of a terrorist attack by an Israeli against Palestinians produces unequivocal condemnation from nearly every quarter in Israel.

text:
The Pied Piper of Hamelin. Thirteen twenty-eight. A German town drowning in rats. Granaries stripped, cellars crawling, children bitten in their sleep. The council offers a thousand guilders to whoever clears them out. A stranger with a flute walks in, plays, and every rat in Hamelin follows him to the river and drowns.
The town throws a feast. Then the bill comes. The council shrugs. Doesn’t pay. The Piper walks back into the square, plays a new tune — slower, sweeter — and one hundred thirty children follow him out the gates, up a hill, into a cave that seals behind them. Gone. The town never recovered. They still count years from that day.
Now the transfer. Today’s Hamelin is Europe. The rats aren’t people — they’re the consequences: churches torched in France, cars burning in Sweden, streets looted in Germany, whole neighborhoods where the state’s authority stopped reaching. That’s the infestation. Visible. Measurable. Impossible to ignore.
The Piper is the ideology. Open borders sold as compassion, as progress, as the moral duty of the age. It played the tune that made a hard problem feel solved — the rats seemed to vanish because the definition of “rat” got rewritten. You don’t have an invasion if you refuse to call it one.
The council is every government that opened the gates, collected the applause, then acted stunned when the bill arrived. And when citizens pointed at the smoke and asked for the thousand guilders back, they got the second tune — the one that calls the questioners bigots, cowards, fascists. That’s not debate. That’s the Piper making sure nobody checks the ledger.
Hamelin didn’t fall to an army. It fell because it believed a melody and stopped counting what it cost. Europe is standing in that square right now, listening to the flute, and the cave is still open.

Evidence against “longer wait times means less views on episodes”.

Some people use the “10 month wait time” excuse to say that episode 80 not getting as much views is fair and justified. Other people say views were always declining even before episode 80 and well into the Astro arc etc. 

But I found that this isn’t exactly the truth. Overall channel views only declined due to less episodes but views per episode were not just constantly declining and in fact the episodes between 79 part 3 and 79 part 1  in fact got just as much as if not more views then other older episodes. 

For these measurements I looked at some 6 episode periods from before. Many of them were still on level, lower or slightly above these episodes in views but you also have to consider that 77 part 3 to 79 part 1 are significantly newer episodes and the ones I’m comparing against are older then it and even still tbe newer episodes effectively equal the views.

I took the mean view counts of several 6 episode periods. Here is the averages I managed to collate. 

77 Part 3 to 79 Part 1 (8 and a half months) = average of 54.17 million views 

75 to 77 part 2 (2 months and 6 days) = average of 36 million views 

71 to 73 part 1 (1 month and 24 days) = 54.83 million views 

67 Part 3 to 68 (full episode) (2 months) = 57.83 million views 

You can notice I put a month counter on each one. This is the months between the upload of the first given episode of each given period and the last episode of each given periods upload date. 

You will notice all of these are 6 upload periods and yet 77 part 3 to 79 part 1 took 3x as much as the rest for it to all come out and are also newer and yet it has significantly higher views then the 6 uploads before it (75-77 part 2) despite it taking 2x as long to upload. 

It even compared literally identically with 71 to 73 part 1 which took less then 2 months for that 6 upload period to come out. 

In fact I even compared it to basically some long form episodes in the prime of the series. Granted most episodes in this period do get significantly more views with some over 100 million but even in this period between 67 part 3 - 68 (full episode), the view average is only 3 million higher then the recent episodes. Of course this doesn’t include short views which were higher back then but it is still insane that years later after the hype died down many episodes still reached more views then some of the episodes in prime skibidi toilet. 

What does this show? 

It shows the times between each upload does NOT necessarily mean less views. In fact 78 had the second longest wait time between uploads and that got the 2nd most views out of any episode in the Astro arc only behind 74. Season 25 took close to 2 months from 77 full episode to come out and was taken down for months right at the start of it being uploaded and still its at 55 million views which is about the average of 71-73 part 1 in views. 

Episode 77 ( full episode ) was also down for about 2-3 months and despite the algorithmic hit that would cause it’s at 61 million views now beating out many older episodes.

Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?
France’s school protests have united students and ‘yellow vest’ supporters, exposing deeper anger over living standards.

Protesters participate in a demonstration against rising living costs and cuts to public services at Place de la Republique in Paris, France, October 17, 2026. [EPA/Yoan Valat]📷
📷

By Caolán Magee
Published On 18 Oct 202618 Oct 2026
Protests are sweeping France as anger over conditions in schools meets frustration with high living costs and a government accused of doing little to address problems facing people.
About 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry. Most marched peacefully, while a small minority attacked buildings, looted shops and clashed with police, who fired tear gas and charged protesters.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were injured. Behind the confrontations lies a political crisis, fuelled by anger at deteriorating services and overstretched household budgets, and compounded by a sense that France’s political institutions offer little hope of change.
Here is how school blockades became a nationwide movement – and what that means for President Emmanuel Macron.
How have the protests spread, what are protesters demanding?
The movement began last month in high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where students protested against teacher shortages and poor facilities. School blockades and demonstrations later spread to cities including Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Lille and Marseille.
Saturday brought together students and trade unions, alongside supporters of the “yellow vest” movement that emerged in 2018 to challenge rising living costs and economic inequality.
Emile Chabal, a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh, told Al Jazeera the demonstrations were “the logical outcome of a series of protests” stretching back to the yellow vests.
That movement was driven by financial pressures and resentment at “the French presidential system”, he told Al Jazeera, alluding to a structure which often leads to the election of a centrist candidate, such as President Emmanuel Macron.
Saturday combined those longstanding grievances with students’ anger at deteriorating state schools. The yellow vests had demanded better public services.

Bringing students’ grievances together with wider social demands, therefore, represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said.

Yes, keep me updated

Students’ immediate demands concern conditions in France’s lycees (public high schools), which generally educate pupils aged 15 to 18. They want smaller classes, enough teachers, better buildings and less exhausting timetables. Their complaints also reflect broader concerns about whether the state can provide the education and opportunities young people need.

But for workers, including school staff, the dispute also concerns wages and the resources available to deliver public services.

The school protests coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s budget plans. Bringing all these concerns together under one umbrella represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said.

It comes as the proposed 2027 budget includes a 54 billion euro ($60.8bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures, which the government says is necessary to reduce France’s deficit. The proposals include freezing the pay scale used to calculate civil servants’ basic salaries, which unions say would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze.

Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, said students were inspiring wider mobilisation around inequality, cuts to public investment and democratic rights, with demands for social welfare spending rather than militarisation.

“They do not want to fight wars; they want a different future,” she told Al Jazeera.
She also linked the movement to young people’s mobilisation over Gaza, with Palestinian flags appearing at demonstrations across several European countries.

How has the government responded?

The government has focused its immediate response on public order, with President Macron saying those responsible for violence would be “prosecuted and punished”.
His comments came as a fire largely destroyed the historic town hall in the city of Limoges, while public buildings and shops were attacked elsewhere.
But those involved in violence represent only a small minority of the much larger mobilisation. Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has accused the government of repressing school students and allowing the confrontation to intensify.
His argument reflects a wider political dispute about whether the government treats the protests chiefly as a security problem or addresses the grievances that have brought different groups together.
Experts say France’s problems extend beyond disagreement over individual budget measures and reflect deeper discontent. Emile Chabal, from the University of Edinburgh, said political paralysis since the 2024 parliamentary elections, which left no bloc with an outright majority, had created “an environment in which no political party or movement is able to channel social discontent”.
That fragmentation makes it difficult to build a durable agreement on spending, taxation or public services. It also leaves protesters questioning whether changing governments produces meaningful changes in policy.
The protests are also “a tough blow for Macron”, Chabal said, whose promises of youthful energy and a reformed, dynamic France have been undermined by “his inability to articulate his political project and his deeply unempathetic persona”.
Chabal added that the unrest included violence sometimes seen on the fringes of French demonstrations, with direct-action tactics associated with the yellow vests. Targets included shops and, more unusually, public buildings. He described the destruction of Limoges’ town hall as particularly significant because of its place in France’s civic history.
Other researchers emphasise the role of policing. Guya Accornero, a specialist in social movements at Lisbon’s University Institute, said previous confrontations had created lasting tensions between protesters and police.
During the current protests, a 15-year-old lost a hand to a police stun grenade, while a 14-year-old suffered a shattered jaw after being struck by a tear gas canister fired at close range, according to Human Rights Watch. The organisation condemned excessive force against children, saying the demonstrations had been overwhelmingly peaceful.
“Young people have been violently repressed also when using non-disruptive tactics,” she told Al Jazeera.
Who could benefit politically?
There is no clear answer from the experts who spoke to Al Jazeera. Paul Smith, an associate professor in French history and politics at the University of Nottingham, believes far-right leader Marine Le Pen stands to gain.
“I see only one beneficiary and that’s Le Pen,” he told Al Jazeera, suggesting the unrest could also damage Melenchon’s presidential prospects.
Chabal cautioned against assuming a far-right gain, but he said fear of disorder had historically benefited conservative or centrist parties in France, including after the 1968 protests.
Le Pen has not entirely dismissed the protesters’ grievances, describing them on X on Saturday as “legitimate social demands”, while claiming they had been “held hostage by the far left”.
The far-right may seek to reap the rewards of public discontent, but experts say it is more likely to channel that anger towards immigration and the scapegoating of migrants, rather than blaming the structures of neoliberalism and capitalism for the protesters’ woes, as Melenchon has suggested.
With a presidential election due in April 2027, candidates face competing pressures, demonstrating that they can restore order while convincing voters they will address the conditions behind the mobilisation.
The challenge, Chabal said, is how to create change in “an environment in which no political party or movement is able to channel social discontent”.

text: Eating Nepali food in restaurants can be tricky. Most Nepali restaurants I know sell restaurant-style food typical of Delhi and the surrounding region, plus momo. This makes sense because, in most places, there isn't enough demand for Nepali cuisine. Occasionally, you may find places that have a wider selection of Nepali food, but they too offer items that are well adapted to being produced in a commercial setting. What I've heard is that Texas is different, especially the Dallas area, where you can find highly specialised Nepali home-style and restaurant-style food. Also, it is worth noting that Nepali cuisine is kind of a misnomer: most food items come from a handful of ethnic groups with rich culinary cultures. The most dominant cultural group in Nepal hardly has what can be termed a “cuisine.”

text:
🧵3. How ballots were counted before computers

For much of American history, counting votes was a manual process.
After polls closed, election officials and designated observers could examine and count the paper ballots. Depending on local law and the type of ballot, officials sorted ballots by candidate, tallied votes, recorded totals, and reported results to higher election authorities.
In an era when elections were relatively local affairs, hand counting was manageable. As the population expanded and ballots grew longer, however, counting became more demanding.
A single ballot might contain choices for president, members of Congress, state legislators, judges, county officials, school boards, and local propositions. Counting thousands or millions of ballots by hand required substantial time and personnel.
Mechanical voting equipment offered one solution.
Mechanical voting machines became prominent in many cities during the 20th century. They reduced the need to count individual paper ballots manually, but they also introduced mechanical complexity and required maintenance.

🧵3. How ballots were counted before computers

For much of American history, counting votes was a manual process.
After polls closed, election officials and designated observers could examine and count the paper ballots. Depending on local law and the type of ballot, officials sorted ballots by candidate, tallied votes, recorded totals, and reported results to higher election authorities.
In an era when elections were relatively local affairs, hand counting was manageable. As the population expanded and ballots grew longer, however, counting became more demanding.
A single ballot might contain choices for president, members of Congress, state legislators, judges, county officials, school boards, and local propositions. Counting thousands or millions of ballots by hand required substantial time and personnel.
Mechanical voting equipment offered one solution.

Mechanical voting machines became prominent in many cities during the 20th century. They reduced the need to count individual paper ballots manually, but they also introduced mechanical complexity and required maintenance.
Punch-card voting became widely known during the 1960s and 1970s. Voters punched holes in cards, which were subsequently tabulated by machines. Problems could arise when holes were incompletely punched or when the intended choice was not clearly registered. text:
National Teen Driver Safety Week is October 18-24! Teen driver safety depends on parent and guardian action. 

Safe driving starts long before anyone gets behind the wheel. This National Teen Driver Safety Week, the Fremont Police Department encourages parents and guardians to discuss safe driving habits with their teens before handing over the keys. 

Car crashes are a leading cause of death for teens (15-18 years old) in the United States. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, in 2024, there were 2,320 people killed in crashes involving a teen driver. That same year, 496 people were killed in crashes on California roads involving drivers aged 20 or younger. 

Teens should understand the dangers of risky driving behaviors, like speeding, texting while driving, not wearing a seat belt and driving under the influence of alcohol and/or drugs.

“Meaningful conversations at home can help shape the choices teens make on the road,” Lt. Kwok said. “Parents and guardians who talk about distractions, speeding and impairment give teens the tools to navigate real world risks and steer them toward safer habits every time they drive.”

Teens are also encouraged to use free, mobile-friendly resources from the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), including the free, mobile-friendly California Quick Reference Driver's Handbook, educational videos and the Teen Driver Roadmap, a step-by-step video guide for teens and their parents to help them prepare to get behind the wheel safely.

The Office of Traffic Safety offers the following tips to support teen drivers:
•Learn about California’s provisional licensing law and Graduated Driver Licensing laws, which places restrictions on passengers and nighttime driving during the first year a teen has a license. 
•Lead by example: Every time you're behind the wheel, it is a chance to model safe driving habits and talk about it with your teen. 
•Establish safe driving behaviors that are not only expected, but also the law. This includes no phone use while driving, eliminating distractions from friends, always following the posted speed limit and always buckling up.
•Friends, family members, parents and guardians can create a teen driving contract to outline specific driving guidelines.
•Speak up for safety: Encourage your teen to say something as a passenger if the driver is speeding, distracted, not wearing their seat belt or otherwise driving unsafely.

Teens, parents, educators, mentors and California drivers can also practice safe driving behaviors in realistic situations on the new, free, web-based driving simulation, The Road Ahead, at https://t.co/xQ49dxbDWu. Additionally, there is a user guide that provides an overview for how to get started and how to facilitate discussions about the game experience.

text:
The History of Guitar Cases and Protection, 1830-2026

Guitar cases evolved from wooden shipping boxes to engineered protection against impact, crushing and climate damage. Twelve designs illustrate that progression.

1830s-1890s - Martin coffin case. C. F. Martin made angular poplar cases with purple felt, brass handles and catches. They protected parlor guitars during storage and stagecoach or railroad shipping.

1930s - Geib & Schaefer red-line case. Suppliers built fitted wood-shell and pressed-fiber cases with fabric coverings and plush interiors. Red piping distinguished some Geib cases used with instruments such as the acoustic Gibson L-5. Cheaper chipboard offered little crush protection.

1950 - Fender thermometer case. Early Esquires and Broadcasters used narrow, shaped cases nicknamed for their outline. Tweed and later brown coverings accompanied Fender’s first solidbodies. The Telecaster name followed in 1951.

1954 - Fender poodle case. Early Stratocasters used contoured brown cases with reddish plush. Telecaster versions could look similar but were not necessarily interchangeable. The design was short-lived.

Mid-1950s - Fender rectangular tweed case. The wood shell and lacquered tweed covering facilitated stacking. An accessory compartment supported the neck. Pocket positions and lining colors changed through the decade.

Late 1950s - Gibson Lifton case. The 1959 Les Paul Standard is closely associated with brown-covered, pink-plush cases, often with five latches. Lifton, Geib and Stone supplied Gibson. A correct case supports historical provenance but cannot alone establish original pairing.

1960s-1970s - Anvil road case. Anvil’s roots date to 1952; heavy-duty touring cases expanded later. Reinforced plywood, aluminum edges, metal corners, strong latches and custom foam protected instruments traveling with professional stage equipment.

1969 onward - Calton. Keith Calton established his business in Aldershot, England. Later fiberglass-composite cases combined rigid shells, fitted interiors and strong hardware, protecting valuable acoustic guitars such as Martin dreadnoughts in transit.

1976 onward - Reunion Blues. Professional padded gig bags offered cushioning, straps and low weight. Later generations added reinforced panels, tougher textiles and improved neck support. Modern hybrids were not features of the original 1976 bags.

1977 onward - SKB. Dave Sanderson and Steve Kottman developed vacuum-formed cases in California. Molded thermoplastic shells enabled consistent mass production. Fender placed a significant case order in 1979.

1985 onward - Hiscox. Molded ABS outer shells, foam cores, fitted interiors and reinforced closures balanced lower weight with impact resistance, departing from heavy plywood construction.

2020s - Hybrid and smart protection. Reinforced gig bags, composite cases and custom foam interiors coexist. Headstock suspension, hygrometers, two-way humidity packs and optional sensors address both impact and changing storage conditions.

Protection depends on correct body and neck support, headstock clearance, shock-absorbing padding and secure latches. Vintage nitrocellulose finishes may react with unsuitable lining materials. Even a hard case needs a padded outer carton for shipping. Acoustic guitars are generally best kept at 45-55% relative humidity. US airline rules permit cabin carriage when suitable safe stowage space is available; they do not guarantee it.

Eritrea at the Heart of Human History: The Discovery of Madam Buya, a One-Million-Year-Old Homo Erectus Skull, and the Danakil’s Place in Human Evolution

Madam Buya: A Landmark Fossil from the Heart of Eritrea

In Buya, Eritrea, Eritrean and Italian scientists discovered one of the oldest known hominid fossils, dating back more than one million years. Known as Madam Buya, the nearly complete Homo erectus skull was excavated between 1995 and 1997 by a team of paleontologists from the National Museum of Eritrea and the University of Florence. The find is considered a possible link between *Homo erectus* and early archaic humans. It remains the oldest skeletal discovery of its kind and offers valuable insight into the evolutionary path toward the earliest anatomically modern humans.

Hand Axe Hill: Thousands of Tools Unearthed in Eritrea’s Ancient Landscape

The Danakil Depression in Eritrea is also believed to have played an important role in human evolution. An international team led by Canadian geologist Bob Walter, working with researchers connected to the University of Toronto, discovered thousands of hand axes in the badlands of Eritrea at a site known as “Hand Axe Hill.” These Acheulean tools, associated with early toolmakers, were found concentrated in one place, offering rare insight into the activities of our ancestors roughly one million years ago. At that time, the area was a lush “Pleistocene Park” with flowing rivers, green forests, and abundant wildlife including crocodiles, hippos, rhinos, elephants, and antelope.

A Coastal Gateway: Eritrea’s Role in the Out of Africa Story

Further discoveries along Eritrea’s Red Sea coast have strengthened the country’s connection to the Out of Africa theory. The team identified the oldest evidence of stone tools near a marine environment, dated to 125,000 years old. Described as the world’s first oyster bar, this find suggests that early human ancestors may have migrated out of Africa northward along the Red Sea coast, using Eritrea’s shoreline as a key route.

All in all, the discovery of Madam Buya, the thousands of hand axes at Hand Axe Hill, and the coastal evidence of early marine adaptation firmly place Eritrea at the heart of human history. These findings by Eritrean and international researchers continue to illuminate both early human evolution in the Danakil and possible pathways out of Africa. #Eritreanhistory #Eritrea

**What people think this is about:** A dramatic Ukrainian escalation deep into Russia proper, hitting civilian-adjacent energy infrastructure in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian power plants, right as Trump tries to force an energy ceasefire.

- St. Petersburg Governor Beglov reported one killed and five injured, fires persisting into the morning, Pulkovo airport restrictions, and damage to residential buildings; Leningrad Governor Drozdenko reported ~144–145 drones downed locally and 20,000 without power from substation hits.[[3]](https://t.co/Yp3ngCrj1v)
- Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point publicly claimed credit with FP-1 long-range drones; monitoring channels noted the 1,000 km flight path across defended airspace.[[1]](https://t.co/x6tTZeDW3g)
- This follows Trump’s Oct 11 “energy ceasefire” announcement (which neither side formally accepted), Russia’s continued strikes on Ukrainian energy (Zelenskyy cited 76 violations), Ukraine’s brief pause, and its resumption after Russian attacks persisted. Trump has publicly called Ukrainian refinery strikes “a disgrace” for raising global diesel prices.[[4]](https://t.co/HierAm32OZ)
- The attack hits export/storage capacity rather than just refining; the terminal handles sea, rail, and river transshipment. No independent confirmation yet on exact throughput loss or duration of disruption.
- Both capitals are using the strikes to signal resolve to domestic audiences and to Washington: Kyiv shows it will not be dictated to on energy targeting; Moscow highlights Ukrainian “terrorism” against civilian infrastructure.

### 3. Snapshot
On the night of October 17–18, 2026, Ukraine conducted one of its largest drone operations of the war, striking energy and logistics targets in and around St. Petersburg. Fires broke out at key petroleum facilities; Russian air defenses claimed a record interception but could not prevent impacts. The strike occurs against the backdrop of a collapsing U.S.-pushed energy truce and Trump’s explicit criticism of Ukrainian deep strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Oct 11, 2026**: Trump announces unilateral “energy ceasefire” effective immediately.[[5]](https://t.co/Q2PuVAhdpU)
- **Mid-Oct 2026**: Russia continues strikes on Ukrainian energy sites; Ukraine pauses refinery attacks briefly then resumes after violations.[[4]](https://t.co/HierAm32OZ)
- **Oct 15–16, 2026**: Trump calls Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries “a disgrace,” criticizes Zelenskyy personally, and notes pressure on Kyiv.[[6]](https://t.co/gtNZEfgqRG)
- **Night of Oct 17–18, 2026**: Ukraine launches massive drone barrage; Russia claims 1,015 downed; fires at Petersburg Oil Terminal and other sites; one fatality reported in St. Petersburg.[[2]](https://t.co/JFrUKTqzIJ)

### 5. Sides
**Ukrainian government / military (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian energy infrastructure, killing civilians and causing blackouts; symmetric response on Russian export capacity is legitimate self-defense and economic pressure.  
Critique: LT — Russia has hit Ukrainian power plants. IT — Deep strikes on Russian oil raise global prices and risk escalation or U.S. support cuts; selective targeting of export terminals vs. pure military sites invites “civilian infrastructure” framing.

**Russian government / military (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilian energy and logistics in a major Russian city, causing casualties and outages; this justifies defensive claims and highlights Kyiv’s unwillingness to de-escalate.  
Critique: LT — Fires and one death occurred. IT — Russia’s own energy strikes on Ukraine predate and continued through the Trump pause; air-defense success claims are inflated when impacts still happen.

**U.S. administration under Trump (IT dominant)**  
Steelman: Halting mutual energy infrastructure attacks reduces global price spikes (especially diesel) and creates space for broader negotiations; both sides should comply.  
Critique: IT — Pressure on Ukraine is asymmetric while Russia continues strikes; threats to cut intelligence/arms risk weakening the partner whose restraint is demanded. LT — Public statements tie Ukrainian actions directly to price effects.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns**: Large-scale Ukrainian drone penetration occurred; specific facilities (Petersburg Oil Terminal, Ruchyi depot, VK data center, Ozon hub) caught fire; Russian claims of 1,015 interceptions; one reported fatality in St. Petersburg; Trump’s public criticism and ceasefire push.[[7]](https://t.co/WYAhh23GYH)
- **Known Unknowns**: Exact extent of damage to terminal throughput or duration of outages; precise number of drones that reached targets vs. intercepted; whether additional unreported strikes occurred deeper in Russia.
- **Unknown Knowns**: Real-time U.S. intelligence on Ukrainian drone operations and targeting; internal Russian assessments of air-defense performance and economic impact.
- **Unknown Unknowns**: Second-order effects on global diesel markets or Russian export logistics if fires persist; potential for further escalation or U.S. policy shift if strikes continue.

### 7. Incentives map
Ukraine gains demonstrated reach, domestic morale, and leverage in any talks by showing it can hit high-value Russian assets despite distance. Russia gains propaganda value from “terrorist” attacks on its second city and justification for its own strikes. Trump administration seeks lower energy prices ahead of midterms and a visible diplomatic win; criticizing Ukrainian strikes aligns with that while avoiding direct confrontation with Russia. Media and engagement incentives favor dramatic fire footage and “escalation” framing over granular damage assessments.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Map the actual damage to export capacity and power restoration timelines before declaring victory or defeat. Both sides treating energy infrastructure as fair game while complaining about the other’s version is predictable; the side that can sustain the pain longer or force third-party intervention wins the attrition round. Watch whether U.S. material support actually changes after this.

**Evil AI Advice:** Keep the fires burning just long enough for the price spike and the viral videos, then offer a “pause” that looks like concession. Blame the other side for every civilian impact; the terminal will be rebuilt faster than the political narrative.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Track independent OSINT on terminal operations and export data in coming days for real impact vs. initial footage.
- Note any shift in U.S. statements or reported aid flows after the strike.
- Distinguish between storage/export terminals and active refineries when assessing economic effects.
- Expect both sides to claim maximal success while downplaying their own vulnerabilities.
- The pattern of tit-for-tat energy targeting is unlikely to stop without external enforcement both parties accept.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Verified independent data showing the Petersburg Oil Terminal returned to full export capacity within 48 hours with minimal throughput loss.
- Public U.S. confirmation that intelligence or arms support to Ukraine was curtailed specifically because of this strike.
- Russian admission or credible evidence that air defenses stopped all drones short of the terminal with zero impacts.
- Zelenskyy publicly committing to a verifiable, monitored halt on Russian energy targets without reciprocal Russian action.

text:
By Newsmax Wires    |   Sunday, 18 October 2026 11:20 AM ED

President Donald Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Sunday, calling him a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and an indispensable American ally in confronting Iran, as Netanyahu faces a closely contested battle to retain power.

In a lengthy Truth Social post addressed “To the Great People of Israel,” Trump offered his strongest possible backing for the Israeli leader.

“Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel,” Trump wrote. “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”

Trump praised Netanyahu’s leadership during the confrontation with Iran, describing him as “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant” despite intense domestic and international opposition.

“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump declared.

The president also warned that Netanyahu’s defeat could complicate America's efforts to counter Tehran.

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote.

Trump's endorsement underscores the unusually close political and personal relationship between the two leaders, who have worked together on some of the Middle East's most consequential diplomatic and security initiatives.

During Trump's first administration, the United States recognized Jerusalem as Israel's capital, moved the American Embassy there, recognized Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights and brokered the Abraham Accords, normalizing relations between Israel and several Arab nations.

Earlier this week in a Newsmax interview Trump hinted at his lean toward Netanyahu.

“I've had a very good relationship with him. We've had good success together,” Trump told Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty, adding “We had a very successful partnership ... in terms of a military partnership.”

The endorsement comes amid a highly competitive Israeli political landscape, with Netanyahu's right-wing and religious coalition facing a potentially decisive challenge from opposition parties seeking to end his long tenure.

Israeli elections are determined by the distribution of seats in the 120-member Knesset, where a governing coalition generally needs at least 61 seats.

A narrow difference between the Netanyahu-aligned bloc and opposition parties could determine whether the prime minister can assemble another government.

Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot has emerged as a significant opposition figure leading the moderate-right Yashar party.

Eisenkot, a former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff and war cabinet member, has emphasized national security, political accountability and the need for new leadership.

Although Eisenkot has extensive military credentials, Netanyahu continues to campaign on his own decades of experience, close relationship with Washington and record of confronting Iran and other regional threats.

Trump's intervention could reinforce Netanyahu's standing among Israeli voters who consider a strong relationship with the United States essential to their country's security.

The president's message left little doubt about his preferred outcome.

“This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much,” Trump wrote.

With the race potentially hinging on only a handful of parliamentary seats, Trump's unequivocal endorsement adds a major international dimension to Israel's increasingly consequential election contest.

text:
🍇 THE DUKE’S VINEYARD — PART 18

THE PRINCE WHO KNEW TOO MUCH

William struggled against Adrian’s grip, but the prince released him almost immediately.

“Quiet,” Adrian whispered. “If Vane discovers you are here, neither of us will leave this palace alive.”

William stared at him with fury.

“You were supposed to be under guard.”

“I escaped.”

“And why should I trust you?”

Adrian glanced toward the chapel.

“Because I know what your mother has spent twenty years trying to hide.”

William’s expression hardened.

“Speak.”

Adrian pulled a folded letter from inside his coat.

“Your father was not executed by the Duke. He was executed by someone who wore the Duke’s face.”

William looked at the letter.

It bore the royal seal, but the signature belonged to a man who had supposedly died before William was born.

“How is this possible?”

“Because the Duke had a twin brother.”

William froze.

Adrian explained that the real Duke had disappeared shortly before William’s father was killed. His twin, Lord Edmund Vale, took his place and secretly controlled the estate. He had spent years searching for the missing royal heir, waiting for the right moment to reveal him and claim power through him.

“And the man in the chapel?” William asked.

Adrian nodded grimly.

“Edmund Vale. The false Duke.”

William’s mind raced.

The man who had welcomed him into the manor, offered him work, and helped him discover his heritage might have been an impostor all along.

But one question remained.

“Where is the real Duke?”

Adrian looked away.

“I don’t know. The last person who saw him alive was your mother.”

A sudden crash echoed from the chapel.

They peered through the opening again.

The false Duke had discovered the hidden passage.

He was holding Margaret by the arm, while Lord Vane stood beside him with a drawn sword.

“Where is William?” the false Duke demanded.

Margaret lifted her chin.

“You will never control him.”

The Duke struck the altar with his fist.

“Then I will destroy everything he loves until he comes to me.”

William started forward, but Adrian stopped him.

“Wait. Look at the altar.”

A narrow compartment had opened beneath the stone surface. Inside lay an old crown, a bloodstained dagger, and a portrait of two identical men.

On the back of the portrait were six words:

ONE BROTHER RULED. THE OTHER SURVIVED.

William looked at Adrian.

“Which one is still alive?”

Before Adrian could answer, a voice came from the darkness behind them.

“The one you have been calling your father.”

Robert stepped into the light.

His face was pale, and blood stained his sleeve.

He looked at William with unbearable sadness.

“Son, I have lied to you about many things.”

He swallowed hard.

“But there is one truth you must hear before the bells ring again.”

Robert pointed toward the chapel.

“The false Duke is not my brother. He is your father.”

William stood motionless.

And inside the chapel, the man wearing the Duke’s face slowly turned toward the hidden passage as if he had heard every word. 👀

text:
The Next Phase of the US Iran War Probably Lies Ahead

This week brought, as forecast, more frequent and heavier attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran claims responsibility for only some of them.

Iran's foreign minister has said that the Iranian seven day offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remains on the table. Iran would open the strait if Washington lifted the blockade of Iranian ports, dropped the sanctions on Iranian oil exports and ended hostilities on all regional fronts. Amid the growing escalation, this comment looks like a reversal, but I do not believe Iran means it. I consider it a formality. The strait will not open, and no agreement will be reached.

I believe Iran is now moving to rungs 2 and 3 of my ladder of war. Here are all the rungs once more:

1. The tankers. A tanker that is hit is an insurance claim, not a supply outage, and it can be replaced. This rung is already in progress.

2. The pipelines, meaning the transport routes on land, and the American bases in the region.

3. Refineries and oil fields, explicitly in the region around Iran, meaning Saudi Arabia and its neighbours, not in the United States. A refinery cannot be replaced, and the outage stays visible for weeks afterwards.

4. The American warships in the Strait of Hormuz. That an American warship will be hit before the midterms, or even sunk, I now consider more likely than not. A warship that is hit is not material damage but an image, and that image will travel around the world and weaken Trump severely going into the midterms.

5. An attack on American soil, however small it turns out to be. What would be hit then is not just a facility. The war would then be in the country itself. This could come through sleeper cells or through drones that are launched from boats off the American coast and detonate on the mainland. I consider this scenario possible, but not likely, because it would be the maximum escalation.

We are 16 days away from the midterm elections in the United States and 9 days away from the elections in Israel. Once those are behind us, Trump has no reason left not to bomb Iran. I believe that from next week Iran and Iran-aligned militias such as the Houthis will escalate step by step to rungs 2 and 3. In the week after that, the escalation could in the worst case even reach rung 4 if the United States answers rungs 2 and 3 with bombs.

What matters most to me:

There are people behind every one of these rungs. In this war innocent people and civilians die, no matter which side they are on. Nothing in this world justifies wars. Civilians are civilians, and warlords are warlords.

Disclosure: I hold no positions related to this topic.

text:
To President Obama, Sir,

You write to the public of a "basic principle of American democracy" , that a government shall not single out a man for his political opinions. I read your words twice, and then a third time, in the manner of a man who cannot believe his own ears. For of all the men who have walked the halls of that house, there is scarce one who trampled that principle more thoroughly than yourself.

You speak of the full weight of the federal government brought down upon a critic. Very well. Let us weigh it. ⚖️

When you sat in the chair, you turned the secret engines of your own intelligence upon the man who would succeed you. Warrants obtained upon a dossier your own faction purchased, whispered into the ear of a tribunal as though it were revelation. Your officers swore to facts they had never troubled themselves to verify. And when the President was cleared, when the special counsel hunted two full years and returned with no collusion, did any man of your party offer apology? Not one. Your faction pronounced the absence of a crime to be itself a crime, and went on hunting.

So mark this, Sir: when you now cry "foul" at the raiding of a congresswoman's house, know that you taught the raiding.

And while your intelligence watched the President-elect, your Secretary, the man your own Vice President raised to guard the southern door, threw it wide open and called the throwing of it policy. Millions entered unrecorded, unvetted, unaccounted for; towns were remade overnight by men who never asked leave. Washington would call it dereliction. A plainer age would call it treason, and not be far wrong.

And when the assassin's ball passed through the President's ear at Butler, Providence stayed its hand and spared us a civil war. Had he fallen, your faction, which speaks of half the nation as a basket of deplorables, which sneers that we "cling to our guns and religion" , would have had no man left to answer to. Your people spoke openly of his death as though it were a remedy. It was not a remedy. It was a near miss of the whole republic.

Now comes Senator Slotkin of Michigan, a woman schooled in the craft of the Central Intelligence, trained in the art of unseating governments abroad, and says aloud what your faction has long intended: that they shall prosecute Republican leaders, and by prosecuting them frighten the young conservatives off the field before they ever reach it. She would have the rising generation believe that to stand with a president is to stand in a dock.

Sir, I warned you of factions. In my Farewell Address I wrote that the spirit of party "agitates the community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms; kindles the animosity of one part against another." That was 1796. You have spent two centuries proving me a prophet.

You complain that a principle is being broken. Sir, you did not break it first, but you broke it well. And a principle broken in your house does not mend itself in another's.

Your most humble and obedient servant, G. Washington

text:
It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts. Congresswoman Omar came to this country with her father when she was 12 years old. Five years later, her father became a naturalized citizen. If Ilhan had been 18 at the time, she would have had to apply for citizenship separately. But because she was 17, she became a naturalized citizen automatically.

Congresswoman Omar went on to graduate from college, work as a community organizer, become the first Somali-American legislator elected to public office in the U.S., and win a seat in Congress. There, she has been one of the Trump Administration’s fiercest critics, which has led the president to repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country.

Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen. Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.

Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it’s not the first time this has happened. Under President Trump, the Justice Department has repeatedly gone after those he considers his political enemies — from the Attorney General of New York, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve.

In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar’s life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she’s been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota.

The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.

text:
🚨Canada Choose India over US, on Largest Ever Trade Mission to Sign Massive $70 Billion FTA with India

In a major shift, Canada has brought its largest-ever trade delegation to India in nearly three decades, with more than 300 business leaders arriving to explore new partnerships and accelerate negotiations for a proposed Free Trade Agreement.

The target is massive, expanding bilateral trade from around $30 billion to approximately $70 billion.

This is not happening in isolation.

For decades, the United States has been Canada's overwhelmingly dominant trading partner, absorbing roughly three-quarters of Canadian exports. But growing uncertainty around US trade policy and tariffs has forced Ottawa to rethink its dependence on a single market.

And India has emerged as one of the most important alternatives.

Canada is now looking toward India's enormous consumer market, rapidly expanding economy, manufacturing capacity and growing demand for energy, technology and critical resources.

The sectors involved could be strategically important: pharmaceuticals, agriculture, textiles, engineering, clean technology, aerospace, energy and critical minerals.

Nuclear cooperation adds another layer. Canada is a major source of uranium, while India's nuclear-power expansion is accelerating. Stronger energy ties could therefore serve both countries' long-term strategic interests.

For Canada, India represents diversification away from excessive dependence on Washington.

For India, Canada offers access to a developed Western market, energy resources, uranium, critical minerals, investment and technology.

The headline may be about a $70 billion trade target, but the larger story is about a changing global economic map.

text:
When the Questioner Becomes the Accused: ABDUL EL-SAYED and the POLITICS of DARVO   

How denial, counterattack, obfuscation, and the reversal of scrutiny threaten political accountability.

A peculiar phenomenon is unfolding in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race: When Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed faces an uncomfortable question, the ensuing exchange can become less about the answer than about the supposed moral failings of the person who dared to ask.

It is a remarkable exercise in political misdirection. And psychology offers a framework for examining it.

DARVO: The Psychology of Reversing Accountability

In 1997, psychologist Jennifer J. Freyd introduced the concept of DARVO: Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender.¹

Originally developed to describe defensive responses to allegations of abuse and wrongdoing,

DARVO identifies three interconnected behaviors:

1. Deny: Reject or minimize the allegation.

2. Attack: Challenge the credibility, motives, or character of the person raising it.

3. Reverse Victim and Offender: Recast the person facing scrutiny as the injured party and the questioner as the aggressor.

Applying this framework to political rhetoric is not a clinical diagnosis, nor does it establish that an allegation is true. But it can expose how a public figure redirects scrutiny through accusation and moral reversal. And El-Sayed’s recent exchanges warrant precisely that examination.

The Tommy Exchange: From Candidate to Prosecutor

At a Michigan town hall, an attendee named Tommy asked whether El-Sayed would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. What followed was a revealing reversal. Instead of unequivocally disavowing it, El-Sayed asked whether Tommy himself had repudiated the organization. He then questioned Tommy’s assumptions, religious beliefs, and understanding of the Constitution.²

Tommy acknowledged that he suspected El-Sayed might hold competing allegiances. Such an assumption deserves scrutiny, especially when it targets someone because of his religion. But the broader political maneuver remains striking: a candidate who had just answered a question turned the exchange into an interrogation of the citizen.

The questioner became the defendant. The candidate became the prosecutor. It was an effective display of rhetorical control. Whether it demonstrated a comparable commitment to transparency is another question entirely.

The NBC Interview: When Evidence Becomes an Offense

The pattern becomes more consequential in El-Sayed’s October interview with NBC’s Tom Llamas. When confronted with historical social media posts from his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, describing their mother’s alleged involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood during the 1970s, El-Sayed dismissed the material as hearsay and challenged the questioning’s seriousness.³

He denied personal and family ties while explaining that he had never discussed the matter with his biological mother. Here, the distinction between allegation and evidence is essential.

A relative’s historical political affiliation does not establish El-Sayed’s own affiliation, ideology, or wrongdoing. The Associated Press has reported no evidence connecting him personally to the Muslim Brotherhood.⁴ Nevertheless, journalists are entitled to ask a candidate to reconcile apparently conflicting public statements. And rather than simply distinguish what he knew, what he disputed, and what remained uncertain, El-Sayed questioned the legitimacy of the inquiry and suggested Llamas was insinuating dishonesty.

As a result, the journalist’s attempt to clarify the record became the controversy. That is the troubling hallmark of political reversal: the demand for an explanation is reframed as an offense that requires its own explanation.

Israel, Iran, and the Art of Rejecting the Question

The October 8 Senate debate offered another example of El-Sayed’s confrontational approach to unwelcome scrutiny. When asked repeatedly whether Israel or Iran posed the greater threat to the United States, he dismissed the comparison as ridiculous and ultimately maintained that both countries presented dangers of different kinds.⁵

A candidate is entitled to reject a false choice. He is also obligated to explain his foreign-policy judgment. Yet insulting the question does not resolve the underlying issue. Nor does redirecting attention to an opponent automatically answer what voters were trying to determine.

This exchange does not, by itself, demonstrate the full DARVO sequence. It does illustrate a related tendency: discredit the premise, challenge the inquiry, and regain control of the political narrative.

Religious Liberty Is Not Political Immunity

Let us establish two principles without equivocation. No American should be presumed disloyal because of religious identity. Equally, no candidate should be insulated from legitimate scrutiny by the suggestion that uncomfortable questions are inherently discriminatory.

Religious freedom protects a candidate’s right to seek public office. It does not extinguish the public’s right to scrutinize that candidate. The distinction is fundamental to constitutional democracy. Freyd herself cautions that DARVO-like behavior cannot establish the truth of an underlying accusation. That warning must be respected.¹ But the repeated use of counterquestions, attacks on an inquiry’s legitimacy, and reversals of moral responsibility deserves examination regardless of political affiliation.

The Final Verdict: Accountability Cannot Be Reversed

The most revealing feature of El-Sayed’s confrontational style is not necessarily what he denies. It is how rapidly he can move from answering a question to questioning the person asking it.

A citizen seeks clarification. A journalist seeks consistency. A moderator seeks a policy judgment. Suddenly, the person conducting the inquiry must defend their intelligence, motives, or moral integrity. And the original subject risks disappearing beneath the spectacle.

That is the political danger of DARVO-style rhetoric. It turns accountability into an accusation and scrutiny into a supposed act of aggression. Abdul El-Sayed may be an accomplished debater. But rhetorical agility and political accountability are not interchangeable virtues.

The United States Senate is not a courtroom in which elected officials prosecute citizens for questioning them.
— Isaac Halevi

The U.S. government is an institution whose members are answerable to the citizens they represent, which includes every American citizen—not only the constituents in their respective state.

And when a politician becomes more determined to discredit the questioner than to clarify the answer, the public should pay very close attention.

French history gives their people an identity blueprint for expressing grievances. And the historical background is terrifying and insane.
1) take to the streets
2) challenge authority
3) defend the republic against a betrayal of its promises.

Follow that script back to its origins. The twists are absolutely brutal.

In 1789, crowds storm the Bastille, challengeing a system built on royal power and inherited privilege. The promise is liberty.

In 1993 the revolution starts consuming its own.

Defending liberty becomes the justification for mass arrests and executions. Danton, a revolutionary leader who urges moderation, goes to the guillotine. Robespierre helps drive movement (known as the Terror) until his colleagues turn on him.

He follows Danton to the blade.

Tens of thousanda die in a civil war and unstable government.

Then, a successful young general offers something desperately appealing: order.

Napoleon Bonaparte seizes power in 1799.

By 1804, he’s the emperor.

Eleven years after executing a king, France has another hereditary ruler.

Then Napoleon’s empire collapses. In 1814, the executed king’s brother, Louis XVIII, takes the throne.

Except Napoleon isn’t finished.

He escapes exile, returns to France, and regains power. Waterloo ends the comeback. The king returns. Again.

Another revolution in 1830 removes one king and installs yet another In 1848, that king falls too.

This time, France elects a president.

His name? Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte.

Napoleon’s nephew.

He stages a coup, then becomes Emperor Napoleon III in 1852.

A republic has elected the man who will replace it with an empire.

Only after his defeat in war in 1870 does France return to a republic without another king or emperor taking over.

This wasn’t one population endlessly changing its mind. Rival factions, foreign armies, hunger, ambition, and fear all shaped the outcome.

But the recurring temptation is familiar: 
overthrow those who abuse power, 

endure the upheaval,

then entrust extraordinary power to whoever promises to end it.
