Hayne's Response on 2/7/1861

Your reply, through your Secretary of the War Department, to my communication of the 31st of January, covering the demand of the Governor of South Carolina for the delivery of Fort Sumter, was received yesterday. Although the very distinct and emphatic refusal of that demand closes my mission, I feel constrained to correct some strange misapprehensions into which your Secretary has fallen.

There has been no modification of the demand authorized to be made, and no change whatever in its character, and of this you were distinctly informed in my communication of the 31st of January. You have the original demand as delivered to me by Governor Pickens on the 12th of January, and you have an extract from the further instructions received by me, expressly stating that he, the Governor, was “confirmed” in the views he entertained on the 12th of January by that very correspondence which you assign as the cause of the alleged modification. You assume that the character of the demand has been modified, yet you have from me but one communication, and that asserts the contrary, and you have nothing from the Governor but the very demand itself, which you say has been modified. What purpose of peace or conciliation your Secretary could have had in view in the introduction of this point at all, it is difficult to perceive.

You next attempt to ridicule the proposal presented “as simply an offer on the part of South Carolina to buy Fort Sumter and contents as property of the United States, sustained by a declaration in effect that if she is not permitted to make the purchase, she will seize the fort by force of arms.” It is difficult to consider this as other than intentional misconstruction. You were told that South Carolina, as a separate, independent sovereignty, would not tolerate the occupation, by foreign troops, of a military post within her limits, but, that inasmuch as you, in repeated messages and in your correspondence, had “laid much stress” upon the character of your duties, arising from considering forts as property, South Carolina, so far as this matter of property, suggested by yourself, was concerned, would make compensation for all injury done the property, in the exercise of her sovereign right of eminent domain. And this your Secretary calls a proposal to purchase! The idea of purchase is entirely inconsistent with the assertion of paramount right in the purchaser. I had supposed that an “interest in property,” as such, could be no other than “purely proprietary,” and if I confined myself to this narrow view of your “relations” to Fort Sumter, you, at least, should not consider it the subject of criticism. Until your letter of yesterday, you chose so to consider your relations, in everything which you have written, or which has been written under your direction. It was precisely because you had yourself chosen to place your action upon the ground of “purely proprietary” right that the proposal of compensation was made, and you now admit that in this view “it (Fort Sumter) would probably be subjected to the exercise of the right of eminent domain.”In your letter of yesterday (through your Secretary) you shift your position. You claim that your Government bears to Fort Sumter “political relations of a much higher and more imposing character.” It was no part of my mission to discuss the “political relations” of the United States Government to anything within the territorial limits of South Carolina. South Carolina claims to have dissolved all political connection with your Government, and to have destroyed all “political relations” of your Government with everything within her borders. She is unquestionably at this moment de facto a separate and independent Government, exercising complete sovereignty over every foot of her soil except Fort Sumter. Now, that the intention is avowed to hold this place as a military post, with a claim of exclusive jurisdiction on the part of a Government foreign to South Carolina, it will be for the authorities to determine what is the course proper to be pursued. It is vain to ignore the fact that South Carolina is, to yours, a foreign Government, and how with this patent fact before you, you can consider the continued occupation of a fort in her harbor a pacific measure, and parcel of a peaceful policy, passes certainly my comprehension.

You say that the fort was garrisoned for our protection, and is held for the same purposes for which it has been ever held, since its construction. Are you not aware, that to hold, in the territory of a foreign power, a fortress against her will, avowedly for the purpose of protecting her citizens, is, perhaps, the highest insult which one government can offer to another? But Fort Sumter was never garrisoned at all until South Carolina had dissolved her connection with your Government. This garrison entered it in the night, with every circumstance of secrecy, after spiking the guns, and burning the gun carriages, and cutting down the flag-staff of an adjacent fort, which was then abandoned. South Carolina had not taken Fort Sumter into her own possession, only, because of her misplaced confidence in a Government which deceived her. A fortress occupied under the circumstances above stated, is considered by you, not only as no cause of irritation, but you represent it as held for our protection!

Your Excellency’s Secretary has indulged in irony on a very grave subject. As to the responsibility for consequences, if, indeed, it does rest on us, I can assure your Excellency we are happily unconscious of the fact.I return to Charleston to-morrow. 

With considerations of high regard, I am, very respectfully,

I. W. HAYNE,
Special Envoy.

text:
An accountant turned an $86 online tournament into $2.5 million. Then millions of people decided they could do it too.

In 2003, Chris Moneymaker was a 27-year-old accountant from Tennessee. He had never played a live poker tournament.

He entered an $86 qualifier on PokerStars. It won him a seat in a bigger qualifier, which won him a $10,000 seat at the World Series of Poker Main Event in Las Vegas. For years the story said $39. PokerStars' own records later showed $86.

There were 839 players. Moneymaker reached the final two against Sam Farha, a seasoned pro.

Then came the hand. Moneymaker had nothing: king-high, no pair. Farha had a pair of nines, the better hand. On the last card, Moneymaker bet everything. That is a bluff: betting big with a weak hand to make your opponent believe you are strong.

Farha thought it over and folded the winning hand.

"I know we're early in the century, but that's the bluff of the century," said ESPN commentator Norman Chad.

Moneymaker went on to win the title and $2.5 million. Three years later, the Main Event drew 8,773 players. The poker boom had a face.

The lesson of that hand is not "be fearless". A bluff only works if the story makes sense. Moneymaker's earlier bets fitted a strong hand, and the cards on the table offered several. Farha wasn't beaten by courage. He was beaten by a believable story.

Have you ever been talked out of something you were right about, just because the other person seemed so sure?

text:
🇮🇱🇰🇷 A Jewish Hero of Korea: Tibor "Ted" Rubin, Holocaust Survivor, Korean War Veteran, Medal of Honor Recipient

He was still a boy when the Holocaust took everything from him. His mother and little sister were murdered in the gas chambers of Auschwitz. His father died in a camp. At fourteen, Tibor "Ted" Rubin was sent to Mauthausen, where every day he asked himself one question:

"When is it my turn?"

In 1945, American soldiers liberated the camp. "They picked us up and brought us back to life," he said. He made a promise that one day he would repay them.

He kept that promise in Korea.

In June 1950, Communist North Korea invaded the South. Ted went to war, first against the North Korean army, and later against the Chinese.

Near the Pusan Perimeter, he held a hill alone for 24 hours, racing from foxhole to foxhole and hurling grenades so the enemy would think an entire unit was dug in. Because he stayed, his battalion escaped.

At Unsan, deep inside North Korea, three men had already died manning the last machine gun. Ted took it. "Nobody wanted to do it, but somebody had to." He fired until the ammunition was gone. Wounded, he was captured by the Chinese and marched to a frozen camp the prisoners called "Death Valley." That winter, men died there by the dozens every day.

By then, his native Hungary had fallen to Soviet control. His captors offered to send him home. It was not mercy. They wanted to pull him away from his fellow Americans and parade him as a soldier who had turned his back on the free world. He refused. He would not betray the country that had freed him, and he would not abandon his dying friends.

For 30 months, the boy who survived Mauthausen kept other men alive. Night after night, knowing that capture meant death, he slipped past the guards to steal food. He made soup from grass. He cleaned wounds with melted snow. He sat up through the night with men too weak to lift their heads. As many as 40 of them came home because of him. One survivor put it simply: "I was skin and bones. He saved my life."

His comrades recommended him four times for the Medal of Honor, America's highest military award. Four times, nothing happened. They later testified that an antisemitic sergeant buried every recommendation. The same sergeant mocked Ted for being Jewish and kept sending him on the most dangerous missions, as if hoping he would never return. Decades later, the U.S. Congress ordered a review of Jewish and Hispanic veterans who had been passed over because of prejudice, and the truth finally came to light. In 2005, 55 years after he fought, Ted Rubin received the Medal of Honor at the White House. He said only this:

"The real heroes are the ones who didn't come home."

Ted died on December 5, 2015, in Garden Grove, California. He was 86. He rests at Mount Sinai Memorial Park in Los Angeles. In 2022, his family gave his Medal of Honor to the 1st Cavalry Division, the unit he fought with in Korea. It is displayed today at division headquarters at Fort Hood, Texas, still among the soldiers he loved.

Ted, you survived a darkness no child should ever know, and then you walked back into the fire for a country that was not your own. The freedom I live in today was built on what you gave. As a Korean, I bow my head to you in deep gratitude.

You never knew my name. And still, you fought and bled for people like me, for generations of Koreans not yet born.

And now, I know yours.

Tibor "Ted" Rubin.

While you were alive, I never knew what you had given for Korea. I never knew that so many of your comrades, many of them Jewish, never made it home, and gave their lives on our soil.

I wish I could thank you in person. 
But I learned too late.

Now that I know, I cannot stay silent. 
As you did for Korea, I will do everything I can so that your people, your descendants, can live in safety and in joy.

Antisemitism cruelly took the family of the man who helped save our nation. 

It even tried to deny him the Medal of Honor he earned saving our people. 

So, my fellow Koreans, what will we do?

Will we not work to drive antisemitism from the face of the earth for good?

We Koreans will repay this debt.

For the Jewish people and for their generations to come, we will stand against antisemitism with everything we have, and help tear it out by the roots.

Today we Koreans walk our streets in freedom. We will not rest until Jewish people everywhere in the world can do the same, walking their streets in safety and living without fear.

We will never forget.

May his memory be a blessing. 🙏🏻

text:
As part of Marc Carney’s extreme militarism, he’s putting $2 billion into one of the most secretive, US aligned parts of the Canadian government. But the media focus has been almost entirely about controversy over data centres.

On Friday the Globe and Mail and several other outlets reported that the Communication Security Establishment (CSE) will construct a data centre in Ottawa expected to cost up to $1.85 billion. The new 60 MW facility would be among the largest such projects in the country though smaller than several planned data centres. According to the paper, “the national security source told The Globe the data centre project is possible now because of the Carney government's significant increase in defence spending.”

Under the Department of National Defence, CSE employs over 3,800 mathematicians, engineers, linguists, analysts, computer scientists, etc. Its annual budget is over $1 billion. The secretive agency has a variety of high-tech gadgets, including surveillance planes. In 2011 CSE moved into a new $1.2 billion home. The seven-building, 110,000 square-metre complex is connected to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service’s (CSIS) headquarters in Ottawa.

Unlike CSIS, CSE is largely foreign focused. It seeks to “protect the computer networks and information of greatest importance to Canada” from international attack. CSE also gathers international signals intelligence (SIGINT), which it defines as “intelligence acquired through the collection of electromagnetic signals.” Historically, CSE largely intercepted electronic communications between embassies in Ottawa and other nations’ capitals. Today, CSE monitors phone calls, radio, microwave and satellite, as well as emails, chat rooms and other Internet exchanges. It engages in various forms of data hacking, sifting through millions of videos and online documents daily.

CSE has long had close ties to its US counterpart. NSA has trained CSE cryptanalysts and in the 1960s the US agency paid part of the cost of modernizing Canadian communications interception facilities. CSE has opened interception posts at Canadian diplomatic outposts at NSA’s behest. CSE long spied for the US from an interception post inside Canada’s embassy in Havana and in the 1970s sought to open a communications site in Algeria to help NSA spy on Muammar Gaddafi’s Libya. CSE also gathered intelligence on Palestinians for Israel. Former CSE intelligence officer Mike Frost wrote, “[former Palestinian Liberation Organization chairman] Yasser Arafat’s name, for instance, was on every [CSE] key word list. NSA was happy about that.”

An NSA history of the US–Canada SIGINT relationship released by whistleblower Edward Snowden labelled Canada a “highly valued second party partner”, which offers “resources for advanced collection, processing and analysis, and has opened covert sites at the request of NSA. CSEC shares with NSA their unique geographic access to areas unavailable to the US.”

As part of the Snowden revelations, it came to light that CSE hacked Mexican computers and spied on Brazil’s Department of Mines and Energy. CSE also planted sophisticated malware on mobile phones and maintained a network of infected computers to attack targets without being detected. To mask their involvement CSE hacked into random computers outside the US/Canada/UK/Australia/New Zealand Five Eyes alliance to use them to launch cyberattacks.

The September 11, 2001, attacks in the US spurred a major expansion of CSE. During this period CSE took an ever more active role in ‘counterterrorism’ and foreign intelligence. The agency’s sophisticated equipment and analytical and linguistic resources contributed significantly to the 2001-14 occupation of Afghanistan. The agency’s website said it played a “vital role” in the central Asian country and CSE head John Adams boasted that they were responsible for more than half the “actionable intelligence” Canadian soldiers used in Afghanistan. That included monitoring Taliban forces and leaders as well as allied Afghan government officials. Information CSE provided protected Canadian troops from attack and helped special forces assassinate Afghans.

CSE contributed intelligence to the March 2006 special forces operation to rescue two Canadians and a British hostage held by insurgents in Iraq. CSE aided the deployment to Iraq-Syria that began in 2014. The agency probably hacked ISIL computers and smartphones, and CSE officials likely staffed a state-of-the-art intelligence centre in Kuwait. (Presumably, CSE supported the 2011 bombing of Libya, 2004 coup in Haiti and other Canadian Forces deployments, but I couldn’t confirm this.)

For more than half a century CSE (and its predecessor) functioned without official mandate. CSE operated under secret orders in council until 2001. That year’s Anti-Terrorism Act (Bill C-36) gave CSE a statutory mandate, which amended the National Defence Act. Among other things, it called on the agency to acquire foreign intelligence from the “global information infrastructure” and detailed the defence minister’s role in authorizing information collection that might “inadvertently” target Canadians’ private communications.

As the Internet came onto the scene CSE was instructed to conduct Computer Network Exploitation. It went from intercepting communications (“data in motion”) to seeking information on foreign computer systems (“data at rest”). According to Bill Robinson, who runs SIGINT focused blog Lux Ex Umbra, “it became a hunter as well as a gatherer.” CSE could hack into computer systems, implant malware and copy information.

In 2017 CSE was further empowered to carry out offensive operations against foreign actors. The Communications Security Establishment Act authorized CSE “to degrade, disrupt, influence, respond to or interfere with the capabilities, intentions or activities” of international targets. In effect the intelligence agency could seek to take a government offline, shutter a power plant, knock a drone out of the sky or interfere in court proceedings and elections in countries Ottawa doesn’t deem “democratic”. There is no requirement that the target threaten Canadian security.

The legislation forbids offensive cyber activities that could cause injury or death or “obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice or democracy.” But these limitations don’t apply if CSE conducts cyberattacks on behalf of a Canadian Forces operation or receives approval of the foreign minister. Additionally, there is no independent oversight of CSE’s new offensive capabilities and CSE is allowed to do “anything that is reasonably necessary to maintain the covert nature of the activity.”

The Communication Security Establishment is a secretive, US aligned government agency. We need a public discussion about putting $2 billion more into bolstering it.

“Divine providence concurs with evil actions, first, by foreknowing them; second, by sustaining nature; third by permitting; fourth by abandoning; fifth by handing over to Satan; sixth by setting their limits beforehand; seventh by eliciting good from them.”

That is from Johann Gerhard in his “Theological Commonplaces: On Creation and Angels, on Providence, on Election and Reprobation, and on the Image of God in Man before the Fall” and another source summarizes:

2. Sustaining of Nature: God preserves the physical substance, life, and natural faculties of the creature while the creature abuses those powers to commit sin.

3. Permission: God allows the sinner to act contrary to His moral law rather than forcibly preventing the exercise of free choice.

4. Forsaking/Desertion: God justly withdraws restraining grace, abandoning stubborn sinners to their own blindness and hardness of heart.

5. Handing Over: God delivers unrepentant sinners over to the power of Satan or their own disordered desires.

6. Setting Limits beforehand: God circumscribes evil, determining in advance how far it may go, its duration, and the individuals it can touch.

7. Directing to a Good End / Ordinatio ad Bonum: God overrules and elicits good from evil acts, turning what was intended for wickedness into a means of Good.

Classical theism further holds that God possesses exhaustive knowledge of reality. In the theology of Thomas Aquinas, divine knowledge is traditionally distinguished as the knowledge of simple intelligence (scientia simplicis intelligentiae), by which God knows all possibles in His own essence, and the knowledge of vision (scientia visionis), by which He knows all actualities across time in light of His eternal decree. Self-knowledge of the divine essence is necessary and identical in every alternative.

More broadly through the Arc of Christendom “God” as the Metaphysical Wellspring of all Ontological Counterfactual Possibility necessarily and eternally houses All Knowledge of All Ontologies, Counterfactual and Otherwise. More narrowly if we zoom in on Thomism specially and then zoom in again on a few schools withing Thomism we will find a more limited “reach” of the “Content” of God’s Knowledge. Specifically withing the framework of those select schools (not all Thomisitic schools), the contingent content of free knowledge (the knowledge of vision) is not identical across the alternatives of creation and non-creation and different creations. If God decrees a created order, free knowledge includes the free choices and events that occur within it; if God refrains from decreeing creation, that contingent content remains purely possible. This variation concerns only contingent terms and the extrinsic termination of divine knowledge. It introduces no real change, temporal transition, or division into the divine act of knowing (actus intelligendi), which remains one, simple, eternal, immutable, and identical to the divine essence across all alternatives.

The Post-Tridentine Schism: Physical Premotion vs. Middle Knowledge

Across all such baselines regarding Agency, Environment (the Ocean of Secondary Causes called “Reality”), and Divine Knowledge a four-century scholastic dispute erupted in the post-Tridentine era. Thomist and Molinist thinkers locked themselves in mutual accusations of fatalism on one side and semi-Pelagianism on the other. The clash centered on the metaphysical character of the will at the exact instant of choosing between opposites, as well as the location of the sufficient cause that effects the transition from potency to act, and also the consequent mechanics of how God knows those choices.

Post-Tridentine Dominican thinkers, most prominently Domingo Báñez, operated within a strict Aristotelian metaphysical principle: nothing moves from potency to act except by something already in act. A power remaining in potency cannot self-actualize into a state of act without an effect existing without a sufficient actual cause. Therefore, the transition from the capacity to choose to the actual willing requires a divine motion applied directly to the will itself—an internal physical premotion (praemotio physica).

On this account, God does not merely establish the world and observe; the divine decree actively and interiorly moves the will to actualize one specific choice. Grounded in the principle that truth requires ontological reality (ens et verum convertuntur), Bañezianism denies that God possesses an independent knowledge of what a free creature would do in hypothetical orders He does not decree. Prior to a divine decree, a counterfactual conditional of creaturely freedom possesses no determinate truth value and lacks the ontological reality required to be knowable. While traditional Bañezian interpreters argue this causal-grounding intuition has material continuity with Aquinas, this specific denial of undecreed counterfactuals is a specialized early-modern consequence.

Seeking to safeguard libertarian freedom and moral accountability, Luis de Molina and the Jesuit school regarded the Bañezian mechanism as rendering the concrete power to do otherwise illusory, collapsing human freedom into theological determinism. Molinists insisted on simultaneous concurrence, where God supplies the general power to act while the creature’s own will and intellect are wielded by the agent. To explain how God retains sovereign foreknowledge without “learning” from creaturely determinations, Molina posited scientia media (middle knowledge)—an eternal category of divine knowledge logically prior to, and independent of, any divine decree. The meaning of the term Molinism is complete if and when two criteria are met: First: God infallibly knows what any free agent would choose in any given set of circumstances, and Second: God consults those truths prior to deciding which world to actualize.

Both the Banezian Overreach and the Molina Overreach operated on the shared assumption that counterfactuals of freedom must either float in mid-air independent of any causal order or else be fixed by a discrete, antecedent predetermining decree upon the creaturely faculty.

The Broader Tradition, Synergy, and the Biblical Witness:

The technical debate over whether counterfactuals require an antecedent divine decree represents an early modern scholastic development rather than the explicit consensus of the broader Christian tradition. For the first sixteen centuries, patristic, medieval, and Eastern Christian sources affirmed God’s exhaustive omniscience alongside genuine creaturely contingency without formulating foreknowledge around either middle knowledge or physical premotion. Biblical texts depicting conditional human actions—such as David at Keilah (1 Samuel 23) or Christ’s warning regarding Tyre and Sidon (Matthew 11:21)—were historically received as genuine expressions of divine counterfactual knowledge, grounded in God’s comprehensive knowledge of circumstances and outcomes without requiring an antecedent causal shove to render them knowable.

The two-thousand-year macro-history of Christian theology displays a dominant footprint composed of four interlocking affirmations:

      •Necessary Grace: Humans are radically incapable of initiating salvation without the prior, unmerited illumination of the Holy Spirit (excluding Pelagianism).
      •Necessary Synergy: Grace does not treat the human soul as a passive block; it heals the will so that active, uncoerced cooperation becomes possible.
      •Resistible Grace: The salvific movement can be definitively and tragically resisted by the human creature.
      •The Hopeful Universal Offer: God genuinely wills the salvation of all, and Christ died for all human beings without exception.

This general arc is the bedrock of the Catholic Catechism, the paradigmatic map of Eastern Orthodoxy, and the vast majority of early Church Fathers like Irenaeus and John Damascene. Narrow historical exceptions to this synergistic consensus have consistently been met with explicit rejection. When Gottschalk of Orbais advanced a doctrine of twin predestination (unconditional election and reprobation) in the ninth century, he was condemned at the Synods of Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849). Similarly, Pope Innocent X’s bull Cum occasione (1653) officially condemned the Jansenist propositions that inner grace in fallen nature can never be resisted.

The historical proof that Báñezianism is not the exclusive Catholic paradigm lies in the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1598–1607). Pope Paul V ultimately permitted both the Dominican and Jesuit schools to be taught but forbade either from condemning the other as heretical. Strict Báñezian Thomism remains a permitted theological opinion, but the magisterium pointedly refused to adopt its specific deterministic mechanics as dogma.

Lonergan’s Retrieval: Aquinas Beyond the Dichotomy

Twentieth-century historical retrieval, most systematically articulated in Bernard Lonergan’s Grace and Freedom: Operative Grace in the Thought of St. Thomas Aquinas, demonstrates that the post-Tridentine apparatus of physical premotion versus middle knowledge was anachronistic relative to Thomas Aquinas. Later commentators read sixteenth-century concerns back into thirteenth-century texts. Lonergan’s analysis yields a framework that dissolves the later dilemma through several foundational observations.

First, for Aquinas, God is the universal transcendent ground of all being. God does not intervene as an extrinsic secondary agent competing with human wills on the same causal plane. God sustains both primary causality and the entire network of secondary causes—the full ecosystem of reasons, agencies, natures, and occasions. Divine providence decrees not only that an event occurs, but the precise mode in which it occurs: necessary things happen necessarily, and contingent, voluntary things happen freely. The will’s free movement is upheld from within by universal providence; no specialized discrete premotion is required to determine the will from outside that ecosystem.

Second, Aquinas distinguishes operative from cooperative grace without pre-determination that bypasses the faculties. Operative grace causes the very willing itself (operatur in nobis velle) and actualizes the intellect’s grasp of the good from within human consciousness, without violating voluntary agency. Cooperative grace concerns the subsequent external execution of that willing.

Third, Lonergan’s central thesis is that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion.

Finally, moral failure is accounted for as a defect: the will’s failure to attend to the rule of reason (non-attentio regulae or defectus regulae). This non-attention is a pure privation, initiated when the creature places an obstacle (ponere obicem). Because sin possesses no positive ontological entity, it is “unintelligible” in Aquinas’s precise sense—it requires no divine causal predetermination in order to be known or permitted. Because the will under sufficient grace retains the real proximate potency (in sensu diviso) not to place the obstacle, the failure remains voluntary and culpable.

Incompatibility with Five-Point Calvinism and Deterministic Compatibilism:

For centuries, a recurring claim has appeared in some Reformed discussions: that selected passages from Thomas Aquinas secretly support a monergistic account of grace and election. However, Five-Point Calvinism’s attempt to appropriate Thomas Aquinas falters because its soteriology relies on a competitive, mechanistic view of divine action that fundamentally contradicts Aquinas’s doctrine of divine transcendence. In Grace and Freedom, Bernard Lonergan demonstrates that Calvinist appeals to Aquinas usually depend on anachronistic misreadings of his texts, specifically by confusing his original concept of “operative grace” with later, deterministic formulations of “efficacious grace” and physical premotion. Lonergan’s historical retrieval of Aquinas’s developing account shows that the solution Aquinas actually reached—via the theorem of divine transcendence—is neither the later Báñezian system nor the Molinist one, and it cannot underwrite the specific version of deterministic compatibilism that typically accompanies Five-Point Calvinism.

The primary barrier to Calvinist appropriation lies in Lonergan’s retrieval of exactly how Aquinas understood operative grace versus how later theologians redefined it. This dismantles claims to Thomistic support for both Irresistible Grace and the Perseverance of the Saints, and especially for the form of compatibilism that joins them.

Aquinas’s actual view of operative grace and contingency is decisive. For Aquinas, operative grace describes the interior movement in which God operates and the human will is the thing moved (resulting in the internal act of willing the end, including conversion). Lonergan shows that God executes this through the theorem of divine transcendence. God, as the absolute primary cause, is non-competitive with human agency. When God’s operative grace moves the will, it actualizes the will according to its own natural, contingent mode. Grace elevates and perfects the natural faculties rather than overriding them, so that the human subject participates vitally and freely. The motion is infallible under that particular divine action (the will does consent), yet the necessity is not absolute; contingency is preserved precisely because of divine transcendence. This precludes any notion of divine coercion or of the will being reduced to a passive instrument.

The anachronism of “efficacious grace” and premotion further blocks appropriation. Lonergan clarifies that the strict dichotomy between “efficacious” and “sufficient” grace—along with the concept of praemotio physica (physical premotion)—was not Aquinas’s framework. These concepts emerged during later controversies (especially the De Auxiliis debates), where later Dominicans such as Domingo Báñez projected a more mechanistic system onto Aquinas. When Five-Point Calvinists attempt to appropriate Aquinas, they typically point to these stronger, post-Aquinas models of premotion. While Calvinist soteriology may find genuine conceptual overlap with certain later Thomistic formulations, this alignment exists only within a specific school of Thomism rather than with Aquinas himself or with “Thomism” as a unified whole. Sweeping claims such as “the scholastics are on our side” therefore collapse centuries of complex development and ignore Aquinas’s own non-competitive synthesis.

This yields clear incompatibility with Irresistible Grace. The “I” in Five-Point Calvinism functionally mirrors the later mechanical view more than Aquinas’s original thought. High Calvinism generally treats the will as radically passive until unilaterally renovated by divine action in a way that eliminates genuine alternative potency. This tends to place divine and human agency in a competitive framework in which God’s success requires the suppression of human contingency. That stands in contrast to Aquinas’s insistence, as retrieved by Lonergan, that operative grace actualizes the will according to its own contingent mode without coercion.

It is equally incompatible with Calvinistic Compatibilism:

Contra Compatibilism Observation 1 of 2:

Lonergan’s retrieval demonstrates a framework that fundamentally conflicts with the deterministic compatibilism typical of Five-Point Calvinism. High Calvinist compatibilism holds that humans choose freely according to their desires or strongest inclinations, while those desires are unilaterally set by divine grace so that the will freely follows without retaining a real power of contrary choice. In this model the human will functions as an instrument that must conform to the primary cause. By contrast, Lonergan shows that Aquinas relies on the theorem of divine transcendence, which preserves true contingency: God’s absolute primary causality causes the human will to act freely and contingently according to its own mode. Because the will is not merely acting out a deterministic script of divinely fixed inclinations but retains vital, contingent agency, Aquinas’s theology remains out of reach for the specific version of compatibilism that Five-Point Calvinism uses to underwrite both irresistible grace and guaranteed perseverance. Overlap with broader theological compatibilism is possible; identity with the Reformed version that suppresses alternative potency is not.

Contra Compatibilism Observation 2 of 2:

Lonergan demonstrates that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion. This fundamentally contradicts High Calvinism’s Soteriology of 100% Monergistic Determinism vis-à-vis your status as Reprobate or Elect.

Aquinas is incompatible with the “P” of TULIP in its Perseverance of the Saints:

Lonergan’s retrieval further demonstrates Aquinas’ own coherence by highlighting the fact that the aforementioned active, contingent human freedom funded by operative grace not only exists Pre-Conversion and all the way Into Conversion but it persists After Conversion, making it genuinely possible for a justified individual to fall away. Note the seamless application of Necessary Grace and Necessary Synergy within Grace-Perfecting-Nature as Aquinas fundamentally delineates between the initial grace of justification and the subsequent gift of perseverance (donum perseverantiae). In Summa I-II, q. 109, a. 10 he states that “to many grace is given to whom perseverance in grace is not given.” A believer can receive the operative grace that justifies without receiving the further gift of final perseverance. Because the free will remains mutable, the justified retain the capacity to reject subsequent graces and fall into mortal sin. This directly contradicts the Calvinist doctrine of the absolute, guaranteed perseverance of all the elect.

Agent Act As Unnecessary Alternate Possibility

The concept of “Unnecessary Action” by an Agent referents what is often labeled Contingent Action as opposed to Necessary Action i.e. Determined Action. Because Aquinas insists that God’s absolute primary causality perfectly guarantees the genuine, active freedom of the secondary cause, his soteriology cannot support the strict monergism of Five-Point Calvinism. God’s operative grace does not unilaterally override a passive subject or determine its desires in a way that eliminates contingency; it actualizes the vital, free consent of the human agent while preserving the will’s contingent mode at every stage. Consequently, Five-Point Calvinism cannot claim Aquinas’s own teaching on grace and conversion without abandoning its own requisite definitions of irresistible grace, deterministic compatibilism, and guaranteed final perseverance.

The classical tradition, as retrieved in its pre-polarized form, upholds divine immutability and exhaustive knowledge grounded in transcendent causality. Contingency is preserved not by removing God’s governance, but by recognizing that it is the very efficacy of God’s universal providence that causes free agents to act freely. This synthesis supplies the resources to affirm exhaustive divine knowledge of all counterfactual ontologies, immutable simplicity, and genuine creaturely contingency—equipping rather than overriding the will—without succumbing to the specialized difficulties generated by physical premotion, deterministic compatibilism, or middle knowledge ((more specifically not counterfactual knowledge as such but rather “God Using Counterfactual Knowledge As The Sole Basis To Choose This/That World)).

Convergence In Various Discussions:

God Is The Wellspring, Root, and Causal Repository — the Explanatory Terminus from Whom all causal ecosystems are drawn, conserved, and explained.

▪️PAP & Unnecessary Alternate Possibility
▪️Ex Nihilo & God CAN WILL OTHERWISE

▪️God’s Eternal Council Can Be Otherwise
▪️Free Will as Liberty of Exercise & Liberty of Specification

▪️All Knowledge is Eternally Present in the Uncreated Wellspring of all Unnecessary Ontological Counterfactual Possibility

▪️Proportionate Causality + Divine Conservation + Divine Concurrence → Imago Dei → Arbiter I|||i
▪️We speak of the Triune God Who Is Procession||Verb||Speech Itself — not of the Static Processionless Verbless God of Aristotelian-Metaphysics — but the Fundamentally Wider God of Aristotelian-Thomistic-Metaphysics.

For centuries, a recurring claim has appeared in some Reformed discussions: that selected passages from Thomas Aquinas secretly support a monergistic account of grace and election. However, Five-Point Calvinism’s attempt to appropriate Thomas Aquinas falters because its soteriology relies on a competitive, mechanistic view of divine action that fundamentally contradicts Aquinas’s doctrine of divine transcendence. In Grace and Freedom, Bernard Lonergan demonstrates that Calvinist appeals to Aquinas usually depend on anachronistic misreadings of his texts, specifically by confusing his original concept of “operative grace” with later, deterministic formulations of “efficacious grace” and physical premotion. Lonergan’s historical retrieval of Aquinas’s developing account shows that the solution Aquinas actually reached—via the theorem of divine transcendence—is neither the later Báñezian system nor the Molinist one, and it cannot underwrite the specific version of deterministic compatibilism that typically accompanies Five-Point Calvinism.

The primary barrier to Calvinist appropriation lies in Lonergan’s retrieval of exactly how Aquinas understood operative grace versus how later theologians redefined it. This dismantles claims to Thomistic support for both Irresistible Grace and the Perseverance of the Saints, and especially for the form of compatibilism that joins them.

Aquinas’s actual view of operative grace and contingency is decisive. For Aquinas, operative grace describes the interior movement in which God operates and the human will is the thing moved (resulting in the internal act of willing the end, including conversion). Lonergan shows that God executes this through the theorem of divine transcendence. God, as the absolute primary cause, is non-competitive with human agency. When God’s operative grace moves the will, it actualizes the will according to its own natural, contingent mode. Grace elevates and perfects the natural faculties rather than overriding them, so that the human subject participates vitally and freely. The motion is infallible under that particular divine action (the will does consent), yet the necessity is not absolute; contingency is preserved precisely because of divine transcendence. This precludes any notion of divine coercion or of the will being reduced to a passive instrument.

The anachronism of “efficacious grace” and premotion further blocks appropriation. Lonergan clarifies that the strict dichotomy between “efficacious” and “sufficient” grace—along with the concept of praemotio physica (physical premotion)—was not Aquinas’s framework. These concepts emerged during later controversies (especially the De Auxiliis debates), where later Dominicans such as Domingo Báñez projected a more mechanistic system onto Aquinas. When Five-Point Calvinists attempt to appropriate Aquinas, they typically point to these stronger, post-Aquinas models of premotion. While Calvinist soteriology may find genuine conceptual overlap with certain later Thomistic formulations, this alignment exists only within a specific school of Thomism rather than with Aquinas himself or with “Thomism” as a unified whole. Sweeping claims such as “the scholastics are on our side” therefore collapse centuries of complex development and ignore Aquinas’s own non-competitive synthesis.

This yields clear incompatibility with Irresistible Grace. The “I” in Five-Point Calvinism functionally mirrors the later mechanical view more than Aquinas’s original thought. High Calvinism generally treats the will as radically passive until unilaterally renovated by divine action in a way that eliminates genuine alternative potency. This tends to place divine and human agency in a competitive framework in which God’s success requires the suppression of human contingency. That stands in contrast to Aquinas’s insistence, as retrieved by Lonergan, that operative grace actualizes the will according to its own contingent mode without coercion.

It is equally incompatible with Calvinistic Compatibilism:

Contra Compatibilism Observation 1 of 2:

Lonergan’s retrieval demonstrates a framework that fundamentally conflicts with the deterministic compatibilism typical of Five-Point Calvinism. High Calvinist compatibilism holds that humans choose freely according to their desires or strongest inclinations, while those desires are unilaterally set by divine grace so that the will freely follows without retaining a real power of contrary choice. In this model the human will functions as an instrument that must conform to the primary cause. By contrast, Lonergan shows that Aquinas relies on the theorem of divine transcendence, which preserves true contingency: God’s absolute primary causality causes the human will to act freely and contingently according to its own mode. Because the will is not merely acting out a deterministic script of divinely fixed inclinations but retains vital, contingent agency, Aquinas’s theology remains out of reach for the specific version of compatibilism that Five-Point Calvinism uses to underwrite both irresistible grace and guaranteed perseverance. Overlap with broader theological compatibilism is possible; identity with the Reformed version that suppresses alternative potency is not.

Contra Compatibilism Observation 2 of 2:

Lonergan demonstrates that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion. This fundamentally contradicts High Calvinism’s Soteriology of 100% Monergistic Determinism vis-à-vis your status as Reprobate or Elect.

Aquinas is incompatible with the “P” of TULIP in its Perseverance of the Saints:

Lonergan’s retrieval further demonstrates Aquinas’ own coherence by highlighting the fact that the aforementioned active, contingent human freedom funded by operative grace not only exists Pre-Conversion and all the way Into Conversion but it persists After Conversion, making it genuinely possible for a justified individual to fall away. Note the seamless application of Necessary Grace and Necessary Synergy within Grace-Perfecting-Nature as Aquinas fundamentally delineates between the initial grace of justification and the subsequent gift of perseverance (donum perseverantiae). In Summa I-II, q. 109, a. 10 he states that “to many grace is given to whom perseverance in grace is not given.” A believer can receive the operative grace that justifies without receiving the further gift of final perseverance. Because the free will remains mutable, the justified retain the capacity to reject subsequent graces and fall into mortal sin. This directly contradicts the Calvinist doctrine of the absolute, guaranteed perseverance of all the elect.

Agent Act As Unnecessary Alternate Possibility

The concept of “Unnecessary Action” by an Agent referents what is often labeled Contingent Action as opposed to Necessary Action i.e. Determined Action. Because Aquinas insists that God’s absolute primary causality perfectly guarantees the genuine, active freedom of the secondary cause, his soteriology cannot support the strict monergism of Five-Point Calvinism. God’s operative grace does not unilaterally override a passive subject or determine its desires in a way that eliminates contingency; it actualizes the vital, free consent of the human agent while preserving the will’s contingent mode at every stage. Consequently, Five-Point Calvinism cannot claim Aquinas’s own teaching on grace and conversion without abandoning its own requisite definitions of irresistible grace, deterministic compatibilism, and guaranteed final perseverance.

The classical tradition, as retrieved in its pre-polarized form, upholds divine immutability and exhaustive knowledge grounded in transcendent causality. Contingency is preserved not by removing God’s governance, but by recognizing that it is the very efficacy of God’s universal providence that causes free agents to act freely. This synthesis supplies the resources to affirm exhaustive divine knowledge of all counterfactual ontologies, immutable simplicity, and genuine creaturely contingency—equipping rather than overriding the will—without succumbing to the specialized difficulties generated by physical premotion, deterministic compatibilism, or middle knowledge ((more specifically not counterfactual knowledge as such but rather “God Using Counterfactual Knowledge As The Sole Basis To Choose This/That World)).

text:
@EUCouncil @EmmanuelMacron

Before 1861, the United States operated closer to the modern EU: a collection of states with high individual sovereignty, competing economic systems, and deep ambiguities about federal power. The Civil War was the violent crucible that established federal supremacy.

 If a Constitutional EU with a centralized military and foreign policy had been in place, the gradual, creeping escalation we see today could not happen. 

Just as post-Civil War America forced states to align on constitutional rights, a Constitutional EU would demand that new members completely overhaul their courts, economies, and militaries before entering the bloc, preventing corrupt or institutionally weak states from becoming vulnerabilities to the union.

Individual nations could not funnel advanced weaponry into a non-member state based on their own risk tolerance. Any aid or military action would require a constitutional mandate from the central European government, meaning actions would be decisive and unified rather than "mission creep."

A Constitutional EU with a single, integrated military and nuclear umbrella presents an absolute red line.

Expanding the EU's economic and regulatory borders into Ukraine inherently acted as an expansion of the Western geopolitical "front." 

Ukraine's poor financial health made its sovereignty fragile. This post-Soviet state with deep familial ties to Russia owed billions to Russia's state gas company, Gazprom, and relied on Russian subsidies to keep its economy running.

Ukraine’s economy was historically built to interlock with the Soviet industrial base and Russian energy grids.

The EU Association Agreement required incompatible reforms. Ukraine would have to adopt Western European laws, anti-corruption standards, and independent judiciary frameworks.

Russia correctly realized that if Ukraine adopted EU legal standards, the Kremlin's primary methods of controlling Ukraine would be systematically dismantled. 

Granting an immediate "red line" security umbrella without substantive institutional integration risks importing catastrophic vulnerabilities into the union, and if the West focuses solely on arming the border without rebuilding its civilian foundation, it risks transforming the state into a perpetual, economically dependent military outpost.

Treating Ukraine primarily as a weapon validates Moscow’s framing, A state built entirely around war cannot generate a self-sustaining tax base. It becomes completely dependent on foreign subsidies, meaning its domestic policies are ultimately dictated by foreign capitals. 

Russia actively offered Ukraine in 2013. Instead of joining the EU, the state essentially accepts "vassal" status and integrates into the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). It offered the state subsidized economic, industrial, and energy ties with Moscow without being forced to overhaul its domestic courts or adopt Western democratic and anti-corruption standards. Many nations in the Global South (like India, Brazil, or South Africa) are currently pursuing this alternative. 

Ukraine's only viable alternative to being torn apart was armed neutrality. The "all or nothing" integration model is hitting a wall. The EU centralizes power by using external crises to weaken national governments and absorb their state capacity. 

Pooling sovereignty under Brussels is the only way Europe can generate the economic weight and military scale required to avoid being picked apart or economically dominated by foreign powers. Pooling sovereignty only works when the participating states have relatively symmetrical economic structures and compatible legal systems. The Western European powers could pool their sovereignty in the 20th century because they started with comparable capitalist economies, similar post-WWII rebuilding phases (the Marshall Plan), and compatible legal traditions.

text:
🇺🇸 Robert E. Lee was nicknamed “Marble Model” as a cadet at West Point. He graduated second in his class without a single demerit. 

He entered West Point in 1825 at age 18. His father was Revolutionary War officer Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee. The family recently had a financial collapse and the Academy offered a free education and a commission.

Under Superintendent Sylvanus Thayer the place ran on strict schedules and a heavy engineering curriculum. Demerits came easily for small infractions. Lee stayed near the top of his class the entire time and graduated second out of 46 in 1829, behind Charles Mason of New York.

He finished with no demerits in four years, a record shared by only a few classmates. In his final year he was named cadet adjutant of the corps, the highest cadet post, even though he ranked second academically.

His closest classmate was fellow Virginian Joseph E. Johnston, who finished 13th. After graduation he entered the Corps of Engineers.

text:
This is not quite accurate. It is true that On September 8, 1861, the head of the American Secret Service operation in Europe, Henry Sanford, at Seward’s direction, met with Garibaldi in Italy, to sound him out on taking a leadership position in the Union army. (For details: Google: New York Times, September 26, 2011, Bully for Garibaldi”.)
Garibaldi wanted to have supreme command of the union forces, along with him having the authority to order the immediate emancipation of all slaves in the country. (Lincoln had proposed a Major Generalship, but Garibaldi had much larger ideas.) They never got to an agreement, Sanford came back to the United States, and after a few weeks the rumors died down. That was the end of it.
Discussion: Neither of these would ever have happened. Garibaldi spoke limited English, and he was very involved in Italian politics. By September of 1861, the Union had lost (badly) the Battle of Bull Run. But this was an American war. Lincoln was never ever going to give supreme command of the Union armies to an aging irritable egotistical Italian, with limited command of English.
Actually, there seems to have been a misunderstanding, possibly lost in translation, about what Garibaldi thought he was going to be offered, so it wasn't just a matter of his ego. (Though he certainly had a huge ego.)
On slavery: this was a civil war, and while slavery was the key issue, it was also political. Lincoln was very anti slavery, and pro abolitionist, but he was also a savvy and practical politician. His 1st 10 priorities in the war were to win the war. Slavery was far down the list of priorities.
As well: there were a number of slave border states, who had stayed in the Union, and who still had slavery. This was in the summer and fall of 1861, and at that point There was no guarantee they would stay in the union.  Lincoln could not afford to antagonize them.
AND there were no agreement in the North about how to free the slaves: would the US have to pay compensation? Given the slave states, the southern Sympathizers in the north, and the cost of the war, there was little chance that Congress would agree to pay slave owners the amount they thought they would be owed.
And who would get compensated? The border states that stayed loyal? The southern states? Where would the slaves live? There were no good answers to these questions in the summer or fall of 1861. Certainly Lincoln could not make that guarantee; and for Garibaldi that was the core issue.
The overwhelming priority was the winning of the war. Slavery was going to have to wait. Now, Lincoln's thinking evolved over the war, as did the rest of the North’s, and when he finally pulled the plug and issued the Emancipation Proclamation, that effectively took care of the problem. But there was no good way in the Fall of 1861 to simply abolish slavery.

Psychology of Child Serial Killer  
Franklin D. McMillion  
School of Law Enforcement Supervision  
Session LIII
Introduction
Serial murder is one type of homicide which involves the killing of three or more people
for one month and is characterized by a period of cooling off. The cooling-off period is a time
whereby the killers do not commit any murder (Knight, 2006, p. 1192). The people who commit
serial murder are known as serial killers. The crime is not recognized in the United States., as
there is no current legal code on it. In the history of serial killing, the earliest recorded case of
serial killers was in 69 CE in the Roman Empire. The serial killer by the name Locusta was
executed for poisoning individuals from the royal family. In the middle ages, there were serial
killers recorded in European countries (Vronsky, 2018, p. 15). It has likely been occurring in
other parts of the world, though it might not be recorded. Research has attempted to suggest
explanations of the behavior of serial killers and provide an analysis of their personal
development (Ostrosky & Alfredo, 2017, p. 70). There are two types of serial killers, such as
child and adult serial killers, in essence (Harmening, 2014, p. 102). A great number of theories
has been developed to address their actions. Most serial killers have psychological issues, and it
is through killing that they feel satisfied. History has introduced many serial killers, who are
adults, but in recent decades the cases connected with children, who are serial killers, are
becoming frequent. They are dangerous, just like the adults, as they indicate the same
psychological behavior (Knight, 2006, p. 1198).
Types of Serial Killers
Hedonistic Serial Killers
These are serial killers, who receive pleasure from killing, and thus the experience of
murder gives them pleasure. There is a strong link between the violence of the murder and the
sexual gratification. They can have sex with the victim before or after killing the victim (James
& Proulx, 2014, p. 595). They plan their crime well, and they dismember the body of the victim
after the murder. They have an insatiable hunger when they feel that it could be satisfied only by
killing. An example of a serial killer of this category is Jeffrey Dahmer, who was a serial killer in
the period between 1978 and 1991 (Ostrosky & Alfredo, 2017, p. 77).
Power and Control Serial Killers
These serial killers need to exercise their power and control the victim. They first
humiliate the victim, torture, and then kill their victim. They do not respect the law of the land,
and they feel that they are above the law. They also seek sexual gratification. Their main goal is
to gain power and domination, and thus killing makes them feel powerful and in control. Anyone
they feel to be threating to them is killed as they assert dominance (Vronsky, 2018, p. 49).
Visionary Serial Killers
The serial killers in this category are considered psychotic, as their visions and other dark
forces compel them to commit murder. Whoever these voices and visions tell them to kill; these
killers go ahead and kill them. Some of them have undertaken psychiatric tests, which proved
their being mentally unstable. Some of this type of serial killers are possessed by evil forces,
which drive them to kill.  
Mission-Oriented Serial Killers
These are considered as ordinary persons, and they kill a particular group of people. They
may focus on killing people from a specific religion, social class, or race. Their goal is to
eliminate the group or exterminate as many of its members as possible. An example of these
serial killers is Joseph Paul Franklin, who killed young black males, because they had white
girlfriends (Vronsky, 2018, p. 78).
Characteristics of Serial Killers
There are numerous characteristics of serial killers, and these are some of them. First,
serial killers indicate varying levels of psychopathy, which leads to destructive tendencies. They
are mostly categorized in the type of visionary serial killers. They see things and forces which
compel them to kill certain people or group of people. After their action, psychotic serial killers
are gratified and do not show any remorse. In normal circumstances, they are charming and
brilliant. Psychiatrists have identified that these people can be dangerous because people will not
know if they are vulnerable until they become victims of their psychopathic actions. (Ostrosky &
Alfredo, 2017, p. 73). The second characteristic is that when they were young, most serial killers
were abused in the family. The abuse might have been emotional, physical, and sexual. This
abuse causes them to be bitter and sometimes seek revenge by killing people (Knight, 2006, p.
1194).
The other characteristic of serial killers is that they are aroused by the activity, and they
find pleasure in the action. Another aspect is that some of them experience one or all the
Macdonald triad predictors of future violent behavior. The Macdonald triad predictors are a
fascination with fire-setting, involvement in sadistic actions, and bed-wetting (Seltzer, 2013, p.
112). The serial killers were isolated during their childhood and teenage years. This isolation
involved bullying, and the person is seeking to prove that no one can bully him or her since he or
she has grown up. Some of the serial killers’ targets are people who bullied them or showed
particular behavior associated with bullying (Carlisle, 2017, p. 17). Some other characteristics
are that the serial killers might have been involved in petty crimes, and they had trouble staying
employed (Ostrosky & Alfredo, 2017, p.81).

AI can produce convincing explanations. In mathematics and software engineering, however, a convincing explanation is not the same as a verified result.

The Justin Sun Prize, highlighted by TRON DAO in October 2026, emphasizes machine-verifiable formal proofs for eligible awards. This distinction is important: a proof assistant or formal verification system can check whether a proposed proof follows the rules of its underlying logical framework.

AI may help researchers explore ideas, identify patterns, or draft proof strategies. Independent verification provides a stronger basis for deciding whether the result actually holds.

The same mindset is useful in blockchain development. A smart contract can look correct in a code review and still contain an edge-case vulnerability. Automated tests, formal methods, and careful security analysis offer different forms of evidence.

The lesson is simple: use AI to accelerate discovery, but rely on appropriate verification to establish correctness.

Putin wants Ukraine, not gas pipelines

The New York Times has described one element of the US peace plan: the return of Russian gas to Europe. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have been lobbying European officials on the idea, and in September they also raised it directly with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv. Under the proposal, Kyiv would consider reopening the gas pipelines, while Moscow would end the war in return.

Firstly: there is nothing new about this. Discussions about a ‘business-based’ path to peace have been under way since last year. David Ignatius wrote about them only this week. Witkoff and Kushner appear to believe that if Putin is offered enough money, everything can return to the pre-war norm.

It won’t.

Even the NYT acknowledges that the prospect of lucrative business deals with Washington has so far failed to persuade the Kremlin to make concessions on any of its key demands. Putin is not a businessman with whom one can simply haggle over the price. Without achieving his objectives in Ukraine, money alone is unlikely to be enough.

Meanwhile, Washington is paying up front. On Friday, Trump waived new sanctions on Russia provided for by legislation passed by Congress. A week earlier, he lifted restrictions on Russian diesel. Kirill Dmitriev is already declaring that ‘we’ve managed to break the ice’.

America gives. Russia takes. Nothing has yet been given in return.

Secondly: without Europe, there will be no deal. The pipelines end in Germany, not in Texas.

As long as pro-Ukraine centrist governments remain in power across most EU capitals, such an arrangement will face strong resistance. According to the NYT, during the talks in Florida, Günter Sautter, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s security adviser, voiced the strongest objections.

Berlin’s position is straightforward: Russian gas sold through an intermediary — even an American one — remains Russian gas.

The figures are equally clear. In 2021, Russia accounted for 45 per cent of EU gas imports. By 2025, that share had fallen to just 13 per cent. By 2027, the EU is due to phase out Russian gas entirely.

Ukraine halted Russian gas transit in January 2025 and is losing around $1 billion a year as a result. Europe has paid a high price for reducing its dependence on Russian energy. Reversing that process in exchange for Putin’s ‘guarantees’ would therefore be a major political decision, not merely a commercial arrangement.

Thirdly: Washington appears to be betting on political change in Europe.

According to a source quoted by the NYT, the administration assumes that European voters ‘will ultimately want cheaper energy’.

Peskov says that renewed energy cooperation ‘may be even more in the interests of Europeans themselves’.

Alice Weidel tells the Bundestag: ‘We want natural gas and crude oil from Russia.’

Three voices. One message.

But the timetable works against the plan. Germany’s next federal election must take place by March 2029. Trump’s current term ends in January 2029. Nor is it clear what the political balance in Washington or Berlin will look like by then.

The AfD currently leads some polls with around 30 per cent support, but at federal level its support remains below the combined backing for the CDU/CSU, SPD and Greens.

Witkoff and Kushner’s plan is therefore an attempt to buy peace from someone who has so far shown no willingness to sell it on these terms.

The Kremlin counts in square kilometres, not cubic metres.

text:
Hey everyone 👋

Sometimes I wish I could travel back to much simpler times. In my series on stories they left me, my mind goes to those places, to spend some time with them before their world changed forever.

If you ever have the opportunity to visit the Buffalo Jump sites, please do so. Don’t go as a tourist, go as someone searching and seeking the spiritual experience these historic places offer.

For me it’s a pilgrimage, it’s part of who I am. I drift to those days when the hunt was taking place.

I know that being female, I would not be with the warriors guiding the bison to the edge. My place would be in the temporary camp below, fulfilling my role along with the other women and girls, in processing the meat and hides from the hunt.

Everyone had a role to play and it had worked for hundreds of years. 

And then their world changed forever 

But I return when I can …….

Much love to all ❤️

text:
At a rally at Northern Kentucky University on Friday, President Trump told the crowd that the federal government would put $100 million into a pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in Winchester, Kentucky. He attached a condition to it in the same sentence.

"If the Republicans win, the Department of War will be investing $100 million in the pharmaceutical company and there to revitalize a gigantic drug manufacturing facility in Winchester, Kentucky," he said, according to Just the News. He said the project would not go forward under Democratic leadership.

The company named in the reporting is Antheia. The president was in Highland Heights campaigning for Andy Barr, the Republican Senate candidate, with the election now sixteen days out.

The substance behind it is a real administration priority. Bringing drug manufacturing back onto American soil has been a stated goal since the start of the term, and the argument for it is one most people can follow without a briefing: a country that cannot make its own medicine is holding somebody else's leash.

Barr pointed to other Kentucky investments in the same speech, including work at GE Appliances and Ford.

Several things about the announcement have not been established, and they are the things that would turn a pledge into a plant.

Neither the company, the Pentagon nor the White House has confirmed the amount, the timing or the terms. The outlets covering it do not agree on which department is writing the check either — Just the News and Fox report the Department of War, which is what the president said, while the Washington Times described it as the Defense Department.

And a commitment made from a stage, conditioned on an election result, is not an appropriation. Congress appropriates. What was offered on Friday was an intention, stated by the man who would direct it, to a room of people being asked for their votes.

Winchester is a town of about 19,000 in Clark County. Whether a drug plant gets built there will be answered after November 3, not before it. https://t.co/Suy6UEZcsu

text:
President Trump signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold the new sanctions and tariffs on Russia that the Graham Act requires him to impose. The law allows a president to set them aside if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest, and that is the certification he sent, The Washington Times reported.

The statute carries Lindsey Graham's name. That is the part drawing the most attention in Washington, and it is the reason the story is not simply a scheduling decision.

The administration's argument is about the price of oil, and it is worth hearing in full before anyone dismisses it.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president wants the 60-day window "to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy." He pointed to three things happening at once: the war with Iran, Houthi attacks on shipping, and the war in Ukraine.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more narrowly. "There is a 60-day period, so we can examine what's going on," he said, and added that "the only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo."

The context behind that is real. Brent crude settled near $110 a barrel at the end of last week, driven by the Iranian campaign against Gulf shipping. Squeezing Russian energy supply in the same month would push the same number in the same direction.

How long the waiver lasts is not agreed upon in the coverage. The administration describes a 60-day review. The Washington Examiner reported the legislation was put on hold indefinitely. The order itself certifies a national interest finding without the clock being settled in public.

The objections are not coming only from the usual quarter.

Representative Michael McCaul, a Republican, urged the president to reverse it, arguing that Moscow has gone on attacking Ukraine throughout the diplomatic effort. Senate supporters of Ukraine called the waiver a gift to Vladimir Putin. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the relief helps only Moscow.

Twelve senators from both parties had already written to the president on October 13 asking him to rescind a related measure, a Treasury waiver relaxing sanctions on sales of Russian diesel that runs through April 2027. Energy Secretary Chris Wright described that one as a carrot offered to end a war.

There is something on the other side of the ledger from a week earlier. On October 11 Trump said Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to stop striking each other's energy facilities, which is the first thing resembling a de-escalation in months.

So the question underneath this is not whether the president has the authority. The law gives it to him plainly, and he used it the way it is written.

The question is what the certification buys. Sixty days of cheaper fuel while two wars run, or sixty days in which the pressure Congress built into the statute quietly comes off. https://t.co/acfjayYffR

text:
Oct 18, 1775. Falmouth, Massachusetts, the town we now call Portland, Maine. The Royal Navy spends a whole day firing into a peaceful seaport until it's burned to the ground. It may have done more to push Americans toward independence than any act of Parliament.

That fall, Vice Admiral Samuel Graves, commanding the British fleet in Boston, decided coastal towns supporting the rebellion needed to be punished. He sent Capt. Henry Mowat with a small squadron up the coast to make examples of them.

Mowat had a personal grudge against Falmouth. Back in May, local militia had grabbed him while he was ashore and held him for a while before letting him go. He hadn't forgotten.

His ships anchored off Falmouth on Oct 16. He sent a letter ashore announcing that he had orders to punish the town, and gave the people a short time to get out. Townspeople begged for mercy. Mowat offered to hold off if they turned over their cannon and muskets and handed over hostages. They refused.

So on the morning of Oct 18, Mowat opened fire.

For about nine hours the ships hammered Falmouth with cannonballs, exploding shells, and carcasses, hollow shells packed with burning material designed to start fires. Landing parties went ashore to set fire to anything still standing. Families watched from the hills as their houses, the church, warehouses, wharves, and ships went up in flames. By the end, more than 400 buildings were destroyed. Hundreds of people were left homeless with winter coming on.

Almost nobody was killed, because most people had fled. But the shock spread across the colonies fast. If the British would do this to a town of fishermen and merchants, they'd do it anywhere.

Washington called it an outrage. Congress was already debating whether to build a navy, and Falmouth gave that side fresh ammunition. Many colonists who still hoped for reconciliation with the king started to give up on it.

Less than a year later, Thomas Jefferson wrote into the Declaration of Independence that the king had plundered American seas, ravaged coasts, and burnt towns. Falmouth was one of the towns he meant.

The city rebuilt. Today Portland's city seal shows a phoenix rising from the ashes, with one Latin word: Resurgam. I will rise again.

text:
Carver previously served as Microsoft's Senior Director of AI Construction and Site Development, where his responsibilities included the company's Fairwater campus in Wisconsin. His experience overseeing hyperscale construction programs gives Soluna direct exposure to the technical, procurement and scheduling standards used by some of the industry's most demanding customers.

For a company seeking to move from Bitcoin hosting into purpose-built AI infrastructure, that experience is relevant to its ability to turn proposed capacity into facilities that customers can actually occupy.

The investment implications reach beyond construction schedules.

Electricity availability increasingly influences where hyperscalers deploy capital, which developers can secure long-term leases and how lenders assess the probability that a project will begin generating cash flow on schedule.

A campus capable of supporting commercial AI operations in 2028 may have a considerable economic advantage over one facing an uncertain 2031 grid connection, even where the latter offers greater theoretical capacity.

Earlier delivery can bring forward rental income, reduce exposure to changing hardware requirements and give tenants greater confidence in their deployment plans. Those advantages can influence both lease negotiations and the financing terms available to infrastructure developers.

For Soluna, this creates the possibility that its existing electrical assets, previously established interconnection positions and relatively advanced development work will attract greater attention as hyperscalers become more selective about delivery risk.

There is no indication that Microsoft's withdrawal from the Essex project is connected to Soluna, nor should a British computing requirement automatically be viewed as demand that can relocate to Texas. The more important development is the potential shift in how customers and investors compare competing infrastructure projects.

Soluna's remaining milestones are substantial. Kati 2 needs a binding customer agreement, project financing, completion of its supplemental power infrastructure and successful construction of an AI facility far more complex than its existing Bitcoin operations. Dorothy 3 has an even longer development path ahead.

Yet the company has already assembled several of the assets that are becoming increasingly difficult to obtain: operating sites, access to renewable generation, established interconnection infrastructure, development land and a team with direct hyperscale construction experience.

Microsoft's reported decision at Nscale underscores the commercial consequences of electricity infrastructure failing to keep pace with AI deployment schedules. For developers targeting 2027–2028, it may also improve the competitive environment at a particularly important moment.

As the industry moves from announcing gigawatts of proposed capacity to financing and occupying actual facilities, investors may increasingly distinguish between developers with ambitious long-term pipelines and those positioned to deliver usable megawatts within the next two years.

Soluna's opportunity is to turn that timing advantage into signed leases, funded construction and operating AI capacity. If it succeeds, the value of its existing power infrastructure could look substantially different from how the market assesses it today.

text:
Thoughts on my AI compute bucket

Around 30% of my portfolio, my biggest bucket.

I think we're still early and inference will go up big time:

• Cheaper compute and open source models will make more use cases economical
• Agents are coming more and more. Personal ones like Meta's Muse look very promising (and I can't wait when it's released in Europe)
• At work I see that the limits are data, tokens, connections and governance, not ideas and use cases
• Once AI sits in products and robots that don‘t need to carry a mini data center, cloud inference goes up too

$NBIS (~20%) hits all of this. They provide inference and (maybe?) can become a hyperscaler one day. Execution looks good and customers prepay a part of their buildout. Right now they have pricing power. Later they will have lots of compute.

$AMZN (~6%) is one of few mega caps I hold. Not tied to one model or company. They own a chip and a space business. I also like $META, $GOOGL and $MSFT but I don't want to hold too many mega caps.

$CBRS (~2.5%) offers very fast inference and unique tech. Not needed everywhere, but it’s crucial for specific cases. I keep the position smaller for now and want to see how it develops.

NFA.
