text:
Africa is seriously falling behind, and Nigeria is a glaring example of this troubling reality.
We idolize thugs, thieves, ex-convicts, fraudsters, criminals, internet fraudsters, ritualists, brainless streamers, and corrupt politicians. 
We celebrate people for their wealth and popularity without asking how they acquired them or what values they represent.
How can a country grow when society celebrates the wrong role models?
How will the next generation develop an interest in technology, innovation, science, and entrepreneurship when the people they admire promote lifestyles that offer no meaningful contribution to society?

How will a girl child aspire to become a scientist, engineer, or successful entrepreneur when the celebrity she looks up to glorifies prostitution and materialism?

How will a boy child dream of becoming a tech innovator when his greatest ambition is to become the next Hushpuppi?

The problem is not just the individuals we celebrate; it is a society that rewards questionable lifestyles with fame, wealth, influence, and admiration while hardworking innovators, educators, and nation-builders struggle to receive the recognition they deserve.
A society that celebrates the wrong values is unknowingly programming its next generation for failure.

My question is simple:
WHO WILL CHANGE THIS NARRATIVE AND HELP SAVE THE NEXT GENERATION?

Will it be the government?
Parents? Schools? Religious institutions? The media? Content creators? Or must we all take responsibility?

The future of Africa depends not only on the leaders we elect but also on the people we choose to celebrate, the values we promote, and the examples we set for our children.
We cannot build a generation of innovators while glorifying the lifestyles of villains.
The change must begin with us.

text:
The current administration's reliance on executive orders, effectively legislating from the Oval Office, represents a profound betrayal of our constitutional compact. This usurpation of authority turns the executive branch into a legislative body, undermining the very foundation of republican government.

Consider the recent proliferation of executive fiats, such as H.R. 1781's mention of orders like "Unleashing American Energy" or "Declaring a National Energy Emergency." These directives, bypassing the legislative process, impose policies with the force of law, yet lack the deliberative consent of the people's representatives. They are but one more instance of executive overreach, chipping away at the liberty bequeathed to us.

Our Founders were explicit: "All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives," as declared in Article I, Section 1 of our Constitution. James Madison, in Federalist No. 47, warned that "The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny." This separation was designed as liberty's bulwark, not a mere suggestion.

Such actions stand in stark contrast to biblical wisdom, which cautions against concentrated power and encourages vigilance against earthly rulers who would oppress. "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places" (Ephesians 6:12). True freedom is a divine gift, not a grant from a monarchical executive, for "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (John 8:36).

To dismantle this encroaching executive tyranny, Congress must reassert its constitutional prerogatives. Bills like H.R. 6971, which proposes requiring congressional approval for major executive orders, offer a pathway to restore balance. Furthermore, the judiciary, upholding its duty under Marbury v. Madison, must invalidate executive orders that lack statutory or constitutional authority, ensuring the President "shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed," not arbitrarily created.

The true remedy, however, lies not in legislative chambers alone, but in the steadfast resolve of sovereign individuals. Cultivate your own sustenance, secure your water, build your shelter, and foster local economies through barter and mutual aid. This self-reliance and biblical stewardship, as commanded in Genesis 2:15 to "dress it and to keep it," is the ultimate defense against an overweening government that seeks to manage every aspect of life. Dependence on government for every solution, a foreign ideology alien to our founding, only strengthens the chains of servitude.

Are we to be a nation governed by carefully deliberated laws, or by the fleeting decrees of a single office?

#ReclaimSovereignty #FoundersVoice

text:
#NFO vs #AFC

Ratings:

Raya: 7
Rarely tested. Solid distribution but occasionally slowed down potential counters. Excellent claiming from corners and crosses.

White: 5
Average. Lacked the overlapping threat this game demanded, something Timber provided much more effectively in the final 30 minutes.

Konsa: 8 
Tough battle against the physical Delap but held his own. That last minute tackle sort of summed up his performance: Poor positioning initially but recovered beautifully and effectively. 

Gabriel: 9
Superb. One of the world's best box defenders. Made several crucial interventions against Forest's counters, including 3 blocks. Faultless defensively.

Calafiori: 6
Quiet game. Forest's narrowness restricted his influence in the LHS, leaving him largely in a supporting role underneath Noni and Eze.

Rice: 7
Solid deliveries and excellent defensive work, particularly with second balls and recoveries. Got his assist but should have converted Timber's cutback. Crucial presence at the base.

Bruno G: 7
Limited central space but consistently tried to make things happen, especially in the first half. Excellent recovery defending and duelling as usual.

Odegaard: 7
Forced deeper than usual. Made some intelligent channel runs behind Murillo but was rarely found. Occasionally too slow in possession when quicker distribution was available.

Saka: 6
Often isolated in 2v1 situations as Arsenal looked to stretch Forest. Largely ineffective until Timber and Gyokeres came on.

Eze: 3
Really poor. Limited involvement due to our right sided bias, but underwhelming when involved. Deserved to come off. Noni should have started.

Havertz: 4
Struggled physically and offered very little involvement or influence. Disappointing performance.

Subs:

Noni: 8
Excellent again on the left, carrying momentum from Leeds. Direct, energetic and consistently dangerous with his crossing. His goal came from an action I saw quite often vs Leeds. 

Timber: 8
Superb impact. Provided exactly what White lacked, making 3 dangerous overlapping runs. Rice should have converted his cutback.

Merino: 7
Immediately brought control. Won fouls under pressure, combined intelligently and fulfilled his shadow striker responsibilities well.

Gyokeres: 7
Effective attacking the channels as we were more direct after scoring. His strengths were well suited to this game, and he arguably should have started.

#மானத்துக்குஎன்னவிலை ? – 
#WhatIsThePriceOfDignity ? – The Price of an Honest Man’s Honour – #EnnaVilai : A Quiet, Powerful Reminder of Dignity and Justice

#ThePriceOfAnHonestMANsHonour
Enna Vilai is a film that remains in the heart long after it ends. It follows the quiet life of an ordinary fisherman named Thavasi, portrayed by actor #Karunas , who lives by simple honesty on the shores of #Rameswaram .

When he finds a valuable gold ornament in the sea, he does what he believes is right and hands it over to the authorities. Instead of being protected for his integrity, he is framed, humiliated, and forced to fight for years to clear his name and restore his family’s honour.

What makes the film deeply moving is its refusal to treat dignity as something secondary. Karunas brings quiet pain and restrained strength to the role of a man who has done everything correctly yet still loses everything that matters. 

#NimishaSajayan , as the lawyer who takes up his case, does more than argue in court. She asks a question the system rarely faces: once an innocent person’s reputation has been destroyed, what does the state truly owe him? Not just freedom, but the restoration of his dignity.

The film holds a mirror to society by showing how a single act of honesty can destroy an ordinary family’s peace when institutions fail. It raises important questions about police conduct, the responsibility of the state, and the long struggle to reclaim lost honour. 

This is precisely why Enna Vilai deserves the highest recognition from the Tamil Nadu government as Best Film. It realistically depicts the vulnerability of the common man and the misuse of power.

Police personnel across the state should be encouraged to watch this film. The actions of the police are among the most critical factors in solving or worsening social problems. When the police and district administration function correctly with integrity and fairness, issues are resolved quickly and justly. 

When they act wrongly, as the film shows through the framing of an honest man, the damage extends far beyond one individual and brings lasting disrepute to the police force, the administration, and the government itself.

Only when higher officials intervene directly and promptly in cases of administrative failure, including lapses by the police, can the problems of affected citizens be truly resolved. 

Enna Vilai serves as a timely reminder that justice is incomplete if it stops at declaring someone innocent; the system must also restore the dignity that was taken away. 

By honouring this film, the state government would recognise outstanding cinema and send a clear message about accountable policing and responsive administration.

More importantly, Enna Vilai offers a clear message for the next generation of lawyers. In a time when people’s rights are easily brushed aside, young lawyers and law students have a special responsibility to stand as examples of integrity and courage. 

Real advocacy is not only about winning cases, but about asking difficult questions and refusing to let an ordinary person’s suffering go unnoticed. 

Every young lawyer and every student of law should watch this film. It reminds them why they chose the profession and what society quietly expects from them.

As an ordinary citizen, I respectfully request the Hon’ble @CMOTamilnadu of Tamil Nadu, Thiru @TVKVijayHQ , to set aside time and watch #EnnaVilai along with his Cabinet ministers and senior officials. 

Just as a single grain of rice can reveal the quality of an entire pot of cooked rice, this film clearly and lawfully illustrates how ordinary people in Tamil Nadu have suffered for years due to lapses in the police and government administration. 

An innocent family’s life is shattered by one administrative and police failure, and the film points this out with clarity and sensitivity as a lesson for correction within the framework of law.

text:
Horizontal overloads offer little value when the opposition congests the spaces between the lines. And that is precisely what has happened here.

Arsenal initially went for the textbook approach: keeping Eze wide while overloading the right flank to create a vertical overload and play through that side. Even the central players were positioned towards the right, which explains why the majority of Arsenal's attacking play came down that flank.

However, Forest have dealt with this quite well, engaging in consistent duels and effectively blocking Arsenal's players in that zone.

The best way to dismantle Forest's structure would be to employ a "Pull-Push" tactic: draw their entire defensive structure towards the ball before releasing a runner in behind. The objective is to manipulate their defensive shape, exploit the space created and ultimately dismantle the structure.

We saw glimpses of this in the 31st minute, when Rice clipped a ball in behind for a runner (most likely Ben White). This could be a valuable tactical weapon for Arsenal in the second half.

A stalemate so far, but a few subtle tactical adjustments could make all the difference.

text:
Aryan and Abrahamic psychosis:

The belief in pseudo-scientific racial and faith-based identity of humanity.

The phrase "Aryan and Abrahamic psychosis" is a provocative sociological and psychological concept used to critique two major historical constructs of exclusive identity: racial supremacy (the "Aryan" myth) and dogmatic religious exclusivism (the core claim of historical absolute Truth in certain interpretations of Abrahamic faiths).

When framed as a collective "psychosis," the term suggests a departure from reality—where abstract constructs like racial purity or divine election overwrite observable human shared biology and shared morality.

The "Aryan Psychosis": Racial Pseudo-Science

The myth of the "Aryan race" originated in 19th-century linguistics and philology, where the term was originally used to describe an ancient Indo-Iranian language family. Through pseudoscientific manipulation, thinkers like Arthur de Gobineau and Houston Stewart Chamberlain transformed a language classification into a racial hierarchy.

Core Features of Racial Exclusivism

Biological Determinism: 

The false premise that culture, intellect, moral capacity, and historical accomplishment are tied directly to genetic traits.

Purity and Contamination: 

A obsessive preoccupation with maintaining "pure bloodlines" and framing other ethnicities as corrupting forces or lower species.

Mythic Past: 

The belief in an ancient, superior "golden age" civilization that was diluted or overthrown by lesser groups, requiring ideological warfare to restore.

The "Abrahamic Psychosis": Exclusive Faith Identity

In a parallel way, exclusive theological frameworks within Abrahamic traditions (Judaism, Christianity, and Islam) have at times been interpreted through rigid, binary dogmas.

Core Features of Religious Exclusivism

​The "Chosen" vs. The Damned:

 A sharp cosmic division between those inside the covenant/faith and outsiders ("infidels," "heathens," or "gentiles").

Monopolization of Truth: 

The belief that a single historical revelation holds exclusive access to divine truth, rendering all other spiritual or worldview frameworks invalid or evil.

Apocalyptic Teleology: 

Framing human history as a zero-sum struggle between good and evil leading toward a final, violent purification or judgment.

The Intersection: Ideological Parallels

When examined side by side, pseudo-scientific race theory and dogmatic religious exclusivism share striking psychological and sociological mechanics:

Dimension"Aryan" Racial Pseudoscientific IdentityDogmatic Abrahamic Exclusivism

Source of AuthorityPseudoscientific eugenics & fake anthropologyLiteralized scriptural dogmatism & divine mandate

View of HumanityHierarchical / Biological tiersBinary / Saved vs. Lost

In-Group MechanismBloodline / Heritage / Physical traits; Orthodoxy / Faith / Absolute adherence

Out-Group Dynamic: Threat of racial degradation / Parasitic threat; Heresy / Sin / Demonic influence

Solution offered: Segregation, eugenics, or eradication; conversion, exile, or spiritual/physical judgment

Why Is It Characterised as "Psychosis"?

Reification of Constructs: 

Treating social, linguistic, or spiritual metaphors as literal, immutable biological or cosmic realities.

Delusional Inversion: 

Replacing empirical observation (that human biology and human morality exist across all geographic and cultural boundaries) with insular, paranoid narratives of persecution and divine or racial destiny.

​Dehumanisation and strategies: 

Stripping the "other" of intrinsic value, making moral atrocities (war, genocide, forced assimilation) feel not only acceptable, but mandatory.

text:
In her twenties, she decided not to sign with a management company.
She built her own instead.

Beyoncé did something almost nobody at the start of a solo career does:
 she walked away from the standard industry split before
 she'd even proven the solo career would work.

In 2008, she founded Parkwood Entertainment, 
named after the street she grew up on in Houston. It wasn't a vanity label.
 It became a vertically integrated company controlling her production, distribution, touring, merchandising, film, and brand partnerships, all under one roof she owned.

That structure changed the math entirely. 
By self-producing her tours and controlling distribution,
 she kept a share of the revenue that artists working through conventional deals never see. Ivy Park, her athleisure line, grew out of the same company. 
None of it answered to a record label.

The part that actually matters in her story.

> Managing herself wasn't a rejection of help.
 It was a rejection of giving away ownership before she had to. 

> A record label and a production company aren't the same thing, and she built the second one specifically so she'd never be stuck depending on the first. 

> Every new venture ran through the same company, not a new deal with a new set of terms. That's what compounding ownership actually looks like.

Beyoncé didn't just become one of the best-selling artists of all time. She built the company that made sure she kept what she earned from it.

That's what figures of authority do.

Inside Top 5% Method®% Method®,
I study Figures of Authority like her for one reason:
the executives who keep what they earn are the ones
who build the structure before anyone offers them a deal.

C'est ça la vraie vie 🌸

text:
Everett Public Schools settled a lawsuit brought by LifeWise Academy, which offers voluntary off-campus Bible instruction during the school day with parental permission. The district had required students to keep Bibles and other materials from the program sealed in envelopes inside their backpacks so other students would not see them. 

It also required weekly parental permission slips instead of a single semester-long form and restricted the program from community events and flyer displays. LifeWise CEO Joel Penton said children felt they were being told to hide their faith “as though it was something to be ashamed of.”

Under the settlement, the district will post a public written apology on its website for six months, send board members to religious liberty training, revise policies on religious activities, and pay $275,000 in attorney’s fees. The district’s apology acknowledges that comments from board members about LifeWise were “offensive and hurtful.” A federal court had previously issued a preliminary injunction finding viewpoint discrimination. The case centered on whether the district treated the Bible program differently from secular activities.

text:
Naive Utilitarianism, the Sacrificial Lamb, and the Open Society’s Inversion of Right

The Open Society project, whatever its rhetorical debt to Popper, operates in practice according to a logic that was already widespread in the progressive and socialist circles of Marx’s day: a naive utilitarianism that treats the good of the many as a calculable aggregate for which particular persons may be sacrificed. This logic is incompatible with natural-rights theory and classical liberalism. It is further incompatible with the Aristotelian cultivation of virtue, the Kantian insistence that persons are ends, and Hegel’s development of that insistence into the concrete institutions of mutual recognition and freedom. When these standards are applied, the Open Society appears not as the institutionalization of critical openness but as the contemporary form of an older willingness to treat some individuals as means for a projected collective improvement.

Naive utilitarianism in the age of Marx.  
The utilitarian ethics that dominated much of nineteenth-century progressive thought, associated above all with Bentham and the early Mill, held that the right action is the one that maximizes the sum of pleasure or welfare across persons. Because the standard is aggregative, it contains no intrinsic barrier to sacrificing the interests, liberty, or life of one or a few when the arithmetic favors the remainder. Bentham’s own formulations treated rights as “nonsense upon stilts” precisely because they obstructed this calculation. The same arithmetic reappears in the more optimistic progressive literature of the period: social reform, public health measures, colonial administration, and early socialist schemes were routinely justified by the claim that temporary or localized hardship would produce a larger net benefit. Marx rejected Bentham’s psychology and the idea of a static calculus of pleasures, yet the historical materialism he advanced retained a teleological structure in which present suffering—expropriation, class conflict, the “dictatorship of the proletariat”—is instrumentally required for the future abundance and freedom of the classless society. The individual or the class that stands in the way is, in the logic of the theory, the necessary cost of the greater historical good. The sacrificial lamb is not an accidental excess; it is what the aggregative or teleological standard licenses once persons are valued only for their contribution to the total.

Direct violation of natural rights and classical liberalism.  
Classical liberalism, as articulated by Locke and carried forward in the constitutional tradition, begins from the opposite premise. Persons possess rights to life, liberty, and property that are not the gift of society and are not subject to cancellation by a calculation of aggregate welfare. These rights function as side-constraints: they limit what may be done to a person even when the violation would produce a larger sum of good. The state exists to secure them, not to optimize an independently defined social product. Once the utilitarian standard is admitted as supreme, the side-constraint disappears. The person who owns productive property, the person who is a net fiscal contributor, the person whose continued presence is said to impose costs on others, can be treated as an input whose sacrifice is justified by the welfare of the larger number. Natural-rights theory rejects that conversion of the person into a resource. Classical liberalism therefore cannot endorse policies whose explicit or implicit justification is that some must bear concentrated losses so that others may enjoy diffuse gains, unless those policies can be defended on grounds that respect the prior rights of each.

Aristotelian virtue.  
Aristotle supplies a further standard that utilitarianism cannot meet. The human good is eudaimonia, an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, not a sum of pleasures or a future state of material abundance. Virtue is cultivated in particular persons through habituation, practical reason, and the institutions that support excellence—friendship, the household, the polity ordered toward the common good of its members. Justice, for Aristotle, is not the maximization of an aggregate; it is giving each what is due according to a standard of merit and reciprocal equality among citizens. A regime that systematically disadvantages the competent, the propertied, or the law-abiding in order to redistribute resources or status to others does not cultivate virtue; it undermines the conditions under which citizens can exercise it. The magnanimous person and the just polity both refuse the premise that one may be used as a mere instrument for the welfare of the rest.

Kantian deontology.  
Kant’s categorical imperative states the prohibition directly. Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law; treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never merely as a means. The second formulation rules out the sacrificial calculation. A person cannot be used as a means to the welfare of others without contradiction, because the maxim that licenses such use cannot be universalized without denying the status of rational agency itself. The kingdom of ends is a systematic union of rational beings under laws they can regard as their own, not an engineered aggregate in which some are expendable for the total. Policies that treat individuals as obstacles to be removed, or as bearers of costs to be socialized, for the sake of an equity metric or a demographic outcome fail this test.

Hegel’s extension of Kantian ethics.  
Hegel takes the Kantian insight that freedom is the ground of right and develops it into concrete institutions. In the *Philosophy of Right*, the free will must give itself an external existence; property is the first such existence. Mutual recognition of persons as free occurs through the recognition of each other’s property and through contract. The master-slave dialectic of the *Phenomenology* shows that one-sided domination is unstable; full freedom requires reciprocal recognition. That recognition is actualized in the rational state, the sphere of ethical life in which individuals find their particular interests mediated by law and institutions that secure personhood. Hegel’s extension of Kant therefore requires the cultivation of freedom wherever it is found—securing the conditions under which persons can exercise and recognize it—rather than its instrumentalization for a collective project. A politics that weakens the security of property, undermines impartial enforcement of law, or treats some categories of persons as permanent claimants upon others reverses this order: it dissolves the media of recognition in the name of a future or aggregate good.

Application to the Open Society.  
The operational record of the Open Society Foundations and its associated political vehicles exhibits the utilitarian pattern. Large-scale funding of progressive prosecutors has produced measurable declines in charging and incarceration for selected offenses; the justification offered is the reduction of systemic harm to larger populations, with the costs borne by victims of the offenses that are deprioritized and by the communities in which disorder increases. Immigration-related advocacy and the support of policies that limit enforcement treat the fiscal, wage, and social costs imposed on existing residents as acceptable externalities of a larger humanitarian or demographic good. Equity frameworks that reallocate educational, professional, or legal advantages according to group categories treat the individuals who lose those advantages as the necessary means to a preferred distribution. In each case the language of openness, rights, and justice is retained, yet the underlying standard is aggregative or historical: present, concentrated burdens on identifiable persons are accepted for the sake of a projected improvement for others. This is the sacrificial logic of naive utilitarianism. It cannot be reconciled with the side-constraints of natural rights, the cultivation of virtue required by Aristotle, the prohibition on using persons as mere means required by Kant, or the institutional actualization of mutual recognition required by Hegel.

The Open Society therefore does not extend the traditions it selectively invokes. It subordinates them to a standard those traditions were developed to resist.

Divine Knowledge, Divine Concurrence, Agent Causation, Soteriology, Created Ecosystems, Lonergan, Aquinas, and High Calvinism 
→ 
Classical Christian theology affirms that human agents exist within complex environments comprising innumerable interconnected variables. Across major traditions, there is agreement that these environmental factors—physical surroundings, timing, psychological stressors, motives, and occasions—incline, influence, and frame options without themselves strictly coercing or determining the will or agent. A free agent situated in a causal ecosystem of secondary causes remains an authentic causal agent in possession of (a) agent-specific causality fundamentally distinct from all causal natures in the environment and in possession of (b) [bracketed] degrees of freedom within which the agent exercises a power called intellect and a power called will. Obviously all causal natures are entirely dependent upon the Trio of Proportionate Causality + Divine Conservation + Divine Concurrence.

Regarding Concurrence, an abbreviated paraphrase:

“Divine providence concurs with evil actions, first, by foreknowing them; second, by sustaining nature; third by permitting; fourth by abandoning; fifth by handing over to Satan; sixth by setting their limits beforehand; seventh by eliciting good from them.”
→ 
That is from Johann Gerhard in his “Theological Commonplaces: On Creation and Angels, on Providence, on Election and Reprobation, and on the Image of God in Man before the Fall” and another source summarizes:

1. Foreknowledge: God foresees evil deeds from eternity without necessitating or directly causing the perverse choice of the created will.

2. Sustaining of Nature: God preserves the physical substance, life, and natural faculties of the creature while the creature abuses those powers to commit sin.

3. Permission: God allows the sinner to act contrary to His moral law rather than forcibly preventing the exercise of free choice.

4. Forsaking/Desertion: God justly withdraws restraining grace, abandoning stubborn sinners to their own blindness and hardness of heart.

5. Handing Over: God delivers unrepentant sinners over to the power of Satan or their own disordered desires.

6. Setting Limits beforehand: God circumscribes evil, determining in advance how far it may go, its duration, and the individuals it can touch.

7. Directing to a Good End / Ordinatio ad Bonum: God overrules and elicits good from evil acts, turning what was intended for wickedness into a means of Good.

Classical theism further holds that God possesses exhaustive knowledge of reality. In the theology of Thomas Aquinas, divine knowledge is traditionally distinguished as the knowledge of simple intelligence (scientia simplicis intelligentiae), by which God knows all possibles in His own essence, and the knowledge of vision (scientia visionis), by which He knows all actualities across time in light of His eternal decree. Self-knowledge of the divine essence is necessary and identical in every alternative.

More broadly through the Arc of Christendom “God” as the Metaphysical Wellspring of all Ontological Counterfactual Possibility necessarily and eternally houses All Knowledge of All Ontologies, Counterfactual and Otherwise. More narrowly if we zoom in on Thomism specially and then zoom in again on a few schools withing Thomism we will find a more limited “reach” of the “Content” of God’s Knowledge. Specifically withing the framework of those select schools (not all Thomisitic schools), the contingent content of free knowledge (the knowledge of vision) is not identical across the alternatives of creation and non-creation and different creations. If God decrees a created order, free knowledge includes the free choices and events that occur within it; if God refrains from decreeing creation, that contingent content remains purely possible. This variation concerns only contingent terms and the extrinsic termination of divine knowledge. It introduces no real change, temporal transition, or division into the divine act of knowing (actus intelligendi), which remains one, simple, eternal, immutable, and identical to the divine essence across all alternatives.

The Post-Tridentine Schism: Physical Premotion vs. Middle Knowledge

Across all such baselines regarding Agency, Environment (the Ocean of Secondary Causes called “Reality”), and Divine Knowledge a four-century scholastic dispute erupted in the post-Tridentine era. Thomist and Molinist thinkers locked themselves in mutual accusations of fatalism on one side and semi-Pelagianism on the other. The clash centered on the metaphysical character of the will at the exact instant of choosing between opposites, as well as the location of the sufficient cause that effects the transition from potency to act, and also the consequent mechanics of how God knows those choices.

Post-Tridentine Dominican thinkers, most prominently Domingo Báñez, operated within a strict Aristotelian metaphysical principle: nothing moves from potency to act except by something already in act. A power remaining in potency cannot self-actualize into a state of act without an effect existing without a sufficient actual cause. Therefore, the transition from the capacity to choose to the actual willing requires a divine motion applied directly to the will itself—an internal physical premotion (praemotio physica).

On this account, God does not merely establish the world and observe; the divine decree actively and interiorly moves the will to actualize one specific choice. Grounded in the principle that truth requires ontological reality (ens et verum convertuntur), Bañezianism denies that God possesses an independent knowledge of what a free creature would do in hypothetical orders He does not decree. Prior to a divine decree, a counterfactual conditional of creaturely freedom possesses no determinate truth value and lacks the ontological reality required to be knowable. While traditional Bañezian interpreters argue this causal-grounding intuition has material continuity with Aquinas, this specific denial of undecreed counterfactuals is a specialized early-modern consequence.

Seeking to safeguard libertarian freedom and moral accountability, Luis de Molina and the Jesuit school regarded the Bañezian mechanism as rendering the concrete power to do otherwise illusory, collapsing human freedom into theological determinism. Molinists insisted on simultaneous concurrence, where God supplies the general power to act while the creature’s own will and intellect are wielded by the agent. To explain how God retains sovereign foreknowledge without “learning” from creaturely determinations, Molina posited scientia media (middle knowledge)—an eternal category of divine knowledge logically prior to, and independent of, any divine decree. The meaning of the term Molinism is complete if and when two criteria are met: First: God infallibly knows what any free agent would choose in any given set of circumstances, and Second: God consults those truths prior to deciding which world to actualize.

Both the Banezian Overreach and the Molina Overreach operated on the shared assumption that counterfactuals of freedom must either float in mid-air independent of any causal order or else be fixed by a discrete, antecedent predetermining decree upon the creaturely faculty.

The Broader Tradition, Synergy, and the Biblical Witness:

The technical debate over whether counterfactuals require an antecedent divine decree represents an early modern scholastic development rather than the explicit consensus of the broader Christian tradition. For the first sixteen centuries, patristic, medieval, and Eastern Christian sources affirmed God’s exhaustive omniscience alongside genuine creaturely contingency without formulating foreknowledge around either middle knowledge or physical premotion. Biblical texts depicting conditional human actions—such as David at Keilah (1 Samuel 23) or Christ’s warning regarding Tyre and Sidon (Matthew 11:21)—were historically received as genuine expressions of divine counterfactual knowledge, grounded in God’s comprehensive knowledge of circumstances and outcomes without requiring an antecedent causal shove to render them knowable.

The two-thousand-year macro-history of Christian theology displays a dominant footprint composed of four interlocking affirmations:

      •Necessary Grace: Humans are radically incapable of initiating salvation without the prior, unmerited illumination of the Holy Spirit (excluding Pelagianism).
      •Necessary Synergy: Grace does not treat the human soul as a passive block; it heals the will so that active, uncoerced cooperation becomes possible.
      •Resistible Grace: The salvific movement can be definitively and tragically resisted by the human creature.
      •The Hopeful Universal Offer: God genuinely wills the salvation of all, and Christ died for all human beings without exception.

This general arc is the bedrock of the Catholic Catechism, the paradigmatic map of Eastern Orthodoxy, and the vast majority of early Church Fathers like Irenaeus and John Damascene. Narrow historical exceptions to this synergistic consensus have consistently been met with explicit rejection. When Gottschalk of Orbais advanced a doctrine of twin predestination (unconditional election and reprobation) in the ninth century, he was condemned at the Synods of Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849). Similarly, Pope Innocent X’s bull Cum occasione (1653) officially condemned the Jansenist propositions that inner grace in fallen nature can never be resisted.

The historical proof that Báñezianism is not the exclusive Catholic paradigm lies in the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1598–1607). Pope Paul V ultimately permitted both the Dominican and Jesuit schools to be taught but forbade either from condemning the other as heretical. Strict Báñezian Thomism remains a permitted theological opinion, but the magisterium pointedly refused to adopt its specific deterministic mechanics as dogma.

Lonergan’s Retrieval: Aquinas Beyond the Dichotomy

Twentieth-century historical retrieval, most systematically articulated in Bernard Lonergan’s Grace and Freedom: Operative Grace in the Thought of St. Thomas Aquinas, demonstrates that the post-Tridentine apparatus of physical premotion versus middle knowledge was anachronistic relative to Thomas Aquinas. Later commentators read sixteenth-century concerns back into thirteenth-century texts. Lonergan’s analysis yields a framework that dissolves the later dilemma through several foundational observations.

First, for Aquinas, God is the universal transcendent ground of all being. God does not intervene as an extrinsic secondary agent competing with human wills on the same causal plane. God sustains both primary causality and the entire network of secondary causes—the full ecosystem of reasons, agencies, natures, and occasions. Divine providence decrees not only that an event occurs, but the precise mode in which it occurs: necessary things happen necessarily, and contingent, voluntary things happen freely. The will’s free movement is upheld from within by universal providence; no specialized discrete premotion is required to determine the will from outside that ecosystem.

Second, Aquinas distinguishes operative from cooperative grace without pre-determination that bypasses the faculties. Operative grace causes the very willing itself (operatur in nobis velle) and actualizes the intellect’s grasp of the good from within human consciousness, without violating voluntary agency. Cooperative grace concerns the subsequent external execution of that willing.

Third, Lonergan’s central thesis is that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion.

Finally, moral failure is accounted for as a defect: the will’s failure to attend to the rule of reason (non-attentio regulae or defectus regulae). This non-attention is a pure privation, initiated when the creature places an obstacle (ponere obicem). Because sin possesses no positive ontological entity, it is “unintelligible” in Aquinas’s precise sense—it requires no divine causal predetermination in order to be known or permitted. Because the will under sufficient grace retains the real proximate potency (in sensu diviso) not to place the obstacle, the failure remains voluntary and culpable.

Incompatibility with Five-Point Calvinism and Deterministic Compatibilism:

For centuries, a recurring claim has appeared in some Reformed discussions: that selected passages from Thomas Aquinas secretly support a monergistic account of grace and election. However, Five-Point Calvinism’s attempt to appropriate Thomas Aquinas falters because its soteriology relies on a competitive, mechanistic view of divine action that fundamentally contradicts Aquinas’s doctrine of divine transcendence. In Grace and Freedom, Bernard Lonergan demonstrates that Calvinist appeals to Aquinas usually depend on anachronistic misreadings of his texts, specifically by confusing his original concept of “operative grace” with later, deterministic formulations of “efficacious grace” and physical premotion. Lonergan’s historical retrieval of Aquinas’s developing account shows that the solution Aquinas actually reached—via the theorem of divine transcendence—is neither the later Báñezian system nor the Molinist one, and it cannot underwrite the specific version of deterministic compatibilism that typically accompanies Five-Point Calvinism.

The primary barrier to Calvinist appropriation lies in Lonergan’s retrieval of exactly how Aquinas understood operative grace versus how later theologians redefined it. This dismantles claims to Thomistic support for both Irresistible Grace and the Perseverance of the Saints, and especially for the form of compatibilism that joins them.

Aquinas’s actual view of operative grace and contingency is decisive. For Aquinas, operative grace describes the interior movement in which God operates and the human will is the thing moved (resulting in the internal act of willing the end, including conversion). Lonergan shows that God executes this through the theorem of divine transcendence. God, as the absolute primary cause, is non-competitive with human agency. When God’s operative grace moves the will, it actualizes the will according to its own natural, contingent mode. Grace elevates and perfects the natural faculties rather than overriding them, so that the human subject participates vitally and freely. The motion is infallible under that particular divine action (the will does consent), yet the necessity is not absolute; contingency is preserved precisely because of divine transcendence. This precludes any notion of divine coercion or of the will being reduced to a passive instrument.

The anachronism of “efficacious grace” and premotion further blocks appropriation. Lonergan clarifies that the strict dichotomy between “efficacious” and “sufficient” grace—along with the concept of praemotio physica (physical premotion)—was not Aquinas’s framework. These concepts emerged during later controversies (especially the De Auxiliis debates), where later Dominicans such as Domingo Báñez projected a more mechanistic system onto Aquinas. When Five-Point Calvinists attempt to appropriate Aquinas, they typically point to these stronger, post-Aquinas models of premotion. While Calvinist soteriology may find genuine conceptual overlap with certain later Thomistic formulations, this alignment exists only within a specific school of Thomism rather than with Aquinas himself or with “Thomism” as a unified whole. Sweeping claims such as “the scholastics are on our side” therefore collapse centuries of complex development and ignore Aquinas’s own non-competitive synthesis.

This yields clear incompatibility with Irresistible Grace. The “I” in Five-Point Calvinism functionally mirrors the later mechanical view more than Aquinas’s original thought. High Calvinism generally treats the will as radically passive until unilaterally renovated by divine action in a way that eliminates genuine alternative potency. This tends to place divine and human agency in a competitive framework in which God’s success requires the suppression of human contingency. That stands in contrast to Aquinas’s insistence, as retrieved by Lonergan, that operative grace actualizes the will according to its own contingent mode without coercion.

It is equally incompatible with Calvinistic Compatibilism:

Contra Compatibilism Observation 1 of 2:

Lonergan’s retrieval demonstrates a framework that fundamentally conflicts with the deterministic compatibilism typical of Five-Point Calvinism. High Calvinist compatibilism holds that humans choose freely according to their desires or strongest inclinations, while those desires are unilaterally set by divine grace so that the will freely follows without retaining a real power of contrary choice. In this model the human will functions as an instrument that must conform to the primary cause. By contrast, Lonergan shows that Aquinas relies on the theorem of divine transcendence, which preserves true contingency: God’s absolute primary causality causes the human will to act freely and contingently according to its own mode. Because the will is not merely acting out a deterministic script of divinely fixed inclinations but retains vital, contingent agency, Aquinas’s theology remains out of reach for the specific version of compatibilism that Five-Point Calvinism uses to underwrite both irresistible grace and guaranteed perseverance. Overlap with broader theological compatibilism is possible; identity with the Reformed version that suppresses alternative potency is not.

Contra Compatibilism Observation 2 of 2:

Lonergan demonstrates that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion. This fundamentally contradicts High Calvinism’s Soteriology of 100% Monergistic Determinism vis-à-vis your status as Reprobate or Elect.

Aquinas is incompatible with the “P” of TULIP in its Perseverance of the Saints:

Lonergan’s retrieval further demonstrates Aquinas’ own coherence by highlighting the fact that the aforementioned active, contingent human freedom funded by operative grace not only exists Pre-Conversion and all the way Into Conversion but it persists After Conversion, making it genuinely possible for a justified individual to fall away. Note the seamless application of Necessary Grace and Necessary Synergy within Grace-Perfecting-Nature as Aquinas fundamentally delineates between the initial grace of justification and the subsequent gift of perseverance (donum perseverantiae). In Summa I-II, q. 109, a. 10 he states that “to many grace is given to whom perseverance in grace is not given.” A believer can receive the operative grace that justifies without receiving the further gift of final perseverance. Because the free will remains mutable, the justified retain the capacity to reject subsequent graces and fall into mortal sin. This directly contradicts the Calvinist doctrine of the absolute, guaranteed perseverance of all the elect.

Agent Act As Unnecessary Alternate Possibility

The concept of “Unnecessary Action” by an Agent referents what is often labeled Contingent Action as opposed to Necessary Action i.e. Determined Action. Because Aquinas insists that God’s absolute primary causality perfectly guarantees the genuine, active freedom of the secondary cause, his soteriology cannot support the strict monergism of Five-Point Calvinism. God’s operative grace does not unilaterally override a passive subject or determine its desires in a way that eliminates contingency; it actualizes the vital, free consent of the human agent while preserving the will’s contingent mode at every stage. Consequently, Five-Point Calvinism cannot claim Aquinas’s own teaching on grace and conversion without abandoning its own requisite definitions of irresistible grace, deterministic compatibilism, and guaranteed final perseverance.

The classical tradition, as retrieved in its pre-polarized form, upholds divine immutability and exhaustive knowledge grounded in transcendent causality. Contingency is preserved not by removing God’s governance, but by recognizing that it is the very efficacy of God’s universal providence that causes free agents to act freely. This synthesis supplies the resources to affirm exhaustive divine knowledge of all counterfactual ontologies, immutable simplicity, and genuine creaturely contingency—equipping rather than overriding the will—without succumbing to the specialized difficulties generated by physical premotion, deterministic compatibilism, or middle knowledge ((more specifically not counterfactual knowledge as such but rather “God Using Counterfactual Knowledge As The Sole Basis To Choose This/That World)).

Convergence In Various Discussions:

God Is The Wellspring, Root, and Causal Repository — the Explanatory Terminus from Whom all causal ecosystems are drawn, conserved, and explained.

▪️PAP & Unnecessary Alternate Possibility
▪️Ex Nihilo & God CAN WILL OTHERWISE

▪️God’s Eternal Council Can Be Otherwise
▪️Free Will as Liberty of Exercise & Liberty of Specification

▪️Free Will as Power To Either Alternative
▪️All Knowledge is Eternally Present in the Uncreated Wellspring of all Unnecessary Ontological Counterfactual Possibility

▪️Proportionate Causality + Divine Conservation + Divine Concurrence → Imago Dei → Arbiter I|||i
▪️We speak of the Triune God Who Is Procession||Verb||Speech Itself — not of the Static Processionless Verbless God of Aristotelian-Metaphysics — but the Fundamentally Wider God of Aristotelian-Thomistic-Metaphysics.

Therefore, the transition from the capacity to choose to the actual willing requires a divine motion applied directly to the will itself—an internal physical premotion (praemotio physica).

On this account, God does not merely establish the world and observe; the divine decree actively and interiorly moves the will to actualize one specific choice. Grounded in the principle that truth requires ontological reality (ens et verum convertuntur), Bañezianism denies that God possesses an independent knowledge of what a free creature would do in hypothetical orders He does not decree. Prior to a divine decree, a counterfactual conditional of creaturely freedom possesses no determinate truth value and lacks the ontological reality required to be knowable. While traditional Bañezian interpreters argue this causal-grounding intuition has material continuity with Aquinas, this specific denial of undecreed counterfactuals is a specialized early-modern consequence.

Seeking to safeguard libertarian freedom and moral accountability, Luis de Molina and the Jesuit school regarded the Bañezian mechanism as rendering the concrete power to do otherwise illusory, collapsing human freedom into theological determinism. Molinists insisted on simultaneous concurrence, where God supplies the general power to act while the creature’s own will and intellect are wielded by the agent. To explain how God retains sovereign foreknowledge without “learning” from creaturely determinations, Molina posited scientia media (middle knowledge)—an eternal category of divine knowledge logically prior to, and independent of, any divine decree. The meaning of the term Molinism is complete if and when two criteria are met: First: God infallibly knows what any free agent would choose in any given set of circumstances, and Second: God consults those truths prior to deciding which world to actualize.

Both the Banezian Overreach and the Molina Overreach operated on the shared assumption that counterfactuals of freedom must either float in mid-air independent of any causal order or else be fixed by a discrete, antecedent predetermining decree upon the creaturely faculty.

The Broader Tradition, Synergy, and the Biblical Witness:

The technical debate over whether counterfactuals require an antecedent divine decree represents an early modern scholastic development rather than the explicit consensus of the broader Christian tradition. For the first sixteen centuries, patristic, medieval, and Eastern Christian sources affirmed God’s exhaustive omniscience alongside genuine creaturely contingency without formulating foreknowledge around either middle knowledge or physical premotion. Biblical texts depicting conditional human actions—such as David at Keilah (1 Samuel 23) or Christ’s warning regarding Tyre and Sidon (Matthew 11:21)—were historically received as genuine expressions of divine counterfactual knowledge, grounded in God’s comprehensive knowledge of circumstances and outcomes without requiring an antecedent causal shove to render them knowable.

The two-thousand-year macro-history of Christian theology displays a dominant footprint composed of four interlocking affirmations:

      •Necessary Grace: Humans are radically incapable of initiating salvation without the prior, unmerited illumination of the Holy Spirit (excluding Pelagianism).
      •Necessary Synergy: Grace does not treat the human soul as a passive block; it heals the will so that active, uncoerced cooperation becomes possible.
      •Resistible Grace: The salvific movement can be definitively and tragically resisted by the human creature.
      •The Hopeful Universal Offer: God genuinely wills the salvation of all, and Christ died for all human beings without exception.

This general arc is the bedrock of the Catholic Catechism, the paradigmatic map of Eastern Orthodoxy, and the vast majority of early Church Fathers like Irenaeus and John Damascene. Narrow historical exceptions to this synergistic consensus have consistently been met with explicit rejection. When Gottschalk of Orbais advanced a doctrine of twin predestination (unconditional election and reprobation) in the ninth century, he was condemned at the Synods of Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849). Similarly, Pope Innocent X’s bull Cum occasione (1653) officially condemned the Jansenist propositions that inner grace in fallen nature can never be resisted.

The historical proof that Báñezianism is not the exclusive Catholic paradigm lies in the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1598–1607). Pope Paul V ultimately permitted both the Dominican and Jesuit schools to be taught but forbade either from condemning the other as heretical. Strict Báñezian Thomism remains a permitted theological opinion, but the magisterium pointedly refused to adopt its specific deterministic mechanics as dogma.

Lonergan’s Retrieval: Aquinas Beyond the Dichotomy

Twentieth-century historical retrieval, most systematically articulated in Bernard Lonergan’s Grace and Freedom: Operative Grace in the Thought of St. Thomas Aquinas, demonstrates that the post-Tridentine apparatus of physical premotion versus middle knowledge was anachronistic relative to Thomas Aquinas. Later commentators read sixteenth-century concerns back into thirteenth-century texts. Lonergan’s analysis yields a framework that dissolves the later dilemma through several foundational observations.

First, for Aquinas, God is the universal transcendent ground of all being. God does not intervene as an extrinsic secondary agent competing with human wills on the same causal plane. God sustains both primary causality and the entire network of secondary causes—the full ecosystem of reasons, agencies, natures, and occasions. Divine providence decrees not only that an event occurs, but the precise mode in which it occurs: necessary things happen necessarily, and contingent, voluntary things happen freely. The will’s free movement is upheld from within by universal providence; no specialized discrete premotion is required to determine the will from outside that ecosystem.

Second, Aquinas distinguishes operative from cooperative grace without pre-determination that bypasses the faculties. Operative grace causes the very willing itself (operatur in nobis velle) and actualizes the intellect’s grasp of the good from within human consciousness, without violating voluntary agency. Cooperative grace concerns the subsequent external execution of that willing.

Third, Lonergan’s central thesis is that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion.

Finally, moral failure is accounted for as a defect: the will’s failure to attend to the rule of reason (non-attentio regulae or defectus regulae). This non-attention is a pure privation, initiated when the creature places an obstacle (ponere obicem). Because sin possesses no positive ontological entity, it is “unintelligible” in Aquinas’s precise sense—it requires no divine causal predetermination in order to be known or permitted. Because the will under sufficient grace retains the real proximate potency (in sensu diviso) not to place the obstacle, the failure remains voluntary and culpable.

In Grace and Freedom, Bernard Lonergan demonstrates that Calvinist appeals to Aquinas usually depend on anachronistic misreadings of his texts, specifically by confusing his original concept of “operative grace” with later, deterministic formulations of “efficacious grace” and physical premotion. Lonergan’s historical retrieval of Aquinas’s developing account shows that the solution Aquinas actually reached—via the theorem of divine transcendence—is neither the later Báñezian system nor the Molinist one, and it cannot underwrite the specific version of deterministic compatibilism that typically accompanies Five-Point Calvinism.

The primary barrier to Calvinist appropriation lies in Lonergan’s retrieval of exactly how Aquinas understood operative grace versus how later theologians redefined it. This dismantles claims to Thomistic support for both Irresistible Grace and the Perseverance of the Saints, and especially for the form of compatibilism that joins them.

For Aquinas, operative grace describes the interior movement in which God operates and the human will is the thing moved (resulting in the internal act of willing the end, including conversion). Lonergan shows that God executes this through the theorem of divine transcendence. God, as the absolute primary cause, is non-competitive with human agency. When God’s operative grace moves the will, it actualizes the will according to its own natural, contingent mode. Grace elevates and perfects the natural faculties rather than overriding them, so that the human subject participates vitally and freely. The motion is infallible under that particular divine action (the will does consent), yet the necessity is not absolute; contingency is preserved precisely because of divine transcendence. This precludes any notion of divine coercion or of the will being reduced to a passive instrument.

Lonergan clarifies that the strict dichotomy between “efficacious” and “sufficient” grace—along with the concept of praemotio physica (physical premotion)—was not Aquinas’s framework. This yields clear incompatibility with Irresistible Grace. The “I” in Five-Point Calvinism functionally mirrors the later mechanical view more than Aquinas’s original thought. High Calvinism generally treats the will as radically passive until unilaterally renovated by divine action in a way that eliminates genuine alternative potency. This tends to place divine and human agency in a competitive framework in which God’s success requires the suppression of human contingency. That stands in contrast to Aquinas’s insistence, as retrieved by Lonergan, that operative grace actualizes the will according to its own contingent mode without coercion.

It is equally incompatible with Calvinistic Compatibilism:

Contra Compatibilism Observation 1 of 2:

Lonergan’s retrieval demonstrates a framework that fundamentally conflicts with the deterministic compatibilism typical of Five-Point Calvinism. High Calvinist compatibilism holds that humans choose freely according to their desires or strongest inclinations, while those desires are unilaterally set by divine grace so that the will freely follows without retaining a real power of contrary choice. In this model the human will functions as an instrument that must conform to the primary cause. By contrast, Lonergan shows that Aquinas relies on the theorem of divine transcendence, which preserves true contingency: God’s absolute primary causality causes the human will to act freely and contingently according to its own mode. Because the will is not merely acting out a deterministic script of divinely fixed inclinations but retains vital, contingent agency, Aquinas’s theology remains out of reach for the specific version of compatibilism that Five-Point Calvinism uses to underwrite both irresistible grace and guaranteed perseverance. This directly contradicts the Calvinist doctrine of the absolute, guaranteed perseverance of all the elect.

The concept of “Unnecessary Action” by an Agent referents what is often labeled Contingent Action as opposed to Necessary Action i.e. Determined Action. Because Aquinas insists that God’s absolute primary causality perfectly guarantees the genuine, active freedom of the secondary cause, his soteriology cannot support the strict monergism of Five-Point Calvinism. God Is The Wellspring, Root, and Causal Repository — the Explanatory Terminus from Whom all causal ecosystems are drawn, conserved, and explained.

▪️All Knowledge is Eternally Present in the Uncreated Wellspring of all Unnecessary Ontological Counterfactual Possibility

That is from Johann Gerhard in his “Theological Commonplaces: On Creation and Angels, on Providence, on Election and Reprobation, and on the Image of God in Man before the Fall” and another source summarizes:

5. Handing Over: God delivers unrepentant sinners over to the power of Satan or their own disordered desires.

6. Setting Limits beforehand: God circumscribes evil, determining in advance how far it may go, its duration, and the individuals it can touch.

Lonergan’s retrieval demonstrates a framework that fundamentally conflicts with the deterministic compatibilism typical of Five-Point Calvinism. High Calvinist compatibilism holds that humans choose freely according to their desires or strongest inclinations, while those desires are unilaterally set by divine grace so that the will freely follows without retaining a real power of contrary choice. In this model the human will functions as an instrument that must conform to the primary cause. By contrast, Lonergan shows that Aquinas relies on the theorem of divine transcendence, which preserves true contingency: God’s absolute primary causality causes the human will to act freely and contingently according to its own mode. Because the will is not merely acting out a deterministic script of divinely fixed inclinations but retains vital, contingent agency, Aquinas’s theology remains out of reach for the specific version of compatibilism that Five-Point Calvinism uses to underwrite both irresistible grace and guaranteed perseverance. Overlap with broader theological compatibilism is possible; identity with the Reformed version that suppresses alternative potency is not.

Contra Compatibilism Observation 2 of 2:

Lonergan demonstrates that Aquinas does not treat sufficient and efficacious grace as two entitatively distinct aids. Unlike post-Tridentine Bannezians—who claimed sufficient grace conferred only the power (posse) while a distinct efficacious grace conferred the actual performance (actu agere)—Aquinas views them as the exact same divine motion. It is called “sufficient” when the will does not consent and “efficacious” when the will does consent. Efficacy is not a stronger or different motion; it is the non-refusal of the same motion. This fundamentally contradicts High Calvinism’s Soteriology of 100% Monergistic Determinism vis-à-vis your status as Reprobate or Elect.

Aquinas is incompatible with the “P” of TULIP in its Perseverance of the Saints:

Lonergan’s retrieval further demonstrates Aquinas’ own coherence by highlighting the fact that the aforementioned active, contingent human freedom funded by operative grace not only exists Pre-Conversion and all the way Into Conversion but it persists After Conversion, making it genuinely possible for a justified individual to fall away. Note the seamless application of Necessary Grace and Necessary Synergy within Grace-Perfecting-Nature as Aquinas fundamentally delineates between the initial grace of justification and the subsequent gift of perseverance (donum perseverantiae). In Summa I-II, q. 109, a. 10 he states that “to many grace is given to whom perseverance in grace is not given.” A believer can receive the operative grace that justifies without receiving the further gift of final perseverance. Because the free will remains mutable, the justified retain the capacity to reject subsequent graces and fall into mortal sin. This directly contradicts the Calvinist doctrine of the absolute, guaranteed perseverance of all the elect.

Agent Act As Unnecessary Alternate Possibility

The concept of “Unnecessary Action” by an Agent referents what is often labeled Contingent Action as opposed to Necessary Action i.e. Determined Action. Because Aquinas insists that God’s absolute primary causality perfectly guarantees the genuine, active freedom of the secondary cause, his soteriology cannot support the strict monergism of Five-Point Calvinism. God’s operative grace does not unilaterally override a passive subject or determine its desires in a way that eliminates contingency; it actualizes the vital, free consent of the human agent while preserving the will’s contingent mode at every stage. Consequently, Five-Point Calvinism cannot claim Aquinas’s own teaching on grace and conversion without abandoning its own requisite definitions of irresistible grace, deterministic compatibilism, and guaranteed final perseverance.

The classical tradition, as retrieved in its pre-polarized form, upholds divine immutability and exhaustive knowledge grounded in transcendent causality. Contingency is preserved not by removing God’s governance, but by recognizing that it is the very efficacy of God’s universal providence that causes free agents to act freely. This synthesis supplies the resources to affirm exhaustive divine knowledge of all counterfactual ontologies, immutable simplicity, and genuine creaturely contingency—equipping rather than overriding the will—without succumbing to the specialized difficulties generated by physical premotion, deterministic compatibilism, or middle knowledge ((more specifically not counterfactual knowledge as such but rather “God Using Counterfactual Knowledge As The Sole Basis To Choose This/That World)).

text:
In 1855, an enslaved teenage girl named Celia fought back against the white man who had repeatedly raped her for years.

Celia had been purchased by Robert Newsom, a white slaveholder in Missouri, when she was about 14 years old. 

For approximately five years, Newsom repeatedly sexually abused her.

She wanted it to stop. 

She warned him. 

She sought help. 

But under a system that treated enslaved Black women as property, her pleas offered her little protection against the man who claimed ownership over her.

On the night of 23 June 1855, Newsom entered her cabin and attempted to assault her again.

This time, Celia fought back.

During the struggle, she struck him with a heavy stick, killing him.

But instead of confronting the years of sexual violence inflicted upon her, the slaveholding state put Celia on trial for murder.

Her defense argued that she had the right to protect herself against sexual assault. 

The court rejected her claim, denying her the legal protection she had sought against her abuser.

Think about that.

A white slaveholder could repeatedly rape an enslaved Black girl, yet the legal system offered her no effective protection from him. When she finally fought back, she became the one facing execution.

Celia was convicted of murder and sentenced to death.

On 21 December 1855, at just 19 years old, she was hanged.

She was enslaved, sexually abused for years, denied meaningful protection, and executed after resisting the man who abused her.

This is the reality behind the romanticized stories of slavery. Enslaved Black women were not only forced to work without pay; they were subjected to sexual violence under a system that denied them control over their own bodies.

Celia refused to surrender her body without a fight.

And for killing the man who had abused her, she paid with her life.

Remember Celia. 

Remember what slavery did to Black women. 

And remember the system that punished a victim who fought back while protecting the power of the man who enslaved her.
